name: A. O. Dennis Willows
text:
A. O. Dennis Willows is a neurobiologist and professor emeritus of biology at the University of Washington who directed Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1972 to 2005. In 1964 he spent a summer at FHL with his PhD advisor Graham Hoyle, a University of Oregon neurobiologist, and there found that the brain of the nudibranch Tritonia has large neurons, many of them individually identifiable. He earned his PhD in 1967 and joined the UW faculty in 1968. He also served as director of the Neurobiology Program of the US National Science Foundation. FHL has a Dennis Willows Director's Endowed Professorship, and a January 2024 conference at FHL honoring his work led to a 2025 review of Tritonia neuroscience in the Journal of Neurophysiology. The census lists 46 FHL-connected papers, 1973–2011, and the report's network records Hoyle as his teacher.

Willows's research asks how nervous systems are wired to produce coherent behavior. In Tritonia diomedea (now T. exsulans) he found that stimulating single identified neurons could produce specific movements, and a 1978 paper showed single central neurons controlling a fixed action pattern. His group traced the neural control of feeding, crawling, gut motility and ciliary beating, and the roles of serotonin and of neuropeptides from identified neurons. A second line of work, combining field observation with electrophysiology, asked how the slugs orient to water flow, odors and the Earth's magnetic field; representative papers report lunar-modulated geomagnetic orientation (1987), a neuron that responds to Earth-strength magnetic fields (1991) and daily tracking of slugs in the field (2011). He also worked on Phestilla, Clione and sea hares, and with engineers on instruments for recording from neurons. His trainee Peter Getting studied central pattern generators, including early realistic modeling of neural circuits.

name: Aaren Freeman
text: Aaren S. Freeman completed a PhD in zoology at the University of New Hampshire in 2007 as a student of James E. Byers, after an MS at Northeastern University (2001). In 2005 Freeman published a study of size-dependent indirect interactions among sea urchin herbivores (Behavioral Ecology) and, with Megan N. Dethier and Susan L. Williams, a study of how stress and herbivory affect seaweed life histories (Ecological Monographs). With Byers, Freeman reported divergent induced responses of mussel populations to an invasive predator (Science, 2006). As professor of biology at Adelphi University, Freeman turned to kelp aquaculture, estuarine nutrient extraction and oyster sustainability.

name: Aaron Ninokawa
text: Aaron T. Ninokawa was a National Science Foundation postdoctoral research fellow at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 2021 to 2023, listed among Emily Carrington's lab postdocs. His fellowship asked how ecosystem engineers shape communities by altering local seawater chemistry. He was first author on the FHL Ocean Observatory seawater datasets of 2022 and 2025 and co-authored a 2023 student report on Olympia oysters (Ostrea lurida) exposed to acidification and low salinity. He earned a PhD in ecology at UC Davis's Bodega Marine Laboratory in 2021 and joined the chemistry department of SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry as assistant professor in 2023, studying shell formation and carbonate chemistry.

name: Aaron Olsen
text: Aaron M. Olsen was a postdoctoral fellow with Elizabeth L. Brainerd at Brown University from 2016, first on a National Science Foundation fellowship and from 2018 as an anatomy teaching and research fellow. Olsen came from a PhD with Mark Westneat at the University of Chicago (2016) on the evolution of feeding in waterfowl, including a 2017 Functional Ecology paper on beak shape. At Brown, Olsen combined XROMM kinematics with biomechanical modeling in ray-finned fishes: a linkage that helps drive mouth expansion in largemouth bass (2017) and the coordination of prey capture and swallowing in channel catfish (Proceedings B, 2019). Olsen also wrote open-source software for shape data and modeling.

name: Aaron W. E. Galloway
text:
Aaron W. E. Galloway is an associate professor of biology at the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, where he leads the Coastal Trophic Ecology Lab. He holds a BA in environmental science and policy from The Evergreen State College (1999), an MS in resource management (wildlife biology) from Central Washington University (2004), with a thesis on ungulate surveys by students along school bus routes, and a PhD in aquatic and fishery sciences from the University of Washington (2013). From 2007 to 2013 he was a graduate research assistant based at Friday Harbor Laboratories, with Kenneth Sebens and Michael Brett among his supervisors. At FHL he held Strathmann and Kohn fellowships (2012), was an NSF GK-12 teaching fellow in Friday Harbor schools and was scheduled to teach a summer course in 2015. Postdoctoral posts followed at the University of Eastern Finland, Stockholm University and Washington State University.

Galloway studies the base of coastal food webs, especially links between algae and their invertebrate grazers. He uses fatty acids and stable isotopes as dietary markers, with field diving, experiments and modeling. His FHL-connected papers examined how habitat and depth shape the distribution of drift seaweeds and their invertebrates (2011), showed that fatty acid signatures distinguish marine macrophytes by order and family (2012) and traced microbe-linked differences between shallow and deep benthic food webs (2013). Others followed the declining food quality of aging kelp (2014) and described kelp detritus as a magnet for animals (2016). Later papers cover algal fatty acids in two urchin species (2018), the food value of urchin feces (2019), red urchins and drift kelp found at 284 m (2020), and how sunflower sea stars eating urchins can help kelp forests recover (2023–2024). Wendel Raymond is linked to him as a trainee in the report's network.

name: Abby van Hemmen
text: Abby van Hemmen was an undergraduate researcher with Petra Ditsche at FHL, in the Aquatic Animals Research Experience course (Fish/Ocean/Biology 479). Their June 2014 report measured pull-off forces of the sea anemone Metridium farcimen on acrylic glass with and without 1.5 mm holes. Attachment was stronger on the surface without holes, suggesting that suction contributes, although the anemones showed no significant preference between the two surfaces when given a choice. Van Hemmen presented a poster on the work at the annual meeting of the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology in West Palm Beach, Florida, in 2015.

name: Abdisalan Hawadle
text: Abdisalan Hawadle was a Carleton College undergraduate who worked with Michael T. Nishizaki in the 2022 FHL REU program. Hawadle's 2022 report compared respiration in the Mediterranean mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis and the bay mussel M. trossulus across five temperatures (5 to 29 °C) and five flow speeds (2 to 20 cm/s) in a fully crossed design. Respiration stayed low at all temperatures in the slowest flow, and Mediterranean mussels showed higher thermal optima only at moderate flow speeds. Hawadle is also a co-author with Nishizaki on a 2025 BCO-DMO dataset of mussel respiration from experiments run at FHL from 2020 to 2023.

name: Abdull J. Massri
text: Abdull J. Massri, known as AJ, was a PhD student of Gregory A. Wray in biology at Duke from 2016 to 2022. Working with Wray and David McClay, Massri applied single-cell RNA sequencing to sea urchin embryos. A 2021 Development paper followed Lytechinus variegatus through eighteen time points in its first 24 hours, and a 2025 Genome Biology and Evolution paper compared it with Heliocidaris erythrogramma, which has a derived life history, to trace changes in cell fate specification. A 2023 EvoDevo paper examined feedback circuits in embryonic gene regulatory networks. As of 2026 Massri was in the Integrative Bioinformatics Support Group at the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences.

name: Abigail Clark
text: Abigail S. Clark completed an MS in zoology at the University of New Hampshire in 2012, advised by Winsor H. Watson III. The thesis compared standard and ventless traps for American lobster (Homarus americanus), measuring catch, lobster size and trap saturation, with time-lapse video of lobsters around the traps. Ventless traps caught about five times as many lobsters. Related papers appeared in Fisheries Research (2015) and Fishery Bulletin (2018, 2019).

text: Abisage Sekarore was an undergraduate in Mackenzie E. Gerringer's lab at SUNY Geneseo, listed among the lab's alumni as class of 2024. text: Adam Haines Krahn earned a PhD in Molecular Genetics and Cell Biology at the University of Chicago in 2025, advised by Benjamin S. Glick, with Edwin Munro on the committee. A related paper with Glick appeared in The EMBO Journal (2026).

name: Adam Horn
text: Adam Horn was listed as a postdoc in William M. Bement's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison on the lab's 2019 roster. Work there moved to zebrafish tissue repair, including a 2026 Development paper on how fibroblasts respond to burn injury in larvae. Horn remained at Wisconsin as of 2026.

name: Adam M. Reitzel
text:
Adam M. Reitzel is a biologist who studies the evolution and development of marine invertebrates. His ORCID record lists a B.A. in biology from Illinois Wesleyan University (1999), an M.S. in zoology from the University of Florida (2002) and a Ph.D. in biology from Boston University (2008), followed by postdoctoral work at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (2007–2012). Since 2012 he has been on the faculty of the Department of Biological Sciences at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, where he is a professor. His FHL-connected papers in the census run from 2004 to 2020. His early papers on sand dollar hormones were written with Andreas Heyland and with Jason Hodin of FHL. A 2012 paper on sand dollar larvae, which gives an FHL address, grew out of a student project in the FHL summer Larval Biology course.

Most of his FHL-connected work concerns echinoderm larvae. A 2004 paper with Heyland and Hodin showed that thyroid hormone lets sand dollar larvae that normally must feed complete metamorphosis without food, and a 2006 paper found that larvae of a facultatively feeding species make the hormone themselves; both bear on the evolutionary loss of larval feeding. Other 2004 papers compared the growth of Dendraster excentricus larvae on natural and laboratory diets and modeled how spawning date relates to larval development time. The 2012 study tracked the depth of sand dollar larvae relative to haloclines, food and fish cues. From 2018 to 2020, with his student Tyler J. Carrier, who held an FHL Charles Lambert Memorial Endowment fellowship, he studied the bacteria of sea urchin larvae and how they shift with diet, location, development and exposure to Vibrio. Venomix (2018), a pipeline for finding toxin genes, grew out of a computing workshop at FHL.

name: Adam P. Summers
text:
Adam P. Summers is a comparative biomechanist and professor at the University of Washington, appointed in the Department of Biology and the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences and based at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics and engineering at Swarthmore College, a master's degree in biology at New York University and a PhD at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he studied tissues of cartilaginous fishes. After a Miller postdoctoral fellowship at the University of California, Berkeley, he joined the faculty of UC Irvine and founded a biomechanics laboratory there in 2001. He moved the lab to FHL in 2009, where he became associate director, and teaches an intensive graduate course there on the biomechanics of fishes. He is a Fellow of the AAAS and held the 2025–26 Rome Prize in Environmental Arts and Humanities. The census lists 116 FHL-connected papers, 2009–2026.

His lab applies engineering and physics to the mechanics, materials and structure of animals, mainly marine fishes, in an evolutionary context. The work relies heavily on museum collections, and the lab's #ScanAllFish project aims to CT-scan all ray-finned fishes. His research has also covered the mechanical properties of cartilage and tendon, shark swimming, and breathing in sharks and rays. Recent FHL-connected papers compare how clingfishes, lumpsuckers and snailfishes stick to rough and soft surfaces (2022), test the armor of poachers and the Pacific spiny lumpsucker and its effect on drag (2023–2026), and analyze jaw mechanics in spotted ratfish (2022), bone density in rattails (2022), tooth indentation in fruit-eating fishes (2025) and the body form of the extinct megatooth shark (2024–2025). He has also co-authored clingfish taxonomy and open-source 3D measurement tools. The report's network links him to more than a dozen students, including Mason Dean and Karly Cohen.

name: Addie Band
text: Addie (Adalena) Band was, as of 2026, a PhD student of James E. Byers in ecology at the University of Georgia, also listed with the Georgia Coastal Ecosystems LTER. After a bachelor's degree in marine science and international studies at Eckerd College, she took up disturbance and ecosystem engineering on coasts, with earlier work on nutrient and hydrologic dynamics in mangroves. In 2026 she held a Georgia Sea Grant research traineeship for a project on mangroves expanding north into Georgia as prolonged freezes become rarer. The project asks whether mangrove root systems help aquatic species establish at the edge of their range.

text: Adrian Dahood, later Adrian Dahood-Fritz, is listed among Billie J. Swalla's former University of Washington lab members. She held an internship at Texas A&M University at Galveston with Bernd Würsig, studying wild dolphins. Her master's research concerned night feeding by dusky dolphins near Kaikōura, New Zealand. She built food web models of the Western Antarctic Peninsula (2019, at George Mason University) and marine protected areas (2020). She died in 2019.

name: Adriana Golding
text: Adriana E. Golding was a graduate student of William M. Bement in the Cell and Molecular Biology program at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, on the lab's rosters from 2016 through 2019. Golding worked on Rho GTPases at the cell cortex and in the repair of single-cell wounds, co-authoring a 2015 review on cell healing with Bement, a 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper on the cortex as an excitable medium, and a 2016 mathematical model of GTPase patterning during wound repair. A first-author 2019 eLife paper, with Ilaria Visco, Peter Bieling and Bement, showed that RhoGDI can extract active as well as inactive RhoGTPases from membranes.

name: Adriana T. Dawes
text:
Adriana T. Dawes is a mathematical biologist who combines modeling with laboratory experiments to study how cells become polarized. Dawes received a Ph.D. in mathematics from the University of British Columbia in 2006. Dawes's three census papers, from 2006, 2008 and 2011, list the University of Washington's Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address. From 2008 to 2011 Dawes was Max Wyman Assistant Professor of Mathematical Biology at the University of Alberta, in its mathematics and statistics department. In 2011 Dawes joined The Ohio State University as an assistant professor in mathematics and molecular genetics, becoming associate professor in 2017 and professor in 2022. Grants listed in Dawes's ORCID record come from NSERC, the National Science Foundation, including a CAREER award, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

Dawes's work asks how signaling molecules and the cytoskeleton set up and maintain distinct regions within a cell. A 2006 paper with Leah Edelstein-Keshet at UBC built a one-dimensional model of a motile cell in which phosphoinositides and Rho-family proteins regulate actin polymerization to start and sustain directed movement. With the Center for Cell Dynamics as an address, Dawes modeled the dimerization of alpha-catenin at adherens junctions in polarized epithelial cells (2008), and with Edwin Munro proposed that oligomerization of the PAR-3 protein could keep PAR protein domains separate in the early Caenorhabditis elegans embryo without depending on actin (2011). Later grant titles describe projects on intracellular polarization, the organization and dynamics of cortical actin, dynein-mediated positioning of centrosomes in polarized cells, and changing phenotypes by modifying signaling networks; other grants equipped a laboratory for confocal microscopy and C. elegans research.

name: Agnes Rouchon
text: Agnes M. Rouchon was a PhD student of Nicole E. Phillips at Victoria University of Wellington, with a 2015 thesis on the effects of metal toxicity on the early life stages of the sea urchin Evechinus chloroticus. With Phillips, Rouchon published a 2018 Marine Environmental Research paper on the same urchin. A month in elevated copper in the laboratory raised copper in adult gonads and nearly halved gonad size. Normal larval development and larval size fell as copper in the mother's gonads rose, while fertilization success was unaffected, showing a maternal effect carried across generations.

name: Alan Barr
text: Alan H. Barr completed a PhD in mathematics at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in 1983 under Garrett M. Odell, with a dissertation titled "Geometric Modeling and Fluid Dynamic Analysis of Swimming Spermatozoa." name: Alan J. Kohn
text:
Alan J. Kohn was a thesis advisor of Richard R. Strathmann, whose CV names Kohn and Karl Banse as thesis advisors at the University of Washington, where Strathmann earned an MS in oceanography (1966) and a PhD in zoology (1970). Kohn joined the university's zoology faculty in 1961 after three years at Florida State University, became professor in 1967 and emeritus in 1998, and held curator appointments in malacology at the Burke Museum. His papers at the University of Washington Libraries include Friday Harbor Laboratories files spanning 1960 to 2017 and photographs labeled as Friday Harbor invertebrate zoology from 1984 to 2015. In a 2009 interview he said he had supervised 22 doctoral students, most on marine mollusks and others on crustaceans, polychaetes, nemerteans and tunicates.

Kohn graduated from Princeton in 1953 and received a Yale PhD in 1957. His research centered on Conus, the venomous cone snails, beginning with work in Hawaii reported in "Piscivorous gastropods of the genus Conus" (PNAS, 1956) and "The Ecology of Conus in Hawaii" (Ecological Monographs, 1959). He took part in the Yale Seychelles Expedition of 1957-58 and the U.S. program of the International Indian Ocean Expedition in 1963. Over about 50 years he studied how Indo-Pacific cones make a living and coexist, why some habitats hold more species, and their taxonomy and phylogeny. He co-authored Manual of the Living Conidae (1995). In the phylogeny work, former postdocs Tom Duda and Chris Meyer did most of the molecular genetics. He died in 2022.

name: Alexander Fodor
text:
Alexander C. A. Fodor (1988–2018) was a graduate student who studied the genomics and evolution of ctenophores and tunicates. Fodor's connection to Friday Harbor Laboratories dates to 2012, when Fodor wrote a report on mesoderm- and muscle-specific genes in the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei for FHL's Marine Genomics Research Apprenticeship; it is held in FHL's student research papers collection. Fodor is a co-author of the 2014 ctenophore genome paper in Nature, with an address at the University of Florida's Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience. He was a graduate student at UW and FHL when he died in 2018. Papers from 2020 to 2023, published after his death, list the Biology Department of the University of Washington and FHL and are co-authored with Billie J. Swalla, whom the report's mentoring network lists as Fodor's teacher.

Fodor's research used genes and genomes to trace the evolution of animal body plans. The 2012 apprenticeship project examined tropomyosin, calponin and beta-catenin in Pleurobrachia and found them expressed in both muscular and epidermal tissues. The 2014 Nature paper reported the genome of Pleurobrachia bachei and proposed that ctenophore neurons and muscles evolved independently of those of other animals. The later FHL papers concern ascidians, tunicates whose tadpole larvae carry a notochord, muscle and dorsal nerve cord in the tail. A 2020 chapter with Swalla and colleagues treats tunicates as transitional chordates. A 2021 paper compares the genomes of the tailed Molgula oculata and the tailless M. occulta, finding much conserved gene order but insertions and deletions that disrupt genes in the tailless species. A 2023 paper shows that the kinase gene cymric, expressed in gonads, eggs and embryos of M. oculata, is a pseudogene in M. occulta.

name: Alexander T. Lowe
text:
Alexander T. (Alex) Lowe is a marine ecologist whose FHL-connected papers date from 2011 to 2016. After a master's degree in Santa Barbara modeling larval Antarctic krill, he worked at FHL in the NSF-funded Spatial Subsidy Lab led by David Duggins and Megan Dethier, where he led a study of food sources for suspension feeders. He then completed a PhD in Biology at the University of Washington; his dissertation (2018), supervised by Jennifer Ruesink, examined how local ecosystem processes modulate ocean acidification and its effects on benthic foundation species. In 2018 he co-taught FHL's Marine Subtidal Ecology course with Aaron Galloway and dive officer Pema Kitaeff, the first FHL academic course to train a full class as scientific divers. He was later a postdoctoral researcher at the Smithsonian Institution, and his website states that he now works at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration on National Environmental Policy Act issues.

Lowe studies how environmental variability shapes coastal food webs using oceanography, community ecology, physiology and fatty acid and stable isotope biomarkers. His FHL work traced the sources and quality of particulate organic matter and kelp detritus in the San Juan Islands: a 2014 Oikos paper identified phytoplankton as the main source of essential fatty acids for suspension feeders, and a 2016 paper linked pulses of fresher water, with salinity below about 30, to more marine-derived organic matter and higher pH. Other papers dealt with drift seaweeds and their invertebrates (2011), the changing food quality of decaying kelp species (2014), the influence of sedentary urchins on bottom communities below the macroalgal zone (2014), kelp detritus as a magnet for fauna (2016) and the food value of urchin feces (2019). His dissertation also tested eelgrass effects on native and Pacific oysters, and with Galloway he reported red urchins with drift kelp at 284 m (2020).

name: Alfred Wegener
text: Alfred Wegener (1880-1930) took his doctorate at the University of Berlin in 1905 under Julius Bauschinger and Wilhelm Förster, with a dissertation applying the astronomical data of the Alfonsine tables to the computing methods of his day. He then worked at the Lindenberg aeronautical observatory, tracking air masses with weather balloons, and joined the first of four Greenland expeditions in 1906. From 1908 he lectured in meteorology, applied astronomy and cosmic physics at Marburg. His book The Origin of Continents and Oceans, setting out continental drift, dates from 1915. He became professor of meteorology and geophysics at Graz in 1924 and died in Greenland in November 1930.

name: Alison Duncan
text: Alison Duncan was listed as a PhD student of Nicole E. Phillips at Te Herenga Waka, Victoria University of Wellington, with a 2023 thesis on heavy metals and reproduction in the mud whelk Cominella glandiformis, a carnivore with an entirely benthic life cycle. Over four weeks of exposure, copper-polluted whelks ate less yet gained weight, and polluted whelks then preferred contaminated prey and foraged less efficiently. Whelks exposed to more than 5 µg of copper per liter began laying egg capsules three weeks later than controls, though they laid a similar number overall. Encapsulated embryos proved more sensitive to the metals than juveniles.

name: Alli N. Cramer
text:
Alli N. Cramer is a marine and aquatic ecologist. Cramer received a B.A. in biology from the University of Oregon in 2010, a master's degree in applied marine and watershed science from California State University, Monterey Bay in 2015, and a Ph.D. in environmental and natural resource sciences from Washington State University in 2020. Postdoctoral positions followed at NOAA Fisheries' Southwest Fisheries Science Center and the Institute of Marine Sciences at the University of California, Santa Cruz. From December 2021 to March 2024 Cramer was an NSF Ocean Sciences Postdoctoral Fellow in the University of Washington Department of Biology, based at Friday Harbor, and census papers with FHL addresses date from 2022 to 2026. Since August 2024 Cramer has been an assistant professor in the School of Mathematical and Natural Sciences at Arizona State University.

Cramer's work looks for general patterns in how primary production and habitat stability organize ecological communities, and makes wide use of open data. Earlier projects used ROV video to map corals and sponges in the Channel Islands, assessed the effects of bottom trawling on soft-sediment fish habitat off central California, assembled a global dataset of lake area, climate and population, and used acoustic telemetry to tell residency from random movement. The NSF fellowship project concerned substrate mobility as a disturbance in hard-rock marine communities. The FHL-connected papers include an essay arguing that shared observational data can restore the naturalist's tradition of description (2022); a review using dimensionless numbers to compare patchy ecologies, from bacteria to gazelles (2022); a report on the Hacking Limnology data-science workshops for aquatic scientists (2023); and a study, with Emily Carrington and others, of an analog sclerometer for measuring the strength of hard coastal substrates (2026).

name: Amanda L. Rychel
text:
Amanda L. Rychel is a biologist whose papers span molecular phylogenetics, the evolution and development of deuterostomes, and plant cell biology. Her first paper (2004), a molecular phylogeny of baleen whales with Tod W. Reeder and Annalisa Berta, gives the Department of Biology at San Diego State University. From 2005 her papers give the University of Washington, where her ORCID record lists a PhD in Biology without dates. Her papers of 2005 to 2009 were written with Billie J. Swalla and give the UW Biology Department and Center for Developmental Biology; the four from 2007 to 2009 also give Friday Harbor Laboratories, and three of these the Kewalo Marine Laboratory of the University of Hawaii. From 2010 to 2019 her address remained the UW Department of Biology, on papers from Keiko U. Torii's group on stomatal development in plants and on two 2011 protein-structure studies.

Her work with Swalla compared chordates with hemichordates and other deuterostomes to trace the origins of chordate features. A 2005 paper reviewed the development of gill slits and their cartilaginous bars and reported that hemichordate gill bars contain collagen and proteoglycans but no cells. A 2007 study found collagen resembling vertebrate type II collagen in the acellular cartilage of hemichordates and cephalochordates, with SoxE gene expression in nearby endoderm. A 2008 paper followed regeneration of the anterior body in the acorn worm Ptychodera flava, and a 2009 book chapter compared regeneration in hemichordates and echinoderms. She also co-authored a 2009 molecular phylogeny of the Hemichordata that updated the status of deep-sea enteropneusts. Her later papers with the Torii group concern the signals and regulators that pattern stomata on leaves, including a 2010 review of small peptide ligands and a 2019 Nature Plants study of how the SCREAM protein couples MAP kinases to SPEECHLESS.

name: Amy L. Moran
text:
Amy L. Moran is a marine invertebrate biologist; she describes herself as a marine physiological ecologist. Her first papers, from 1997 to 2001, came from the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (OIMB), including work with Richard B. Emlet. Papers of 2000 to 2002 give a Friday Harbor Laboratories address; the 2002 paper also lists the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama. Papers of 2003 to 2005 list the University of Southern California and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. She then published from Clemson University's Department of Biological Sciences (from 2007) and from the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (from about 2013). In 2025 she returned to the University of Oregon, where she is Professor and Director of OIMB. The census counts three FHL-address papers (2000–2002) and five later papers (2007–2020) that are in the FHL bibliography or mention FHL in their text.

Moran's lab studies the ecology, evolution and physiology of marine invertebrates, especially life histories, larval ecology, and responses of larvae and adults to temperature and oxygen, from the tropics to the Antarctic. Her FHL-address papers tested the dye calcein as a marker for newly hatched snails (2000); used field outplants of the snail Nucella ostrina, with Emlet, to show that larger hatchlings grew faster and survived better (2001); and, with Peter B. Marko, linked egg-size divergence to changes in a mitochondrial protein among bivalve sister species separated by the Isthmus of Panama (2002). With H. Arthur Woods she measured and modeled oxygen supply to embryos in gelatinous egg masses (2007, 2008) and compared nudibranch egg masses from Friday Harbor and McMurdo Sound (2010). Papers of 2016 and 2020 with Steven Lane, Caitlin Shishido and Woods examined epibionts and temperature–oxygen limits on body size in two temperate Achelia sea spiders.

name: Amy T. Sewell
text:
Amy T. Sewell is a co-author of ecological and developmental studies carried out at Friday Harbor Laboratories between 1989 and 2020. Four of her five papers in the census, published in 1989, 1990, 1993 and 2020, give her address as Friday Harbor Laboratories, University of Washington; the fifth, a 2020 book chapter, lists no address for her. Her co-authors in kelp studies of 1989 and 1990 were David O. Duggins of FHL and James E. Eckman of the Skidaway Institute of Oceanography in Georgia. In later work on marine larvae they were Richard R. Strathmann and Megumi F. Strathmann of FHL and Lucienne Fenaux, whose 2020 address is the marine station at Villefranche-sur-Mer.

The first two papers, led by Eckman and Duggins, examined understory kelp environments: the 1989 paper measured how kelps alter water flow and particle transport near the bottom, and the 1990 paper tested how kelps affect the recruitment of benthic invertebrates. Her later papers with the Strathmanns concern how larval development responds to food supply. A 1993 study found that veligers of the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas reared at a low food concentration had larger velar lobes and longer prototrochal cilia than well-fed larvae, a response like that known in sea urchin plutei. A 2020 paper described how the posterior coeloms of a brittle star larva first appear, as separate clusters of mesenchyme-like cells near the base of the posterolateral arms, and reported plasticity in larval structures. A 2020 book chapter compared such plasticity in response to food across classes of echinoderm larvae.

text:
Andrea B. Kohn works in Leonid L. Moroz's group on the genomics and neurobiology of marine invertebrates. Her ORCID record lists the University of Florida, and her papers from 2011 to 2020 give the university's Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience in St. Augustine, Florida, as her address. Her FHL-connected papers in the census run from 2011 to 2020 and center on the sea gooseberry Pleurobrachia bachei, a comb jelly (ctenophore) collected from the FHL docks. In spring and summer 2012 she was a co-author, with Moroz and Billie J. Swalla, of student reports from FHL's Marine Genomics Research Apprenticeship and its summer undergraduate internships, and one student thanked her for teaching molecular biology. One of those students, Rebecca Bruders, is linked to her in the report's mentoring network.

Her work addresses how nervous systems evolved, using ctenophores as a test case. A 2011 paper described the small, fast-evolving mitochondrial genome of Pleurobrachia bachei, from animals collected at FHL in 2008–2010. A 2016 review with Moroz argued from genomic and chemical data that neurons and synapses arose more than once in animal evolution. The 2012 student projects at FHL used transcriptome data and in situ hybridization to map where Pleurobrachia expresses developmental and signaling genes, including Wnt pathway genes, LIM homeobox genes, Brachyury, collagens and genes for glutamate signaling. A 2020 preprint used capillary electrophoresis to measure D-glutamate and D-aspartate, amino acids that can act as signaling molecules, in ctenophores, cnidarians, sponges and placozoans, and found D-glutamate dominant only in ctenophores. She was also a co-author of the 2014 paper reporting the Pleurobrachia bachei genome, on which Moroz gave FHL as one of his addresses.

name: Andreas Hejnol
text:
Andreas Hejnol is a zoologist who works in evolutionary developmental biology. He studied biology at the Freie Universität Berlin (diploma 1996) and earned his doctorate at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin in 2002 with a thesis on cell lineage and gene expression in the germ band of two crustaceans. He was a postdoctoral researcher at the Technische Universität Braunschweig (2002–2004) and at the University of Hawaii's Kewalo Marine Laboratory (2004–2009). From 2009 to 2019 he was a principal investigator at the Sars International Centre for Marine Molecular Biology in Bergen, Norway, and from 2019 a professor at the University of Bergen. Since 2021 he has been a professor at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and director of its Phyletic Museum. He received the A. O. Kovalevsky Medal of the St. Petersburg Society of Naturalists in 2018. His FHL-connected papers, from 2011 to 2024, mostly use brachiopods collected near FHL.

His group compares embryos and larvae across animal phyla to ask when developmental mechanisms, organ systems and body openings first appeared, often in less-studied invertebrates such as brachiopods, bryozoans, priapulids and horsehair worms. In his census papers the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa recurs: adults were dredged from rocky seabeds around Friday Harbor, with help from FHL staff and the crew of the R/V Centennial, and kept in FHL seawater tables. Studies from 2011 to 2024 use it to examine larval eyes (2011), the larval anterior nervous system (2012), mesoderm (2015), Hox genes in larvae and juveniles (2017, 2019), a neuropeptide that triggers defensive behavior in larvae (2017) and Wnt signaling along the head-to-tail axis (2024). Broader comparisons include convergent evolution of nerve cords (2017) and the repeated evolution of protostome and deuterostome development (2017). With his student Ludwik Gąsiorowski he reported evidence for a single origin of ultrafiltration-based excretory organs (2021).

name: Andreas Heyland
text:
Andreas Heyland, a professor in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of Guelph, studies metamorphosis in marine invertebrates and its hormonal control. He received BSc (1996) and MSc (1999) degrees from the University of Zurich and a PhD from the University of Florida (2004), begun in Larry McEdward's laboratory and later advised by David Julian. In 1999 he took two summer courses at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where Jason Hodin introduced him to the idea that thyroid hormones may act in echinoderm metamorphosis, the subject of his PhD. During his PhD he spent several summers at FHL doing research and teaching. From 2004 to 2007 he was a postdoctoral fellow with Leonid Moroz at the University of Florida's Whitney Laboratory, funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation, studying larval development and metamorphosis in Aplysia californica. His FHL-addressed papers date from 2004 to 2012.

Heyland's work concerns the molecular and physiological mechanisms of life-history transitions and their evolution. His FHL-connected work, much of it with Hodin, centered on thyroid hormones in echinoderm larvae. Papers in 2004 showed that thyroid hormone shifts developmental timing in sand dollar larvae, with implications for how nonfeeding development evolves, and a 2006 study found that larvae of the sand dollar Clypeaster rosaceus, which can develop with or without feeding, make the hormone themselves. He also reviewed hormone signaling in non-model organisms (2004) and co-wrote 2006 symposium papers on what metamorphosis is and how it is signaled and timed. A 2012 paper with Luke Hoekstra described histamine- and FMRFamide-like cells in the sea cucumber Leptosynapta clarki. Later papers cover larval staging, juvenile structures, asymmetry, growth and Vibrio resistance in the purple sea urchin (2014–2020) and thyroid hormone signaling in echinoderm skeleton formation (2024).

name: Andrew E. Christie
text:
Andrew E. Christie is a neurobiologist who studies peptide hormones and neuromodulators in crustaceans and other arthropods. The addresses on his papers trace his career. In the mid-1990s he was at Brandeis University, co-authoring work with Eve Marder and Katherine Graubard on the crab stomatogastric nervous system, and a 1997 paper gives an address at the University of Pennsylvania. By 2003 he was in the Department of Biology at the University of Washington, where a stomatogastric research directory lists him as an associate of Graubard's laboratory, and his papers from 2004 to 2007 carry a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. By 2010 he was at the Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory in Maine, and from at least 2015 at the Békésy Laboratory of Neurobiology, Pacific Biosciences Research Center, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa.

Christie identifies the peptide hormones and neuromodulators of decapod crustaceans and studies how they act on small neural circuits, such as those of the stomatogastric and cardiac systems, using anatomical, mass spectrometric, molecular and physiological methods. The FHL-connected papers center on Cancer crabs, especially the red rock crab Cancer productus. They describe a neurosecretory site within the stomatogastric nervous system (2004); the hormones of the sinus gland and pericardial organ, a tachykinin-containing neuroendocrine organ and members of the crustacean hyperglycemic hormone family (2005–2006); a novel FMRFamide-like peptide (2006); and the cloning of hyperglycemic hormone precursors (2007). Others cover SIFamide in the American lobster (2006) and a peptide whose end resembles vertebrate neuropeptide Y (2007). A 2008 study found that the pyloric circuit of the herbivorous crab Pugettia producta responds weakly to several neuromodulators. His later work mines transcriptomes to predict the neuropeptides of lobsters, crabs, copepods and other arthropods.

name: Andrew Hunter
text: Andrew Hunter is listed among former graduate students of Linda G. Wordeman's lab in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington. Hunter's work concerned the mitotic centromere-associated kinesin MCAK. Papers with Wordeman showed its importance in anaphase chromosome segregation (Maney et al., 1998) and reviewed how motor proteins influence microtubule polymerization dynamics (Hunter and Wordeman, 2000). Hunter's first-authored 2003 Molecular Cell paper, with Wordeman, J. Howard and others, showed that MCAK is an ATPase that catalytically depolymerizes microtubules from their ends.

A 2014 Marine Environmental Research paper reported fatty acid and pigment results from the plume, with addresses at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute and the University of Tasmania. text: Andrew N. Spencer did a PhD with George O. Mackie, whose memoir traces the work with Richard Strathmann to a meeting at Friday Harbor Laboratories. At the University of Alberta, Spencer studied neurons and muscle of the jellyfish Polyorchis penicillatus, and coauthored a 1985 study of swimming in the pteropod Clione limacina.

name: Andrew Pershing
text:
Andrew Pershing was a PhD student of Charles H. Greene at Cornell University, completing a dissertation in 2001 on the response of large marine ecosystems to climate variability, and then worked with Greene as a postdoctoral researcher from 2001 to 2003. Papers with Greene link North Atlantic climate to ocean circulation, plankton and ecosystem change. They include "The flip-side of the North Atlantic Oscillation and modal shifts in slope-water circulation patterns" (Limnology and Oceanography, 2003), a study of climate and the recovery of endangered North Atlantic right whales (Oceanography, 2003), and "Climate Drives Sea Change" (Science, 2007).

Pershing held a Brown University BS in aquatic biology (1995). He was an assistant professor in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at Cornell from 2004 to 2006, then became a research assistant professor in the University of Maine School of Marine Sciences in 2006, based at the Gulf of Maine Research Institute, where he was chief scientific officer from 2014 to 2020. Papers from these years include a 2015 Science study tying rapid warming to the collapse of the Gulf of Maine cod fishery and a 2010 PLoS ONE paper on whaling and the ocean carbon cycle. He joined Climate Central in 2020 as director of climate science and was listed as its vice president for science in 2023.

text: Angela Cheer appears among the postdocs on M. A. R. Koehl's lab page at the University of California, Berkeley, and earned a Berkeley PhD in 1981. text: Angela M. Kita was a graduate student of William M. Bement at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where the work concerned actin in cell division. text: Ani Michaud was a PhD student of William M. Bement in cell and molecular biology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, entering in 2016. name: Anja Kleinteich
text: Anja Kleinteich was a postdoctoral fellow with Adam P. Summers from 2009 to 2011. With Dylan K. Wainwright, Thomas Kleinteich, Stanislav N. Gorb and Summers, Kleinteich published a 2013 Biology Letters paper, with Friday Harbor Laboratories as Kleinteich's affiliation, on suction adhesion in the northern clingfish, Gobiesox maeandricus. The fish held equally well on surfaces from the finest sandpaper to textures used for removing floor finish, with adhesive forces 80 to 230 times body weight, and outperformed man-made suction cups. The authors related this tenacity to hierarchically structured microvilli around the edge of the adhesive disc.

name: Ann Miller
text:
Ann L. Miller was a postdoctoral fellow in William M. Bement's laboratory at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Working in Xenopus laevis embryos, she showed that MgcRacGAP activity keeps RhoA activity focused throughout cytokinesis, a mechanism called Rho GTPase flux (Miller and Bement, Nature Cell Biology, 2009). Papers with Bement and George von Dassow from these years include "Rho GTPase activity zones and transient contractile arrays" (BioEssays, 2006), "Control of the cytokinetic apparatus by flux of the Rho GTPases" (Biochemical Society Transactions, 2008) and "Action at a distance during cytokinesis" (Journal of Cell Biology, 2009). In 2017 she described a collaborative project with Bement, von Dassow and Andrew Goryachev.

Miller studied biochemistry at Gustavus Adolphus College and earned a Yale PhD in Tony Koleske's laboratory, where she examined how the Arg nonreceptor tyrosine kinase regulates cytoskeletal structure, cell shape and movement. She began her own group as an assistant professor at the University of Michigan in 2011 and was named Arthur F. Thurnau Professor in 2025. Her laboratory uses the epithelium of Xenopus embryos and live imaging to ask how epithelial junctions keep cells adhered and sealed while the cells change shape during cytokinesis and morphogenesis, with attention to RhoA and to Anillin, MgcRacGAP and Vinculin.

name: Anna Sokac
text: Anna Marie Sokac was a graduate student of William M. Bement at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, with a PhD in cellular and molecular biology (1994-2001). Papers with Bement include a 2000 review of unconventional myosins and a 2006 Developmental Cell study showing that myosin-1c couples assembling actin to membranes during compensatory endocytosis in Xenopus eggs. Sokac then joined the faculty at Baylor College of Medicine (2010-2019) and moved in 2019 to the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as associate professor of cell and developmental biology, with a laboratory studying the actin cytoskeleton in Drosophila embryos.

name: Anthony De Tomaso
text:
Anthony W. De Tomaso hosted Federico D. Brown, then a PhD student of Billie J. Swalla at the University of Washington and Friday Harbor Laboratories, when Brown visited his laboratory at Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station during doctoral research (2002-2008). Publications on ascidians that carry both names include the chapter "Regeneration and Stem Cells in Ascidians" (2008), with Stefano Tiozzo, and "Early lineage specification of long-lived germline precursors in the colonial ascidian Botryllus schlosseri" (Development, 2009), which also carried Swalla as an author.

De Tomaso received a BS from Stanford in 1987 and a PhD in cellular and molecular biology at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, with a thesis on assembly and targeting of multi-subunit proteins, using the rodent Na,K-ATPase. As an NIH fellow in Irving Weissman's laboratory at Stanford, he worked on allorecognition and regeneration in the colonial chordate Botryllus schlosseri, and he was first author of "Isolation and characterization of a protochordate histocompatibility locus" (Nature, 2005). He moved from Hopkins Marine Station to Molecular, Cellular and Developmental Biology at the University of California, Santa Barbara, as an assistant professor, welcomed in the department's 2008 newsletter, and later became a professor. His group has studied allorecognition, germline stem cells and regeneration in Botryllus.

name: Antonio C. Marques
text:
Antonio Carlos Marques is a Brazilian marine biologist who specializes in cnidarians. His ORCID record lists a Ph.D. in zoology from the Universidade de São Paulo (1993–1997) and a position in zoology there from 2000, with the title of full professor. His papers give two addresses at the university: the Departamento de Zoologia of the Instituto de Biociências and the Centro de Biologia Marinha in São Sebastião. He has no FHL address of his own. His five census papers, from 2011 to 2017, are FHL-connected mainly through co-author Claudia E. Mills of FHL and the UW Department of Biology, who worked with Marques and his student Lucília S. Miranda on stalked jellyfishes. A 2011 paper is included because it appears in the FHL bibliography.

His research covers the taxonomy, phylogeny and evolution of cnidarians, especially medusozoans such as hydroids, box jellies and stalked jellyfishes. His publications listed on Wikispecies also include work on fossil conulariids, bryozoans and areas of endemism in the Southwestern Atlantic. The FHL-connected papers center on Staurozoa, the stalked jellyfishes. In 2012, with Miranda and Mills, he recorded Lucernariopsis capensis in Brazil, its first record outside its type locality in South Africa. In 2016 the same group used mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences to propose the first phylogenetic classification of Staurozoa. It found that the traditional suborders, defined by the presence or absence of a claustrum, are not natural groups, and divided the class into two new groups. Other papers compared staurozoan internal anatomy (2016) and reviewed the group's global diversity and natural history (2017). The 2011 paper named the Bonaire banded box jelly, Tamoya ohboya.

name: Arthur H. Whiteley
text:
Arthur H. Whiteley (1916–2013) was a developmental biologist who studied sea urchin embryos at the University of Washington and Friday Harbor Laboratories. He received a BA in biology from Kalamazoo College (1938), an MS in zoology from the University of Wisconsin (1939) and a PhD in biology from Princeton (1945), where he did war-related research with E. Newton Harvey, and then held posts in Galveston and at Caltech. He began teaching at UW in 1947, the start of a long association with FHL, where he had a laboratory. He headed an NIH-sponsored interdepartmental developmental biology training program for 20 years and retired in 1985 as professor emeritus of zoology. He founded the Helen Riaboff Whiteley Center at FHL. The census lists 33 FHL-connected papers, 1953–2011.

Whiteley's research moved from the metabolism of echinoid embryos to the genetic mechanisms controlling development, mostly in the purple sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus. His FHL-connected papers of the 1950s and 1960s dealt with respiration and DNA synthesis, the enzymes urease and malate dehydrogenase, and the uptake and transport of phosphate. From about 1970 he turned to RNA: the conservation of early-development RNA sequences among echinoderms, the expression of maternal and paternal genomes in hybrid embryos, histone gene expression, and comparisons with limpet and oyster embryos. In the 1980s his group isolated and cultured micromeres and primary mesenchyme cells, the cell line that forms the larval skeleton, and followed their protein synthesis and gene expression. Later papers address spawning in a chiton (2003) and the history of embryology at FHL (2011). Students in the report's network include Michael Harkey and Hironobu Ozaki.

text: Ashley E. M. Miller was a PhD student of Andreas Heyland at the University of Guelph, with a 2013 thesis on iodine uptake in larvae of the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus. The work compared sodium-dependent transport with hydrogen peroxide-dependent diffusion. Larvae took up iodine from microalgal food and through the body surface; perchlorate had no effect, while added peroxide raised uptake and peroxidase inhibitors lowered it, supporting diffusion. Miller and Heyland reported the result in the Journal of Experimental Biology in 2013. They also published a 2010 General and Comparative Endocrinology paper on exogenous hormone sources from plants and the evolution of hormone signaling.

name: Aurel Wintner
text:
Aurel Wintner (1903–1958) was a Hungarian-born mathematician who worked in analysis, probability, number theory, differential equations and celestial mechanics. He studied at the University of Budapest and then at the University of Leipzig, where he received his doctorate; Wikipedia gives the year as 1928 and the MacTutor archive as 1929. Wikipedia names Leon Lichtenstein as his doctoral adviser. MacTutor says Lichtenstein encouraged his doctoral work and employed him as an assistant, and Wikidata also lists Julius Bauschinger as an adviser. After stays in Rome and Copenhagen in 1929–30, he joined Johns Hopkins University in 1930, became a full professor in 1946 and stayed until his death. He spent 1937–38 at the Institute for Advanced Study and was associate editor of the American Journal of Mathematics from 1936 and editor from 1944. He has no FHL papers.

Wintner published proofs of basic facts about Hilbert spaces in 1929 and wrote several papers that put George W. Hill's lunar theory on a rigorous footing. Wikipedia counts him among the founders of probabilistic number theory, and the Jessen–Wintner and Wiener–Wintner theorems carry his name. MacTutor credits him with about 437 papers and nine monographs. His books include a work on the spectral theory of infinite matrices (1929), The Analytical Foundations of Celestial Mechanics (1941) and The Fourier Transforms of Probability Distributions (1947). His tie to FHL is a line of doctoral advisers recorded in Wikidata. His student Monroe H. Martin supervised Simon A. Levin, whose FHL-connected papers in the census deal with plankton-feeding fishes (2002) and marine ecosystem-based management (2008). Levin's own student Daniel Grünbaum later taught in FHL's summer Larval Biology course.

text: Ayana T. Moore earned a PhD at the University of Washington in 2005 as a graduate student in Linda G. Wordeman's lab in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics, with a thesis on regions of the kinesin MCAK outside its motor domain. Moore was first author of a 2005 Journal of Cell Biology paper, with Wordeman and George von Dassow of the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories among the coauthors. It showed that MCAK tracks the tips of polymerizing microtubules in living cells, and that this tracking is inhibited by phosphorylation and depends on the protein's extreme C-terminal tail.

text: Baixue Yao earned a PhD in cell and molecular biology at the University of Chicago in 2022, advised by Edwin Munro and Michael Rust, and is listed as a former graduate student of Munro's lab. text: Barbara L. Gartner is listed among the postdocs of M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley. text: Baylen M. Ratliff was a University of Washington undergraduate in the College of the Environment who studied eelgrass, Zostera marina, at Friday Harbor Laboratories. name: Benjamin G. Miner
text:
Benjamin G. Miner took an embryology course at Friday Harbor Laboratories at the end of his undergraduate degree, and went on to a PhD in zoology at the University of Florida (1998-2003), co-advised by Larry R. McEdward, Colette St. Mary and Craig Osenberg. His papers include a study of feeding structures in opheliid and echiurid larvae with Eric Sanford, Richard R. Strathmann, Bruno Pernet and Richard B. Emlet (Biological Bulletin, 1999), one on postlarval chromatophores and ultraviolet radiation (2000), and work with McEdward on echinoderm larval and life-cycle patterns (Canadian Journal of Zoology, 2001) and fecundity-time models of reproductive strategies (Marine Ecology Progress Series, 2003).

Miner earned a BA in marine sciences at the University of California, Santa Cruz (1996), with John Pearse and Grant Pogson as advisors. He was a postdoctoral researcher at the Bodega Marine Laboratory of UC Davis from 2003 to 2006, then joined the Biology Department at Western Washington University in 2006, where he became a professor. His research asks how phenotypic plasticity in morphology and behavior affects ecological and evolutionary processes, typically in near-shore marine invertebrates, as in "Ecological consequences of phenotypic plasticity" (Trends in Ecology and Evolution, 2005). He also worked on sea star wasting, including the densovirus study in PNAS (2014) and a 2022 review of asteroid biology in the Biological Bulletin.

name: Benjamin Gutzler
text: Benjamin C. Gutzler completed a PhD at the University of New Hampshire in 2019 with Winsor H. Watson as first advisor. The dissertation asked how warming, more acidic Gulf of Maine waters may affect American lobsters, Homarus americanus. It developed a way to quantify sperm in spermatophores, tested effects of shell disease on mating and of lower pH on foraging, and used accelerometers and a custom datalogger on free-moving animals. An MS at Old Dominion University (2014) preceded a 2015 paper on casitas and juvenile Caribbean spiny lobsters. Gutzler became a research scientist at the Wells National Estuarine Research Reserve in 2020, publishing on lobsters and green crabs.

name: Beth Okamura
text: Beth Okamura earned a PhD in zoology at the University of California, Berkeley, as a graduate student in M. A. R. Koehl's lab. That work addressed flow and suspension feeders: the effects of ambient flow, colony size and upstream colonies on feeding in the bryozoans Bugula stolonifera (1984) and Conopeum reticulum (1985), and aggregations of Mytilus edulis (1986). After postdoctoral fellowships at Bangor, the Smithsonian Marine Station and Dalhousie, Okamura held posts at Oxford, Bristol and Reading, where Okamura was professor (2005-2007), then became a research leader at the Natural History Museum in 2007, working on Bryozoa and Myxozoa.

text: Betul Senay Aras was a PhD student in mathematics at Ohio State University from 2014 to 2017, listed on the lab page of Adriana T. Dawes. With Dawes, Ching-Shan Chou and Y. C. name: Billie J. Swalla
text:
Billie J. Swalla is an evolutionary developmental biologist and professor emerita at the University of Washington, based at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She earned her BS, MS and PhD (1988) at the University of Iowa, then studied ascidian eggs as a postdoctoral fellow with William R. Jeffery at the University of Texas at Austin and was an assistant research developmental biologist at the University of California, Davis's Bodega Marine Laboratory (1991–94). She was an assistant professor at Vanderbilt University (1994–97) and Pennsylvania State University (1997–99), joined UW Zoology in 1999, and was professor from 2009 until becoming emerita in 2023. She was FHL's interim director from 2012 and director from 2014 to 2019, the first woman to hold the post, and taught FHL courses on the evolution and development of marine invertebrates. She was president of the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology (2013–15). The census lists 72 FHL-connected papers, 2001–2024.

Her research uses tunicates, especially ascidians, and hemichordates to study how the chordate body plan evolved, combining embryology, gene expression, phylogenetics and genomics. Long-running themes include the loss of the larval tail in molgulid ascidians such as Molgula occulta, metamorphosis and coloniality in ascidians, regeneration in the acorn worm Ptychodera flava, and the relationships among deuterostome groups. Her FHL-connected papers include a cold-water clade of acorn worms (2013), phylogenomic analyses of hemichordates and echinoderms (2014) and of the major tunicate lineages (2017), a survey of hemichordate diversity (2016), a study of the disrupted Cymric gene in tailless Molgula (2023), and reviews of tunicates and vertebrate origins (2020) and of deuterostome ancestors (2024). She is also a co-author of FHL Ocean Observatory seawater datasets covering 2018 to 2024. Her former PhD students include Brad Davidson, Federico Brown, Amanda Rychel, Max Maliska and Shawn Luttrell.

text: Bionda Morelissen was a PhD student of Nicole E. Phillips at Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand, with a thesis dated 2012. name: Brad Davidson
text:
Brad Davidson is a developmental biologist and Associate Professor of Biology at Swarthmore College, where he earned a B.S. in biology in 1991. He took a Ph.D. in zoology at the University of Washington (1997–2002), was a postdoctoral fellow in Molecular and Cellular Biology at the University of California, Berkeley (2002–2006), and was an assistant professor of Molecular and Cellular Biology at the University of Arizona (2007–2012) before returning to Swarthmore in 2012. His FHL connection comes from his doctoral-era research on ascidian metamorphosis with Billie J. Swalla; their 2002 paper lists both the UW Zoology Department and Friday Harbor Laboratories. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 2002 to 2007, and the FHL bibliography also lists a 2013 paper on which he is senior author.

Davidson's lab uses the sea squirt Ciona intestinalis, whose simple embryos share many heart genes with vertebrates, to study the first steps of heart formation. It examines how fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling directs early heart cells, and has described an 'invasive signaling' mechanism, involving the neighboring epidermis, that boosts it and may bear on cancer metastasis. His FHL-connected papers concern the solitary ascidian Boltenia villosa. In 2002 he and Swalla compared larval and juvenile transcripts by PCR subtraction and found that many genes expressed at metamorphosis match innate immune genes, suggesting an immune-like role in remodeling larval tissues. A 2003 paper characterized the morphology and gene expression of B. villosa metamorphosis, and a 2007 paper led by Brock Roberts proposed that a complement response may help trigger it. The 2013 paper showed that adhesion to the extracellular matrix controls where heart progenitors are induced in Ciona.

name: Brian Burkel
text: Brian M. Burkel was a PhD student of William M. Bement at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. With George von Dassow and Bement, Burkel described fluorescent probes for actin filaments based on the calponin homology domain of utrophin, which bind filaments without stabilizing them in vitro (2007). A 2012 Developmental Cell paper, also with von Dassow, showed a Rho GTPase signal treadmill driving contractile array closure in cellular wound repair. Burkel then held a postdoctoral fellowship at the Laboratory for Optical and Computational Instrumentation, and later an associate scientist post in Wisconsin's Department of Cell and Regenerative Biology, publishing on imaging of the mammary tumor microenvironment (2022).

name: Brian Burrows
text: Brian Burrows earned an MS in 2005 in the lab of Esther M. Leise at the University of North Carolina Greensboro. Burrows labeled dividing cells with BrdU in larvae of the snail Ilyanassa obsoleta to ask whether nitric oxide controls larval neurogenesis; the lab reported that the rate of neurogenesis declined during planktonic larval development.

name: Brian Helmuth
text:
Brian Helmuth is a marine ecologist and Professor in the Department of Marine and Environmental Sciences at Northeastern University, with a joint appointment in the School of Public Policy and Urban Affairs, based at its Marine Science Center in Nahant, Massachusetts. He earned a BS at Cornell University (1989), where C. Drew Harvell supervised his research, an MS at Northeastern (1991) and a PhD in zoology at the University of Washington (1997) with Thomas Daniel, and was a postdoctoral researcher with Mark Denny at Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station (1997–1999). He was on the University of South Carolina faculty from 1999 to 2012 and moved to Northeastern in 2013. His CV lists an FHL seminar in May 2002, and FHL's list of visitors in the Whiteley Center's first two years names him, with Gretchen Hofmann, Ann Kinzig and Bruce Menge, in a group studying how environmental stress shapes rocky intertidal distributions.

Helmuth's research forecasts the ecological effects of climate change on coastal ecosystems, with a focus on the body temperatures of intertidal animals such as mussels. His group builds and deploys mussel-like temperature loggers ('robomussels'), runs physiological experiments and maps species' vulnerability to inform marine spatial planning. His FHL-connected papers run from 1996 to 2016. The first, with Dianna Padilla, Drew Harvell and Jessica Marks, examined inducible aggression and competition for space in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea. Later papers treat latitudinal patterns of intertidal thermal stress (2002), the value of mechanistic biophysics for climate-change ecology (2005, with Joel Kingsolver and Emily Carrington), wave exposure and mosaic patterns of thermal stress on rocky shores (2006), temperature-dependent photosynthesis in the alga Fucus gardneri (2014, with Carrington and his doctoral student Nicholas Colvard, who held an FHL Alan and Marian Kohn Fellowship), and a long-term record of mussel-bed temperatures from biomimetic sensors (2016).

name: Brian Rivest
text: Brian R. Rivest completed a PhD as a student of Richard R. Strathmann of the University of Washington, and papers from 1984 and 1992 list the State University of New York at Cortland. Rivest studied the reproduction and development of marine gastropods. A 1978 paper described larval development of the nudibranch Cuthona nana and its tie to a hydroid living on hermit crab shells. A 1984 paper described how Palio zosterae and P. dubia copulate by piercing the body wall with a barbed cirrus. A 1992 study used light, electron and fluorescence microscopy on the larval kidneys of Searlesia dira and Nucella canaliculata.

name: Brian S. Leander
text:
Brian S. Leander is a Professor in the Departments of Zoology and Botany at the University of British Columbia, where he was Assistant Professor from 2003, Associate Professor from 2008 and Professor from 2013. He earned a BSc in engineering science at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo (1993), a BSc and MA in comparative zoology at what is now Cal Poly Humboldt and a PhD in comparative biology at the University of Georgia (2001), and was an NSF postdoctoral fellow in UBC's Program in Microbial Biology (2001–2003). He was a Fellow and Senior Fellow of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (2003–2017) and a Tula Investigator (2007–2017), and has been a Hakai Research Affiliate since 2018. In his 2017–2019 census papers FHL is a collecting site, not an address: his group towed a plankton net off the FHL dock in June 2016, and FHL hosted one of its flatworm sampling campaigns.

Leander's laboratory studies the diversity, ultrastructure and evolution of marine microbial eukaryotes and tiny animals, with a focus on predatory protists. Its questions include how complex organelles such as the eye-like ocelloids and harpoon-like extrusive organelles of dinoflagellates arose, how parasitic gregarine apicomplexans evolved from free-living ancestors, and why unrelated lineages converge on similar traits. The group combines electron microscopy, including FIB-SEM, with transcriptomics, single-cell genomics and molecular phylogenetics, and collects at sites including Calvert Island, Bamfield and Curaçao. Its three FHL-connected papers are a 2017 study, led by his former doctoral student and postdoctoral fellow Gregory Gavelis, showing that the nematocyst-like organelles of dinoflagellates such as Polykrikos and Nematodinium arose independently of those of cnidarians; a 2018 molecular phylogeny of trigonostomine flatworms, with postdoctoral fellow Niels Van Steenkiste, that described four new northeast Pacific species; and a 2019 description of a 'nuclear net' of membranes inside the dinoflagellate nucleus.

name: Brian S. Ort
text: Brian S. Ort was a postdoctoral researcher with Sarah Cohen at San Francisco State University's Romberg Tiburon Center, after a PhD at the University of California, Santa Cruz. The work, with Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria of Friday Harbor Laboratories as co-author, concerned eelgrass (Zostera marina) population genetics. A 2012 paper compared six San Francisco Bay locations with seven microsatellite loci, and a 2014 paper tested buoy-deployed seeding for keeping genetic diversity in mesocosms. Earlier work with G. H. Pogson (2007) compared male and female mitochondrial DNA of the California sea mussel. Ort was later a research associate at UC Berkeley and published on invasive Spartina after ten years of management (2016).

text: Brianna Delaney Reynolds earned an MS in Biology at Montclair State University in January 2024, with Colette J. Feehan as thesis sponsor. name: Brooke Flammang
text:
Brooke E. Flammang is a fish biomechanist and functional morphologist, a professor of biological sciences at the New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT) as of 2026; her group there is the Fluid Locomotion Laboratory. Her tie to FHL began during her master's work at Moss Landing Marine Laboratories with Greg Cailliet, when Lara Ferry urged her to take the FHL fish course taught by Adam Summers. Finishing a dissection early, she went on to dissect the rest of the shark and found a bright red muscle in the tail that the manual did not list, and it became her course project. Her 2010 paper treats the functional morphology of the radialis muscle in shark tails.

Flammang earned a BS in marine biology at Fairleigh Dickinson University (1998), an MS in marine science at California State University, Monterey Bay (2005), and a PhD at Harvard with George Lauder (2010), and held a Harvard postdoctoral fellowship through 2013. Her work combines anatomy, fluid dynamics and robotics, using remoras, shark tails and the walking cavefish Cryptotora thamicola. Stephanie B. Crofts was a postdoctoral research associate in the NJIT lab, studying caudal fins of sharks and extinct marine reptiles; their 2019 paper asks what shark tails show about ichthyosaur swimming. Papers naming FHL include a 2008 study of elastic recoil in pipefish prey capture and a 2020 study of the soft tissues of the remora adhesive disc.

name: Brooke L. Weigel
text:
Brooke L. Weigel is a marine ecologist who studies kelp forests and the microbes that live on kelp. She holds a BA in biology and environmental studies from St. Olaf College (2013), an MS in marine biology from the University of North Carolina Wilmington (2016) and a PhD in evolutionary biology from the University of Chicago (2021). During her doctoral research on kelp forest ecology on Tatoosh Island, Washington, she began studying kelp-associated microbes. She was then the Kelp Conservation Postdoctoral Researcher at FHL, studying why kelp are declining in Puget Sound, and a National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellow at Western Washington University. She is now assistant professor of oceans at Stanford University, with her laboratory at Hopkins Marine Station. The census counts seven FHL-address papers by her, from 2022 to 2025.

Her research examines the feedbacks between climate change, kelp forests, microbes and ocean carbon cycling, using field and laboratory experiments, algal culturing, genomics, bioinformatics and scientific diving. At FHL she worked on the bull kelp, Nereocystis luetkeana, whose life cycle includes microscopic stages. A 2022 student report she co-authored and a 2023 paper test how temperature and nutrients affect gametophytes and young sporophytes, and another 2023 paper compares the effects of temperature and nitrogen on bull kelp and sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima). This work identified temperature thresholds for growth, survival and reproduction across the bull kelp life cycle. Her microbiome papers describe the diversity and functional capacity of microbes on coastal macrophytes (2022), map the kelp microbiome at micron scales (2022) and show that warm, nutrient-poor seawater changes the microbial community on a canopy kelp (2025). She also co-authored a 2025 population-genomic study of genetic drift in bull and giant kelp, aimed at guiding conservation.

text: Brooke Z. Torjman did undergraduate research with Erika V. Iyengar at Muhlenberg College (BS 2019). name: Bruce Alberts
text:
Bruce Alberts is a biochemist who studied the protein machinery of DNA replication, including the reconstitution of a replication system from seven purified proteins. He took a BS at Harvard College (1960) and a PhD in biophysics at Harvard with Paul Doty (1966), then worked at the University of Geneva with Richard H. Epstein on phage T4 replication genes. He was on the Princeton faculty from 1966 to 1976, joined the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) in 1976 and chaired biochemistry and biophysics there from 1985 to 1990. He was president of the National Academy of Sciences from 1993 to 2005 and editor-in-chief of Science from 2008 to 2013, and he is a co-author of the textbook Molecular Biology of the Cell.

His tie to FHL runs through Victoria E. Foe, who did her postdoctoral work with him at UCSF and was later a founding member of the Center for Cell Dynamics at FHL. Their joint papers describe early Drosophila development: a 1983 study in the Journal of Cell Science followed nuclear and cytoplasmic behavior through the five mitotic cycles that precede gastrulation, and a 1985 paper in The Journal of Cell Biology used anoxia to induce reversible chromosome condensation in embryos as a way to see interphase nuclear organization. The 1985 paper's acknowledgments thank FHL for the use of laboratory facilities for part of the work.

text: Bruce Allen Miller earned a Biology MS at the University of Oregon in 1995 under Richard B. Emlet, after serving as a fisheries biologist with the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (1977-93). The thesis tracked larval abundance and settlement of red and purple sea urchins on the southern Oregon coast, tying settlement to upwelling relaxation events. Papers with Emlet followed in 1997 and 1999 on settlement and juvenile development.

name: Bruce Monger
text:
Bruce C. Monger is an oceanographer, a senior lecturer in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at Cornell University as of 2024, whose listed interests include ocean ecosystems, climate change and satellite ocean remote sensing. Monger's tie to FHL core scientists runs through Charles H. Greene, who lists Monger as a postdoctoral advisee at Cornell in 1993-1994. The two had already published together: a 1986 paper in Ecology with Michael R. Landry examined foraging and prey selection by the ambush entangling predator Pleurobrachia bachei, and it appears in FHL's own bibliography. A 1998 paper led by Monger, which names FHL in its main text, concerned sound scattering by the gelatinous zooplankters Aequorea victoria and Pleurobrachia bachei.

Monger completed a PhD in oceanography at the University of Hawaii in August 1993, with Landry as dissertation committee chair. The dissertation built a numerical model of prey capture by heterotrophic marine nanoflagellates that weighed hydrodynamic, van der Waals, electrostatic and solvation forces, then tested the effects of prey size and surface hydrophobicity with feeding experiments. A paper on flow cytometric analysis of marine bacteria with Hoechst 33342 appeared with Landry in 1993. At Cornell, Monger shared NASA funding with Greene for an undergraduate course on satellite remote sensing in biological oceanography (1999-2002) and NOAA funding with Andrew J. Pershing and Greene for work on right whales and their Calanus prey (2001-2003). Later papers with Greene include a 2013 study of climate-forced regime shifts in Northwest Atlantic shelf ecosystems.

name: Bruce W. Frost
text:
Bruce W. Frost, an oceanographer specializing in marine zooplankton, published his first paper in 1967, on a new harpacticoid copepod from Kodiak Island, Alaska, from the University of California's oceanography department at La Jolla; from 1974 his papers give the University of Washington as his institution. Rosters of the UW–FHL Advisory Board and Advisory Committee archived in 2004 list him, as Director of the UW School of Oceanography, among the members of both. His FHL-connected papers in the census date from 1990 to 2000. Most are studies of copepod behavior written with Stephen M. Bollens, and FHL's 2000 list of publications resulting from research at the laboratories includes the series. The last is a 2000 progress report, with Christopher D. Jones of UW's Applied Physics Laboratory, on a portable acoustic laboratory first tested from the FHL pier.

Frost's papers range over copepod taxonomy, including the 1974 description of Calanus marshallae, copepod feeding and subarctic Pacific plankton ecology. His FHL-connected work centers on diel vertical migration in copepods and what drives it. With Bollens he examined how ultraviolet light affects the vertical distribution of Acartia hudsonica (1990) and, in 1991, reported enclosure experiments in which A. hudsonica quickly changed its depth and migration behavior when threespine sticklebacks were present, which they read as behavioral flexibility of individuals rather than genetic change caused by selective predation. Further papers gave field evidence for the predator-avoidance hypothesis (1992), compared the vertical distributions and vulnerability to vertebrate predators of Metridia lucens and Calanus pacificus (1993), and tested chemical, mechanical and visual cues for migration (1994). The 2000 report, which names Frost as principal investigator of the project's UW part, concerns how organisms and biogenic structures affect sound propagation in seabed sediments.

name: Bruno Pernet
text:
Bruno Pernet is a professor of biological sciences at California State University, Long Beach, who studies the development, functional morphology and evolution of marine invertebrate larvae. He received a BA in biology from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington; his papers from the late 1990s give addresses in UW's Department of Zoology and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. After postdoctoral research at the Smithsonian Marine Station at Fort Pierce, Florida, he spent several years teaching and doing research at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology and at Friday Harbor Laboratories before moving to Long Beach. His FHL-addressed papers date from 1996 to 2004, and several later papers also draw on work at the laboratories. At Long Beach he led an NSF-funded project comparing how larvae with different ciliary feeding mechanisms capture food particles of different sizes.

Pernet's work centers on larval form and feeding, especially in annelids. His FHL-connected papers describe the capture of large particles by scaleworm larvae (1996), egg masses and development of the syllid Amblyosyllis speciosa (1998), opposed ciliary bands and large mouths in opheliid and echiurid larvae (1999), gamete interactions and genetic differentiation among three co-occurring polychaetes (1999), a scaleworm's setal "snorkel" and the reproduction of symbiotic scaleworms (2000), and ancestral feeding structures that persist in nonfeeding annelid larvae (2003). In 2004 he described the cryptic filtering house of an invertebrate larva and showed that dichromate oxidation underestimates the energy content of annelid eggs. Later work examined feeding by larvae of two developmental modes in Streblospio benedicti (2006), the risks of moving ghost shrimp as live bait (2008), larval feeding in a capitellid (2015), surveys for the annelid Ficopomatus enigmaticus (2017) and methods for rearing echinoderm larvae through metamorphosis (2018).

text: Bryce Wolcott was a graduate student in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley, working on size and scaling.
