name: C. Drew Harvell
text:
C. Drew Harvell (Catherine Drew Harvell) is a marine ecologist and Professor Emerita of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at Cornell University, which she joined in 1986. She earned BSc (1978) and MSc (1981) degrees in zoology at the University of Alberta, the latter with Fu-Shiang Chia, and a PhD in zoology at the University of Washington (1985) with a thesis on partial predation and inducible defenses in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea. She is affiliate faculty in UW's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences and has taught Cornell's invertebrate biology course at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where her current research is based. She has led an NSF research coordination network on marine disease and curated Cornell's Blaschka glass invertebrate collection. Her honors include fellowship of the Ecological Society of America and the Society of American Naturalists' Jasper Loftus-Hills Award. Her books include A Sea of Glass (2016) and Ocean Outbreak (2019).

Harvell's FHL-connected papers run from 1984 to 2026. Her early work concerned inducible defenses in bryozoans: a 1984 Science paper reported a predator-induced defense in a marine bryozoan, and papers through 1998 examined the cues, costs, genetic variation and evolution of inducible spines and polymorphism in Membranipora and other colonial animals. She later turned to disease in a warming ocean. Since 2015 her group's FHL-connected work has covered the sea star wasting epizootic, including ochre star mortality and the stars' immune responses; 2025 papers identified Vibrio pectenicida as a cause of the disease in the sunflower sea star. A parallel series on eelgrass wasting disease in the San Juan Islands finds that deeper, cooler meadows act as refuges, that grazers influence the disease and that altering the eelgrass microbiome can reduce its severity. Students linked to her in the report's network include Erika Iyengar and Olivia Graham.

Shishido has also worked as a fish and wildlife biologist with the US Fish and Wildlife Service.

text: Carla A. Narvaez was one of the FHL postdoctoral fellows on Emily Carrington's lab page, focusing on sea urchin recruitment and podia adhesion, oceanographic conditions, temperature stress, and microbiomes. Earlier work included a 2020 paper on marine heatwaves and the collapse of marginal North Atlantic kelp forests. From Villanova University, with Michael P. Russell, she published on tube foot regeneration in sea urchins under fluctuating hydrodynamic conditions (2022). Papers with Russell in 2023 and 2024, listing her at Friday Harbor Laboratories and Rhode Island College, showed that low salinity impairs tube foot coordination and adhesion. She became an assistant professor of biology at Rhode Island College in 2023.

name: Carmen Theresa Sanchez-Reddick
text: Carmen Theresa Sanchez-Reddick wrote a University of Oregon thesis, issued in May 2022 in the Clark Honors College collection, advised by Aaron W. E. Galloway and Craig Young. The thesis compared adults of the stalked ascidian Boltenia villosa from Washington and Oregon, using morphometrics, scanning electron microscopy, oocyte diameters and dissections. It reported differences in body proportions, spine character and reproduction despite genetic similarity between the populations, and raised the possibility of an undescribed subspecies. Sanchez-Reddick also contributed a 2023 art feature, "Precipice of Discovery," on the submersible Alvin.

name: Caroline Beth Albertin
text: Caroline Beth Albertin completed a PhD in Organismal Biology and Anatomy at the University of Chicago in 2016, advised by Clifton W. Ragsdale and Edwin M. Munro. The dissertation, on the molecular embryology of Octopus bimaculoides, drew on genome and transcriptome sequencing and traced cephalopod-specific genes, gene family expansions, neural development and Hox expression. At the Marine Biological Laboratory, Albertin was a Hibbitt Fellow (2018-2023) and assistant scientist (2023-2025); 2023 work included an albino squid line made by CRISPR-Cas9 and a review of cephalopod nervous system evolution. In 2026 Albertin became assistant professor of organismic and evolutionary biology at Harvard and curator of malacology at its Museum of Comparative Zoology.

name: Carolyn C. deRoos
text:
Carolyn C. deRoos published research on the endocrinology of sharks and their relatives from 1962 to 1992. A 2015 notice in the Journal of the San Juans says she studied at the University of California, Berkeley, and describes her as the research partner of the comparative endocrinologist Roger McLean deRoos (1930–2015). He earned a PhD in zoology at Berkeley under Howard Bern and joined the University of Missouri faculty in 1961. According to the notice, the two spent most summers at FHL, where they studied glucose regulation in the spiny dogfish. The census lists eight FHL-connected papers by her, from 1962 to 1992; seven of them give FHL as an address.

Her papers trace how the pituitary and the interrenal glands, which make corticosteroid hormones, work in cartilaginous fishes. The 1962 paper, with Bern and E. G. Biglieri, identified aldosterone and other corticosteroids from chondrichthyan interrenal glands, and a 1967 paper reported corticotropin (ACTH) activity in their pituitary glands. From 1973, working with Roger deRoos, she published a series of studies on blood glucose in the spiny dogfish, Squalus acanthias. These showed that mammalian ACTH (1973) and catecholamines (1978) raise plasma glucose, described severe hypoglycemia caused by insulin (1979), and found that glucose rises after partial removal of the pituitary or after sham surgery (1980). Later papers measured glucose, alanine, lactate and beta-hydroxybutyrate in unfed dogfish after surgery and insulin infusion (1985), and the effects of ACTH on fuels and gluconeogenic substrates in the blood (1992). All eight papers appeared in General and Comparative Endocrinology.

name: Carolyn Keogh
text: Carolyn Keogh completed a PhD in ecology in 2016 with James E. Byers at the University of Georgia's Odum School of Ecology, after a BS in environmental sciences at Emory University. Keogh's research addresses parasite-host interactions in marine invertebrates, including Littorina snails and the invasive shore crabs Carcinus maenas and Hemigrapsus sanguineus. A 2016 Oecologia paper compared local adaptation to trematode parasites in three co-occurring littorinid snail species, and a 2017 Ecology paper on Hemigrapsus sanguineus, with O. Miura and T. Nishimura, found an invasive host to be less infected but more infectable. Keogh went on to the faculty of Environmental Sciences at Emory University as an associate teaching professor.

name: Carroll Williams
text:
Carroll M. Williams (died 1991) was an insect physiologist and developmental biologist at Harvard. He earned a PhD in zoology there in 1941 under Charles Brues, with a thesis on the flight of Drosophila, then became a junior fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows and took an MD at Harvard Medical School in 1946. Appointed assistant professor that year, he chaired biology from 1959 to 1962 and was Benjamin Bussey Professor of Biology from 1966 until he retired in 1987. Working on the giant silkworm Hyalophora cecropia, he used carbon dioxide as a surgical anesthetic, studied the endocrine control of diapause and metamorphosis, and worked on juvenile hormone, later proposing hormone analogs as pesticides.

His link to FHL runs through Lynn M. Riddiford. As a Radcliffe College student she did her senior research thesis in his laboratory, searching vertebrate tissues for insect juvenile hormone. After a first postdoctoral stint in protein chemistry and two years teaching at Wellesley College, she returned to his laboratory for a year as a research fellow, before joining the Harvard biology faculty in 1966. Their joint papers of 1967 covered the effects of juvenile hormone analogs on silkworm embryos and a volatile factor in oak leaves that governs mating in polyphemus moths. Riddiford set up a laboratory at FHL in 2016.

text: Carson C. Keever joined Michael W. Hart's lab at Simon Fraser University as a PhD student in 2004, coming from Rick Grosberg's lab at UC Davis. Her 2009 Evolution paper found a strong phylogeographic break at Queen Charlotte Sound in the sea star Patiria miniata, and a 2013 Biology Letters paper reported extreme loss of genetic diversity in viviparous Parvulastra sea stars. Papers from 2016 and 2017 give her affiliation as the Department of Biology at Kwantlen Polytechnic University in British Columbia.

name: Cascade Sorte
text: Cascade Sorte was a PhD student of Susan L. Williams at the University of California, Davis, working from Bodega Marine Laboratory. A 2010 Ecology paper with Williams and R. A. Zerebecki tested ocean warming on a marine fouling community in Bodega Harbor and found that introduced species tolerated higher temperatures than natives. Sorte and Williams coauthored a 2006 Ecology Letters review on climate change in coastal marine systems. Later papers from the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of California, Irvine, address coastal pH (2023), observed and potential range shifts of native and nonnative species (2024), and the effects of marine range expansions (2026).

name: Cassandra M. Donatelli
text:
Cassandra M. Donatelli is a comparative biomechanist and an assistant professor in the School of Engineering and Technology at the University of Washington Tacoma since 2024, working on biomechanics and bio-inspired design with fishes. She came to FHL in summer 2013 through the BLINKS/REU internship, after her junior year at the University of Rochester, and worked with Marianne E. Porter on how vertebral shape affects body mechanics and swimming. In 2014 she took the FHL fish course taught by Adam P. Summers and Misty Paig-Tran, where her software for analyzing elongate fish swimming became the basis of her Tufts PhD with Eric D. Tytell (2014-2019), with Summers on her committee. She returned as teaching assistant (2016, 2018), REU mentor (2017, 2021) and course instructor (2020, 2022).

After a postdoctoral fellowship with Emily Standen at the University of Ottawa (2019-2022) and a faculty post at Chapman University (2022-2024), she continued to work at FHL on fish locomotion and armor. Her papers include a 2017 study of long-axis twisting in swimming elongate fishes with Summers and Tytell, a 2021 paper relating vertebral shape to behavior and ecology, and work on poacher (Agonidae) armor, including a 2020 study of swimming and defense across ontogeny and a 2026 paper on the armor's mechanical limits. She has also worked on MorphoCloud, a platform that moves CT-scan processing to an external cluster.

Loudon joined the University of California, Irvine, faculty in 2006, working on insect antennae and on leaf-inspired surfaces that trap bed bugs.

name: Cathy McFadden
text: Catherine S. (Cathy) McFadden is listed among the completed PhD students of Richard R. Strathmann at the University of Washington. Her papers on soft corals include a study of colony fission and particle capture (1986), a demographic analysis of clonal reproduction in a temperate species (1991), and population structure in Alcyonium rudyi (1997). After postdoctoral work at the University of California, Davis, and a NATO fellowship at the Port Erin Marine Laboratory, she joined Harvey Mudd College, where she became Vivian and D. Kenneth Baker Professor in the Life Sciences. Her lab used molecular methods to study octocoral phylogeny, species boundaries in the family Alcyoniidae, and hybridization in Alcyonium.

name: Cecelia Miles
text: Cecelia M. Miles was a PhD student of Larry R. McEdward of the University of Florida, listed among his students in 2001, the year McEdward died. With Adam M. Reitzel, Andreas Heyland, Jonathan D. Cowart and McEdward, Miles co-authored a 2005 study of the facultative feeding period in echinoid larvae. Later work used artificial selection on egg size, first in the polychaete Hydroides elegans (2007, 2009, with M. L. Wayne), then in Drosophila melanogaster at the University of Chicago, where a 2011 paper with Martin Kreitman and others reported shifts in early embryonic patterning. Miles was in the Department of Biology at Augustana University, Sioux Falls, as of 2026.

text: Celia Beron, from the University of Texas at Austin, worked with James A. Murray in the 2014 Blinks-NSF REU-BEACON program at Friday Harbor Laboratories, testing responses of the sea slug Tritonia tetraquetra to magnetic distortion. name: Celina Scott-Buechler
text: Celina M. Scott-Buechler was a thesis student of Charles H. Greene at Cornell University, completing a 2018 College Scholar honors thesis on climate drivers of Caribbean coral bleaching and a 2021 MS thesis in atmospheric science, chaired by Greene, on marine microalgae for human nutrition. With Greene, Scott-Buechler wrote a book chapter on the ocean's role in climate stabilization and 2022 papers on algae and marine aquaculture in PLoS Biology and Oceanography. Listing a Stanford University affiliation on the PLoS Biology paper, Scott-Buechler later published on community attitudes toward direct air capture of carbon dioxide and became an assistant professor at Duke University's Sanford School of Public Policy.

name: Chantel Taylor
text: Chantel Taylor is listed among the undergraduate alumni of the XROMM project, directed by Elizabeth L. Brainerd at Brown University. Taylor co-authored a 2015 Journal of Morphology paper with Nicholas J. Gidmark, Eric LoPresti and Brainerd on durophagy in the black carp, Mylopharyngodon piceus, which crushes snails and other mollusks with robust pharyngeal jaws. The study combined gross morphology, histological sectioning and X-ray reconstruction of moving morphology to examine how the jaws, their molariform teeth and the bone they bite against work together.

text: Charlotte E. (Char) Konikoff was an NSF BEACON postdoctoral fellow in Billie J. Swalla's lab at the University of Washington, named in the lab's December 2010 photo. From Arizona State University, Konikoff published with S. J. Newfeld on the molecular evolution of TGF-beta and Wnt signaling pathways (2008, 2010) and with S. Kumar and Newfeld on embryonic gene expression in Drosophila using the FlyExpress platform (2012). In the Swalla lab the work turned to hemichordates: a 2012 paper with S. Luttrell and others comparing neurulation in ptychoderid hemichordates and chordates, and a 2016 PLoS One survey of the global diversity of Hemichordata.

name: Charles Bradley Shuster
text:
Charles Bradley (Brad) Shuster is a cell biologist at New Mexico State University (NMSU). The faculty directory lists him as professor and head of the Department of Biology, with research on the regulation of the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons. A 2015 NMSU announcement, when he was an associate professor, described two grants worth more than $1.2 million together: one from the National Science Foundation on G-protein regulation of the actin cytoskeleton in the cleavage-stage embryo, and one from the National Institutes of Health on spindle orientation in echinoderm embryos. A 2017 seminar listing named him director of NMSU's Molecular Biology graduate program. His laboratory and John Henson's at Dickinson College share an NSF-supported study of cytokinesis, and the two groups work together in summers at FHL, using its sea urchins. The census lists seven FHL-address papers by him, from 2012 to 2024.

Shuster studies how dividing embryonic cells build and position the cleavage furrow, using live imaging of sea urchin, sea star and sand dollar eggs injected with fluorescent fusion proteins. A 2012 paper with Victoria Foe and others tracked the centralspindlin and chromosomal passenger complexes in echinoderm embryos, in both normal and so-called Rappaport furrows. Papers with Henson's group describe the arrangement of actin and myosin II filaments in the contractile ring (2017), the ring's start as clusters of myosin II, anillin and septin (2021), and its later maturation, including the recruitment of alpha-actinin (2024). Other papers cover the role of Cdc42 in shaping sea urchin primary mesenchyme cells (2018), polar lobe formation in scallop embryos (2019) and the Wnt-pathway protein Dishevelled in the vegetal cortex of the egg (2021). His census list also includes a 2008 biochemistry paper on the signaling protein Grb7, which is listed in FHL's research bibliography.

name: Charles Brues
text: Charles Thomas Brues (1879-1955) was an entomologist at Harvard University and the doctoral advisor of Carroll Williams, whose 1941 thesis analyzed the flight of Drosophila. Brues edited the journal Psyche from 1910, coauthored A Key to the Families of North American Insects (1915) with Axel Leonard Melander and wrote Insect Dietary (1945), an account of the food habits of insects.

name: Charles C. Lambert
text:
Charles C. Lambert (died 2011) was a developmental and reproductive biologist who worked mainly on ascidians (sea squirts). An FHL centennial timeline records that his association with the laboratories began in summer 1964, when as a graduate student he took the Invertebrate Zoology course; Gretchen Lambert, his research partner and co-author on many papers, began hers the same summer. He taught in the Department of Biological Science at California State University, Fullerton, for 28 years and was its campus Outstanding Professor for 1986. After retiring in 1998 he moved to Seattle to continue research in association with the University of Washington. He co-taught FHL's summer Comparative Invertebrate Embryology course in 1999 with Steve Stricker and in another year with Mark Martindale, and co-edited the 2001 volume The Biology of Ascidians. The census credits him with 23 FHL-connected papers, 1971-2014.

Lambert's research centered on fertilization and early development in ascidians. Early papers dealt with gene transcription during development and metamorphosis of Ascidia callosa (1971) and with light-triggered larval release in compound ascidians (1973); a 1978 Science paper with Gretchen Lambert showed that tunicate eggs use ammonium ions for flotation. Much of his later work examined gamete interactions: the ascidian sperm reaction and sperm mitochondrial movement (1982, 1984), a glycosidase released by eggs that helps block polyspermy (1989-1994), sperm-surface proteases (1994, 2001), and the block to hybridization and self-fertilization between two Ciona species (2000). He also studied sperm formation in the ratfish Hydrolagus colliei (1985, 1990), signaling pathways in oocyte maturation and the roles of follicle cells (2005-2011), and took part in rapid-assessment surveys of non-native species in harbors of California and southern England (2002-2006). His 2011 oocyte-maturation paper came from a symposium held at FHL in 2010.

name: Charles H. Greene
text:
Charles H. Greene is a biological oceanographer. He received a B.A. in biological oceanography from the University of Colorado in 1978 and a Ph.D. from the University of Washington in 1985, then spent a year as a postdoctoral fellow at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. He joined Cornell University in 1986 as a visiting assistant professor in the Division of Biological Sciences and became a professor in the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. He directed Cornell's Biological Resources Program and its Ocean Resources and Ecosystems Program, and his Cornell page now lists him as professor emeritus. His graduate-era papers on plankton predators (1985–1986) are in the FHL bibliography, and many later papers mention FHL or its Whiteley Center in their text. Since 2022 he has published with a Friday Harbor Laboratories affiliation, and the census counts three FHL-address papers (2022–2025).

Greene's early work asked how zooplankton predators choose prey. Papers of 1985 and 1986, two with Michael R. Landry, studied prey selection by the copepod Euchaeta elongata and the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei and grouped planktivores by how they encounter and capture prey. He then turned to bioacoustics, using high-frequency sound to measure zooplankton size distributions (1989) and studying sound scattering by gelatinous animals such as Aequorea victoria (1998). From 1993 he organized field courses in marine bioacoustics. In 2000 he organized the MERCINA working group on North Atlantic ecosystems and climate. Papers from 2003 to 2021 trace how climate shifts and Arctic change have affected Northwest Atlantic shelf ecosystems and the endangered North Atlantic right whale. Erin Meyer-Gutbrod, his student in the network, led a 2022 paper on shifting right whale habitat use. Since 2022 his papers have also proposed marine algae as a basis for sustainable aquaculture.

name: Charles J. O’Kelly
text:
Charles J. O'Kelly is a phycologist and protistologist who studies the diversity and evolution of algae and protists. His earliest papers, around 1980, came from the University of Washington's botany department and dealt with marine Chaetophoraceae, small green algae. From 1982 to 1985 his address was the botany department at Ohio State University, and his later papers list Massey University in New Zealand, the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences in Maine and the University of Hawaii. At Bigelow he and Robert Andersen led an NSF-funded project (2000–2004) toward a monograph of the Ulvellaceae, and he took part in 2003 NASA Astrobiology Institute projects on eukaryotic origins. His papers from 2011 to 2022 give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, and the census counts 11 of them; a 2022 review also lists him as Director of Applied Research at Cyanotech Corporation in Hawaii.

O'Kelly uses cultures, microscopy and gene sequences to define species and lineages of small algae and protists. In the 1980s he studied the flagellar apparatus of algal motile cells as evidence on green algal phylogeny. He co-described the flagellate Malawimonas jakobiformis (1999) and co-authored the 2011 description of Subulatomonas tetraspora, a member of a previously unrecognized major clade of eukaryotes, and a 2017 study of Paramoeba amoebae and their endosymbionts. His FHL-period papers treat algal systematics: red algal orders around the genus Rhodella (2011), a new family for the green alga Cloniophora (2011), the Aegagropila clade of Cladophorales (2012), Ulva of Narragansett Bay (2013), a revision of Ulvella from cultured strains and tufA gene sequences (2013), new Ulvaceae from mesophotic Hawaiian habitats (2015), the genus Wittrockiella (2017) and Ostreobium, a green alga that lives inside rock (2022). Two 2012 papers concern amoebae and other contaminants of microalgal production cultures.

name: Charles L. Asbury
text: Charles L. Asbury is a professor in the Department of Neurobiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington who chaired the PhD committees of Andrew D. Franck (2012), Kwaku Nyame Opoku (2016) and Bonnibelle Kroeker Leeds (2026). Their dissertations concerned kinetochores, the structures that attach chromosomes to spindle microtubules. Asbury received a Packard Fellowship in 2006 and was elected a fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology in 2018.

name: Charles Laird
text:
Charles D. Laird is a geneticist and professor emeritus of biology at the University of Washington as of 2026, who was also associate director for fragile X research in the university's Center on Human Development and Disability and a faculty member in Genome Sciences. He took a BS at the University of Oregon and a PhD at Stanford, and taught at the University of Texas at Austin before joining UW in 1971. His tie to FHL core scientists runs through Victoria E. Foe, who completed her PhD with Laird at UW, with a thesis dated 1975. Their 1976 papers analyzed active transcription units in the milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus and chromatin-associated fiber arrays. A 1971 paper with Charles C. Lambert on the molecular properties of tunicate DNA carries an FHL affiliation.

Laird's early papers treated Bacillus subtilis with W. F. Bodmer (1967, 1968) and the Drosophila genome with B. J. McCarthy (1968-1969), followed by work on the DNA and transcription of Drosophila chromosomes. From 1987 his work turned to human fragile X syndrome, beginning with a proposed mechanism of its inheritance and expression in Genetics; a 1993 paper in Cell associated the syndrome with delayed replication of the FMR1 gene. His group then developed hairpin-bisulfite PCR (2004), which reads methylation patterns on both strands of individual DNA molecules, and applied it to the fidelity of epigenetic inheritance. He also taught or did research at Cold Spring Harbor, Zurich, the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, Bergen and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center.

name: Charles Lang
text: Charles F. Lang was a graduate student in Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago, in the Committee on Genetics, Genomics, and Systems Biology, from 2014 to 2022. With Munro, Lang wrote a 2017 review of PAR proteins and cell polarity, then studied how oligomerization shapes polarization, in a 2022 Biophysical Journal paper and in work on PAR-3 asymmetries in the C. elegans zygote (2026). Lang moved in 2022 to a postdoctoral position in Lucy Erin O'Brien's lab at the Stanford University School of Medicine; a 2024 preprint from that lab, co-authored by Lang, examined how organ injury speeds stem cell differentiation in the adult Drosophila intestine.

name: Charles Stephen
text: Charles Stephen was a PhD student in biological sciences at Auburn University (2022), advised by Jonathan Armbruster, with Kenneth M. Halanych on the committee. The dissertation used RADseq data from more than 100 caves in ten states, with morphometrics, to revise cave-obligate Hesperochernes pseudoscorpions, retaining H. mirabilis as the valid name. Stephen was a visiting assistant professor at Missouri State University (2021-2023) and joined Georgia State University as an assistant professor in 2023.

name: Charlie Endris
text: Charlie Endris worked with H. Gary Greene as a geologist and GIS specialist at the Center for Habitat Studies, Moss Landing Marine Laboratories. A 1998 geology graduate of Hamilton College, Endris spent three years as a marine lab specialist with the Ocean Drilling Program aboard JOIDES Resolution, assisting in the paleomagnetism lab and curating deep-sea cores, and completed an MS in geological oceanography at Moss Landing in 2008. With Greene, Endris co-authored a 2013 review of subtidal benthic habitats of central San Francisco Bay and a 2023 paper mapping offshore infrastructure from Cannery Row in Monterey. Other work includes drone surveys for tidal marsh restoration in California (2021).

name: Charlotte Boyd
text: Charlotte Boyd was a PhD student at the University of Washington School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (2012), with Daniel Grünbaum as Graduate Student Representative and André E. Punt and Glenn R. VanBlaricom as co-chairs. The dissertation modeled how Peruvian Boobies and Guanay Cormorants forage on patchy anchoveta. Later papers estimated cetacean populations, including Cook Inlet belugas (2020), and applied the Key Biodiversity Area standard to sharks (2025).

name: Charlotte Clubley
text: Charlotte Clubley was a PhD student at the University of Plymouth, advised by Antony M. Knights, with James E. Byers as committee member or outside examiner (2024). The thesis examined community assembly in the Anthropocene through environmental filtering at multiple scales. Publications treated biodiversity on coastal structures and enemy shells as refuges from grazing. Clubley became a postdoctoral fellow at Aarhus University in 2024, with work on larval connectivity and dispersal corridors.

name: Charlotte Loring Dohrn
text: Charlotte Loring Dohrn was an MS student of Terrie Klinger in marine affairs at the University of Washington (2020). The thesis built a preliminary habitat suitability index for Olympia oyster (Ostrea lurida) restoration in the southern Salish Sea from six variables, including tidal elevation, salinity and temperature, checked it against oysters at restored sites, and showed how it could bring climate change into restoration planning.

name: Chelsea L. Wood
text: Chelsea L. Wood is on the faculty of the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences and advised Evan Fiorenza's 2019 master's thesis on tracking change in marine parasite abundance over time. The two published a 2020 paper showing that fluid preservation caused minimal reduction of parasite detectability in fish specimens. Wood earned a PhD at Stanford University.

name: Chessa Scullin
text: Chessa Scullin completed a PhD in biomedical sciences at the University of New Mexico in 2010 under Lloyd Donald (L. D.) Partridge Jr. The thesis examined how presynaptic calcium handling and short-term plasticity develop at Schaffer collateral synapses onto CA1 pyramidal neurons in mouse hippocampal slices. The slow component of residual calcium decay fell from over 80 percent in newborn mice to about 50 percent in animals older than postnatal day 24. With Partridge, Scullin published on developmental changes in presynaptic calcium clearance (2010), on SERCA pumps and ryanodine-sensitive stores (2010), and on pregnenolone sulfate in the hippocampal trisynaptic circuit (2012).

text: Ching-Hsin (Glory) Ho was a University of Washington biology student in the ZooBot Research Apprenticeship at FHL in spring 2011, with Megan Dethier and Adam Summers as professors and Michael Nishizaki as teaching assistant. The report tested how salinity changes contraction, expansion and locomotion in the sea anemone Anthopleura elegantissima: individuals closed faster in high salinity and opened more slowly in both low and high salinity.

name: Chinyere Mary-Cynthia Awaogu
text: Chinyere Mary-Cynthia Awaogu was a member of the lab of Charles Bradley Shuster at New Mexico State University (2026). Awaogu spent four weeks at FHL in summer 2026, studying genetic networks needed for muscle regulation in the sea star Pisaster ochraceus from its natural habitat, as part of research on sea stars and urchins. Awaogu also served on an early career subcommittee of the Genetics Society of America.

name: Chisato Kitazawa
text: Chisato Kitazawa was a member of Gregory A. Wray's lab at Duke University and coauthor with Wray of a 2004 methods chapter on culturing echinoderm larvae through metamorphosis. The lab lists Kitazawa as a research professor at Yamaguchi University, whose Faculty of Education is the address on papers about development in temnopleurid sea urchins, including blastula formation and gastrulation (2016) and larval axis specification (2017).

name: Chloe Beck
text: Chloe Beck's 2024 MS thesis in Environmental Sciences at Western Washington University lists Robin Kodner as a thesis advisor, with Andrew Godard Bunn and Rebecca Bunn. The thesis described snow algae biodiversity at Mount Watson in the North Cascades, comparing snow fields, glacial snow and melt ponds with amplicon sequencing over three years.

name: Chloe Schwab
text: Chloe J. Schwab worked as a research assistant in Jason Hodin's lab at Friday Harbor Laboratories, in the captive breeding program for the sunflower star, Pycnopodia helianthoides. The lab's June 2024 newsletter shows Schwab with Vannessa Valdez placing stars into a sea table. Schwab was an author, credited with data curation and methodology, on the lab's 2025 PLoS ONE paper, which studied embryos, larvae, settling stars and juveniles through eight months of growth at temperatures from about 10 to 20 degrees C. Embryos and larvae grew best at 16 to 18 degrees C, above the roughly 14 degrees C typical summer maximum in the region.

name: Chris Cameron
text: Christopher B. (Chris) Cameron visited Billie J. Swalla's lab at Vanderbilt University in 1997 as a PhD student from the University of Alberta, finishing the degree in 2000 with A. Richard Palmer. With Swalla, Cameron co-authored studies of deuterostome relationships: a 2000 PNAS phylogeny bearing on the chordate body plan, a 2000 Systematic Biology paper on urochordate monophyly, and a 2002 ribosomal DNA analysis. Two 2002 Biological Bulletin papers described the enteropneust Harrimania planktophilus and its filter-feeding pharynx. Cameron became a full professor at the Université de Montréal, working on invertebrate evolution, including living hemichordates and Cambrian tubicolous enteropneusts (Nature, 2013).

name: Chris Lowe
text: Christopher Lowe was a graduate student of Gregory A. Wray at SUNY Stony Brook, taking a PhD in ecology and evolution in 1998 with work on the evolution of body plans and the origin of echinoderms. Lowe and Wray's 1997 Nature paper examined changing roles of homeobox genes in echinoderm evolution. As a Miller Fellow at UC Berkeley (1998-2001) he studied chordate origins with Mike Levine, John Gerhart and Marc Kirschner. He joined the University of Chicago in 2005 and moved to Stanford in 2010. As of 2026 he was De Nault Professor of Marine Science at Hopkins Marine Station, with work on hemichordates such as Saccoglossus kowalevskii.

name: Chris Schoff
text: Chris Schoff was a University of Washington graduate student listed at the UW Center for Cell Dynamics, directed by Garrett M. Odell. In the center's 2003 course on gene network dynamics and cell behavior, Schoff joined Adriana Dawes, Alex Hart and Eliana Hechter on Team Worm. The team studied how the one-cell Caenorhabditis elegans embryo sets up its anterior-posterior axis before first cleavage, combining experiments and modeling of feedback loops between regulatory proteins and the cortical actomyosin mesh.

text: Christian Bojorquez was an MS student in ecology and evolution in Colette J. Feehan's lab at Montclair State University (2020). name: Christiane H. Biermann
text:
Christiane H. Biermann is an evolutionary biologist whose research concerns how marine invertebrates, especially sea urchins, become reproductively isolated. Bibliographic records link her papers from 1996 to 1999 to Stony Brook University. From about 1999 she was a postdoctoral researcher at FHL, studying the evolution of reproductive barriers and the population genetics of gamete-recognition proteins; FHL's 2002 program review lists 2001 funding to her and Jeb Byers through the UC Davis Marine Ecosystem Health Project. In 2004 UW described her as a research associate at FHL and adjunct biology faculty at Portland State University, and later FHL researcher listings give her affiliation as Portland State. Her FHL-connected papers date from 1999 to 2008. The census also holds a 1992 FHL paper by C. H. Biermann, with G. O. Schinner and Richard Strathmann, on how sunlight, algal fouling and currents affect egg-laying sites and embryo survival in a dorid nudibranch.

Most of her work concerns strongylocentrotid sea urchins and the molecules by which sperm and eggs recognize their own species. A 1998 single-author paper traced the molecular evolution of the sperm protein bindin in six species. Later papers described geographic divergence of gamete recognition in two Strongylocentrotus species (1999), showed with Paulo Mourão's group in Rio de Janeiro that sulfated fucans in the egg jelly of S. droebachiensis and S. pallidus ensure species-specific fertilization (2002), and, using green sea urchins from the San Juan Islands, proposed carbohydrate-based recognition as another route to speciation (2004). With Jessica Marks and colleagues she compared sperm polymorphism in Pacific and Atlantic populations of S. droebachiensis (2008). With Stephen Palumbi she studied the phylogeny of strongylocentrotid urchins as model species (2003), and with Erik Sotka and Jennifer Hempelmann she found genetic evidence of postglacial population expansion in the Puget Sound rockfish Sebastes emphaeus (2005).

name: Christina Geierman
text: Christina Geierman was an MS student of Richard B. Emlet at the University of Oregon (2007). The thesis compared feeding behavior, cirral anatomy, Reynolds numbers and cirral fan leakiness across size classes of the acorn barnacles Balanus glandula, Semibalanus cariosus and Balanus nubilus, finding that newly metamorphosed B. glandula fed at Reynolds numbers below one. A 2009 paper with Emlet reported the B. glandula results.

text: Christina I. Ellison was a PhD student of Svetlana Maslakova at the University of Oregon (2025), with Richard B. Emlet as a core committee member. Christina I. Ellison used COI sequences and the appearance of living worms to assess ribbon worm (Nemertea) diversity in Northern California and the Panama Bight, finding 124 benthic species, most of them undescribed, and describing 36 species from the Panama Bight.

name: Christina Linkem
text: Christina Linkem studied fish ecology as a summer REU student from the University of Hawaii at Manoa, working with Petra Ditsche in the Blinks-BEACON internship program at FHL. With Lisa Truong, Linkem documented the natural habitat of the northern clingfish, Gobiesox maeandricus, at a San Juan Island site, measuring rock roughness, fouling, rock size, substrate and flow. An FHL report dates from August 2014, and the results went to the 2015 SICB meeting. The 2017 paper with Ditsche, Madeline Hicks, Truong and Adam Summers found that some natural rocks were rougher than any surface the fish could attach to in the lab. Linkem later coauthored a 2018 Animal Behaviour paper on the color and size cues that trigger flight in perching damselflies.

name: Christopher Alexander Quintanilla
text: Christopher Alexander Quintanilla was a PhD student at the University of Chicago (2020), advised by Robert K. Ho and Sally Horne-Badovinac, with Edwin Munro on the committee. The dissertation studied what positions the pectoral fin field along the body axis in early zebrafish embryos, finding that retinoic acid and the Cdx factors Cdx4 and Cdx1a act in parallel during gastrulation to restrict where the field forms.

name: Christopher David Wells
text: Christopher David Wells, who published as Christopher D. Wells and was also listed as Chris Wells, took a University of Washington PhD in biology in 2019, with Kenneth P. Sebens as major advisor and chair, and Megan N. Dethier, Jennifer L. Ruesink and Daniel Grünbaum on the committee. The dissertation, on hexacorallians of the San Juan Archipelago, described dye marking of the anemone Metridium farcimen (PLoS ONE, 2017), used DNA metabarcoding on its diet (Environmental DNA, 2022) and examined the distribution of common hard-bottom species. Wells spent time at FHL during the degree. After an MSc at the University of New Hampshire (2013), Wells was a postdoctoral associate at the University at Buffalo (2019-2023), publishing on Caribbean octocorals, and became a Doherty Marine Biology Postdoctoral Scholar at Bowdoin College in 2024.

name: Christopher Goatley
text: Christopher Goatley was a Fulbright Fellow visiting Adam P. Summers's lab in 2021, while a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of New England, Australia (2017-2022). Goatley holds a BSc from Newcastle University and a PhD in marine biology from James Cook University (2015). The work concerns reef fish ecology and anatomy, including cryptobenthic reef fishes (Current Biology, 2017; Science, 2019) and a CT-based study of a double-tailed surgeonfish (2018), with later contributions on anglerfish feeding morphology (2023) and pufferfish diversification (2024). Goatley became Lecturer in Marine Biology at the University of Southampton in 2022 and co-chair of the IUCN Gobies and Blennies Specialist Group in 2025.

name: Christopher Harley
text: A 2021 tribute to Susan Lynn Williams names Christopher D. G. Harley among people at the University of California, Davis, to whom Williams provided important input. With Williams, Harley wrote a 2006 coastal climate change review from Bodega Marine Laboratory. Harley earned a University of Washington zoology PhD (2001) and joined the University of British Columbia faculty in 2005. A 2011 Science paper linked warming to lost predator-free space on rocky shores. Harley's kelp biomechanics work with Emily Carrington included a 2013 Functional Ecology paper on frond strength and self-pruning.

name: Christopher W. Petersen
text:
Christopher W. Petersen is a biologist who studies the reproductive behavior and ecology of marine fishes. He completed a doctoral dissertation at the University of Arizona in 1985 on the mating systems of tropical reef fishes in the Gulf of California, with case studies of simultaneous hermaphroditism and paternal care. His papers of 1986 to 1989 list the University of Arizona or the Department of Psychology at the University of Washington, and those of 1989 to 1991 list the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama and Friday Harbor Laboratories. Since 1992 his papers have come from the College of the Atlantic in Bar Harbor, Maine, most recently in 2025 and 2026. The census counts three FHL-address papers, from 1989 to 1991. A 2013 paper on plainfin midshipman fish in his census list is by a namesake, Christopher L. Petersen of Brooklyn College.

Petersen's research asks how mating systems, sex allocation and parental care evolve in reef fishes. His FHL-era papers include a 1989 study, with Karen Marchetti, of filial cannibalism (parents eating their own eggs) in the Cortez damselfish Stegastes rectifraenum and a 1989 paper showing that female carmine triplefins prefer males that are already mating. Two 1990 papers related population density, body size and mating tactics to reproductive success and gonad allocation in the hermaphroditic sea bass Serranus fasciatus. A 1990 paper with D. Ross Robertson and Jeffrey Brawn examined lunar spawning cycles in bottom-brooding reef fishes, and a 1991 study with Helen Hess examined spawning synchrony in a Caribbean damselfish. Later papers concern fertilization in the bluehead wrasse (1992), sex allocation in the chalk bass (1996), osmoregulation (2006) and spawning (2010) in the mummichog, shellfish and river herring co-management in Maine (2025) and intertidal hydroids of Mount Desert Rock (2026).

name: Clara F. Asnes
text:
Clara F. Asnes is a cell biologist who worked on microtubules and their protein, tubulin. Her earliest papers, from 1976 to 1981, were written with Leslie Wilson, and a 1979 paper gives her address as the Department of Biological Sciences at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Her papers from 1979 to 1983 carry a Friday Harbor Laboratories address, and the five FHL-connected papers in the census fall in those years. From 1984 to 1986 she published from the Department of Biology at the University of Rochester, including work with Joanna Olmsted on the microtubule-associated protein MAP 4. From 1999 to 2015 her name appears on papers from the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, with Elliot Elson and others, on cell contractility, growth cone motility and engineered heart tissue.

At Friday Harbor she worked with sea urchin eggs and sperm flagella. With Thomas E. Schroeder she examined the fine structure of cleaving eggs and reported evidence against the idea that aster microtubules stimulate the cleavage furrow at the cell's equator (1979). With Wilson she analyzed inhibitors of microtubule assembly in sea urchin egg extracts and found evidence that a protease was responsible (1981). This followed a 1976 study that measured the tubulin content of unfertilized eggs of the sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus by colchicine binding. With Melvyn Little, Richard Ludueña and colleagues she compared how alpha- and beta-tubulins from distantly related species are cut by proteases (1981), and they proposed two major types of alpha-tubulin (1982). A 1983 paper with Jerome Parness and Susan Band Horwitz reported that the drug taxol binds differently to sperm-tail outer-doublet microtubules than to microtubules reassembled from their tubulin.

name: Claudia E. Mills
text:
Claudia E. Mills is a marine biologist who studies gelatinous zooplankton, especially medusae and ctenophores. She earned a B.A. in biology at Colorado College (1972), an M.S. in zoology at Florida State University (1976) with Richard N. Mariscal, and a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Victoria in Canada (1982) with George O. Mackie. She took summer courses at Friday Harbor Laboratories in 1974 and 1976, has been based at FHL since 1978 and works there year-round. She is an affiliate professor in the University of Washington Department of Biology and describes herself as an independent research scientist. She has held visiting postdoctoral or research posts of several months in New Zealand, at the marine stations of Villefranche-sur-Mer and Roscoff in France, and at Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution in Florida. The census counts 31 FHL-address papers by her from 1981 to 2023.

Mills's work ranges from individual behavior to the structure of midwater communities. Early FHL papers dealt with swimming behavior and feeding in hydromedusae (1981) and with how medusae and ctenophores change density and ion balance with salinity (1984). Dives in manned submersibles in the Ligurian Sea and the western Atlantic (1989, 1991) gave in situ observations of foraging and of the small-scale distribution of macroplankton, and papers on nematocysts and kleptocnidism related stinging-cell types to diet. She described a new medusa (1985) and a new colonial hydroid (1993) from the waters of British Columbia and Washington, documented two Black Sea hydromedusae introduced to San Francisco Bay (1995), and asked whether jellyfish blooms are increasing worldwide (2001, 2012). Recent work covers the anatomy and systematics of stalked jellyfishes (Staurozoa), including Haliclystus sanjuanensis (2023), and contributions to the 2014 ctenophore genome paper and to studies of trachymedusan swimming and ctenophore speciation.

name: Clyde Manwell
text:
Clyde Manwell was a zoologist and comparative biochemist who studied respiratory pigments and, later, protein variation in animals. His FHL-connected papers, from 1957 to 1960, give his address as the Department of Biological Sciences at Stanford University together with the University of Washington's marine laboratories at Friday Harbor. A 1963 paper lists the University of Illinois at Urbana, a 1969 paper the Marine Biological Association laboratory at Plymouth, England, and by the early 1970s he was a professor in the Department of Zoology at the University of Adelaide. With C. M. Ann Baker he wrote Molecular Biology and the Origin of Species: Heterosis, Protein Polymorphism and Animal Breeding (1970). In the early 1970s he publicly criticized aspects of the South Australian government's fruit-fly spraying; a complaint by his head of department led to an attempt to dismiss him, which failed after about four years. He retired in 1986.

Manwell's FHL-period papers used oxygen-equilibrium and alkaline-denaturation measurements to compare hemoglobins and related pigments across animal groups. He described changes in hemoglobin during development in the cabezon, Scorpaenichthys marmoratus (1957), and the skate Raja binoculata (1958), and compared the hemoglobins of two diving birds (1958). He measured the hemocyanin and myoglobin of the gumboot chiton Cryptochiton stelleri (1958), annelid hemoglobins (1959), the hemoglobin of the sea cucumber Cucumaria miniata, which lacks a Bohr effect (1959), and heme–heme interactions in invertebrate myoglobins (1960). A 1960 paper compared body-cavity and muscle hemoglobins in the polychaete Travisia pupa and the echiuran Arhynchite pugettensis. From the 1960s, often with Baker, he used starch-gel electrophoresis to study protein polymorphism, hybrid vigor and species differences in animals from sea cucumbers to birds, sheep and cattle.

name: Colette J. Feehan
text:
Colette J. Feehan is a marine ecologist and Associate Professor of Biology at Montclair State University in New Jersey. She completed a doctoral thesis at Dalhousie University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 2015 on the regulation of sea urchin populations in Nova Scotian kelp beds. Her papers of 2010 to 2015 come from Dalhousie's Department of Biology, many written with Robert E. Scheibling. She then published from the Department of Marine and Coastal Sciences at Rutgers University and, from 2017, from Montclair State. Her papers of 2017 and 2018 also list Friday Harbor Laboratories and report sea urchin studies with FHL-based co-authors, among them Richard R. Strathmann, Megan N. Dethier and David O. Duggins. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 2017 to 2018.

Montclair State lists her research interests as marine ecosystems, host–pathogen and predator–prey interactions, disease ecology and climate-change ecology. In Nova Scotia she studied outbreaks of an amoebic disease that kill sea urchins and help kelp beds persist; a 2016 paper linked these outbreaks to storms, and a 2015 paper with Karen Filbee-Dexter and Scheibling documented large-scale degradation of kelp beds in an ocean-warming hotspot. Her FHL papers concern Northeast Pacific sea urchins. With Dara Yiu she showed in 2017 that articulated coralline algae shelter juvenile urchins from predatory crabs. Another 2017 paper found that detritus from the kelp Nereocystis luetkeana is high-quality food for urchin larvae. A 2018 study, prompted by the 2013–2016 warm 'Blob', found that warm water combined with scarce phytoplankton or a kelp-detritus diet slowed development and raised mortality in larvae of Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis. Later papers address kelp forests, Caribbean Diadema urchins and tropical cyclones.

St. Mary's research covers behavioral and evolutionary ecology, including sexual selection and the evolution of parental care, mainly in fish.

name: Colin Beal
text: Colin M. Beal was a postdoctoral researcher with Charles H. Greene at Cornell University from 2011 to 2013. The work concerned the sustainability of algal production. With Greene, Beal published a techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment of a 100-hectare algal facility (Algal Research, 2015), a study integrating algae with bioenergy carbon capture and storage (Earth's Future, 2018), and an assessment of marine microalgae for fisheries and aquaculture (Scientific Reports, 2018). Earlier papers from the University of Texas at Austin covered lipid analysis of Neochloris oleoabundans by NMR (2010) and energy return on algal biofuel coupled with wastewater treatment (2012).

name: Colin Lee
text:
Colin A. Lee trained as a neuroscientist working on feeding and behavioral state in sea slugs, with an MS in zoology from the University of New Hampshire (2012-2015) and a doctorate from the Neuroscience Program at the University of Illinois (2015-2021). Lee's tie to FHL runs through the nudibranch Melibe leonina. Animals for the New Hampshire work came from eelgrass beds near FHL and from Monterey Bay, and were kept at FHL or shipped to Durham. The Friday Harbor Labs Summer Graduate Fellowship Program helped support Lee. The 2015 thesis, "Mechanisms of satiation in the nudibranch Melibe leonina," had Winsor H. Watson as first advisor, with Leslie J. Curren and James M. Newcomb as second and third advisors.

The thesis found that stomach distention lowered the drive to feed. A 2022 Frontiers in Physiology paper with Watson found that the posterior nerves communicate that distention. Earlier work included a 2014 Biological Bulletin study of circadian crawling and swimming and a 2020 paper on small cardioactive peptide, both with Newcomb and Watson. Lee is listed among alumni of Rhanor Gillette's lab at Illinois. A 2021 Frontiers in Physiology paper with Gillette and Jonathan Sweedler compared neuropeptides in homologous interneurons of Hermissenda, Melibe and Pleurobranchaea, using Melibe collected in the San Juan Islands and kept at FHL, with support from an FHL fellowship endowment. A 2023 Journal of Neuroscience paper with Gillette examined serotonergic neurons and locomotion in Pleurobranchaea.

name: Colleen Burge
text:
Colleen A. Burge is a marine disease ecologist who works on host, pathogen and environment interactions in shellfish and seagrass. She took a BS (2002) and PhD (2010) in Aquatic and Fishery Sciences at the University of Washington; a 2006 paper with Carolyn Friedman addressed oyster mortality and herpesvirus infection in Tomales Bay. Postdoctoral positions followed at Cornell, in C. Drew Harvell's lab, and at UW. From December 2014 to June 2021 she was on the faculty of the Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology, with appointments at UMBC and the University of Maryland Baltimore. Papers from 2024 to 2026 place her at the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, at UC Davis's Bodega Marine Laboratory, where a seminar biography says she runs the Shellfish Health Laboratory.

Sea star wasting was one subject of Burge's research: a 2015 PLoS ONE study of immune and nervous system responses used animals from sites including FHL. Eelgrass wasting disease, caused by Labyrinthula zosterae, was another. A 2024 Royal Society Open Science paper with Morgan Eisenlord tested waterborne transmission at field sites in the San Juan Islands, with shoots brought to FHL, and a 2025 Ecology paper examined invertebrate herbivores and the disease. A 2022 FHL student report with Maya Groner and Harvell found that oysters moved from infected water could pass the disease to eelgrass. The oyster herpesvirus OsHV-1 has been her other main subject, including a search for resistance genes (2017) and a 2026 paper on viral shedding.

name: Colleen Cavanaugh
text: Colleen M. Cavanaugh was a Harvard PhD student of Kenneth P. Sebens from 1979 to 1985, with J. McCarthy as co-advisor, working on bacteria-invertebrate associations. Her 1981 Science paper identified prokaryotic cells in the vent tube worm Riftia pachyptila as possible chemoautotrophic symbionts, and her 1985 dissertation addressed such symbioses in marine invertebrates. After a Harvard Junior Fellowship (1986-1989) she joined the faculty in Organismic and Evolutionary Biology in 1989, becoming a full professor in 1995 and holding the Edward C. Jeffrey Professorship by 2002. Later work covered symbionts of the clam Solemya velum and microbiomes of the human mouth and Darwin's finches. She became an AAAS Fellow in 1996.

name: Colton Miller
text: Colton Miller was a PhD student in UW's School of Environmental and Forest Sciences with Megan N. Dethier on the committee. Miller's 2022 dissertation, advised by Ernesto Alvarado and Monika Moskal, modeled uncertainty in burn severity from the Composite Burn Index and remote sensing, using the King Fire. An MS (2013, with Darlene Zabowski) tested Douglas-fir reforestation of surface-mined land. Miller was a forest health scientist at the Washington State Department of Natural Resources as of 2025.

name: Colton Skavicus
text: Colton Skavicus was a University of Washington undergraduate who co-authored a 2014 Friday Harbor Laboratories student paper with Petra Ditsche in the spring Aquatic Animals Research Experience. The project ran flume tests on 3D-printed models of a snail (Calliostoma ligatum), a chiton (Tonicella lineata) and a limpet (Lottia pelta) at Reynolds numbers simulating currents up to 6 m/s; at high flow the snail shape took much greater drag. Skavicus thanked Hilary Hayford for guidance. A 2015 senior thesis for Oceanography 445, naming and thanking Julian Sachs, tested Nootka Sound sediments for dioxins from a former pulp mill.

name: Constance Amanda Sullivan
text: Constance Amanda Sullivan was a Master of Marine Affairs student at the University of Washington (2012), advised by Terrie Klinger, with Jan Newton and Thomas Leschine on the committee. name: Corrine Avidan
text: Corrine Avidan is listed as a postdoctoral fellow among recent alumni of Elizabeth Brainerd's lab at Brown University. Avidan's ORCID record gives a BS in marine science from Coastal Carolina University (2011), a PhD in zoology from Tel Aviv University (2015-2020) and a Brown postdoc from 2020. Publishing first as Corrine Jacobs, Avidan worked with Roi Holzman at Tel Aviv and the Inter-University Institute for Marine Sciences in Eilat, comparing suction-feeding flows across aquatic vertebrates (2018). Later papers measured suction flows in seahorses, which store elastic energy for feeding (2021), and traced the power for head swing and suction to two elastic tendons (2023).

name: Courtney Babbitt
text: Courtney Babbitt was a postdoctoral researcher in Gregory Wray's lab at Duke University, studying how gene regulation evolved in primates. The work included adaptive noncoding change in human evolution (2010), diet-related genomic signatures in human origins (2011) and gene expression during reproductive maturation in wild baboons (2012). Babbitt also co-authored a 2012 study of temperature stress in a sea urchin gene network with Dan Runcie. Babbitt then moved to the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where the Babbitt Lab for Evolutionary Genomics has compared metabolic gene expression in human and chimpanzee astrocytes (2024).

name: Courtney Couch
text: Courtney Couch completed a Cornell University PhD in ecology in 2014, with C. Drew Harvell as committee chair. The dissertation examined coral health and disease along the west coast of Hawai'i Island and the timing of the cellular immune response in a Caribbean sea fan. Papers with Harvell covered immune defenses in Montastraea faveolata (2009), eelgrass wasting disease in the San Juan Archipelago, Washington (2014), and plastic waste and coral disease (Science, 2018). Couch led a study of the 2014 mass bleaching in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (2017). As of 2025 Couch's address was the Cooperative Institute for Marine and Atmospheric Research and NOAA's Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center.

name: Courtney Greiner
text: Courtney Greiner was a Master of Marine Affairs student of Terrie Klinger at the University of Washington (2017), with Jennifer Ruesink on the committee. Greiner tested shell hash and macrophytes as ocean acidification adaptation strategies for juvenile clams (Venerupis philippinarum) at Fidalgo Bay and Skokomish Delta, finding no support for either (published 2018). A 2019 clam synchrony paper gives the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community Fisheries Department as affiliation.

name: Craig Mandato
text: Craig Mandato was a postdoctoral fellow in William Bement's lab in the Department of Zoology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, and holds a PhD from the University of Waterloo. The work used Xenopus oocytes to study how microtubules and actin interact, including how actomyosin rings assemble and close around membrane wounds (Journal of Cell Biology, 2001; Current Biology, 2003). Mandato moved to the Department of Anatomy and Cell Biology at McGill University, later serving as department chair, with research on the cytoskeleton in cell division, motility and wound healing, including mitochondria at the cleavage furrow (2013).

text: Craig Osenberg is a population and community ecologist and professor in the University of Georgia's Odum School of Ecology. name: Cristina Quesada Candela
text: Cristina Quesada Candela completed a doctoral thesis at Miguel Hernández University in Elche, Spain, on the pancreatic alpha cell in late pregnancy in the mouse, with Iván Quesada and Ángel Nadal as advisors. As first author in Metabolism (2020), with Quesada and Nadal, Quesada Candela compared pregnant and non-pregnant C57BL/6 mice and their isolated pancreatic islets, and tested pregnancy hormones on glucagon-secreting cells. In late pregnancy alpha cells grew in size and mass, mainly through proliferation, while glucagon secretion from islets at low glucose fell.

name: Cydney Wolff
text: Cydney Wolff was an MS student of Colette J. Feehan in marine biology and coastal sciences at Montclair State University (2024). Wolff counted macrofauna on settlement plates deployed for a month in June 2023 at two coral reef sites in the Florida Keys, Delta Shoal and Pelican Shoal. Plates held about 6,000 organisms from seven animal phyla, with no clear pattern between sites or plate heights.

name: D. A. Dorsett
text:
D. A. Dorsett is a neurobiologist who studied the nervous systems and behavior of marine invertebrates, especially opisthobranch mollusks. His publications, from 1961 to 1991, give the Department of Zoology at Queen Mary College, London (1961), University College Ibadan in Nigeria (1962) and, from 1962, the Marine Science Laboratories at Menai Bridge, Anglesey, of the University College of North Wales; papers of 1989 to 1991 give its biology schools at Bangor. A 1980 paper describes him as Reader in Marine Biology at the University College of North Wales. His work on Tritonia with A. O. D. Willows and Graham Hoyle began with a 1969 paper whose addresses include the University of Oregon. Three 1973 papers with Willows and Hoyle give Dorsett's address as Friday Harbor Laboratories, and a 1975 paper with Willows gives both FHL and Menai Bridge.

Dorsett's early papers concerned tube-building and reproduction in the polychaete Polydora ciliata, flight preparation in hawk-moths, and the innervation, sense organs and glands of the ragworm Nereis. From 1967 he worked on giant neurons in the brain of the nudibranch Tritonia. The FHL-connected series with Willows and Hoyle mapped the functional organization of the central nervous system of Tritonia diomedea, proposed a standard system of abbreviations and cell numbers for its ganglia, nerve trunks and giant cells, and showed that the motor pattern of escape swimming, a fixed action pattern, originates centrally and can be produced by the isolated brain. Papers in 1974 and 1975 compared the neurons controlling branchial tuft withdrawal in T. hombergi and T. diomedea and related the evolution of swimming to its neural correlates. His later work examined feeding circuits of T. hombergi, barnacle proprioceptors, and the buccal neurons and muscles of Philine aperta.

name: Damien S. Waits
text: Damien S. Waits completed an MS in biological sciences at Auburn University in 2015 under Kenneth Halanych, after a computer science bachelor's there. At Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2014, in the course Deep Sea Biodiversity, Connectivity and Ecosystem Function, Waits sequenced COI from Osedax bone-eating worms found on whalebones off Oregon and Antarctica. The thesis and a 2016 Journal of Molecular Evolution paper examined sulfur-binding hemoglobins in Siboglinidae, with attention to Osedax. Waits also co-authored phylogenomic studies of hemichordates and echinoderms (2014) and Lophotrochozoa (2016), and later led a study from Auburn on reptile blood transcriptomes (2020).

name: Dan Nicolau
text: Dan Nicolau Jr was a Miller Postdoctoral Fellow in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley, on biocomputation and stochasticity in biological systems. He took a DPhil in mathematics at Oxford under Philip Maini and a medical degree there. Papers with a Berkeley Integrative Biology address mapped hydrophobicity on protein surfaces (2014) and used molecular-motor-propelled agents in nanofabricated networks for parallel computation (PNAS, 2016). King's College London lists him as a Reader in the Peter Gorer Department of Immunobiology, where he applies mathematics and computer science to immune networks, disease, inflammation and aging, including epithelial cells in COVID-19 (2021).

text: Dan R. Matthews was an MS student at the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (1983), whose thesis was approved by Robert C. Terwilliger. Matthews studied the feeding ecology of the common murre (Uria aalge), with strip transects off Coos Bay (1979 to 1982), Newport and the Columbia River (1982) and analysis of stomach contents, which held 37 species of fish, crustaceans and cephalopods and suggested opportunistic feeding.

name: Dan Runcie
text: Dan Runcie was a graduate student in Gregory Wray's lab at Duke University, finishing a PhD in 2012. The work asked how environment shapes development in sea urchin larvae, using gene expression under variation in food, temperature and pH. A 2012 paper asked how warmer water alters genetic variation in gene expression within a Strongylocentrotus purpuratus gene network, and a 2016 paper with Wray studied genetic variability and tolerance to lower pH in larvae of S. droebachiensis. At the University of California, Davis, Department of Plant Sciences, Runcie has worked on statistical methods for genomic prediction in plants, including MegaLMM, linear mixed models for thousands of traits (2021).

name: Dan Shapiro
text: Dan Shapiro is listed with a PhD among graduate student alumni of C. Drew Harvell's lab at Cornell University. Working at Friday Harbor Laboratories on the encrusting bryozoan Membranipora membranacea, taken from kelp near Turn Island, Shapiro reported in 1996 that genetically different colonies share a partial, temporary neural link that ends as they grow, with support from Harvell's NSF grants. A 1992 paper described coordinated zooid behavior and a new class of pore plates between colonies. The Harvell page lists Shapiro as a professor at California State University, Monterey Bay, where ORCID gives a faculty post in Applied Environmental Science from 1997.

name: Daniel A. Janies
text: Daniel A. Janies earned a PhD in zoology at the University of Florida in 1995 under Larry McEdward. The dissertation reconstructed morphogenesis and dispersal in velatid asteroids; a 1993 paper with McEdward described coelomic development in Pteraster tesselatus, and a 1997 paper treated echinoderm larvae and life cycles. The dissertation names Friday Harbor Laboratories in its text. Papers from 1999 to 2002 list Janies at the American Museum of Natural History. Janies then worked at Ohio State's College of Medicine (2003-2012), before UNC Charlotte's bioinformatics department. Later work covered echinoderm phylogeny including Xyloplax (2011), EchinoDB (2016), and pathogen spread, including Zika (2017).

name: Daniel G. Burton
text: Daniel G. Burton held a Blinks Research Fellowship at Friday Harbor Laboratories in 2012, working with Charles J. O’Kelly while affiliated with the Department of Biology at Gallaudet University. Their report asked how marine amoebae that contaminate commercial algal cultures grown for biodiesel differ in what they eat. Neoparamoeba, Paramoeba and Thecamoeba isolates from two field sites in Kailua-Kona, Hawai’i, were given five marine algae, with algal density tracked by spectrophotometer absorbance, and bacterial prey, with migration rate measured along agar raceways. Feeding ability varied widely across algal and bacterial prey.

text: Daniel Geldof was an undergraduate researcher advised by Nicholas J. Gidmark at Friday Harbor Laboratories in 2014, with funding from the University of Washington’s Mary Gates Endowment. Geldof cleared and stained 36 specimens of the soft sculpin Psychrolutes sigalutes, collected from the FHL docks, to link skeletal development to known behavioral shifts during growth. A 2016 Copeia paper with Gidmark compared P. sigalutes with the tadpole sculpin P. paradoxus and reported heterochrony: P. sigalutes transforms over three to four months and exceeds 40 mm before settling.

name: Daniel Grünbaum
text:
Daniel Grünbaum is an oceanographer who applies mathematical models and fluid mechanics to biological questions. He received his PhD from Cornell University in 1992 under Simon A. Levin, with a dissertation modeling bryozoan feeding currents and density-dependent aggregation in Antarctic krill. His papers of the late 1990s give Cornell, the mathematics departments of the University of Utah and the University of British Columbia, and the UW Department of Zoology; from 2008 they give the UW School of Oceanography, where a 2014 BioScience paper lists him as an associate professor. His bryozoan papers of 1995 to 1998 mention FHL or appear in its bibliographies, and the census counts FHL-connected papers from 2010 to 2020. Kit Yu Karen Chan, listed in Wikidata as his doctoral student, and Sasha K. Seroy were his co-authors on this larval and ocean-acidification work. He is also an author of 2018–2020 datasets from the sensor array of the Friday Harbor Laboratories Ocean Observatory.

His work asks how small organisms feed, swim and aggregate. Papers of 1995 to 1998 modeled feeding currents in encrusting bryozoans, showing interference between zooids within a colony, analyzed the hydromechanics of colony organization and the cost of defense in Membranipora membranacea, and examined the geometry of ciliated tentacle arrays in suspension feeders. A 2008 paper tested whether advection–diffusion equations describe swarming and schooling groups. From 2010 his FHL-connected work centered on ciliated larvae: with Tansy W. Clay he examined how swimming performance constrains the form of echinoid plutei and how morphology and flow lead to stage-selective vertical transport of sand dollar larvae in shear, and with Chan he studied how temperature, diet and acidification-induced changes in shape alter larval swimming and feeding. Later papers addressed ocean acidification and the interaction between Membranipora and the nudibranch Corambe steinbergae near FHL (2018, with Seroy) and the vertical distribution of echinoid larvae in pH-stratified water (2020).

name: Daniel Harris
text: R. Daniel Harris, listed as Daniel Harris on James E. Byers’s lab page, completed a PhD with Byers at the University of Georgia in 2025 on ecosystem engineers in coastal systems, especially oysters. With Byers and labmate Julie A. Blaze, Harris published a 2023 paper in the Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology on facilitation between two dominant ecosystem engineers. name: Dara S. Yiu
text:
Dara S. Yiu is a marine ecologist whose published work deals with nearshore communities in Washington State and, more recently, kelp forests and turf reefs in the Gulf of Maine. All three census papers, from 2017, 2019 and 2024, give Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address, and the 2019 paper also lists the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences. A 2022 paper lists Montclair State University in New Jersey together with that UW school, and papers from 2025 and 2026 list the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences in East Boothbay and the University of Maine. Co-authors on the FHL papers are Colette Feehan, Megan Dethier, Julia Kobelt, Lindsay Wentzel and Jennifer Ruesink.

Yiu's research concerns how habitat structure, predators and physical conditions shape the survival of young invertebrates, and how kelp loss changes reef ecosystems. The FHL-connected papers show that articulated coralline algae give juvenile sea urchins a refuge from predatory crabs (2017, with Colette Feehan), examine how the influence of abiotic and biotic factors on the performance of juvenile clams depends on context (2019), and describe how clam recruitment varies among beaches and years in Washington State (2024). A 2022 multi-author study found that warming speeds kelp decomposition and lowers the carbon sink potential of kelp forests. Papers from 2025 and 2026 examine how the replacement of kelp forests by turf algae changes reef chemistry, the reef microbiome, energy flow to predators and functional diversity, and a 2025 University of Maine thesis listed under Yiu's name compares reef fish communities on kelp- and turf-dominated reefs in the Gulf of Maine.

name: David H. Gire
text:
David H. Gire is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Washington, in its Neural Systems and Behavior area, and was promoted with tenure in 2022; a 2022 paper also lists him in the UW Astrobiology Program. He trained at the University of Colorado at Denver School of Medicine (2009). His FHL-connected papers date from 2021 to 2025 and come from octopus research done at the laboratories. A 2021 paper notes that Gire and Dominic Sivitilli, whose UW PhD (2023) Gire advised, received funding and research support from FHL. Gire was also the UW faculty mentor and a close collaborator for Willem Weertman's master's research at Alaska Pacific University, whose experiments took place at FHL.

Gire's laboratory studies how neural circuits process sensory signals during active sensing to guide behaviors such as finding food, with a focus on mammalian olfaction and comparisons across species; its methods include electrophysiology, calcium imaging, optogenetics and automated analysis of behavior. At FHL the group has turned these questions to octopuses. Papers with Sivitilli argue that the octopus's distributed nervous system offers lessons for soft robotics (2022, with Joshua Smith) and show that arm search without visual feedback relies on contact and local coordination among suckers (2023); Sivitilli's dissertation identified sucker recruitment as a key search mechanism. Gire was also a coauthor of a 2021 paper presenting the lesser Pacific striped octopus, Octopus chierchiae, as a laboratory model. Work with Weertman, David Scheel and Venkatesh Gopal, reported from 2021 and published in PLOS ONE in 2025, showed in a flume at FHL that Octopus rubescens tracks odor plumes to find food.

name: David Julian
text:
David Julian is a comparative physiologist who studies how animals and their cells respond to environmental stressors such as hydrogen sulfide, oxygen, salinity and temperature. Julian joined the University of Florida's Department of Biology as an assistant professor in 2000, became an associate professor with tenure in 2006, and as of 2024 also held a position in the Department of Physiology & Aging. The tie to FHL is through Andreas Heyland, whose Zoology PhD (2000-2004) Julian chaired, co-advised with Larry McEdward; Heyland then held a postdoctoral appointment at FHL. Julian also chaired the MS committee of Adam Reitzel (2000-2002), again co-advising with McEdward.

Julian took a BS (1988) and MA (1991) at San Francisco State University, a PhD in physiology at UC San Francisco (1997), and postdoctoral positions at San Francisco State (1999) and the University of Dusseldorf (2000). With Alissa Arp, Julian published on sulfide physiology in the echiuran worm Urechis caupo, including sulfide permeability (1992) and neuromuscular sensitivity (1998), and on sulfide uptake through the roots of the seep tubeworm Lamellibrachia (1999). At Florida the work moved to the bloodworm Glycera dibranchiata, with papers on mitochondrial depolarization (2005) and oxidative damage to RNA and DNA (2010), then to multi-stressor tolerance in horseshoe crab embryos (2015, 2017). Julian was a Visiting Science Education Fellow at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in 2018-2019.

name: David O. Duggins
text:
David O. Duggins is a marine ecologist who worked as a research scientist at Friday Harbor Laboratories for 40 years before retiring in 2016. He earned a bachelor's degree in zoology and a Ph.D. in wildlife biology at the University of Washington. His academic expertise is the effect of disturbance on ecological communities, studied mainly in marine systems. At FHL he founded and directed the Marine Science Outreach Program, a partnership among the university, public and private schools and government agencies for K-12 science education and stewardship. He was also among the FHL supervisors of graduate student Aaron Galloway (2007-2013), with whom he published fatty acid studies of nearshore food webs. The census counts 32 FHL-address papers from 1981 to 2026; his co-authored papers continue after his retirement.

Duggins's research concerns kelp forests and the food webs they support. Early papers examined growth and longevity in a crustose red alga (1979), facilitation among benthic grazers and sea urchin responses to short-term diet changes (1981), and herbivory and algal competition in a low intertidal habitat (1985). A 1989 Science paper with Charles Simenstad and James Estes used a natural experiment to show that benthic suspension feeders grew much faster where kelp detritus was present and that kelp-derived carbon is found throughout the nearshore food web. Related studies covered how understory kelps affect water flow, invertebrate recruitment and suspension-feeder growth (1989-1994), chemical defenses in kelps and rockweeds, and kelp gametophytes living inside red algae (1999). Later FHL work used fatty acid and stable isotope biomarkers to trace kelp detritus through benthic food webs, and examined drift kelp as habitat for invertebrates and as food for sea urchins and their larvae (2011-2019).

name: Dawn Vaughn
text:
Dawn Vaughn is a marine biologist who has studied the defenses of planktonic invertebrate larvae and the effects of warming on intertidal snails. Her FHL-connected papers, from 2007 to 2011, give her address as the University of Washington Department of Biology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and in 2008 news coverage described her as a biology doctoral student at FHL. She then worked at FHL as a postdoctoral researcher in Emily Carrington's laboratory. FHL's autumn 2012 newsletter reported that she had left for a faculty position at California State University, Northridge, and FHL's December 2013 Tide Bites newsletter described her postdoctoral research on snails.

Most of her FHL work asks how planktonic larvae respond to predators. In a 2007 paper, larvae of the snail Littorina scutulata reared with crab larvae developed rounder shells with smaller openings and survived predation better. In 2008 Vaughn and Richard Strathmann reported in Science that larvae of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus clone in response to predator cues: exposed to fish mucus, they produced clones within a day, and the clones were smaller, which may help against fish that hunt by sight. Later papers asked whether mothers influence this response (2009), showed with Kathryn McDonald that an abrupt increase in food can also trigger cloning (2010), and presented cloning and smaller size as an inducible defense (2010). As a postdoctoral researcher she used heat lamps over outdoor tanks at FHL to test how warmer low-tide air affects foraging and growth of male and female snails, including Nucella ostrina in a 2011 student project.
