name: Dean Grubbs
text:
R. Dean Grubbs is a fish ecologist who studies sharks and rays, on the research faculty of Florida State University's Coastal and Marine Laboratory since 2007 and, as of 2025, its associate director of research. The tie to FHL runs through Matthew A. Kolmann, who took an MSc at Florida State (2009-2012) and was an FHL postdoctoral fellow (2016-2018). The two published on the feeding apparatus of rays, including batoid cranial muscles (Journal of Morphology, 2014) and cownose ray feeding biomechanics over ontogeny (Journal of Anatomy, 2015). Their 2018 Journal of Zoology paper on intraspecific variation in bite force in durophagous stingrays gives Kolmann's address as Friday Harbor Laboratories.

Grubbs took a BSc at the University of Miami (1992) and a PhD at the College of William & Mary (2001) through the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. An EPA STAR graduate fellowship (1996-2001) supported work on sandbar sharks in lower Chesapeake Bay nursery grounds, along with coordination of the institute's longline program under J. A. Musick. Grubbs was a postdoctoral researcher and faculty member at the Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology before joining Florida State. Later work covered smalltooth sawfish in Florida and the Bahamas, deep-sea sharks including the effects of the Deepwater Horizon spill, and coastal sharks and bycatch. Grubbs was first author of a 2016 Scientific Reports paper reassessing a purported marine trophic cascade, and became a scientific adviser to the Save Our Seas Foundation in 2015.

name: Dean Jacobson
text: Dean M. Jacobson was curator of the Provasoli-Guillard culture collection at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences from 1990 to 1993, during Robert A. Andersen’s term as director, and co-authored its 1991 strain catalog with him. A 1987 MIT and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution monograph treated the ecology and feeding biology of thecate heterotrophic dinoflagellates, alongside papers with Donald M. Anderson on feeding mechanisms (1986) and on growth and grazing in Protoperidinium hirobis (1993). With Andersen, Jacobson reported food vacuoles and mixotrophy in Dinophysis (Phycologia, 1994). A 2024 paper on the dinoflagellate Oxytoxum lohmannii gives the College of the Marshall Islands.

name: Dean Pentcheff
text: N. Dean Pentcheff was a graduate student of M. A. R. Koehl at the University of California, Berkeley. Koehl's lab page lists Pentcheff's 1991 Marine Biology paper on how the barnacle Balanus glandula resists crushing by wave-borne debris; a 1987 paper addressed stipe shapes and material properties of seaweeds in different exposure regimes. At the University of South Carolina's Baruch Institute, Pentcheff studied odor plumes and navigation in crabs and orientation in spiny lobsters (1995). From 2001 Pentcheff was program coordinator of the Marine Biodiversity Center at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, with later work on decapod classification (2009) and environmental DNA surveys of California (2021).

name: Deborah A. Giles
text:
Deborah A. Giles is a marine mammal biologist who studies the endangered Southern Resident killer whales (Orcinus orca) of the Salish Sea. She received her PhD from the University of California, Davis, in 2014, with a dissertation on the Southern Residents. From 2009 to 2021 she worked as a vessel captain for the University of Washington, using a scat-detection dog to find floating killer whale feces for monitoring the whales' physiological health. That program is now run by the nonprofit Wild Orca, where she is science and research director. She is a resident scientist and lecturer at FHL, where she teaches Marine Mammals of the Salish Sea and Marine Biology. The census lists twelve FHL-connected items by her from 2018 to 2026, both journal papers and conference abstracts.

Her work combines non-invasive sampling with behavioral and acoustic study of free-ranging whales. A 2018 paper profiled contaminants in Southern Resident fecal samples as a baseline before any oil spill and found signs of possible exposure to vessel exhaust. Most of her other FHL-connected papers come from a collaborative study, with Marla Holt, Jennifer Tennessen and others, in which archival tags recorded the movements and sounds of individual fish-eating killer whales. Two 2019 papers used hidden Markov models to describe daily patterns of behavior, and identified the movement signatures of prey capture, finding differences between males and females. Papers in 2021 and 2024 report that vessels and their noise reduce prey-capture effort and success, in part through auditory masking. A 2023 paper compares foraging strategies between killer whale populations that share the same waters, and a 2026 paper describes daily cycles of echolocation-based foraging.

name: Deborah Eastman
text: Deborah Eastman is a professor of biology at Connecticut College and advised Erica Hildebrand's undergraduate research and 2010 honors thesis there on Tramtrack69 and gene expression in Drosophila. Eastman studies how signaling pathways and transcriptional regulation control cell specialization during development, with earlier work on Notch signaling in fruit flies and later work on taste bud development in the axolotl.

name: Deborah L. Penry
text:
Deborah L. Penry worked in oceanography and marine invertebrate physiology, applying chemical reactor theory to animal digestion, and was based at the University of California, Berkeley from 1992. Penry trained at the University of Washington, where Peter A. Jumars supervised her and she completed a PhD in oceanography in 1988. The dissertation, "Digestion theory and applications to deposit feeders," built gut models from batch, plug-flow and stirred-tank reactors and treated deposit feeders with simple tubular guts as modified plug-flow reactors. Her papers with Jumars appeared in BioScience (1986), The American Naturalist (1987) and Oecologia (1990). FHL's bibliography lists these three and her 1989 test of gut models in the sea cucumber Parastichopus californicus and the polychaete Amphicteis scaphobranchiata.

With Bruce W. Frost she reexamined the gut-fullness method for inferring ingestion rates in suspension-feeding copepods (1990) and studied chlorophyll degradation by Calanus pacificus (1991). NSF funded her work on digestive enzymes in deposit feeders through the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science (1991) and then Berkeley (1992), and a 1995 paper with Miller and Glibert addressed trophic interactions and nitrogen regeneration in Chesapeake Bay. In 1993 she received NSF's Alan T. Waterman Award, cited for applying chemical engineering principles and chemical-reactor theory to digestion in marine invertebrates, along with an NSF Young Investigator award. From Berkeley's Department of Integrative Biology she then studied contaminant uptake, including digestive controls on benzo[a]pyrene and phenanthrene bioaccumulation in a deposit-feeding polychaete (1998).

name: Deborah Sills
text: Deborah Sills was a postdoc of Charles H. Greene at Cornell University from 2011 to 2013, after an MS (2005) and PhD (2011) there in environmental engineering. Papers with J. M. Gossett (2011, 2012) covered hemicellulases and the use of FTIR spectroscopy to predict saccharification of alkali-pretreated biomass. Sills was first author, with Greene and J. W. Tester as co-authors, of a 2013 Environmental Science & Technology analysis of uncertainty in life cycle assessment of algal biofuel production. Sills joined Bucknell University as an assistant professor in 2013 and later held the Claire W. Carlson Chair in Environmental Engineering there, with research on life cycle assessment, biomass conversion and biorefineries.

name: Debra Murray

Otto's papers of those years addressed F-actin in sea urchin eggs and starfish oocytes (1996), following earlier work with T. E. Schroeder on actin and myosin in the contractile ring (1990).

name: Delaney St. Pierre
text: Delaney St. Pierre was an MS student at Montclair State University (2025), sponsored by Paul A. X. Bologna, with Colette J. Feehan and Alexis Khursigara on the committee. St. Pierre's throw-trap sampling in Barnegat Bay, New Jersey, in summer 2024 found blue crabs, grass shrimp, sand shrimp and four-spined stickleback denser in Ruppia maritima than in Zostera marina beds, arguing for the habitat value of widgeon grass.

name: Delany Rodriguez
text: Delany Rodriguez was a PhD student of Charles Bradley Shuster at New Mexico State University, completing the degree in December 2009 with a dissertation on the spatial regulation of cytokinesis, using chemical and physical micromanipulation of sea urchin embryos. An earlier MS (2005), advised by William Lott, dealt with separating capacitated and non-capacitated sperm. A 2011 paper with Shuster described tritylthioethanamine inhibitors of the mitotic kinesin KSP. Rodriguez then moved to the University of California, Santa Barbara, as a postdoctoral fellow (2010-2015) and from 2016 a research specialist, publishing with Anthony De Tomaso on germ cells, vasculature and aging in the colonial tunicate Botryllus schlosseri.

name: Dennis Dunninger
text: Dennis Robert Dunninger was a doctoral student of Monroe H. Martin at the University of Maryland, College Park, finishing the PhD in 1966 with a dissertation on uniqueness and comparison theorems for harmonic functions under boundary conditions, published under that title in 1967. Jim Cushing (1968) and Simon Levin (1964) are listed among Martin's other students. Dunninger's later papers treated uniqueness theorems and maximum principles for differential equations, including a 1971 paper with J. M. Cushing on quasi-linear elliptic equations and a 1976 paper with Howard A. Levine on singular boundary value problems. The Mathematics Genealogy Project lists two doctoral students of Dunninger at Michigan State University (1973, 1997).

text: Devya Hemraj-Naraine was a PhD student of Matthew A. name: Diana DiMarco
text: Diana DiMarco was mentored by Lyda S. T. Harris at Friday Harbor Laboratories in 2016, while at Seattle University, on a project on how microplastic and silt affect the clearance rate of marine mussels. DiMarco later co-authored, with a University of Washington affiliation, the 2023 Marine Pollution Bulletin paper led by Harris on microparticles in mussels across the Salish Sea. That study processed mussel tissue collected at regional and localized scales, found a mean of 0.75 particles per gram of wet tissue, and identified 20 percent of a subset of particles as synthetic materials.

text: Diana T. White was a PhD student of Adriana T. Dawes in mathematics at the University of Alberta from 2008 to 2013. name: Dianna K. Padilla
text:
Dianna K. Padilla is Professor in the Department of Ecology and Evolution at Stony Brook University, where she joined the faculty in 1998 and became Professor in 2006, with an affiliated appointment in the School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences. She earned BAs in zoology and biological oceanography at the University of Washington (1978), an MS at Oregon State University (1982) and a PhD in zoology at the University of Alberta (1987), was a postdoc at Cornell (1987–1989) and was on the zoology faculty at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (1989–1998). She was an NSF program director in Integrative Organismal Systems (2006–2007) and president of the American Malacological Society (2004–2005). Her FHL ties include doctoral fieldwork partly done at FHL, seminars there in 1990–1992, a 1994 honors thesis she supervised at FHL, the FHL Academic Advisory Board from 2002, research at FHL in 2012–2016 and co-teaching Advanced Invertebrate Biology there in 2014.

Padilla studies phenotypic plasticity, especially inducible offences and defenses in marine invertebrates, and the ecology of introduced species. Her doctoral work related seaweed calcification and form to how herbivores feed, and a 1993 paper described 'rip stop' features that limit herbivore damage in algae. FHL-based papers examined inducible aggression and competition for space in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea (1996, with Drew Harvell, Jessica Marks and Brian Helmuth) and radula production and diet-induced radula change in Lacuna snails (1996, 1998); her later FHL research turned to the snails' crab and sea-star predators. Other FHL-connected papers treat the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas as a non-native ecosystem engineer (2010) and its larval food selection (2020), and predator-induced phenotypes in a marine snail (2019); several acknowledge the Whiteley Center. Many census entries concern the spread and impacts of zebra and quagga mussels, much of it with collaborator Alexander Karatayev.

text: Diethard Tautz is a German geneticist who was a professor at Ludwig Maximilians University Munich when Ralf Sommer earned a PhD in the Tautz lab in 1992. name: Dina F. Mandoli
text:
Dina F. Mandoli is a plant developmental biologist. Her early papers (1981–1985) came from the Carnegie Institution of Washington's Department of Plant Biology at Stanford and concerned phytochrome and light-piping in plant tissues such as etiolated oat seedlings. From 1990 her papers give the University of Washington's Department of Botany as her address, and her 2006 paper the UW Department of Biology and Center for Developmental Biology. Her FHL-connected papers, from 1999 to 2006, come from her laboratory's work on the green alga Acetabularia acetabulum. FHL course lists name her, alongside G. M. Odell, as an instructor of research apprenticeships on development and morphogenesis in Acetabularia (2000) and on the cell biology of morphogenesis and development (2002), and a 2004 paper acknowledges an FHL apprenticeship course among its sources of support. She also edited a 2000 collection on emerging models in plant biology for the Journal of Plant Growth Regulation.

Mandoli's research uses Acetabularia, a giant single-celled green alga of the Dasycladales, as a model for subcellular localization and morphogenesis during development. Her FHL-listed papers address the roles of light and the nucleus in timing reproductive onset (1999, with René Kratz), physiological factors that help zygotes and juveniles differentiate (1999), and the developmentally regulated subcellular localization of Aaknox1, a knotted1-like homeobox gene (1999, with Kyle Serikawa). Others found subcellular domains of calcification and of proton and oxygen flux along the cell (2000), related growth, shape and wall stress in the stalk (2001, with Michelangelo von Dassow and G. M. Odell), compared expressed sequence tags from juvenile and adult phases (2004), and showed with spectroscopy and biochemistry that walls of the diploid phase are mainly a para-crystalline mannan, while the haploid gametangia have cellulose-based walls (2006).

name: Dmitry Sakharov
text:
Dmitry A. Sakharov (died 2024) was a Soviet and Russian neurobiologist of invertebrates, based at the Koltsov Institute of Developmental Biology in Moscow. His tie to FHL core scientists runs through Leonid L. Moroz, whose CV names Sakharov as mentor for a 1985–1989 PhD at that institute. Sakharov graduated from Moscow State University in 1953, defended a candidate's dissertation on the development of motor behavior in amphibians in 1957, and took a doctorate in 1973 with a thesis on the transmitter specificity of neurons and its origin and evolution. Moroz and V. E. Dyakonova name Kh. S. Koshtoyants as his teacher.

His 1974 book Genealogy of Neurons argued that neurons differ chiefly because they have different origins, and that their chemical diversity has functional meaning. He also proposed non-synaptic volume transmission as a basis for neuronal ensembles. Moroz and Dyakonova, revisiting these hypotheses in 2024, trace the work to his 1958 rediscovery of the sea angel Clione limacina as a neurobiological model; Moroz's photograph of the species in their article shows an animal from Friday Harbor. Later papers used the pond snail Lymnaea, from transmitter-dependent switching of respiratory interneurons (2000) to behavioral experience stored in single neurons (2019). Sakharov also published poetry as Dmitry Sukharev, and received the Bulat Okudzhava State Prize (2001) and a state medal citing his contribution to science (2022).

name: Dominic M. Sivitilli
text:
Dominic M. Sivitilli is a neuroscientist of octopus behavior who earned a dual-title PhD in psychology and astrobiology at the University of Washington in 2023, advised by David H. Gire. He did research in Seattle and at Friday Harbor Labs, combining lab studies of octopus locomotion, foraging and exploration in computer-designed environments with SCUBA work on the effects of giant Pacific octopus predation. He first studied the smaller red octopus, then Enteroctopus dofleini at FHL, including an animal he met about 45 feet down off San Juan County Park, which he and colleagues brought into the lab.

His dissertation, Reverse Engineering the Octopus Arm, identified sucker recruitment as a key mechanism of arm search when vision is limited, and designed a soft robotic arm from repeated segments modeled on sucker units. Papers with Gire and Joshua R. Smith covered lessons for robotics from octopus control architecture (2022) and arm search without visual feedback (2023). He co-authored a 2025 PLoS ONE paper with Willem Weertman, Venkatesh Gopal, David Scheel and Gire on octopus tracking chemosensory plumes to find food, and a 2023 paper with Aaron W. E. Galloway and others on sunflower sea star predation on urchins. In 2024 he accepted a postdoctoral position at UW's Applied Physics Laboratory, developing octopus-inspired soft robots for underwater manipulation.

name: Dorothy Hinshaw Patent
text:
Dorothy Hinshaw Patent is a zoologist and an author of nonfiction books for young readers. She earned a B.A. from Stanford University in 1962, and an M.A. (1965) and Ph.D. (1968) in zoology from the University of California, Berkeley, and studied at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1965 to 1967. She was a postdoctoral fellow at Sinai Hospital in Detroit (1968–1969) and a postdoctoral researcher at the Stazione Zoologica in Naples (1970–1971). She later held faculty affiliate appointments at the University of Montana in zoology (1975–1990, including a term as acting assistant professor in 1977) and in environmental studies (from 1995). Rather than become a professor or researcher, she chose to focus mainly on writing for young readers. The census counts three FHL-address papers, from 1969 and 1970, which give both the Berkeley zoology department and FHL as her address.

Her FHL papers deal with basket stars of the genus Gorgonocephalus, brittle stars with branching arms. A 1969 paper followed the reproductive cycle of G. caryi through monthly gonad samples, finding an annual cycle with spawning spread over six months, and a 1970 paper described its early embryology. A second 1970 paper described the life history of G. eucnemis in the San Juan Islands and reported very small young living inside polyps of the soft coral Gersemia, where it suggested the embryos develop. She has since written more than 100 nonfiction books for children, including The Lives of Spiders (Golden Kite Award, 1980). With Vicki Cobb she co-founded iNK Think Tank, a group of nonfiction writers for young readers. She received the American Nature Study Society's Eva L. Gordon Award (1987) and the Washington Post/Children's Book Guild Nonfiction Award (2004).

name: Douglas J. Eernisse
text:
Douglas J. Eernisse is a marine biologist and Professor in the Department of Biological Science at California State University, Fullerton, where he has worked since 1994. He received a BS in zoology from the University of Washington and a PhD from the University of California, Santa Cruz. His 1986 monograph on the chiton genus Lepidochitona, part of his doctoral work, gives his former address as UC Santa Cruz's Institute of Marine Sciences and his present address as FHL, and says its final revisions were made while he held an FHL postdoctoral fellowship. A 1988 paper with Diarmaid Ó Foighil also gives FHL as the authors' address. FHL's list of visitors in the Whiteley Center's first two years records him co-writing a book synthesizing animal relationships, and his 2010 description of a new sea star was supported by FHL and an NSF grant held with Richard Strathmann, with drafts prepared during Whiteley Center visits.

Eernisse's papers concern the systematics, reproduction and evolution of marine invertebrates, especially chitons (Polyplacophora), and his FHL-connected papers span 1986 to 2010. His 1986 revision of Lepidochitona in the Oregonian and Californian provinces described three new species, among them L. fernaldi, a brooding hermaphroditic chiton named for Robert L. Fernald, whom the monograph calls a teacher of invertebrate reproduction at FHL; a 1993 paper with John Buckland-Nicks described its sperm and egg ultrastructure and mechanism of fertilization. He also reported tissue hemoglobins in the red foot of a lepidopleurid chiton (1988, with Nora and Robert Terwilliger) and, with Ó Foighil, used enzyme variation to identify widespread, non-hybridizing sympatric strains of the brooding clam Lasaea (1988). With Richard Strathmann he reviewed what molecular phylogenies show about the evolution of larval forms (1994), and with Megumi and Richard Strathmann he described the brooding sea star Henricia pumila (2010).

name: Dylan K. Wainwright
text:
Dylan K. Wainwright is a fish biomechanist and functional morphologist who joined Purdue University's Department of Biological Sciences as an assistant professor in 2022. Wainwright's tie to FHL dates from summer 2011, as a Duke University biology major on a Blinks/REU project at Friday Harbor Labs with Adam P. Summers, then assistant director, and postdoctoral researcher Thomas Kleinteich. The project compared how well northern clingfish, Gobiesox maeandricus, adhered to surfaces of differing roughness. A 2013 Biology Letters paper reported that the fish adhered about equally across a broad range of roughness, with forces of 80 to 230 times body weight. Further clingfish papers followed with Petra Ditsche and Summers (2014) and with Jonathan M. Huie, Summers and Karly E. Cohen (2022).

Wainwright took a PhD in organismic and evolutionary biology at Harvard (2013–2019), publishing with George V. Lauder on scale structure in bluegill sunfish (2016) and bigeye tuna (2018), on shark denticles (2018), and on skin ridges in dolphins and other odontocetes (2019). A postdoctoral fellowship in Thomas Near's lab group at Yale followed from 2019 to 2022; a study with Near on chromosomal inversion and speciation in darters, a group of riverine fishes, appeared in 2023. The Wainwright lab at Purdue uses 3D imaging, biomechanical performance testing and comparisons across species, mainly in bony fishes, to connect form, function and evolution.

name: E. B. Ridgway
text:
Ellis B. Ridgway, a physiologist, studied calcium signals in muscle, nerve cells and eggs using aequorin, a calcium-sensitive photoprotein from jellyfish. His papers of 1988 and 1993 give the Department of Physiology at the Medical College of Virginia in Richmond as his address. Wikipedia's article on aequorin cites his 1967 paper with C. C. Ashley on calcium transients in single muscle fibers for the first experiments in which injected aequorin was used to visualize the release of calcium, in barnacle muscle fibers. In 1970 he and Ashley related membrane potential, calcium transient and tension in barnacle fibers, and in 1971 he published with P. F. Baker and A. L. Hodgkin on calcium entry in squid giant axons. His papers with a Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) address or acknowledgment run from 1976 to 1999, and several thank the FHL director and staff for their hospitality.

At FHL, Ridgway worked mainly with the giant barnacle Balanus nubilus, whose large muscle fibers he injected with aequorin; the barnacles were dredged from Lopez Pass and kept in the laboratory's running seawater. With Albert M. Gordon of the University of Washington he showed that calcium release depends on fiber length (1976), then studied how shortening and stretch after stimulation change calcium binding to the activating sites and how this relates to cross-bridge attachment and force (1984–1993); they also measured resting free calcium with modified aequorins (1993, 1995). In 1977 he co-authored a study of calcium entry in aequorin-injected mollusk neurons with Roger Eckert and D. L. Tillotson. From 1987 to 1999 he worked with Gary Freeman of the University of Texas on hydrozoans such as Phialidium, studying oocyte maturation and using the animals' own photoproteins to follow calcium during fertilization, cleavage and larval metamorphosis, and calcium fluxes tied to exocytosis and endocytosis.

name: E. J. Lund
text:
Elmer Julius Lund (1884–1969) was an American physiologist who studied bioelectricity and growth. He received a bachelor's degree from Hamline University in 1910 and a PhD from Johns Hopkins University in 1914. In 1926 he joined the Department of Zoology at the University of Texas, where he was a professor until 1949. After investigating a large fish kill at Port Aransas in 1935, later attributed to a red tide, he persuaded the university to build a marine laboratory on the Texas coast. The Institute of Marine Science was formally founded there in 1941, with Lund as its first director until 1949. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 1921 to 1931, when the station was the Puget Sound Biological Station. Four of them appeared in the station's own Publications series in 1929 and 1930.

Lund asked whether steady electrical potentials in living tissue are tied to cell oxidation and help set the polarity of growth. A five-part series in the Journal of Experimental Zoology (1921–1925) used regenerating stem segments of the hydroid Obelia to show the colony's normal electrical polarity, and measured how applied currents of different density and orientation delay or inhibit polyp formation. Later papers showed that cyanide, ether and chloroform reversibly suppress the electrical polarity of Obelia and frog skin (1926), and related bioelectric potential quantitatively to cell oxidation (1928). From 1929 to 1931 he mapped electric polarity in the Douglas fir, including the electrical dominance of growing tips and the potentials between living cells of cortex and wood. He summarized this program in the book Bioelectric Fields and Growth (1947). At Port Aransas he and his student Gordon Gunter studied Texas marine fishes and fouling on ships' bottoms.

name: E. Sanford Branscomb
text:
E. Sanford Branscomb's published work, from 1976 to 2014, concerns the larvae of barnacles and crabs. The two 1976 papers come from the University of Maryland's Chesapeake Biological Laboratory at Solomons. One, with S. D. Sulkin and Robert E. Miller, concerns inducing winter spawning and rearing larvae of the blue crab; the other, a single-author study, examines causes of death limiting the distribution and abundance of the barnacle Balanus improvisus in Chesapeake Bay. The 1981 paper lists the University of Washington Zoology Department at Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the 1982 paper lists FHL. Papers of 1984 and 1985, with Dan Rittschof and John D. Costlow, list the Duke University Marine Laboratory in Beaufort, North Carolina. A 2014 paper again lists FHL and the UW Department of Biology. The census counts three FHL-address papers (1981, 1982 and 2014).

Branscomb's FHL work, with Karen Vedder and Richard R. Strathmann, concerns how barnacle larvae develop, settle and hatch. The 1981 paper treated settlement where young barnacles die as a cost of larval dispersal and examined how intertidal plants and algae affect settlement. The 1982 paper described the naupliar stages of three Puget Sound barnacles, Balanus glandula, B. cariosus and B. crenatus; the larvae of the first two had not been described before. The 2014 paper found that B. glandula broods reaching hatching stages at different times over winter all hatched within about two weeks in spring. Crabs breaking a brooding barnacle's shell set off hatching, while whelks, which leave the shell plates in place, posed a greater risk to the brooded larvae. At Duke the work concerned settlement in relation to water flow and surfaces, low-frequency sound as a deterrent, and settlement inhibitors from the whip coral Leptogorgia virgulata.

name: E. W. Misty Paig-Tran
text:
E. W. Misty Paig-Tran is a functional morphologist and biomechanist who works mainly on fishes, especially cartilaginous filter feeders. She received a B.S. in marine biology from California State University, Long Beach (2006) and a Ph.D. in biology from the University of Washington (2012). Her supervisory committee was chaired by Adam P. Summers, then associate director of FHL. Since 2014 she has been in the Department of Biological Sciences at California State University, Fullerton, where her ORCID record lists her as professor. Her 2011 paper gives FHL as her address, and her doctoral papers through 2014 list FHL among the authors' addresses. A Strathmann Fellowship paid for her housing at FHL, and excised gill arches were shipped to FHL for examination for her thesis. Later papers, through 2025, have FHL-based co-authors, and some used micro-CT scanning at FHL's Karel F. Liem imaging center.

Her research asks how the shape and material of biological structures determine how they perform. Her dissertation examined filtration in the devil rays (Mobulidae) using dissection, scanning electron microscopy, histology, modeling and measurements of live feeding. It described rigid, chevron-shaped cartilaginous filter pads and a flow path that turns abruptly through the filter pores. Related papers used physical models of ram-feeding fishes to predict how swimming speed and gill-slit design affect size selectivity and filtering efficiency (2011), described variation in devil ray filter pads (2013) and compared the branchial filters of suspension-feeding sharks and rays (2014). Later FHL-linked papers covered jaw protrusion in the king-of-the-salmon (2019), the scales of a small armored catfish (2020) and baleen structure in rorqual whales (2023). A 2025 group of papers concerns biological armor, armadillo-inspired tiles, mobulid filters and bioinspiration. Her ORCID record also lists work on whale sharks, manta rays and megamouth sharks.

name: Edgar Meyhöfer
text:
Edgar Meyhöfer is a researcher in biomechanics and single-molecule biophysics who joined the University of Michigan's mechanical engineering faculty in 2001. In 1985 Meyhöfer and M. Patricia Morse were at Northeastern University's Marine Science Laboratory at Nahant, and with William E. Robinson they reported morphological evidence for ultrafiltration by podocytes in bivalves. Morse, Meyhöfer and colleagues reported a hemocyanin respiratory pigment in bivalves in Science in 1986. A 1988 comparison of bivalve hemocyanins added Nora B. and Robert C. Terwilliger as co-authors. Work with Morse continued in a 1990 chapter on the heart-kidney complex of protobranchs and a 1996 paper on ultrafiltration in Mytilus edulis, Chlamys hastata and Mercenaria mercenaria.

Meyhöfer entered the University of Washington's Department of Zoology in 1985 and finished a PhD in 1991. With Thomas L. Daniel, Meyhöfer analyzed escape locomotion in the dock shrimp Pandalus danae (1989) and, with Joel G. Kingsolver, nectar-feeding energetics in butterflies (1989). As a senior fellow in UW Physiology and Biophysics from 1991 to 1994, Meyhöfer worked with J. Howard on kinesin, including a 1995 PNAS measurement of the force generated by a single kinesin molecule. After Hannover Medical School (1994–2001), the Michigan work ranged from single-molecule tracking of kinesin in mammalian cells (2007) to near-field radiative heat transfer (2015) and thermal transport in single-atom junctions (2017).

name: Edsel A. Caine
text:
Edsel A. Caine is a marine invertebrate zoologist whose papers, from 1974 to 1998, deal mainly with caprellid amphipods (skeleton shrimps). His earliest papers, of 1974 and 1975, several giving Florida State University, covered feeding morphology in caprellids of the northwestern Florida Gulf coast, feeding in crabs and anomurans, and the zoogeography of Florida's cave crayfishes. The census counts four FHL-address papers from 1976 to 1980; the first gives both the Department of Biology at the University of Tampa and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and a 1978 paper gives the Department of Zoology at Mississippi State University. From 1980 his papers give the Department of Marine Science at the University of South Carolina at Beaufort, often with the Belle W. Baruch Institute for Marine Biology and Coastal Research, and in 1998 the Department of Biology at USC Beaufort.

Caine studied how caprellids feed, groom, swim and use their habitats. His FHL papers concern caprellids of Puget Sound and the Washington shore: a 1976 paper compared cleansing (grooming) mechanisms of North American caprellids, a 1977 paper related feeding mechanisms to possible resource partitioning among Puget Sound species, and papers in 1979 and 1980 described the population structure of two species and the ecology of two littoral species in Washington. Related papers of the same years examined habitat adaptations of North American caprellids (1978) and the function of their swimming setae (1979). In South Carolina he went on to study community interactions of Caprella penantis on sea whips, epibionts on the carapaces of nesting loggerhead turtles, floating-dock fouling communities, wave exposure and caprellid robustness, caprellid behavior under fish predation, reproductive behavior and sexual dimorphism, and a caprellid–hydrozoan mutualism (1998).

name: Edward J. DeVillez
text:
Edward J. DeVillez is a comparative physiologist and biochemist whose published research, from 1964 to 1986, concerns the digestive enzymes of invertebrates. A 1965 paper gives the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Illinois, Urbana. From 1967 to 1985 his papers give the Department of Zoology and Physiology, later the Department of Zoology, at Miami University in Oxford, Ohio. Three papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address: the 1964 note lists FHL alone, and the 1967 and 1975 papers list it alongside Miami University.

His papers deal with proteolytic enzymes, especially trypsin-like enzymes, that invertebrates use in digestion. Early papers isolated and characterized proteinases from the gastric juice of the crayfish Orconectes virilis. From Miami University he published on the molecular weight of crustacean trypsin, the digestive proteinases of the earthworm Lumbricus terrestris and where its trypsin is produced and secreted, polychaete trypsin, and trypsin secretion in the esophagus of the polychaete Nereis virens. Later papers described a chymotrypsin-like enzyme from the sipunculan Phascolopsis gouldii (1982) and hepatopancreatic cell types in the crayfish Orconectes rusticus (1986). His FHL-connected papers belong to the same line of work: a 1964 note on preparative acrylamide electrophoresis using a conventional vertical starch-gel apparatus, a 1967 survey with Karen Buschlen of a tryptic digestive enzyme across crustacean species, and a 1975 study of proteolytic enzymes in the digestive fluid of the barnacle Balanus nubilus.

name: Edwin Munro
text:
Edwin Munro is a cell and developmental biologist who studies how cells and embryos generate polarity, force and shape. He studied at Hampshire College and earned a PhD in cell and developmental biology at the University of Washington, where around 2000 he co-authored, with George von Dassow, Eli Meir and Garrett Odell, a model of the Drosophila segment polarity network. An FHL centennial timeline lists him as one of the postdoctoral scholars, resident at FHL from about 2000, on the team awarded a 2002 National Institute of General Medical Sciences grant that set up the Center for Cell Dynamics at FHL. He was also a postdoctoral fellow at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center; his papers of 2004-2011 give the Center for Cell Dynamics as his address. He is now Professor of Molecular Genetics and Cell Biology at the University of Chicago. The census lists 18 FHL-connected papers, 2002-2015.

Munro combines live imaging, quantitative image analysis and computer modeling. His FHL-connected papers fall into three groups. Work on ascidian embryos showed that notochord patterning is regulative and robust and that polarized basolateral cell motility drives notochord invagination and convergent extension (2002), and went on to the role of the polarity gene prickle (2005), FGF3 signaling from the floor plate in Ciona (2008) and the sequential apical and basolateral contractions that drive endoderm invagination (2010). Work on the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans showed that cortical flows powered by asymmetric contraction carry PAR proteins to set up anterior-posterior polarity in the early embryo (2004), with later papers on symmetry breaking (2009) and PAR-3 oligomerization (2011). Modeling and biophysical papers covered gene networks (2002), clustering of self-aggregating particles (2012, 2014) and force generation by myosin II filament isoforms (2015).

name: Ehab Abouheif
text: Ehab Abouheif completed a PhD in biology at Duke University in 2002 and is listed among former members of Gregory A. Wray's lab. He co-authored with Wray the 1997 Trends in Genetics paper on homology and developmental genes and a 2002 Science paper on the evolution of the gene network underlying wing polyphenism in ants. After postdoctoral fellowships at the University of Chicago and UC Berkeley, he joined McGill University in 2004, became full professor in 2015, and moved to Zhejiang University in 2025. His later ant research includes a 2012 Science paper on ancestral developmental potential. He held Sloan (2006), Steacie (2014) and Guggenheim (2017) fellowships.

text: Eileen Bates is listed for 2017 in the Pelagic Ecosystem Function Research Apprenticeship at Friday Harbor Laboratories, with a project on sediment type and the distribution of Pacific sand lance in the San Juan Archipelago. Padilla-Gamiño, on trace metals in Salish Sea bivalves and climate stress in pinto abalone (Scientific Reports, 2025), and joined the Puget Sound Restoration Fund's abalone team in 2024.

name: Eli Meir
text: Eli Meir wrote a 1992 undergraduate honors thesis at Cornell University under Charles H. Greene on Langmuir circulation and the patchiness of pelagic animals, and co-authored a 1998 paper with Greene on sound scattering by Aequorea victoria and Pleurobrachia bachei. Meir completed a PhD in zoology at the University of Washington in 2003. With George von Dassow, Edwin Munro and Garrett M. Odell, Meir built computer models of gene networks: the segment polarity network (Nature, 2000), the Ingeneue software (2002) and the neurogenic network (2002). Meir also published on extinction risk (1999 to 2001) and on simulation-based teaching of biology, including natural selection (2009) and experimental design (2024).

text: Elias Taylor worked with Andreas Heyland in Integrative Biology at the University of Guelph, completing a 2017 master's thesis on thyroid hormones and larval skeletogenesis in the sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and a 2024 PhD thesis on thyroid hormone regulation of skeletogenesis and metamorphosis in echinoderms. text: Eliott Drucker is listed on Adam P. Summers's postdocs page as a National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellow from 2001 to 2003. Publishing as Eliot G. name: Elisabeth Rennert
text: Elisabeth Rennert completed a 2026 dissertation in Biophysical Sciences at the University of Chicago, advised by Suriyanarayanan Vaikuntanathan, with Edwin Munro on the committee. The work combined minimal thermodynamic models, dimensionality reduction and generative machine learning to study branched actin networks, reaction-diffusion waves and simulated actomyosin cortex. A 2025 eLife paper with Vaikuntanathan treated force and morphology tradeoffs in branched actin.

name: Eliza C. Heery
text:
Eliza C. Heery is a marine ecologist who studies how coastal urbanization affects seafloor (benthic) ecosystems. She received a BS from Emory University, an MS from Virginia Tech and, in 2017, a PhD from the University of Washington Department of Biology, advised by Kenneth P. Sebens of Friday Harbor Laboratories. As a doctoral candidate she was also a graduate fellow in UW's IGERT Program on Ocean Change. She was then a postdoctoral researcher at the National University of Singapore before moving to the Smithsonian's MarineGEO program; some of her 2020 and 2021 papers give her address as MarineGEO at Friday Harbor Laboratories. In December 2022 she joined the University of Washington Tacoma as an Assistant Professor in Ecology. Her census papers run from 2018 to 2026, and FHL's 2026 people page lists her on its Research Advisory Committee.

Her research asks how marine life responds to the artificial structures and armored shorelines of coastal cities. For her doctoral work she dived at natural rocky outcrops and at breakwaters, fishing reefs and riprap-covered pipelines in Puget Sound, from north of Everett to south of Tacoma, photographing standard areas of seafloor to compare communities along an urbanization gradient. Papers from this work show that artificial structures can raise detrital loads in nearby sediments (2018) and describe how giant Pacific octopuses use urban habitats (2018). With colleagues in Singapore she tested ways of making seawalls and shorelines better habitat, among them added microhabitats for fishes, seaweed farming and lower-pH concrete, which gave little biodiversity gain (all 2020). She also co-authored a global estimate of the extent of marine built structures (2020). A 2026 paper presents a tool that measures urbanization across seascapes and predicts where habitat-forming seaweeds occur in the Salish Sea.

name: Elizabeth Anne Sosik
text:
Elizabeth Anne Sosik studied coastal food webs for an MS at the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (2012). Charles Simenstad chaired the committee, with David O. Duggins and Tim Essington as members, and an NSF grant to Duggins and co-investigators funded most of the work. The thesis credits guidance from Friday Harbor Labs colleagues Megan Dethier, Alex Lowe, Aaron Galloway and Kevin Britton-Simmons. In July and August 2011, in the San Juan Islands, Sosik decomposed blades of the kelps Saccharina subsimplex and Agarum fimbriatum for five weeks in complete darkness in a flow-through seawater system, to measure how microbes alter stable isotope values.

Microbial counts rose more than threefold on S. subsimplex and its isotope values changed, while counts on A. fimbriatum stayed low and its isotopes showed no significant change. Sosik related the contrast to phlorotannin concentrations, which were consistently high in Agarum. The thesis, Isotopic evidence of microbial pathways in macroalgal detritus-based coastal food webs, proposed that microbial biofilms may act as a distinct trophic level and can add error to mixing models. Sosik and Simenstad published on the role of microbes in these food webs in Marine Ecology Progress Series in 2013. Sosik also co-authored papers on drift macrophytes in a Washington marine basin (2012), biomarkers across depths (2013), variation in macrophyte isotopes and fatty acids (2013), and the food quality of aging kelp (2014).

name: Elizabeth G. Boulding
text:
Elizabeth G. Boulding is an evolutionary biologist and Professor in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of Guelph, where she is also affiliated with the One Health Institute. She earned a BSc at the University of British Columbia (1980), an MSc at the University of Alberta (1983) and a PhD at the University of Washington (1990). Her FHL-connected papers run from 1983 to 2010. Her Alberta master's thesis on crab predation on buried bivalves thanks the director and staff of Friday Harbor Laboratories and Bamfield Marine Station for the use of their facilities. A 1993 paper from her doctoral years gives a University of Washington, Friday Harbor Laboratories address, and later papers from her Guelph group are listed in the FHL research bibliography. In the report's network she is linked to Hyuk Je Lee, whose Guelph doctoral thesis examined population genetic structure in five northeastern Pacific Littorina species.

Boulding's lab asks whether a population can adapt to a change in its biological environment without going extinct, using field experiments, quantitative genetics and genomics. Her early FHL-connected papers concern shell-breaking crabs and their prey. A 1986 study with Michael LaBarbera showed that repeated loading lets crabs open larger bivalves, and papers with Sylvia Behrens Yamada (1996, 1998) looked at how mobile crab predators shape the zonation of intertidal snails and how claw form relates to prey size selection. In 1993 she examined the quantitative genetics of shell form in an intertidal snail and the survival and growth of two Littorina species on wave-exposed and protected shores. Later papers concern male mate choice in Littorina subrotundata (2008), hatchery pedigrees of northern abalone and the population structure of salmon lice (2009), and, with Lee, larval development and genetic structure in littorinid snails (2009) and body size clines in Littorina keenae (2010).

Jewett became director of NOAA's Ocean Acidification Program in 2011, and later coauthored work on ocean change, including a 2020 Frontiers in Marine Science paper on acidification in the U.S. Southeast and a 2021 overview of ocean climate change indicators.

name: Elizabeth L. Brainerd
text:
Elizabeth L. Brainerd is a vertebrate functional morphologist and biomechanist. She received an A.B. (1985) and a Ph.D. (1991) from Harvard University and was a Junior Fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows from 1990 to 1993. She was on the faculty of the University of Massachusetts Amherst from 1994 to 2005, then moved to Brown University, where she has been Robert P. Brown Professor of Biology and Professor of Medical Science since 2020. She was president of the International Society of Vertebrate Morphology (2016-2019) and the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology (2019-2021), and received the Joseph S. Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award in Ichthyology (2021) and the Society for Experimental Biology's Bidder Prize Lecture (2023). The census lists ten FHL-connected items by her from 1993 to 2020, including two 2015 reports from FHL's Blinks-NSF REU-BEACON internship program; her own 2018 and 2020 papers list an FHL address.

Brainerd's research combines anatomy of the musculoskeletal system with methods from engineering to study how vertebrates breathe, feed and move, including the evolution of lung ventilation, prey capture in fishes and fish escape responses. She is one of the developers of XROMM (X-ray Reconstruction of Moving Morphology), which combines CT scans with biplanar X-ray video to show skeletal motion in three dimensions, and has directed Brown's Keck XROMM Core Facility since 2008. Her FHL-connected papers deal with Northeast Pacific fishes: lift and ground effect during pectoral-fin swimming in the northern spearnose poacher (2009), the move from water into sand in sand lances (2011), pectoral-fin movements during turns in the Pacific spiny dogfish (2018), and neurocranial motion and the sternohyoideus muscle in suction feeding (2018, 2020). Nicholas Gidmark and Yordano Jimenez, listed in the report's network as her students, are first authors of the 2011 sand lance and 2018 neurocranial papers.

text: Elska Kaczmarek worked as an undergraduate with Nicholas Gidmark, producing a 2015 report on the force-length relationship in the adductor mandibulae of pink and king salmon and a 2020 Journal of Experimental Biology paper on bite force across gape in the two species, with a Friday Harbor Laboratories affiliation. name: Emily A. Roberts
text:
Emily A. Roberts is a marine biologist who studies the energetics of marine invertebrates and their responses to temperature, food and seawater chemistry. After a professional master's degree in marine biology at Northeastern University (2011), she completed a PhD in Biology at the University of Washington (2014–2019), advised by Emily Carrington. Her papers from these years give the UW Department of Biology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and a 2015 paper gives FHL alone. Her FHL-connected papers and datasets in the census run from 2015 to 2025. She was then a postdoctoral fellow in the Keck Science Department of Claremont McKenna College (2019–2021), a National Academies postdoctoral researcher at the NOAA Fisheries laboratory in Milford, Connecticut (2021–2023), a quantitative research ecologist there (2023–2024), and from 2024 a postdoctoral associate in Stony Brook University's School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences.

Her doctoral research measured the energetic cost of byssal attachment in mussels. With Mytilus trossulus and M. galloprovincialis, she combined laboratory temperature and food experiments and field studies with scope-for-growth energy budgets. A 2021 Functional Ecology paper showed that cutting threads to induce extra thread production reduced shell and tissue growth in M. trossulus, at an estimated cost of about 1 joule per thread, and a 2023 paper found that energetic scope limited growth but not thread production in two mytilid species. Earlier she co-authored FHL seawater studies: a 2015 analysis of a 2011–2013 time series from the FHL dock pump house, describing an inland sea with high nitrate, low chlorophyll and naturally high pCO2, and a 2016 paper relating freshwater influence to particulate organic matter and pH in the San Juan Archipelago. With Carrington she released FHL's Cantilever Point weather station records for 2006–2021 (2022). Later work models ocean and air warming effects on the barnacle Balanus glandula (2025).

name: Emily Carrington
text:
Emily Carrington is a marine biomechanist and professor of biology at the University of Washington, working on the Seattle campus and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She received a BA from Cornell University (1985) and a PhD from Stanford University (1992), advised by Mark Denny, then was a Killam Postdoctoral Fellow with John Gosline at the University of British Columbia and a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station. She was on the faculty of the University of Rhode Island from 1996 to 2005, then joined UW Biology and FHL as associate professor in 2005, becoming professor in 2010. At FHL she directed the Ocean Acidification Environmental Laboratory (2012–14) and was named a Turn Point Faculty Fellow in 2020. From 2016 to 2019 she was a program director at the National Science Foundation, and she was named an AAAS Fellow in 2021. The census lists 50 FHL-connected items, 2007–2026.

Her work combines materials science, fluid mechanics, organismal biology and environmental science to understand how organisms of wave-swept shores stay attached and how they will fare in changing oceans. Mussel byssal threads are a central system: her group has measured how attachment varies with season, wave action, temperature, low oxygen and ocean acidification, and how thread production trades off against growth. She has also studied drag on seaweeds, feeding in barnacles and the thermal behavior of intertidal snails. Recent FHL-connected papers cover the energetic cost of byssus production (2021, 2023), microplastics and mussel biodeposits (2021), kelp physiology under different temperatures and nitrogen levels (2023) and seasonal thermal sensitivity (2025). Many census entries are datasets: her lab launched an FHL weather station in 2005, and she is a co-author of FHL Ocean Observatory seawater records. Her PhD students include Michael Nishizaki, Laura Newcomb, Hilary Hayford and Matthew George.

name: Emília P. Martins
text:
Emília P. Martins is an evolutionary biologist and professor in the School of Life Sciences at Arizona State University, where she leads the Martins Lab. Her lab page describes her main interest as the evolution of complex and multimodal communication. Her connection to FHL comes through its imaging facility. The census holds two of her papers, from 2024 and 2026, that name FHL in the text but not in the author addresses. For the 2024 study, lizard specimens were micro-CT scanned at the Karel F. Liem Bio-Imaging Center at Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the authors thanked Adam Summers, Mackenzie Gerringer and FHL staff for help with collecting and analyzing the CT data. The 2026 paper's acknowledgments also name FHL and the Liem center. The report's network links her to Julio A. Rivera, a postdoctoral researcher in her lab from 2017 to 2021 and first author of the 2024 paper.

Martins's lab studies body form and communication in Sceloporus lizards and sensory biology in fishes. One current project asks whether closely related Sceloporus species living in the same areas differ in body form and ecology. It works in Mexico and the southwestern United States, using CT scans of museum specimens, field surveys and phylogenetic analyses. Another project, with the Arizona Game and Fish Department as a partner, tests how temperature, acidity, water flow and light affect the senses of zebrafish and of native and non-native desert minnows. Both FHL-connected papers apply phylogenetic comparative methods to CT data. The 2024 paper, on male skulls of 57 Sceloporus species, found that evolutionary shifts to larger body size went with more compact skulls. The 2026 paper found that in two of three live-bearing lineages, larger body size evolved with flatter, wider female pelvises, which the authors related to habitat rather than to reproduction.

name: Eric D. Tytell
text:
Eric D. Tytell is a biologist at Tufts University, where his faculty page lists him as Associate Professor of Biology and where he leads the Tytell Laboratory. He received a BA in biology and physics from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (1998), an MPhil in zoology from the University of Cambridge (1999) and a PhD in biology from Harvard University (2005). His FHL connection comes through collaboration: the census holds three papers from 2017 to 2022 written with Adam P. Summers and Karly E. Cohen, colleagues affiliated with Friday Harbor Laboratories. Cassandra M. Donatelli, who completed her PhD with Tytell at Tufts between 2014 and 2019, is a co-author on all three, and the report's network links her to him. On these papers Tytell's own address is Tufts; FHL appears through his co-authors' affiliations and the specimens used.

Tytell studies the biomechanics and neural control of locomotion, mainly in fishes. His work asks how fishes produce the forces that move them forward and let them maneuver, and how they keep their swimming stable in changing environments. His lab also asks how sensory systems detect such changes and how neural circuits control movement, combining experimental measurements, physical models and computational simulations. The FHL-connected papers deal with the fish body axis. The 2017 study measured long-axis twisting, or 'wobble', during swimming in six elongate fishes from intertidal, nearshore and subtidal habitats and found that species from the same habitat moved alike. A 2021 paper tested whether vertebral shape predicts the behavior and ecology of fishes. A 2022 study used micro-CT scans of 79 species, with specimens donated from the FHL ichthyology collection, and found vertebral features that point to more flexible spines in bottom-dwelling fishes than in open-water swimmers.

name: Erich Kähler
text: Erich Kähler (1906-2000) took his doctorate under Leon Lichtenstein at the University of Leipzig in 1928, with a dissertation on equilibrium solutions of rotating liquids derived from the n-body problem. A German mathematician, he joined the University of Hamburg's mathematics department in 1930, took a professorship at Leipzig in 1948 and a lectureship at Technische Universität Berlin in 1958, and returned to Hamburg in 1964. His name is attached to Kähler metrics and manifolds, the Cartan-Kähler theorem on non-linear analytic differential systems, and Kähler differentials, an algebraic theory adopted in algebraic geometry.

name: Erika V. Iyengar
text:
Erika V. Iyengar is an invertebrate ecologist and Professor of Biology at Muhlenberg College in Allentown, Pennsylvania. She holds a BS with honors from Stanford University and a PhD from Cornell University. Her FHL-connected papers run from 2001 to 2024. The earliest, written with C. Drew Harvell in 2001 and 2002, deal with defenses in marine invertebrates. Most of the later papers come from summer research at Friday Harbor Laboratories. Her college profile says her summer research often takes place there and that many Muhlenberg students have come with her. Several held NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates positions at FHL, among them Kerry L. McGowan, co-author of the epibiont studies. The report's network links her to McGowan and to Brooke Z. Torjman, whose hermit crab studies with her (2021, 2024) were supported by FHL's Blinks-NSF REU-BEACON program.

Iyengar studies interactions between species, especially feeding and defense, and uses present-day ecology to address evolutionary questions. A central subject is the snail Trichotropis cancellata, which steals food from the tube worm Serpula columbiana. Her papers describe this kleptoparasitism (2002), the snail's performance on different hosts (2004), its seasonal changes in feeding mode (2005) and the function of the flexible hairs on its shell (2008). A 2008 review compared kleptoparasitism across the animal kingdom. With Harvell she studied predator deterrence in the early stages of sea stars and sea cucumbers with yolk-feeding larvae (2001) and the cues that trigger defensive spines in the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea (2002). Later work with students covers host specificity in Crepidula adunca (2011), epibionts on intertidal snail shells (2014, 2017), feeding by the native slug Ariolimax columbianus and the invasive Arion rufus (2014–2015), and the cost to hermit crabs of carrying heavy shells (2024).

name: Ernst Hölder
text: Ernst Hölder (1901-1990), a German mathematician, was a doctoral student of Leon Lichtenstein at the University of Leipzig, taking a PhD in 1926 with a dissertation on fluid dynamics and habilitating in 1929 on celestial mechanics. The research covered partial differential equations and continuum mechanics. Hölder was an assistant at Leipzig and then Privatdozent there (1929-1939), a scientific member of the German Aeronautical Research Institute in Braunschweig (1939-1945), and after the war head of Leipzig's Mathematical Institute. From 1958 Hölder was a professor at the University of Mainz, retiring in 1969. Memberships included the Leopoldina and the Saxon Academy of Sciences.

name: Esther M. Leise
text:
Esther M. Leise is a neurobiologist and invertebrate zoologist who studies the development of molluscan nervous systems and metamorphosis. She received a B.S. in zoology from the University of Maryland University College (1975) and a Ph.D. in zoology from the University of Washington (1983), where she was also a teaching assistant. She was a postdoctoral fellow at the University of California, Davis (1983–1988) and a postdoctoral researcher at Georgia State University (1988–1990), then an assistant researcher at the University of Hawaii's Kewalo Marine Laboratory (1990–1991). In 1991 she joined the Department of Biology at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro as assistant professor, becoming associate professor in 1998 and professor in 2008. Her FHL-connected papers, from 1979 to 1986, come from her graduate work, and a 2009 study used a diatom culture isolated at FHL.

As a graduate student she studied molluscan larvae and juveniles. A 1979 paper with Richard R. Strathmann, for which FHL provided space, filmed the beating of cilia and the paths of food particles to study feeding mechanisms and clearance rates in molluscan veligers. Her papers of 1984 and 1986 followed the integument of the chiton Mopalia muscosa through metamorphosis and the development of its sensory organs in juveniles. A 1988 paper described sensory organs in the hairy girdles of mopaliid chitons. As a postdoctoral researcher she worked on crayfish neurophysiology, including sensory afferents, motor neurons and the lateral giant escape neuron. At Greensboro she has studied metamorphosis in the mud snail Ilyanassa obsoleta, testing how serotonin, nitric oxide, GABA, programmed cell death in the larval apical ganglion and cues from benthic diatoms regulate the change from larva to juvenile.

name: Ethan T. Ellis
text: Ethan Tanner Ellis, of the University of Washington Department of Biology, took part in the Aquatic Animals Research Experience in spring 2014 and was lead author, with Petra Ditsche of Friday Harbor Laboratories and Katie Dobkowski, of "Prey Choice of Intertidally Foraging Water Birds." The study made four observations at 4th of July Beach in May 2014, at low and high tide, sorting prey into fish, crustaceans and other. Only gulls were seen, mostly California gulls. Crustaceans were eaten significantly more often than the other categories, and no feeding was seen at high tide. The authors suggested that these birds could exert top-down control on intertidal ecosystems.

name: Eugene N. Kozloff
text:
Eugene N. Kozloff (1920–2017) was a marine biologist and botanist known especially for his field guides to the plants and animals of the Pacific Northwest. He earned master's and doctoral degrees at the University of California, Berkeley, and taught biology and invertebrate zoology at Lewis & Clark College in Portland, Oregon, before joining the University of Washington's Friday Harbor Laboratories in 1966. He later became emeritus professor at FHL. With Richard Norris he started a course that combines marine zoology and botany, and he took his turn teaching on the Seattle campus. He also worked at marine laboratories in Roscoff, France, and in Tunisia. From 2007 he continued his research for several years at Western Washington University's Shannon Point Marine Center. The census counts 15 FHL-address papers by him, from 1965 to 2008.

Much of Kozloff's research concerned small parasites and symbionts of marine invertebrates. He described a new orthonectid from a tube-building polychaete (1965) and later the plasmodium of the orthonectid Rhopalura ophiocomae (1994). Other papers described new acoel flatworms (1965), a ciliate without cilia that parasitizes a sabellid worm (1966, 1967), reproduction in the acoel Otocelis luteola (1999–2000) and umagillid flatworms from echinoderm intestines, among them a new species from the sea cucumber Stichopus californicus (1987). From 2001 to 2008 he published on the ciliate Orchitophrya stellarum as a parasite of Leptasterias and other sea stars. His books include Seashore Life of Puget Sound, the Strait of Georgia, and the San Juan Archipelago (1973), a key to the region's marine invertebrates (1974), Seashore Life of the Northern Pacific Coast (1983), Marine Invertebrates of the Pacific Northwest (1987) and the textbook Invertebrates (1990). Two genera and nine species are named after him.

name: Eugenia del Pino
text:
Eugenia M. del Pino is an Ecuadorian developmental biologist who was Professor of Biology at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador (PUCE) in Quito from 1972 to 2013. Federico D. Brown, an FHL core scientist, took part in del Pino's 1999 developmental biology seminar at PUCE, and del Pino wrote that all its participants later did research and prepared theses in developmental biology under del Pino's guidance. Brown received the licenciado at PUCE in 2001, and both were authors of a 2002 paper on lamina-associated polypeptide 2 in fish and amphibians. Del Pino earned a licenciatura at PUCE (1967), an MS at Vassar College (1969) and a PhD at Emory University (1972), where she worked with Asa Alan Humphries Jr. on the role of egg jelly in fertilization of Xenopus laevis.

She first saw the marsupial frog Gastrotheca riobambae in the PUCE gardens in 1972 and built her research on it, comparing its oogenesis and early development with X. laevis and other tropical frogs. With Humphries she described multinucleated oogenesis in Flectonotus pygmaeus and other marsupial frogs (1978), and with Richard P. Elinson a novel developmental pattern in G. riobambae, with an embryonic disk at gastrulation (1983). She later described two gastrulation modes in frogs, linked to egg size and reproductive mode. PUCE had no doctoral program, and students contributed through undergraduate licenciatura theses she directed. She was named a foreign associate of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences in 2006 and received the L'Oréal-UNESCO Award for Latin America in 2000.

name: Federico D. Brown
text:
Federico D. Brown is an evolutionary developmental biologist at the University of São Paulo (USP), where he has been Professor Doutor in the Institute of Biosciences since 2013 and also works at USP's Centro de Biologia Marinha (CEBIMar). He studied biology at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador (Licenciado, 2001), working in Eugenia del Pino's laboratory. With a Fulbright, he did his PhD (2002-2008) in Billie Swalla's laboratory at the University of Washington and Friday Harbor Laboratories, with visits to Anthony De Tomaso's laboratory at Hopkins Marine Station, and took FHL's Comparative Embryology course taught by Swalla and George von Dassow. He was a postdoctoral researcher in Ralf Sommer's laboratory at the Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology and an assistant professor at the Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá (2010-2013). He is an elected member of the Ecuadorean Academy of Sciences. His FHL-connected papers date from 2007 to 2012.

Brown studies how colonial animals are built, focusing on germ cells, budding and regeneration in colonial ascidians (sea squirts); as a student he also studied developmental modes of Neotropical frogs. His FHL-connected papers on the colonial ascidian Botrylloides violaceus describe expression of the germline gene vasa (2007, with Swalla) and whole-body regeneration (2009). With De Tomaso and Stefano Tiozzo he traced the early specification of long-lived germline precursors in Botryllus schlosseri (2009), evidence that a clonal animal sets aside its germline early, and reviewed regeneration and stem cells in ascidians (2008). A 2008 review with Andrew Prendergast and Swalla examined chordate origins, and a 2012 paper with Swalla used ascidian coloniality as a case study in the evolution of budding by stem cells. At CEBIMar he has coordinated graduate courses on the comparative embryology of marine invertebrates and on coloniality and modularity.

name: Fernanda X. Oyarzún
text:
Fernanda X. Oyarzún is a marine biologist and visual artist who studies the reproduction and development of marine invertebrates. She holds a bachelor's degree in biology from the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile and a PhD in Biology from the University of Washington (2010), with a thesis on brooding, sibling rivalry and population structure in the polychaete Boccardia proboscidea. As a UW graduate student she took FHL's Comparative Embryology course in 2004, taught by Richard Strathmann and George von Dassow, which led her to change her thesis. She later held a Fondecyt postdoctoral project and worked at the Universidad Católica de la Santísima Concepción in Chile; in 2024 FHL described her as an associate researcher at the Coastal Social-Ecological Millennium Institute (SECOS), directing its art and science research. A Fulbright scholar, she was an FHL artist in residence in autumn 2023. Her FHL-connected papers date from 2006 to 2019.

Her research centers on poecilogony, the production of more than one type of larva within a single species, in spionid polychaete worms of the genus Boccardia. With Billie Swalla and colleagues she described the population structure of B. proboscidea along the US Pacific coast and found that worms of different reproductive types can share the same mitochondrial haplotype (2011). Experiments on egg capsules from San Juan Island worms indicated that larval type is fixed early in development, while nurse-egg supply and cannibalism by sibling larvae affect hatching size and survival (2014). A 2009 study found genetic similarity between North American B. proboscidea and worms on cultured abalone in South Africa. With Strathmann she reviewed plasticity in hatching and in the length of planktonic development (2011), and with Stephanie Kamel and Richard Grosberg she discussed family conflict and offspring size (2010). Other papers concern clam digging (2006) and larval feeding while swimming (2019).

name: Fleur P. Anteau
text:
Fleur P. Anteau worked in marine invertebrate and algal biology and was a research assistant on Jason Hodin's sunflower star (Pycnopodia helianthoides) captive rearing program at FHL, shown in a 2021 University of Washington news story checking year-old juveniles in the lab. Anteau came to FHL as a University of Washington student in the spring 2019 course FHL 470, Research in Marine Biology. The resulting report on zoospores of the alga Ulva fenestrata found equal settlement on bacterial biofilms from different tidal heights and motility lasting up to about three and a half hours. It thanks Hodin for teaching on metamorphosis and larval settlement and Tom Mumford for guidance in phycology.

Anteau was an author of the 2021 Biological Bulletin paper by Hodin and colleagues on complete life-cycle culture of the sunflower star, which reported on holding and distinguishing adults, reproductive seasonality, larval development, settlement inducers and early juvenile growth. Anteau was second author, with an FHL affiliation, of the 2025 PLoS ONE paper on temperature tolerance in the species, which placed the optimum for early life stages more than 4°C above ambient Salish Sea temperatures.

text: Florence I. M. Thomas appears under graduate students on the publication list of M. A. R. With a University of South Florida address in 1999, Thomas studied shear stress on echinoderm eggs during spawning; other work covered ammonium uptake by seagrass communities under flow (Ecology, 2000). A later address was the Hawai'i Institute of Marine Biology, with 2014 papers on sea urchin fertilization and coral reef temperature, oxygen and pH.

name: Francois Robin
text: François Robin was a postdoctoral fellow with Edwin Munro, first at the University of Washington and then at the University of Chicago (2009-2014), after a PhD with Patrick Lemaire at the Institut de Biologie du Développement de Marseille (2004-2008). In 2009 he was an instructor at the Center for Cell Dynamics, Friday Harbor Laboratories. His ascidian work included a 2010 Current Biology paper on endoderm invagination with Kristin Sherrard, Lemaire and Munro. He then moved to C. elegans, developing single-molecule imaging of the embryo cell surface (Nature Methods, 2014). From 2016 he led an ATIP/Avenir group on actomyosin dynamics at the Institut de Biologie Paris-Seine, as an Inserm researcher.

name: Frank H. Johnson
text:
Frank Harris Johnson (1908–1990) was a professor of biology at Princeton University who studied bioluminescence. His papers carry a Princeton address from 1931 to 1980. In 1960 he brought Osamu Shimomura from Japan to his laboratory and asked him to purify the light-emitting substance from jellyfish light organs. In the summer of 1961 Johnson, Shimomura and a small team collected the jellyfish Aequorea at Friday Harbor, cutting strips from the luminous rings and taking extracts from about 10,000 animals back to Princeton. Johnson's five FHL-connected papers date from 1962 and 1963 and list the Friday Harbor Laboratories alongside Princeton's Department of Biology or Moffett Biological Laboratory. Shimomura and Johnson collected at Friday Harbor over many summers. When Shimomura resumed the work in Johnson's laboratory in 1967, Johnson built a machine that sped up cutting the rings.

Johnson's papers from the 1930s dealt with respiration and light production in luminous bacteria, and he applied reaction-rate theory to biological processes. His books include The Kinetic Basis of Molecular Biology (1954) and The Theory of Rate Processes in Biology and Medicine (1974), written with Henry Eyring and Betsy Jones Stover. Four of his FHL-connected papers, with Shimomura and Yo Saiga, report the discovery and early study of aequorin: its extraction and purification (1962), further data on its properties (1963), a similar protein, halistaurin, from the hydromedusa Halistaura (1963), and the use of its light to measure small amounts of calcium (Science, 1963). A footnote in the 1962 paper mentioned the green protein later known as green fluorescent protein, for which Shimomura shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The fifth, a 1962 Science note with Dixy Lee Ray, gave a simple method of collecting the isopod Limnoria.

name: Frederick D. Dooley
text:
Frederick D. Dooley is a biologist who has worked on the physiology of seagrasses and on the biology of the cephalopod Nautilus. He earned a BS in biology and a BA in anthropology at the University of Washington in 2009 and a PhD in Biology there in 2015, with a dissertation on the tolerance of seagrasses to hydrogen sulfide advised by Peter D. Ward. His dissertation vita records that he took part in the ZooBot class of 2008 at Friday Harbor Laboratories, with Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria as his advisor there, and was a research technician in the seagrass laboratory at Friday Harbor in 2009–2010. Wyllie-Echeverria co-authored his seagrass papers, which give UW Biology and FHL as addresses; his experiments used containers with flowing seawater at FHL. The census counts four FHL-connected papers from 2012 to 2016. Papers of 2026 give the School of Biology, Everett Community College, Washington.

His dissertation starts from the loss of eelgrass, Zostera marina, from Westcott Bay on San Juan Island in the late 1990s and early 2000s. His FHL-connected papers showed that eelgrass seedlings are sensitive to hydrogen sulfide (2012), that seedlings of the surfgrass Phyllospadix scouleri tolerate even less sulfide (2015), and that stored eelgrass seed loses viability over time (2013). Sampling at eight embayments in the San Juan Archipelago and nearby Salish Sea in 2014 linked sediment sulfide levels to the presence or absence of eelgrass, and he suggested sediment capping as a restoration option for high-sulfide sites. With Ward he also reported increased growth and germination in plants given hydrogen sulfide (2013). His Nautilus work with Ward, Gregory J. Barord, Lauren E. Vandepas and Billie J. Swalla includes baited underwater video surveys in the Philippines, Australia, Fiji and American Samoa (2014), a 2016 phylogeography of Nautilus pompilius, and 2026 studies using acoustic telemetry and stable isotopes.

name: Frederick Dowell
text: Frederick Dowell completed a 2024 University of Washington master's thesis in marine affairs, advised by Terrie Klinger. It scored nine seaweed species, sugar kelp among them, on existing knowledge, global cultivation production, known and future temperature tolerance and amenability to land-based aquaculture. It concluded that sugar kelp was a good crop for Washington and that other native species were also feasible.

name: Frederick Duerr
text:
Frederick G. Duerr worked in the comparative physiology of snails and fish and advised William B. Stickle's doctoral research on the intertidal snail Thais lamellosa. Stickle's thesis, submitted to the University of Saskatchewan, Regina Campus, and dated 1970, used snails collected about monthly at Turn Island, Washington, and taken to FHL. Stickle's 1975 Biological Bulletin paper thanks "Dr. Frederick Duerr, my advisor." Stickle and Duerr published together in 1970 in Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology on how starvation affects respiration and major nutrient stores in T. lamellosa.

Duerr's other papers in that journal include a 1967 study of how digenetic trematode parasitism changes the size-metabolic rate relationship in the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis appressa, a 1967 paper on uric acid in prosobranch and pulmonate snails, and a 1968 study of ammonia and urea excretion in seven marine prosobranchs. Duerr was also an author of papers on starvation in Littorina planaxis (1967) and osmotic adjustment in Tegula funebralis (1969). Two 1975 papers with R. A. Ahokas addressed salinity tolerance and osmoregulation in the fishes Culaea inconstans and Fundulus diaphanus.

Paine finished a Ph.D. at Michigan in 1961. With Nelson Hairston and Lawrence Slobodkin, Smith wrote the 1960 paper "Community Structure, Population Control, and Competition," which set out the green world hypothesis.

name: Frederike Klimm
text: Frederike Klimm was a DAAD scholar from Albert Ludwigs Universität in 2018, listed among the visiting scholars of Adam P. Summers at Friday Harbor Laboratories. With Summers and Thomas Speck, Klimm published a 2026 study of the attachment disc of the brown alga Fucus distichus, with laboratory tests run at FHL and fieldwork in the rocky intertidal zone in front of the laboratories. The study used a setup for continuous in situ mechanical tests, dislodging young individuals and cross-validating with laboratory tensile tests. In the Plant Biomechanics Group at the University of Freiburg, Klimm also published on the tendrils and adhesive pads of climbing passion flowers (2022, 2023, 2024).
