name: Fu-Shiang Chia
text:
Fu-Shiang Chia (1931–2011) was a marine invertebrate zoologist. After a BS in biology from Taiwan Normal University, he earned an MS (1962) and a PhD in zoology (1964) at the University of Washington, doing his graduate research at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He taught for 24 years at the University of Alberta, including five years as chair of zoology and ten as dean of the Faculty of Graduate Studies and Research. He then moved to the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, retired from there in 1997, and directed Taipei Sea World for three years. His obituary credits him with more than 200 research papers and more than 40 graduate degrees supervised. His FHL-connected papers span 1966 to 1995. He was a frequent researcher at the laboratories and served on the FHL Advancement Board.

Chia's research dealt with the reproduction, development and larval biology of marine invertebrates. His early FHL papers described the development of the cushion star Pteraster tesselatus (1966, based on work in the summers of 1960 and 1963), changes in the pyloric caeca of the brooding sea star Leptasterias hexactis (1969), and settlement and delayed metamorphosis in the sea star Mediaster aequalis (1971, with Charles Birkeland and Richard Strathmann). Later work with Alberta students and colleagues covered sea anemones, including a revision of the genus Epiactis (1986), predation on planktonic larvae, a test of Garstang's hypothesis on gastropod torsion (1985), larval settlement cues and sperm formation in chitons. The report's network records him as supervisor of two Alberta doctoral students: J. Timothy Pennington (PhD 1986), on the meroplankton of San Juan Channel and predation on larvae, and Glenys D. Gibson (PhD 1993), on development in the sea slug Haminaea callidegenita.

name: Fujio Egami
text: Fujio Egami (1910-1982), a Japanese biochemist, became a professor at Nagoya Imperial University in 1943 and returned to the University of Tokyo as a professor in 1958. Yoshimasa Hirata worked under Egami at Ueda in wartime and took a Nagoya University doctorate in 1949; English Wikipedia's infobox names Egami as his doctoral advisor. Egami co-wrote a 1949 book on immunochemistry, directed the Mitsubishi Kasei Institute of Life Sciences from 1971 to 1980, and from 1977 was president of the International Society for the Study of the Origin of Life.

text: Gabi (Gabriella N. M.) Mukai was a PhD student of Amy L. Moran in the Zoology program at the University of Hawai'i at Mānoa, defending in March 2025. name: Gareth J. Fraser
text:
Gareth J. Fraser is an evolutionary developmental biologist and Associate Professor in the Department of Biology at the University of Florida, where he is listed as Term Professor for 2024–2027. He received his PhD from King's College London, in the Department of Craniofacial Development and Stem Cell Biology at the Dental Institute. His 2019 paper on pufferfish lists him at both the University of Sheffield (Department of Animal and Plant Sciences and Bateson Centre) and the University of Florida. His FHL-connected papers run from 2019 to 2025. An FHL New Faculty Fellowship supported his ratfish collections. The report's network links him to Karly E. Cohen, a postdoctoral researcher in his group who has also held an FHL affiliation. In 2022 Fraser and Cohen mentored an NSF REU student at FHL.

Fraser's lab studies how evolution, development and regeneration are linked in vertebrate teeth, skin appendages and sensory structures, working mainly with sharks, pufferfishes and cichlids. Recent work covers stem cell niches in the continuously replaced teeth of sharks, the tooth-to-beak transition in pufferfish and a Turing-like patterning mechanism for shark skin denticles. Among the FHL-connected papers, a 2019 study showed that pufferfish skin spines develop through EDA signaling, a pathway shared with other vertebrate skin appendages, and thanked FHL colleagues for pufferfish CT scans. A 2022 REU project described the denticles of the Pacific spiny dogfish. In 2025, with Cohen and Michael Coates, he reported in PNAS that the head clasper of male spotted ratfish carries true teeth grown from a dental lamina. Another 2025 paper described a possible ratfish nursery site in San Juan Channel.

name: Garrett M. Odell
text:
Garrett M. (Garry) Odell was a mathematical and computational biologist at the University of Washington, in the Department of Zoology and later Biology, where he was Professor of Biology. Bibliographic records place his earlier papers at Johns Hopkins University and then Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (1975-1988). FHL describes him as a long-time researcher at the laboratories. He directed the NIH Center for Cell Dynamics, located at FHL from 2002 to 2010, which modeled cell and developmental processes; FHL traces this $14 million center, funded by NIH and UW, to one of its early research apprenticeship teams in cell biology. In 2002 he and Victoria Foe were working at FHL's Whiteley Center on the dynamics of actin and microtubules in cell shape change and division in early embryos of marine invertebrates. His FHL-connected papers in the census date from 1989 to 2012. He died in May 2018.

Odell built mathematical and computer models to ask how gene networks, proteins and mechanical forces produce pattern and shape in embryos and cells. With Victoria Foe he studied mitotic domains in fly embryos (1989) and, with Christine Field, the distribution of actin and myosin in the early Drosophila embryo (2000). With George von Dassow, Eli Meir and Edwin Munro he modeled the Drosophila segment polarity gene network, reporting in Nature (2000) that it behaves as a robust developmental module, and followed with the Ingeneue modeling software and a study of lateral inhibition in the neurogenic network (2002). With Munro he showed that ascidian notochord formation is regulative and driven by polarized cell movements (2002). Later work modeled actin-based propulsion of the bacterium Listeria with Jonathan Alberts (2004, 2009), modeled how microtubules position the cleavage furrow (2008, with Foe), and explored parameters of fisheries food-web models with Sarah Gaichas and colleagues (2012).

name: Gary Freeman
text:
Gary Freeman is an experimental embryologist whose papers give addresses at the University of Texas at Austin, first in the Department of Zoology's Center for Developmental Biology and later in the Section of Integrative Biology. He has used embryos from many animal groups, including ctenophores, hydrozoans, phoronids, brachiopods and mollusks, to compare how embryonic axes and regional fates are established, working at marine stations that include FHL, the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute's Naos Marine Laboratory in Panama and the Kristineberg Marine Research Station in Sweden. Many of his papers from 1981 to 2009 list Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address, some jointly with Texas, and the census credits him with 16 FHL-connected papers from 1976 to 2009.

Freeman's experiments manipulate eggs and early embryos to find when and how axes and cell fates are specified. In ctenophores he altered cleavage planes to study the localization of developmental potential (1976) and traced the establishment of the oral-aboral axis (1977). In hydrozoans he showed that the site where cleavage begins establishes the posterior pole of the embryo (1981) and that eggs can be fertilized only at the site of polar body formation (1982). Other hydrozoan studies covered direct-developing trachyline and siphonophore embryos (1983), calcium signaling at fertilization and metamorphosis (1987-1993, with Ellis B. Ridgway) and how larval age affects the polyp prepattern of the planula (2005, 2009). Work on lophophorates traced regional specification in Phoronis larvae (1991) and in brachiopod embryos, including Terebratalia (1993, 2003), and, with Mark Q. Martindale, the origin of mesoderm in phoronids (2002). A 2006 paper related egg organization in the limpet Lottia to axial specification.

name: George B. Craig
text:
George B. Craig Jr. (1930-1995) was an entomologist and mosquito geneticist at the University of Notre Dame, which he joined in 1957 and where he was named Clark Professor of Biology in 1974. His tie to FHL core scientists is through James W. Truman, who was introduced to biological research as a Notre Dame undergraduate in Craig's laboratory, drawn by Craig's work on hormonal regulation of mosquito mating behavior; Truman later did research at FHL. Craig took a BA in zoology at Indiana University (1951) and an MS (1952) and PhD (1956) in entomology at the University of Illinois, with dissertation research in the laboratory of William R. Horsfall.

Craig built Notre Dame's Mosquito Genetics Project into the Vector Biology Laboratory, centered on Aedes mosquitoes. His work included genetic mutants and linkage maps in Aedes aegypti, among them 87 mutants described in a 1967 study with W. A. Hickey; matrone, a male-produced factor that induces monogamy in inseminated females; variation in vector competence for La Crosse virus among populations of Aedes triseriatus (1977); and the probable introduction of Aedes albopictus to North America in used tires from northern Asia (1987). He directed more than forty PhD students and mentored 39 postdoctoral fellows. He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1983 and received the Walter Reed Medal.

name: George O. Mackie
text:
George O. Mackie (1929-2023) was a comparative physiologist and Professor of Biology at the University of Victoria from 1968 to 1994, emeritus from 1995. He first visited FHL in 1960 as a guest of Joe and Margaret Connell and, by his own account, kept up spring visits on and off for more than 40 years. He began work there on the siphonophore Nanomia in 1961 and studied hydromedusae such as Sarsia with Mac Passano during several summers. He advised Claudia E. Mills for a University of Victoria PhD (1982). With C. L. Singla they published on giant nerve axons and escape swimming in hydromedusae (1985) and on the prehensile tentilla of the ctenophore Euplokamis (1988).

Mackie trained at Oxford (BA 1953, D.Phil. 1957) under W. H. Holmes, with doctoral work on siphonophores, and taught at the University of Alberta from 1956 to 1968. His research asked how nerves, muscles and excitable epithelia produce behavior. At FHL in 1969, with Richard Strathmann and Mackie's PhD student Andrew Spencer, he recorded electrical signals tied to ciliary arrest in echinoderm larvae. With Robert Meech, over many FHL summers, he found axons in the jellyfish Aglantha digitale that conduct both sodium and calcium impulses; with Sally Leys he recorded electrical impulses in glass sponges. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada (1982) and of the Royal Society (1991).

name: George von Dassow
text:
George von Dassow is a cell and developmental biologist who studies cell behavior in embryos and larvae of marine invertebrates. At the University of Washington he worked with Eli Meir, Edwin Munro and Garrett Odell on a computer model showing that the Drosophila segment polarity gene network is a robust developmental module (2000). An FHL centennial timeline names him, with Victoria Foe and Odell, as a recipient of a 2000 Seaver Institute grant for a second confocal microscope at FHL. It also lists him among the postdoctoral scholars, resident at FHL from about 2000, on the team awarded a 2002 federal grant that set up the Center for Cell Dynamics there. He co-taught an undergraduate research apprenticeship and became a regular instructor in FHL's summer Comparative Embryology course. By 2009 he had moved to the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, where he is Associate Professor.

His FHL-connected papers, dated 2002 to 2011 in the census, span genetic network modeling and the cell biology of division. Papers from 2002-2003 introduced Ingeneue, a software tool for reconstituting genetic networks, and explored robustness in the segment polarity and neurogenic networks and in evolution. He then worked mainly on cytokinesis in echinoderm embryos and other cells: light microscopy methods for echinoderm embryos (2004), a microtubule-dependent zone of active RhoA that marks the cleavage plane (2005), fluorescent actin probes based on the actin-binding domain of utrophin (2007), how stable and dynamic microtubules shape the zone of myosin activation (2008), and how asters sharpen a furrow-positioning signal from the spindle (2009). He also contributed to studies of the microtubule regulators MCAK (2005, 2007) and Kif18A (2008) and to larval biology, including the mitraria larva of the polychaete Owenia collaris (2009). At Oregon he has studied nemertean pilidium larvae.

name: Gerald J. Audesirk
text:
Gerald J. Audesirk is a neurobiologist and textbook author who taught at the University of Colorado Denver. He earned a doctorate in neurobiology at the California Institute of Technology, with a 1975 thesis on the organization of the eye of the sea hare Aplysia californica and the relationship between two neuronal circadian oscillators in that animal. He and Teresa Audesirk then worked as postdoctoral researchers at the University of Washington's marine laboratories, and his papers from 1978 to 1980 give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address. From 1982 to 2006 the two taught introductory biology and neurobiology at the University of Colorado Denver, where both are now emeritus professors of biology. With Bruce Byers they are authors of the introductory textbook Biology: Life on Earth, which had reached an eleventh edition by 2016.

At Friday Harbor, Audesirk studied the neural basis of behavior in the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea, a sea slug much used in neuroethology, the study of how nervous systems control behavior. His six FHL-connected papers (1978 to 1980) follow one line of work. A 1978 Nature report and a companion paper describe central motor neurons that drive the cilia the animal uses to crawl. A 1979 study with Richard McCaman and A. O. Dennis Willows examined the role of serotonin when identified neurons control ciliary activity on the foot. Papers in 1979 and 1980 with Teresa Audesirk describe mechanoreceptors of the mouth and other complex mechanoreceptors. At Colorado Denver, with funding mainly from the National Institutes of Health, the Audesirks' laboratory studied how low levels of environmental pollutants harm neurons and how estrogen protects them.

name: Glenys D. Gibson
text: Glenys D. Gibson earned a PhD in the Department of Zoology at the University of Alberta in 1993 under Fu-Shiang Chia, after a 1987 Alberta thesis describing a new species of Haminoea. The thesis acknowledgments record use of Friday Harbor Laboratories, by permission of A. O. D. Willows, throughout most of the work. The research showed that Haminaea callidegenita releases both swimming larvae and non-swimming juveniles from each egg mass, depending on time of metamorphosis and an inducer in the egg mass jelly (Biological Bulletin, 1989 and 1994). At Acadia University, Gibson studied poecilogony and nurse eggs in spionid annelids including Polydora cornuta and Boccardia proboscidea (2004, 2012, 2013).

name: Gordon Gunter
text: Gordon Gunter was a student of Elmer J. Lund at the University of Texas, where he took an MA (1931) and a PhD in physiology and zoology (1945). For the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries (1932-1939) he studied shrimp and oysters in Louisiana and Florida, and studied ichthyology at Scripps. He then worked for the Texas Fish, Game and Oyster Commission, was acting director and director of Texas's Institute of Marine Science (1949-1955), which Lund had first directed, and directed the Gulf Coast Research Laboratory in Mississippi (1955-1971), founding Gulf Research Reports in 1961. He wrote on Gulf fisheries and on salinity and temperature in marine life. He died in 1998.

name: Grace A. Crandall
text:
Grace A. Crandall works on disease and immune response in marine invertebrates and eelgrass. She began a PhD in Aquatic and Fishery Sciences at the University of Washington in fall 2023, advised by Steven Roberts and C. Drew Harvell. Her FHL ties run through Harvell's lab, where she was a research technician from 2021 on sea star wasting disease experiments and from 2022 on the eelgrass team in the San Juan Islands, using eDNA and qPCR to monitor the pathogen Labyrinthula zosterae. She took a BS (2016) and an MS (2020) at the University of Washington, starting as an undergraduate volunteer in Roberts's lab with a capstone on reproductive maturation in geoduck clams.

She was second author of the 2025 Nature Ecology & Evolution paper identifying Vibrio pectenicida strain FHCF-3 as a causative agent of sea star wasting disease, and first author of a 2026 Ecology and Evolution paper comparing juvenile and adult sunflower star (Pycnopodia helianthoides) transcriptomic responses to disease challenge. Her eelgrass papers cover the microbiome under heat stress (2025) and the biogeography of L. zosterae (2026). Her master's thesis, advised by Roberts and Pamela C. Jensen, addressed temperature and the molecular response of shellfish, including gene expression in Tanner crab (Chionoecetes bairdi) threatened by the parasite Hematodinium, with a 2021 preprint.

name: Grace Leuchtenberger
text:
Grace Leuchtenberger, who publishes as Sara Grace Leuchtenberger, is a marine biologist working on the ecophysiology and biomechanics of marine invertebrates and, as of 2026, a Ph.D. candidate in biology at the University of Washington, in Emily Carrington's lab since 2022. In 2020, as a Carleton College undergraduate, she was an REU student at FHL mentored by Michael T. Nishizaki, designing an experiment on how the bay mussel Mytilus trossulus responds to field temperature fluctuations. After her 2021 B.A. in biology she coordinated research in Nishizaki's Carleton lab until March 2022. From April to September 2022 she was a research technician at FHL, running ecomechanics experiments for graduate and undergraduate students in the Carrington lab.

A 2022 PLOS ONE paper with Nishizaki measured thermal performance of fertilization and sperm swimming in the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus and the red urchin Mesocentrotus franciscanus, and combined effects of temperature and pH in the sand dollar. A 2026 Philosophical Transactions B paper with Nishizaki compared mussel respiration under alternating and field-based temperature regimes. With Carrington she worked on mussel byssal thread attachment and coauthored the published FHL Cantilever Point weather station record (2006 to 2021). She coauthored a 2026 method for estimating the surface strength of marine rock with an analog sclerometer. Her doctoral research uses modeling, water quality measurements and field experiments on how oyster reefs influence environmental variability. She was an NSF Graduate Research Fellow and received a 2026 Katherine S. McCarter Graduate Student Policy Award.

name: Grace Phillips
text: Grace Phillips completed a Bachelor of Science with Honours at St. Francis Xavier University in April 2013, co-supervised by Russell C. Wyeth and C. Bishop. The thesis was a baseline survey of biofouling communities at four harbors in northeastern Nova Scotia, using test plates suspended underwater for six weeks and sampled weekly, with temperature, light and approximate water flow recorded. The dominant organisms were the invasive solitary tunicate Ciona intestinalis, two colonial tunicates and the green alga Ulva. Fouling patterns varied widely between and within sites, differences the thesis proposed could guide the choice of locations for field-testing antifouling solutions aimed at specific organisms.

name: Graham Hoyle
text:
Graham Hoyle was an English neurophysiologist who studied neuromuscular transmission in a wide range of invertebrates. His 1960 paper on the swimming sea anemone Stomphia coccinea gives his address as the Department of Zoology, University of Glasgow, together with the marine biological laboratories at Puget Sound. A 2021 column by Dennis Willows says Hoyle had recently moved to the University of Oregon from University College London when he was among the visiting scientists at Friday Harbor Laboratories in the summer of 1963. His FHL-connected papers run from 1960 to 1973. Willows, who later directed FHL, was Hoyle's graduate student, and a 2025 review of Tritonia research places him in the FHL marine invertebrate zoology course in the summer of 1964. The report's network links the two as advisor and student.

In 1963, with Thomas Smyth, Hoyle described the neuromuscular physiology of the giant muscle fibers of the barnacle Balanus nubilus. Willows's column recounts how Hoyle used a glass electrode to show that each fiber is a single cell, the largest muscle cell found in any animal. A 1965 paper with H. L. Atwood and Smyth dealt with single crab muscle fibers. With Willows and D. A. Dorsett he then turned to the nudibranch Tritonia. Papers in 1969 and a four-part series in the Journal of Neurobiology in 1973 described the organization of its central nervous system, how nerve impulse patterns relate to muscle contraction, and the neuronal mechanism of a fixed action pattern, shown to originate centrally in the isolated brain. He also studied horseshoe crabs, sea squirts and locusts, and in 1984 published an essay in Behavioral and Brain Sciences on the scope of neuroethology.

name: Graham Lobert
text: Graham Lobert was a PhD student of Amy L. Moran in the Zoology program at the University of Hawai'i at Manoa, finishing in May 2025. Toh he described spawning and larval development of the giant Antarctic sea spider Colossendeis megalonyx (Ecology, 2024), and he coauthored a 2026 preprint on temperature, oxygen and conductivity on the nearshore benthos around McMurdo Sound. He was a lecturer in biology at Alma College from 2025 and at Central Michigan University from 2026.

name: Gregory A. Wray
text:
Gregory A. Wray is an evolutionary biologist at Duke University. His ORCID record dates his biology professorship there from 1999, and Scholars@Duke also lists professorships in Evolutionary Anthropology (from 2008) and Cell Biology (from 2022). He received a BS from the College of William and Mary in 1981 and a PhD from Duke in 1987. Several papers of 1989 to 1991 give Indiana University, all of them with Rudolf A. Raff. Papers of 1991 and 1992, two of them with Raff, give his address as Friday Harbor Laboratories and the UW Department of Zoology. From 1993 to 1999 he was assistant and then associate professor of ecology and evolution at Stony Brook University. FHL's research bibliographies also list several of his papers from 1996 to 2000, and a 1997 Nature paper with Christopher J. Lowe mentions FHL in its text.

Wray studies how genes and genomes evolve, focusing on changes in gene expression; his main study systems are sea urchins and primates, including humans. His current projects examine how variants in regulatory DNA affect gene function and fitness and how natural selection acts on regulatory elements. His FHL-period papers dealt with the evolution of development in marine invertebrates: the wrinkled blastula of the sea urchin Heliocidaris erythrogramma (1991), a review with Raff of how developmental strategies evolve in marine invertebrates (1991), rates of evolution in developmental processes (1992), and changes in larval form during the post-Paleozoic radiation of echinoids (1992). Later FHL-listed work used molecular data to argue for deep Precambrian divergences among animal phyla (1996), traced changes in the roles of homeobox and other regulatory genes during echinoderm evolution (1997, 2000), studied gene expression during echinoderm metamorphosis (2000), and addressed the systematics of sea stars (2000).

name: Gretchen Lambert
text:
Gretchen Lambert is an ascidian biologist and taxonomist. An FHL centennial timeline records that her association with the laboratories began in summer 1964, when as a graduate student she took the Marine Algology course; Charles Lambert, her long-time research partner, began his the same summer. Until 1998 the Lamberts were based in the Department of Biological Science at California State University, Fullerton. That year they moved to Seattle to do research in association with the University of Washington, and in 2016 an FHL newsletter described her as a long-time FHL researcher and Whiteley Scholar. She has compiled the twice-yearly bulletin Ascidian News since 1975 (with Charles Lambert until 2011), had organized and taught at least 25 ascidian taxonomy workshops by 2023, and in 2016 was one of eight Ascidiacea editors of the World Register of Marine Species. The census lists 23 FHL-connected papers, 1978-2023.

Her research spans the ecology, physiology and especially the systematics of ascidians. A 1968 paper described the ecology and growth of the solitary ascidian Corella willmeriana, and papers with Charles Lambert reported ammonium-based flotation of tunicate eggs (1978) and uric acid accumulation in Corella inflata (1998); she has also studied spicule formation in ascidians. Since 2000 most of her FHL-connected papers have documented non-native ascidians: a global overview of introductions (2001), rapid-assessment surveys of harbors and marinas in southern California, San Francisco Bay, the northeastern United States and southern England (2002-2006), the identity of the invasive colonial ascidian Didemnum vexillum (2009), and records from the Panama Canal (2011), the Galapagos (2019), Puerto Rico (2021) and southern California (through 2023). She described Distaplia alaskensis as a new species (2001) and has reported ascidian faunas from Singapore, Madeira and British Columbia.

text: Guillermina Ramirez San Juan, who also publishes as Ramirez-San Juan, completed a PhD in biophysical sciences at the University of Chicago in 2017, advised by Margaret L. name: H. A. Lessios
text:
H. A. (Harilaos A.) Lessios is a marine evolutionary biologist who studies sea urchins and sand dollars. His papers with FHL-connected co-authors give his address as the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in Balboa, Panama. He has no FHL address of his own; his tie to the laboratory runs through Kirk S. Zigler. Zigler gave both STRI and Friday Harbor Laboratories as affiliations on a 2005 paper with Lessios, and the report's network records Lessios as his probable postdoctoral supervisor at STRI around 2002–2005. Their joint papers in the census run from 2003 to 2013. Some list FHL in an author affiliation or appear in the FHL research bibliography. The acknowledgments of the 2008 and 2013 papers credit fellowships to Zigler from FHL and the Smithsonian Institution.

Lessios's research concerns speciation and the evolution of reproductive isolation in echinoids. It combines phylogeography, molecular evolution and fertilization data. With Zigler he traced the evolution of the sperm protein bindin. A 2003 paper reviewed 250 million years of bindin evolution. Another 2003 paper linked adaptive bindin evolution in Heliocidaris to the shift to direct development. A 2004 study followed speciation and bindin evolution in Lytechinus along New World coasts. A 2005 analysis of five sea urchin genera found that amino-acid divergence in bindin predicts whether gametes of different species can fertilize each other, with as few as ten changes giving complete incompatibility. A 2013 study of 185 Mellita sand dollars from 31 localities recognized eleven species, six of them cryptic. Only one split was clearly caused by the closing of the Isthmus of Panama, about 3 million years ago.

name: H. Gary Greene
text:
H. Gary Greene is a marine geologist. Moss Landing Marine Laboratories (San José State University) lists him among its emeritus faculty as Professor of Geological Oceanography, with a Ph.D. from Stanford University (1977). Bibliographic records place him at the U.S. Geological Survey from about 1969 into the early 1990s and at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute from about 1996 to 2008, alongside a long association with Moss Landing. Since the mid-2010s his papers have given addresses at the Tombolo Mapping Lab on Orcas Island, the SeaDoc Society, Moss Landing's Center for Habitat Studies and Friday Harbor Laboratories. The census counts four papers with an FHL address between 2016 and 2023, among ten FHL-connected items from 2016 to 2025, and lists him as still connected with FHL.

His listed research interests are marine geology, benthic habitats, submarine canyons and landslides, tsunamis and coastal processes. His FHL-connected work maps the seafloor habitat of the Pacific sand lance (Ammodytes personatus), a forage fish that burrows into sandy bottoms in the San Juan Archipelago. A 2016 study with Joseph Bizzarro, Adam Summers and others described the fish's burrowing behavior and functional morphology, using fish held at FHL. A 2017 paper combined sediment sampling, acoustic Doppler current profiling and multibeam bathymetry and found that a large subtidal sand-wave field kept its shape over the years studied. With Matthew Baker of FHL and others he surveyed sand lance habitat from a crewed submersible with a stereo-camera array (2021), assessed hazards to the sand-wave field (2021) and compiled an atlas of sand lance habitat (2024). He also produced oil-spill assessment maps of central Salish Sea seafloor and coastal habitats (2023).

name: Haluk Lacin
text:
Haluk Lacin is a Drosophila developmental neurobiologist who became an assistant professor in the School of Science and Engineering at the University of Missouri-Kansas City in 2023. His tie to FHL runs through James W. Truman, under whose mentorship he did postdoctoral work at HHMI's Janelia Research Campus, where he was based from 2012 to 2018. Truman's affiliations on their 2019 and 2020 eLife papers include FHL. Lacin took a BS at Bogazici University in Istanbul, worked for a year as a research assistant at Baylor College of Medicine, and completed a PhD in developmental biology in James B. Skeath's laboratory at Washington University in St. Louis (2004 to 2010).

His research asks how neuronal lineages, groups of neurons descended from one stem cell, assemble into circuits in the fly ventral nerve cord. With Truman he traced the embryonic neuroblast origins of adult lineages (eLife, 2016) and mapped neurotransmitter use across the nerve cord, finding that all neurons in a hemilineage use the same fast-acting transmitter (eLife, 2019). A 2020 eLife paper showed that the transcription factor Unc-4 promotes cholinergic identity in lineage 11A and proper leg projections and take-off behavior in lineage 7B. He was research faculty in genetics at Washington University from 2018 until the end of 2022. A 2025 eLife paper from his UMKC group, with Truman and Skeath among the authors, presented a split-GAL4 driver library targeting most hemilineages through development.

text: Hannah Tess Scotch was listed as a student co-supervised by Patsy S. Dickinson at Bowdoin College (2022). More specialized species made a larger proportion of correct choices in the learning task.

name: Hans Jørgen Fyhn
text:
Hans Jørgen Fyhn is a Norwegian zoophysiologist who spent most of his career at the University of Bergen. At the University of Oslo he received the cand.real. degree in 1970 and the dr.philos. in 1976, and he held posts there from 1965 to 1980, the last as associate professor (førsteamanuensis) at the Institute of Physiology. He became professor at the University of Bergen in 1981, and Norwegian Wikipedia lists his employment there until 2007. His research stays abroad included Cambridge, the University of Washington, Duke University and Aarhus University. He was a subject adviser to the European Union's CODEST program and sat on the board of the European Society for Comparative Physiology and Biochemistry. His FHL-connected work is three papers from 1972 to 1974, written with J. A. Petersen and Kjell Johansen, that give a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. The 1974 paper also gives the Department of Zoophysiology at Aarhus.

Fyhn's research concerns how animals adapt their physiology to their environment. It covers intertidal invertebrates, environmental toxicology and the physiology of fish larvae. His 1976 Oslo work dealt with physiological adaptations to intertidal life, and a 1986 Bergen work with fish larval physiology and anatomy. He also studied mollusks at the Australian Institute of Marine Science and land crabs in Panama and Venezuela. His FHL papers concern the gooseneck barnacle Pollicipes polymerus. The 1972 paper combined field and laboratory work on body temperature, water loss from the stalk and the regulation of body fluids during air exposure and in diluted seawater. A 1973 report in Science described rhythmic, temperature-dependent hemolymph pressures that are unusually high for an invertebrate and attributed them to a functional heart. A 1974 paper compared gas exchange in water and air over the tidal cycle.

name: Harold A. Scheraga
text:
Harold A. Scheraga (1921–2020) was an American biophysicist who worked on the physical chemistry of proteins. He received a B.S. from the City College of New York in 1941 and a Ph.D. from Duke University in 1946, with a thesis on the kinetics of a chlorination reaction, and first worked on proteins during a postdoctoral year with John Edsall at Harvard Medical School. He joined Cornell University as an instructor in 1947, became full professor in 1958 and George W. and Grace L. Todd Professor of Chemistry in 1965, chaired the chemistry department from 1960 to 1967, and became emeritus in 1992. His honors included a Guggenheim Fellowship (1956), the Eli Lilly Award in Biological Chemistry (1957), election to the National Academy of Sciences (1966) and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1967), and the William H. Nichols Medal (1974). He has no FHL-connected papers in the census.

Scheraga's research concerned how proteins interact with water, the part the hydrophobic effect plays in protein folding, and how polypeptide chains fold into their native structures. He developed statistical-mechanical models of the hydrophobic effect, contributed to early molecular-mechanics models and force fields for simulating proteins and peptides, and in later work compared molecular dynamics simulations of folding with NMR measurements. His place in the report's network comes through one student. Lynn Riddiford earned her Ph.D. in zoology at Cornell in 1961, advised by Marcus Singer and Scheraga, and went on to faculty positions at Harvard and the University of Washington. Wikipedia lists Riddiford as the doctoral advisor of James W. Truman, and in 2016 the two set up their laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories. This places Scheraga two academic generations before FHL's recent work on insect development and metamorphosis.

text: Harsimran Gill is listed among the undergraduate students (honors, REU and similar) in Emily Carrington's lab at the University of Washington. Gill was mentored by Lyda S. T. Harris from 2018 to 2020, on a project using Raman spectroscopy to analyze the polymers in marine debris from the Salish Sea, and coauthored, with Harris and Carrington, a 2021 Marine Pollution Bulletin paper on mussels and microplastic, from the university's Department of Biology. The study measured biodeposits from mussels fed with and without microplastic: those from the microplastic treatment sank 34 to 37 percent more slowly and resuspended at 7 to 22 percent lower shear velocities than those from the algae treatment, so they may disperse farther and shift nutrients from the mussel bed to other communities.

text: Heather Shimamoto was an undergraduate in Billie J. Swalla's lab at the University of Washington during the 2001-2002 school year. text: Heidi Pye, who also published as Heidi Pye Henninger, was a master's candidate with Winsor Watson at the University of New Hampshire in spring 2004. name: Helen Hess
text: Helen Hess was a PhD student of Richard R. Strathmann at the University of Washington, earning a PhD in zoology there in 1991 after a BS at UCLA (1985). Her research concerned the reproductive biology of marine organisms: genetic differentiation in the brooding holothuroid Leptosynapta clarki (1988), spawning synchrony in a Caribbean damselfish (1991, with Christopher W. Petersen), parental care in brooding spirorbid polychaetes (American Naturalist, 1993), and, with Strathmann, oxygen supply and desiccation in marine egg masses (1999). She joined the faculty of College of the Atlantic, later holding emeritus status in biology, biomechanics and zoology, and studied the reproduction of a local sea cucumber with students there.

name: Helen R. Whiteley
text:
Helen Riaboff Whiteley (1921–1990) was a microbiologist at the University of Washington (UW). She received a B.S. in microbiology from the University of California, Berkeley (1941), a master's degree from the University of Texas in Galveston and a Ph.D. from UW (1951). She then returned to California and worked for two years for the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, rejoining UW in 1953; she became a full professor in 1965. She chaired the physiology division and the publications board of the American Society for Microbiology and served as its president in 1976. Her census papers with a Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) address run from 1960 to 1988; most were written with the UW zoologist Arthur H. Whiteley, who later founded the Helen Riaboff Whiteley Center at FHL in her memory, a working retreat for scientists, scholars and artists.

Her research centered on bacterial physiology. With Ernest Schnepf she studied the insecticidal crystal (Cry) proteins of Bacillus thuringiensis, work her Wikipedia entry credits with laying the foundation for genetically modified organisms that express them. Her first FHL-address paper (1960) surveyed the formate-activating enzyme and related tetrahydrofolate enzymes across animal tissues; her later FHL papers concern echinoderm development. With Arthur Whiteley, Brian McCarthy and others she compared base sequences of the RNA used in early development across echinoderms (1970), and followed the replication and expression of maternal and paternal genomes in a blocked echinoid hybrid (1972) and histone gene expression in interspecies hybrid embryos (1974). With Shigeki Mizuno she traced egg-type RNA among the blastomeres of cleaving embryos of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus (1973–1975). A 1988 paper with Michael Harkey described five transcripts that accumulate together in primary mesenchyme cells during skeleton formation in sea urchin embryos.

text: Hidehiko Hashimoto was a postdoctoral scholar in Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago, working on neural tube closure in the ascidian Ciona, a basal chordate. name: Hilary A. Hayford
text:
Hilary A. Hayford is a marine ecologist and Habitat Research Director at the Puget Sound Restoration Fund (PSRF). She joined PSRF in 2020 to develop and carry out science-based plans for restoring Olympia oyster and bull kelp habitat. She received a Ph.D. in biology from the University of Washington in 2016, and her PSRF biography notes earlier work with Friday Harbor Laboratories and the Partnership for Interdisciplinary Studies of Coastal Oceans (PISCO). Her dissertation examined how tidal migration patterns moderate thermal risk in the intertidal snail Nucella ostrina, with experiments run at FHL in 2014; the report's network lists Emily Carrington as her thesis teacher. The census counts four FHL-address papers from 2014 to 2017, and her 2017 paper acknowledges Ragen, Strathmann and Behavior & Neurobiology fellowships from FHL.

Hayford's FHL work asked how intertidal animals avoid heat stress. In field experiments on San Juan Island with Sarah Gilman and Carrington, she showed that Nucella ostrina forages on the coolest available rock faces and at the coolest points in the tidal cycle, which limits its exposure to heat (2014). They also measured body temperatures of a barnacle and two whelk predators in relation to shore height, solar aspect and microhabitat (2015). Other papers examined seasonal changes in gastropod tolerance of heat and desiccation (with William Stickle, 2016), used radio tracking to detect behavioral thermoregulation in snails (2017) and showed how tidal cues reduce the thermal risk of climate change for a foraging snail (2021). At PSRF she has co-authored studies of an unprecedented heatwave's effects on Salish Sea intertidal shellfish (2022, 2024) and a 2026 metric for rating stressors on kelp.

The data proved unsuitable for detecting change over time.

name: Hilda Florence Rosene
text: Hilda Florence Rosene was a doctoral student of E. J. Lund at the University of Texas at Austin, earning a PhD in 1933. She had studied and taught for several years at the Puget Sound Biological Station, later Friday Harbor Laboratories, where Lund was on the summer faculty, and did summer research there from 1924 to 1929 while teaching at the Washington State Normal School in Bellingham. She held University of Washington degrees (BS 1922, MS 1924). She taught zoology at Texas from 1933 until retiring in 1958. Her work on water absorption by plant roots began on a 1939-1940 Guggenheim Fellowship. She died in 1978.

name: Hironobu Ozaki
text:
Hironobu Ozaki (died 2018) was a developmental biochemist who worked on the eggs and embryos of sea urchins and sand dollars from the mid-1960s to the mid-1980s. Sea urchin papers under the name H. Ozaki begin in 1965–1967 with A. Tyler and colleagues on protein and RNA synthesis in eggs, oocytes and early embryos, work that the census record associates with the California Institute of Technology. With Arthur H. Whiteley he studied malate dehydrogenase in the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus (1967, 1970), in papers with an FHL address. A 1974 paper on acetylcholinesterase gives Kitasato University School of Medicine in Japan as his address, and a 1976 paper on the same enzyme lists Michigan State University's Department of Zoology together with FHL. His census papers with an FHL address run from 1967 to 1986. He was a professor emeritus of Michigan State University's College of Natural Science.

Ozaki's research followed how enzymes, nucleic acids and proteins change as sea urchin embryos develop. With Whiteley he characterized L-malate dehydrogenase and its changes during development of S. purpuratus. Other papers examined chromatin from embryos and sperm (1967, 1971), histones of unfertilized eggs and their changes at fertilization (1973, 1979), and RNA and protein synthesis in normal and animalized embryos with W. R. Eckberg (1972–1975). His acetylcholinesterase studies described the enzyme's multiple molecular forms and its localization and differentiation in embryos (1974, 1976). In the 1980s he turned to yolk and egg formation. A 1980 paper characterized yolk proteins of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus. Two 1986 papers showed that the major yolk glycoprotein precursor is secreted by coelomocytes into the coelomic plasma and described a glycoprotein in the accessory cells of the echinoid ovary and its role in vitellogenesis.

name: Hoi-Ying Elsie Yu
text: Hoi-Ying Elsie Yu is listed as a former PhD student of William M. Bement in the Program in Cellular and Molecular Biology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The work used Xenopus eggs to study actin assembly around exocytosing cortical granules. Yu and Bement reported in 2007 (Nature Cell Biology) that mixing of plasma membrane and granule membrane contents triggers local actin assembly, acting through diacylglycerol and protein kinase C beta. A second 2007 paper (Molecular Biology of the Cell) showed roles for myosin-2 and myosin-1e in actin coat compression during compensatory endocytosis. Yu also coauthored a 2009 study of wound responses from the same lab.

name: Holly Barton Keammerer
text: Holly Barton Keammerer earned a PhD in biology at the University of Oregon in March 2011 with Richard B. Emlet as advisor, after a BA in biology at Pomona College (2006). The dissertation examined six salt marshes along the estuarine salinity gradient in Coos Bay, Oregon, covering community structure, seed banks, plant interactions and seedling performance. Four major community types recurred across the estuary, seed banks were more alike within a marsh than within a community type, and interactions between seedlings and established vegetation were highly competitive. A 2013 paper with Sally Hacker reported that negative and neutral plant interactions dominated early life stages.

name: Howard Bern
text:
Howard A. Bern (1920-2012) was a comparative endocrinologist who spent his career at the University of California, Berkeley, joining the Department of Zoology as an instructor in 1948, becoming assistant professor in 1950 and retiring in 1990 as professor of integrative biology. His tie to FHL runs through his PhD student Roger deRoos, who later spent most summers at the laboratories studying glucose regulation in the spiny dogfish. His papers include a 1962 study of aldosterone and other corticosteroids from chondrichthyan interrenal glands, with Carolyn C. deRoos and Edward G. Biglieri, and a 1964 study of prolactin and the pituitary glands of fishes, with Charles S. Nicoll. Bern took his B.A. (1941) and Ph.D. (1948) at UCLA.

His research on diethylstilbestrol (DES), begun in the 1960s, found that exposure during development caused a range of problems in female offspring and helped clarify the drug's role in causing cancer; DES was later identified as an endocrine disruptor, and he coauthored a book on its developmental effects. Later work, partly at the Bodega Marine Laboratory, followed hormone changes in salmon and striped bass moving between fresh and salt water. With Aubrey Gorbman, a former University of Washington zoology professor, he wrote A Textbook of Comparative Endocrinology (1962). He supervised more than 46 PhD students and 36 master's students, mentored more than 90 postdoctoral fellows and visiting professors, and was a member of the National Academy of Sciences.

name: Hugh Forrest
text:
Hugh S. Forrest worked on the biochemistry and genetics of pteridines and of insect development, in papers from 1957 into the 1970s from the Department of Zoology and the Genetics Foundation at the University of Texas at Austin. The tie to FHL runs through Victoria E. Foe, who began her PhD work with Forrest at Texas and finished it at the University of Washington with Charles Laird, later becoming a founding member of the Center for Cell Dynamics at FHL. Foe's 1975 thesis concerned transcription units in embryos of the milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus, an insect Forrest and coworkers had studied since at least 1967, including RNA and DNA synthesis in its eggs (Science, 1967). Forrest and Laird coauthored a 1973 Chromosoma paper on repeat DNA sequences in Oncopeltus.

Pteridines ran through much of Forrest's work. With H. K. Mitchell, Forrest isolated pteridines from Drosophila melanogaster (Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1954 and 1955). With C. Van Baalen and J. Myers, Forrest reported pteridines in a blue-green alga (Science, 1957). Genetic studies followed, including the maroon-like mutant of Drosophila with J. L. Hubby (Genetics, 1960), the terminal synthesis of the brown eye pigment xanthommatin with J. P. Phillips (Biochemical Genetics, 1970), and differential under-replication of satellite DNAs during fly development with M. Blumenfeld (1972). In 1979, with S. A. Salisbury, W. B. T. Cruse and O. Kennard, Forrest described a novel coenzyme from bacterial primary alcohol dehydrogenases (Nature), and Forrest and Salisbury then published on the coenzyme methoxatin (1980, 1981).

name: Hugh P. Stanley
text:
Hugh P. Stanley, a cell biologist and electron microscopist, studied how sperm cells form in fishes, amphibians and insects. Publication records list two Oregon State theses by him, on the reproductive tracts of the nutria (1957) and on reproduction in the ratfish Hydrolagus colliei (1961), and his papers of 1958 to 1963 give the Department of Zoology at Oregon State as his address. Papers from 1965 to 1971 also list the University of Washington School of Medicine, the Zoological Station of Naples and the University of Minnesota. From 1966 to 1990 his papers list Utah State University in Logan, first its Department of Zoology and later its Department of Biology. All five of his FHL-connected papers, from 1983 to 1990, give both Utah State and Friday Harbor Laboratories.

His papers describe, at the level of fine structure, how sperm cells develop and are released. In the 1960s and early 1970s he studied the testis or sperm formation of a goby (1965), the catshark Scyliorhinus and the ray Torpedo (1966), a lamprey (1967), the tidepool sculpin Oligocottus maculosus (1969), the dogfish Squalus suckleyi (1971) and the clawed toad Xenopus laevis (1972). With James T. Bowman and colleagues at Utah State he used male-sterile mutants of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster to study genetic control of sperm development (1972 to 1977). His FHL papers return to the ratfish. He described its sperm (1983) and, with Harold Kasinsky and Niels Bols, reported chromatin diminution during meiosis (1984). With Charles Lambert he examined how an actin-myosin system in Sertoli cells forms sperm bundles (1985) and the fate of mitochondria in maturing sperm (1990); a further 1990 paper described sperm release (spermiation).

name: Hugo von Seeliger
text:
Hugo von Seeliger (1849-1924) was a German astronomer and, from 1882 until his death, professor of astronomy and director of the observatory at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. His tie to FHL is one of academic descent: he supervised the 1884 Munich doctorate of Julius Bauschinger, on the motion of the planet Mercury, and a line of doctoral students runs from Bauschinger through Aurel Wintner, Monroe H. Martin and Simon Levin to Daniel Grünbaum, a scientist at FHL. Seeliger took his doctorate at Leipzig in 1872 under Carl Christian Bruhns. He was at the University of Bonn Observatory until 1877, as an assistant to Friedrich Wilhelm Argelander, directed the German expedition to the Auckland Islands for the 1874 transit of Venus, and became director of the Gotha Observatory in 1881.

Seeliger's main interest was stellar statistics: what the star counts of the Bonner Durchmusterung and the Astronomische Gesellschaft catalogs implied about the structure of the universe. He studied how the albedo of Saturn's rings varies, which supported James Clerk Maxwell's view of their composition, and the brightening of the rings at opposition carries his name as the Seeliger effect. He identified an apparent paradox in Newton's gravitational law, offered an explanation of the anomalous motion of Mercury's perihelion, and proposed that novae arise when a star collides with a gas cloud. He opposed Einstein's relativity. He was president of the Astronomische Gesellschaft from 1897 to 1921 and an Associate of the Royal Astronomical Society from 1892. His later doctoral students at Munich included Karl Schwarzschild and Gustav Herglotz.

name: Hwan Su Yoon
text:
Hwan Su Yoon is a South Korean phycologist who leads the SKKU Evolutionary Genomics Laboratory in the Department of Biological Sciences at Sungkyunkwan University in Suwon. He earned his B.S., M.S. and Ph.D. (1999) in biology at Chungnam National University, with a doctoral thesis on the molecular phylogeny of the kelp families Alariaceae and Laminariaceae. He was a postdoctoral fellow and then senior scientist at the University of Iowa (2000–2007) and a principal investigator at the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences (2007–2011), then joined Sungkyunkwan University in 2011 and became professor in 2014. He was vice president of the International Society of Protistologists (2012–2013) and an associate editor of Phycologia (2012–2014). The FHL affiliation on his 19 census papers (2011–2026) comes from co-authors: FHL's Robert A. Andersen is a co-author on all but one, and Charles J. O'Kelly on the 2011 Rhodella paper.

Yoon's laboratory studies the diversity and genome evolution of algae, especially red algae and the groups whose plastids descend from them, such as cryptophytes, haptophytes, stramenopiles and dinoflagellates. It combines field collection with genome sequencing, including sequencing from single protist cells. Current projects address early plastid evolution in Paulinella, sex in the yellow-green alga Vaucheria, heat and acid tolerance in Cyanidiophyceae, and multicellularity in brown algae. His FHL-connected papers are of two kinds. Taxonomic papers re-examine algal genera using material from their type localities, among them Chrysotila (2014), Ochromonas (2017) and Sarcinochrysis (2018), and describe new species, new genera and a new class, Phaeosacciophyceae (2020). Genomic papers use single-cell genome data to link phagotrophy with the origin of plastids (2012), compare the plastid genomes of dictyochophytes (2019) and cyanidiophytes (2023), and date the origin of brown algae to the Ordovician (2024).

name: Hyuk Je Lee
text: Hyuk Je Lee was a PhD student of Elizabeth G. Boulding in Integrative Biology at the University of Guelph (2003–2008). The thesis compared spatial and temporal population genetic structure in five northeastern Pacific littorinid gastropods with and without a planktotrophic larval phase; two papers with Boulding (2009, 2010) are listed in FHL's bibliography. Lee then held a postdoctoral post at the University of Konstanz (2008–2013), studying mouth asymmetry and handed foraging in the scale-eating cichlid Perissodus microlepis. Lee joined Sangji University in South Korea in 2013, with later work on Korean chum salmon genetics (2022) and environmental DNA surveys of freshwater fish and insects.

text: Hélène Benink was a PhD student of William M. Bement at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Benink's papers with Bement covered cortical flow (2000) and concentric zones of active RhoA and Cdc42 that form around single wounds in Xenopus oocytes (2005). A 2005 Journal of Cell Biology paper with Bement and George von Dassow, which carries an FHL affiliation, showed that microtubules direct a bounded zone of active RhoA before cytokinesis in four echinoderm species and in Xenopus. Later papers address HaloTag protein labeling and imaging reporters (2011–2015).

name: Ian Brosnan
text: Ian Brosnan was a PhD student of Charles H. Greene at Cornell University (Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, 2010–2014), after a BS at the US Coast Guard Academy (2003) and a master's in marine affairs at the University of Washington (2010). The dissertation, "Death of a Salmon," used acoustic telemetry to follow survival and migration of juvenile yearling Chinook salmon in the lower Columbia River and ocean plume. Brosnan was first author of a 2018 paper on a five-stage training pathway for implanting acoustic transmitters in fish. Brosnan joined NASA Ames Research Center in 2014 and has published there on remote sensing in infectious disease ecology (2024).

name: Ian Mahone
text: Ian Mahone was an undergraduate from Michigan State University who worked with Billie J. Swalla and Leonid L. Moroz at FHL in summer 2012, in an FHL Blinks/BEACON/REU internship. The resulting paper, with Swalla, Andrea Kohn and Moroz, cloned the transcription factors brachyury and forkhead from the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei and mapped their expression in adults by in situ hybridization: brachyury in the esophagus and stomach, forkhead in the tentacles and comb rows. Genomic analysis identified 24 forkhead genes in the ctenophore genome.

name: Ila Leigh Cote
text: Ila Leigh Cote was a PhD student in biology at the University of New Mexico; Lloyd Donald (L. D.) Partridge chaired the 1979 dissertation committee. The dissertation used voltage clamp recordings from neurons of the mollusk Aplysia californica to measure how phenobarbital and pentobarbital alter postsynaptic responses to acetylcholine and GABA. Related papers with committee member W. A. Wilson appeared in Nature (1978) and the Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics (1980). A 1990 paper on cancer risk from 1,3-butadiene and a 2017 paper on the use of epigenetic data in health risk assessment list Cote at the US Environmental Protection Agency.

text: Irit Altman was a PhD student of James E. Byers, listed on the Byers lab page with a 2009 degree. name: Irving Weissman

name: Iván Quesada
text:
Iván Quesada is a biologist at the Universidad Miguel Hernández (UMH) in Elche, Spain. His ORCID record lists him as Professor of Nutrition at UMH since 2018. His recent papers also give addresses at UMH's Instituto de Investigación, Desarrollo e Innovación en Biotecnología Sanitaria de Elche (IDiBE) and at CIBERDEM, the Spanish biomedical research network for diabetes and associated metabolic diseases. Bibliographic records show papers with UMH addresses from 1999 onward. From 2003 to 2006 his papers gave addresses in the Department of Bioengineering and at Friday Harbor Laboratories of the University of Washington, where he worked with Pedro Verdugo, who is listed as his teacher in the report's network. The census counts four FHL-address papers from 2003 to 2006, and the FHL research bibliography lists his papers from 2003 to 2007.

His ORCID keywords describe his current research: pancreatic beta and alpha cells, insulin, glucagon, diabetes and obesity. His FHL-connected papers concern calcium signaling and regulated secretion. With Wei-Chun Chin and Verdugo he reported ATP-independent oscillations and release of calcium and hydrogen ions from mast-cell secretory granules (2003). With Verdugo he described InsP3-driven, pulse-modulated calcium signals in the nucleus of ciliated airway epithelial cells (2005). Two papers extended the work to marine phytoplankton: they demonstrated regulated exocytosis in the single-celled alga Phaeocystis globosa (2004) and analyzed the signal transduction behind its light-stimulated secretion (2006). Later conference abstracts, listed by FHL or giving a Friday Harbor address, dealt with modeling calcium and proton oscillations in secretory granules (2007), airway defense (2010) and the storage and release of brevetoxin in the dinoflagellate Karenia brevis (2012).

name: J. A. Petersen
text:
Jorge A. Petersen, who usually published as J. A. Petersen, worked on the zoology and comparative physiology of marine invertebrates. His papers, from the 1960s to 1986, came mainly from the Universidade de São Paulo, including its Department of General and Animal Physiology and Institute of Marine Biology. In the late 1960s he worked with Kjell Johansen on oxygen uptake in a tube-dwelling polychaete worm, and with Johansen, Claude Lenfant and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen on breathing in the electric eel (1968) and a freshwater turtle (1970); those papers list São Paulo, Duke University and the University of Washington. His five FHL-connected papers, from 1971 to 1974, give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, two of them with the UW Department of Zoology. A 1986 paper again lists São Paulo.

In Brazil he studied acorn worms (enteropneusts): a 1964 note in Nature with C. Burdon-Jones described a giant enteropneust, and a 1971 paper reported asexual reproduction in Glossobalanus crozieri. He also wrote a long series of biochemical studies of worms, snails and other invertebrates with F. B. De Jorge. At Friday Harbor he turned to the breathing and circulation of local marine invertebrates. With Johansen he measured gas exchange and active ventilation in the starfish Pteraster tesselatus (1971) and gas exchange in the giant chiton Cryptochiton stelleri (1973). With Hans J. Fyhn and Johansen he studied the ecophysiology of the intertidal barnacle Pollicipes polymerus (1972) and its breathing in water and in air (1974), and the three reported heart activity and high-pressure circulation in barnacles in Science (1973). A 1986 paper with John P. Sutherland and S. Ortega examined the patch dynamics of mussel beds near São Sebastião, Brazil.

name: J. Timothy Pennington
text:
J. Timothy Pennington, a larval ecologist, took a PhD in zoology at the University of Alberta in 1986 with Fu-Shiang Chia, doing all the thesis research at FHL with almost daily advice from Richard R. Strathmann. The thesis described two years of bimonthly plankton samples from San Juan Channel, in which barnacle and bivalve larvae were most abundant, and tested predation on embryos and larvae. Experiments covered the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus, setae of Sabellaria cementarium trochophores, which deterred predators, and hydromedusae feeding on hydrozoan eggs and planulae.

With Chia (Biological Bulletin, 1985), Pennington offered veligers of the abalone Haliotis kamtschatkana to planktonic predators to test Garstang's hypothesis and found that torsion gave little defense. Other work showed how sperm dilution limits fertilization in the urchin Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis (1985) and, with Richard B. Emlet, traced vertical migration of Dendraster larvae (1986). A 1990 Biological Bulletin paper with Strathmann examined how the calcite skeletons of echinoderm larvae affect orientation, swimming and shape.

name: Jack Litle
text:
Jack Litle is an intertidal physiological ecologist who completed a University of Washington PhD in biology in 2026 with Emily Carrington. He first came to Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) in 2017 as a Blinks-REU-BEACON fellow while an undergraduate at Pomona College (bachelor's degree 2018), where he studied herbivory in coastal sage scrub. As a graduate student he divided his year between Seattle and FHL, with support from the Charles Lambert Memorial Endowment, the Richard and Megumi Strathmann Endowed Fellowship, the Riddiford-Truman Award and a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship. In a 2023 FHL essay he named Carrington as his PhD advisor and Richard Strathmann as a mentor.

His dissertation, "Traits, behavior, and seasonal physiological shifts mediate thermal stress in intertidal mollusks," used two species. In embryos of the bubble snail Haminoea vesicula, studied at False Bay on San Juan Island, habitat temperatures usually sat far below those that maximize growth and development, while the high optima let embryos survive heat spikes (Litle and Carrington, Journal of Animal Ecology, 2025). Adults timed egg laying to semilunar tidal cycles, laying less when embryos were predicted to face lethal heat. In the California mussel Mytilus californianus at Cattle Point, the 2021 heat dome favored small mussels on the high shore and large mussels on the low shore, a result examined with heat-budget simulations (data set with Robin Fales, Kindall Murie and Carrington, 2026).

name: James A. Murray
text:
James A. Murray is a neuroethologist who studies how nervous systems control orientation and navigation, mainly in sea slugs. He received a B.S. in neurobiology and behavior from Cornell University (1988) and a Ph.D. in zoology from the University of Washington (1994). His ORCID record lists a National Institute of Mental Health fellowship, from 1995, for research on social communication and reproduction in electric fish. He was associate professor of biology at the University of Central Arkansas (1999–2007), and since 2008 has been associate professor of biological sciences at California State University, East Bay. His FHL-connected work began with papers of 1992 and 1996 co-authored with A. O. Dennis Willows, who gave an FHL address on the 1992 paper. It continued through a 2011 field study that relied on FHL staff for slug collection and dive equipment, and through FHL student research reports he co-authored from 2013 to 2015.

Murray's research uses the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea (now T. tetraquetra) to link identified neurons to behavior. His early papers showed that pedal neurons sensitive to water flow help the slug orient to currents (1992) and identified the nerves that carry out this orientation (1996). Later papers showed that a single identified cell, pedal neuron 3, helps the slug turn while crawling (2005), and reviewed work on the neural basis of orientation and navigation (2006). A 2011 study tracked slugs in the wild day by day to measure how water flow affects their orientation, crawling and drag. He also contributed to a 2000 confocal-montaging method for imaging neural networks and a 2015 study of nudibranch mitochondrial genomes. FHL student reports he co-authored tested for magnetic sensitivity in Tritonia (2013) and in the nudibranch Armina californica (2015), and he co-authored a 2014 paper giving evidence of magnetic sensitivity in chitons.

name: James B. McClintock
text:
James B. McClintock is a marine biologist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB), which he joined in 1987 and where he is Endowed University Professor of Polar and Marine Biology. He received a B.S. from the University of California, Santa Cruz in 1978 and a Ph.D. from the University of South Florida in 1984, followed by a National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellowship at Santa Cruz. Since 1989 he has led or co-directed fourteen U.S. Antarctic Program expeditions, working from McMurdo and Palmer Stations. McClintock Point in McMurdo Sound was named for him in 1998, and he was elected a Fellow of the AAAS in 1999. His eight census papers (1993–2017) are linked to FHL mainly through the laboratories' research bibliography and through work there by his doctoral student Minako Vickery.

McClintock's research centers on the chemical ecology of Antarctic marine organisms, the effects of warming and ocean acidification on calcified marine organisms, and the possible impact of king crabs entering Antarctic shelf waters on seafloor communities. His FHL-linked papers include work on the energy content and chemical defenses of an Antarctic brachiopod (1993), a 2014 research framework for ocean acidification, and a 2017 study of the diets of seaweed-associated amphipods on the western Antarctic Peninsula, whose fatty-acid extractions were done at FHL. The largest group comes from work with Vickery, who conducted most of her research at FHL: a 1998 Nature note on regeneration in larvae, a 2000 comparison of sea star tube feet, two 2001 papers on larval regeneration and on genes expressed early in sea star larval regeneration, and a 2002 study of regrowth in sea star larvae and in larvae of the echinoid Dendraster excentricus cultured at FHL.

name: James E. Byers
text:
James E. (Jeb) Byers is a marine ecologist at the University of Georgia's Odum School of Ecology, where his ORCID record lists him from 2008, now as Professor and Associate Dean. He received his PhD in ecology, evolution and marine biology from the University of California, Santa Barbara, in 1999. FHL's fall 1999 newsletter announced that he would start a two-year FHL postdoctoral fellowship on 1 January 2000, to study how non-native species affect resident invertebrates and whether those effects are greater in marine reserves than in harvested areas. From 2001 to 2008 he was on the zoology faculty of the University of New Hampshire, starting as assistant professor. He has been a visiting fellow at the University of Wollongong and the University of Technology Sydney (2007 to 2008) and a Fulbright fellow at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile (2017). His FHL-connected papers run from 2000 to 2006.

Byers measures the impacts of non-indigenous species on native species, and also studies parasites, ecosystem engineers and marine reserves, mostly working with mollusks and crustaceans. His first papers with a Friday Harbor address (2000, 2001) came from a northern California salt marsh, where the introduced mudsnail Batillaria attramentaria is displacing the native Cerithidea californica. They showed that the invader converts food into growth more efficiently and better survives low oxygen, and, in a model built with Lloyd Goldwasser, that its lower mortality alone could drive the native snail extinct. In the San Juan Islands he showed that crab predation and sediment type confine the introduced clam Nuttallia obscurata to sandy upper-shore sediments (2002), and that marine reserves raised the abundance, but not the competitive impact, of the harvested non-native clam Venerupis philippinarum (2005). With John J. Meyer he found that cropping of clam siphons, as fishes do, nearly doubled the predation mortality of Venerupis (2005).

name: James L. Dimond
text:
James L. Dimond is a marine scientist who works on population genomics and symbiosis in invertebrates. Dimond's ORCID record lists a post as research assistant professor at Western Washington University's Shannon Point Marine Center, the address on papers through 2026. After a year as a technician and research assistant in Emily Carrington's lab at the University of Rhode Island, studying byssal attachment in mussels, Dimond earned an MS with Carrington in 2006 and wrote two papers with her on the temperate coral Astrangia poculata, on seasonal variation in symbiosis and growth (2007) and on zooxanthellae division and expulsion (2008), and was a coauthor on her 2009 field test of a model predicting wave dislodgment of mussel beds. Dimond later took a University of Washington PhD (2019) with Steven B. Roberts in the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences, with Kenneth P. Sebens on the graduate committee from 2014 to 2019.

Working from Shannon Point, Dimond studied the sea anemone Anthopleura elegantissima and its algal symbionts with Brian Bingham and Gisele Muller-Parker, including a 2011 study of aerial exposure and body temperature whose field samples were collected with FHL permission. The dissertation, "Patterns, dynamics, and potential roles of DNA methylation in reef corals and their allies," drew on transcriptome data from six coral species and Porites colonies from Belize. Later papers applied genomic methods to the basket cockle Clinocardium nuttallii (2022), with Puget Sound Restoration Fund among the addresses, pinto abalone Haliotis kamtschatkana (2024) and Dungeness crab (2026). Dimond also coauthored the 2026 PNAS report of a transmissible cancer outbreak in Puget Sound soft-shell clams.

name: James M. Newcomb
text:
James M. Newcomb is a neurobiologist who studies the nervous system and behavior of nudibranch sea slugs. His early papers, from 2001 to 2004, were written with Winsor H. Watson III, and those on the nudibranch Melibe leonina give addresses at the Zoology Department and Center for Marine Biology of the University of New Hampshire and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He then worked with Paul S. Katz at the Neuroscience Institute of Georgia State University, and his later papers give the Department of Biology and Health Science at New England College in Henniker, New Hampshire, as his address. The census counts five papers with an FHL address (2001 to 2004) and ten FHL-connected papers in all, running to 2021; the later ones describe animals collected at FHL and experiments done there, and several thank the laboratories' staff.

All of Newcomb's FHL-connected papers concern Melibe leonina. The early ones mapped neurons in its central nervous system that appear to produce nitric oxide (2001), showed that nitric oxide modulates swimming (2002), described neural activity correlated with swimming (2002) and tested how light affects locomotion (2004). With Katz he compared Melibe with Tritonia diomedea, which swims differently, and showed that homologous serotonergic interneurons and serotonin play different roles in the two species' swimming, so that the evolution of the behavior involved changes in the functions of the same identified neurons (2009). Later papers with Watson examined daily rhythms of crawling and swimming (2014), putative circadian clock transcripts in the brain (2018), a small cardioactive peptide that may promote nighttime arousal, feeding and swimming (2020), and whether the digestive diverticula harbor photosynthetic symbionts, which they do not (2021).

name: James S. Albert
text:
James S. Albert is an ichthyologist and professor of biology at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. He earned a B.S. in zoology at the University of California, Berkeley in 1987 and an M.S. and Ph.D. in zoology at the University of Michigan. He has written more than 100 papers on the evolution and diversity of fishes, and he and colleagues have described 50 new species. He co-edited Historical Biogeography of Neotropical Freshwater Fishes (2011, with Roberto E. Reis), which explores how the Amazon and other Neotropical fish faunas formed, and the Field Guide to the Fishes of the Amazon, Orinoco, and Guianas (2017, with Peter van der Sleen). His eight census papers (2018–2026) come from work with Kassandra Ford, whom the report's network links to him as a student, with Kory Evans, and with FHL's Adam Summers. Several rely on CT scans of fish specimens made at FHL.

Albert's research centers on the systematics and biodiversity of Neotropical electric fishes (order Gymnotiformes). His FHL-connected papers concern the shape of the electric-fish head and skull. Two from 2018 examine sexually dimorphic head shapes in Neotropical electric fishes, treated as weapons, including how they scale with body size and their performance trade-offs. A 2020 paper redescribes a deep-channel ghost knifefish and assigns it to a new genus. In 2022 Ford, Albert and colleagues compared skull shape in 391 specimens of 78 species of South American Apteronotidae and African Mormyridae, CT-scanned at FHL, and found the convergence between the two families incomplete, or 'only skin deep'. Other 2022 papers trace mosaic craniofacial evolution in ghost knifefishes and relate functional diversity to abiotic gradients. A 2023 review surveys methods for comparative anatomical studies, and a 2026 paper treats craniofacial evolution in mormyrids.

name: James William Truman
text:
James W. Truman is an insect neurobiologist and endocrinologist. After undergraduate work at the University of Notre Dame in the mosquito laboratory of George B. Craig, he earned a Ph.D. at Harvard University in 1970 under Lynn Riddiford and was a junior fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows until 1973. He joined the University of Washington zoology faculty in 1973 and stayed for 34 years; in 2007 he became a group leader at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus. After nine years there he retired and returned to the University of Washington as professor emeritus of biology, continuing his research at Friday Harbor Laboratories. His honors include the Newcomb Cleveland Prize (1970), a Guggenheim Fellowship (1986) and election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2009) and the National Academy of Sciences (2022). The census counts 26 FHL-address papers from 2017 to 2026.

Truman's research concerns how hormones direct the development and function of the insect nervous system, especially its remaking at molting and metamorphosis. His thesis work on adult emergence in giant silkmoths led to the isolation of eclosion hormone, and later work in moths, including the hornworm Manduca sexta, examined how ecdysone and juvenile hormone govern neurogenesis, neuronal death and remodeling. He later turned to Drosophila, mapping neuronal lineages and circuits. His FHL-connected papers include a systematic nomenclature for the Drosophila ventral nerve cord (2020), studies of larval circuits for navigation, chemotaxis and forward and backward crawling (2018-2019), and a 2023 account of how memory circuits are rebuilt at metamorphosis. A parallel line on juvenile hormone, including its embryonic role in the firebrat Thermobia domestica (2023) and reviews of the evolution of insect metamorphosis (2019, 2026), asks how complete metamorphosis arose.

name: Janet L. Leonard
text:
Janet L. Leonard is a biologist who studies invertebrate behavior, especially in cnidarians and gastropod mollusks, and the evolution of hermaphrodite mating systems. Her five FHL papers (1980–1983) give addresses at the Department of Zoology of the University of Wisconsin–Madison and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. The 1982 Journal of Experimental Biology paper reports observations made at FHL in 1976 and 1977, thanks the laboratories' staff, and gives her current address as the Division of Medical Physiology at the University of Calgary. Her later papers give addresses at Calgary, the University of California, San Diego, and the University of Oklahoma in the 1980s and early 1990s, then at Oregon State University's Hatfield Marine Science Center and, from 1999, the Joseph M. Long Marine Laboratory of the University of California, Santa Cruz.

Leonard's FHL papers analyze how a simple animal organizes its behavior. Working with the hydromedusa Sarsia tubulosa, she described the temporal organization of its swimming (1980) and its density regulation (1980), used maximum entropy spectral analysis to find transient rhythms in swimming (1982), made an experimental test of the 'Jennings hypothesis' of behavioral organization (1982) and tested the effect of environmental factors on swimming (1983). She proposed that switching among several short-lived rhythms, which may arise in the marginal pacemaker system, accounts for much of the variability in Sarsia's swimming. Her later work turned to gastropods: ethograms of the sea slugs Navanax inermis (1984) and Aplysia californica (1986), studies of the Aplysia gill-withdrawal reflex, and a long series on mating in simultaneous hermaphrodites, from sperm trading in Navanax (1984) to theory on sexual selection and sexual systems and the reproductive biology of Ariolimax slugs.

name: Jaquan M. Horton
text:
Jaquan M. Horton is a comparative biomechanist who has studied the mechanical properties of fish tissues and the locomotion of fishes and amphibians. His first paper (2004) gives Organismic and Evolutionary Biology at the University of Massachusetts Amherst as his address. A 2009 paper gives the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of California, Irvine, together with Friday Harbor Laboratories, and his locomotion papers of 2009 and 2011 give FHL alone. He completed a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington in 2020. A 2022 paper from that thesis was supported in part by an FHL fellowship awarded to him and Emily Carrington. His FHL-connected work runs from 2009 to 2022.

His FHL-connected papers apply materials testing and motion analysis to fishes. With Adam P. Summers he used bending tests on the ribs of the great sculpin, Myoxocephalus polyacanthocephalus, to measure the stiffness of acellular bone (2009). Two studies with Summers and Elizabeth L. Brainerd, led by Bryan Nowroozi and Nicholas J. Gidmark, measured lift and ground effect in the northern spearnose poacher Agonopsis vulsa swimming with its pectoral fins (2009) and how sand lances change their undulating movements as they pass from water into sand (2011). For his thesis he built a pressure-inflation method to measure the passive mechanics of the intestine in two stomachless surfperches, Cymatogaster aggregata and Embiotoca lateralis. The front part of the intestine was stronger, more extensible and tougher than the rear, which suggests it works like a stomach. He reported the C. aggregata results with John M. Gosline and Carrington in 2022.
