name: Jason Hodin
text:
Jason Hodin is a developmental and evolutionary biologist who studies the larvae of marine invertebrates. He received a BA in biology from Wesleyan University (1991) and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington (1999), with a dissertation supervised by Lynn Riddiford on the evolution of reproductive strategies in dipteran insects. Between 1999 and 2004 he taught at several colleges in Seattle and California, and from 2005 he worked with David Epel at Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station as co-principal investigator and staff scientist on the high-school education projects Virtual Urchin and I2SEA. Since October 2015 he has been a Senior Research Scientist at FHL, where he taught Research in Marine Biology (FHL 470) in 2019 and has led the University of Washington's captive rearing of the sunflower sea star, Pycnopodia helianthoides, in a partnership with The Nature Conservancy. The census lists 19 FHL-connected papers, 2004-2026.

Hodin's research asks how hormones and environmental cues shape larval development and the timing of metamorphosis and settlement. Papers in 2004 showed that thyroid hormone shifts developmental timing in sand dollar larvae and can determine their developmental mode, followed by reviews on hormone signaling and metamorphosis (2004-2006). A later series examined how turbulence affects larvae: turbulent shear spurs settlement in sea urchin larvae (2013), late-stage sand dollar larvae respond more readily to it, and brief intense turbulence produces a lasting life-history shift (2015-2019). He has also published a staging scheme for late larval development in the purple sea urchin (2014) and methods for rearing echinoderm larvae (2018). His papers since 2021 center on the sunflower star: life-cycle culture (2021), its predation on urchins and kelp forest recovery (2023), larval tolerance of warming (2025), and sea star wasting disease, including the 2025 identification of Vibrio pectenicida as a causative agent.

name: Jason Olmstead
text: Olmstead was a UW undergraduate in the Marine Biology Research Apprenticeship at FHL in spring 2011, mentored by Charles O'Kelly. The pilot study grew the diatoms Asterionellopsis glacialis, Thalassiosira sp. and Chaetoceros sp. from the FHL culture collection at different temperatures and nutrient levels to gauge biofuel potential, and identified A. glacialis as the best candidate.

name: Jason Pitt
text: Jason Pitt rotated through Billie Swalla's lab at the University of Washington in autumn 2001, and the lab's page says Pitt then did research at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center. Papers by Jason N. Pitt with A. R. Ferré-D'Amaré dealt with RNA ligase ribozymes (2009), listing the University of Washington's Molecular and Cellular Biology Program, and empirical RNA fitness landscapes (Science 2010), listing Fred Hutchinson.

name: Jason Stumpff
text: Jason Stumpff was a postdoctoral fellow in Linda G. Wordeman's lab at the University of Washington (2005-2011), after a 2004 PhD at the University of Colorado Boulder. Stumpff studied how the kinesin-8 motor Kif18A controls chromosome movement during mitosis; a 2008 Developmental Cell paper with George von Dassow of Friday Harbor Laboratories, Michael Wagenbach, Charles L. Asbury and Wordeman showed that it suppresses kinetochore movements to align chromosomes. Stumpff joined the University of Vermont in 2011 and became professor of molecular physiology and biophysics in 2024, leading a lab on kinesins, cell division and cancer.

name: Jay Barlow
text: Jay Barlow, who worked at NOAA's Southwest Fisheries Science Center from 1982 to 2022, co-mentored Jessica M. Kendall-Bar with Dave Weller during a 2015 Hollings Scholarship internship in La Jolla on pilot whale photo-identification. Barlow earned a PhD in biological oceanography at Scripps Institution of Oceanography and published on cetacean abundance and distribution, including in a changing climate.

name: Jay Raveill
text: Jay Raveill appears among Billie J. Swalla's lab members at Vanderbilt University for 1995-96, around his 1995 Vanderbilt PhD. His earlier degrees came from Northwest Missouri State University and Southern Illinois University. Papers from those years with David E. McCauley addressed founding events and genetic structure in plant populations, including chloroplast DNA and allozyme variation in Silene alba (1995, 1996). He moved to Central Missouri State University; at the University of Central Missouri he was professor of biology as of 2025, curating its 20,000-specimen herbarium (WARM) and studying the taxonomy and phylogeny of the legume genus Desmodium and related genera.

Parrish, a professor of biology at the University of Washington, chaired the committees for Jiae Lee's 2016 PhD on dendrite growth in Drosophila and Melissa Eng's 2016 master's thesis on microtubule dynamics in neurons. name: Jayna Devore
text: Jayna DeVore was a postdoctoral associate with James E. Byers at the University of Georgia's Odum School of Ecology in 2012-13, after a University of Georgia PhD through the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources. A 2014 Ecology paper with Jeffrey T. Wright, Byers and Erik E. Sotka examined mechanisms of facilitation by a habitat-forming invasive seaweed. DeVore then studied invasive cane toads with Richard Shine at the University of Sydney (2013-2018), including a 2021 PNAS paper on the evolution of targeted cannibalism. DeVore was a University of Washington research scientist (2021-2023) and, as of 2026, at the University of French Polynesia, working on seabirds and atoll ecosystems.

name: Jeannette Zamon
text: Zamon earned an MSc at Cornell University in 1993 under Charles Greene, on penguin-krill patchiness in the Antarctic, and a PhD at UC Irvine under George L. Hunt Jr., on tidal forcing of plankton-fish-predator interactions in the San Juan Islands (papers 2001-2003). She held a postdoctoral fellowship with David Welch in Nanaimo, then joined NOAA's Northwest Fisheries Science Center in 2002, working on bird predation on Columbia River salmon.

name: Jeannine Fischer
text: Fischer was an MS student of Nicole Phillips at Victoria University of Wellington, with a 2012 thesis on how environmental stressors affect early development of intertidal and subtidal gastropod embryos. A 2014 Global Change Biology paper with Phillips showed that stress on Siphonaria australis egg masses carried over to larvae exposed to elevated UVB and temperature.

name: Jeff Beauvais
text: Jeff Beauvais was a PhD student of James E. Byers at the University of Georgia's Odum School of Ecology, finishing in integrative conservation in 2023. Papers with Byers mapped coastal infrastructure in the southeastern United States: a 2023 Ecological Applications paper on access to public and private structures and a 2024 Scientific Reports paper on the growth of private docks in South Carolina. Beauvais earlier wrote on predator-prey cascades with Marc Weissburg at Georgia Institute of Technology (2015). A 2023-24 Knauss Marine Policy Fellowship through Georgia Sea Grant and contract GIS analysis for NOAA followed, and from 2025 a post with the Georgia coastal conservation group One Hundred Miles.

name: Jeff Brown
text: Jeff Brown is listed as an assistant curator, 2007-2016, at the Provasoli-Guillard National Center for Marine Algae and Microbiota at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences, the culture collection Robert A. Andersen directed from 1989 to 2009. The center's history records that in autumn 1981 Brown and Robert Guillard drove the collection, first housed at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, to Bigelow in Maine. Brown's listed curatorial years overlapped the last years of Andersen's directorship.

name: Jeff Shimeta
text: Jeff Shimeta was a postdoctoral fellow with M. A. R. Koehl at the University of California, Berkeley (Miller Institute, 1993-1995), after a 1993 University of Washington PhD in oceanography. The work concerned how suspension feeders capture particles: a 1995 study with Peter A. Jumars and Evelyn J. Lessard on turbulence and feeding by planktonic protozoa, a 1996 paper on particle selection by the spionid polychaete Pseudopolydora paucibranchiata, and a 1997 paper with Koehl on selection mechanisms. Shimeta then worked at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and taught at Franklin & Marshall College (1997-2005). Shimeta joined RMIT University in Australia in 2007; later papers address biofilm ciliates, microbeads and pollutants.

name: Jeffrey D. Laurence-Chasen
text: Jeffrey D. Laurence-Chasen was a 2015 Blinks-REU-Beacon summer intern at Friday Harbor Laboratories with Elizabeth L. Brainerd, while an undergraduate at Brown University. The project developed Video Reconstruction of Moving Morphology, using biplanar video and 3-D models to test the opercular linkage in two sculpins, Leptocottus armatus and Hemilepidotus hemilepidotus; a companion report examined vertebral bending in suction feeding. Laurence-Chasen earned a 2021 University of Chicago PhD on primate tongue neuromechanics, advised by Callum F. Ross, with a 2023 Nature Communications paper on cortical encoding of tongue shape. A later affiliation is the National Laboratory of the Rockies, in data, analysis and visualization.

name: Jeffrey Maynard
text:
Jeffrey Maynard is a coral reef scientist who works on climate projections and reef management. Maynard's ORCID record lists a BSc and MAppSc at James Cook University, a PhD in global change biology and environmental risk at the University of Melbourne, and the post of director at SymbioSeas, a marine applied research group. Maynard was a postdoctoral associate in C. Drew Harvell's lab at Cornell University. A May 2015 news release named Maynard as a postdoctoral researcher in ecology and evolutionary biology and lead author of a Nature Climate Change paper projecting the climate conditions that raise coral susceptibility to disease and pathogen virulence, with global maps of disease risk for reef managers.

Maynard and Harvell coauthored a 2015 Science letter, "Emergency response for marine diseases"; a 2016 review, "Managing marine disease emergencies in an era of rapid change," from a research network with logistical support from FHL; and a 2016 study of ochre star mortality during the 2014 wasting disease epizootic, covering Pisaster ochraceus in the San Juan Islands and elsewhere in Washington, with a temperature experiment at FHL. Maynard's earlier work included the ReefTemp bleaching monitoring system (2008) and frameworks for responding to coral bleaching (2009) and coral disease outbreaks (2012). Later titles include global warming and bleaching trends for reefs (2016) and a manager's guide to reef restoration planning (2020).

name: Jeffrey Paul Thomas
text: Thomas earned a Master of Marine Affairs at the University of Washington in 2015, with David Fluharty as chair and Terrie Klinger on the reading committee. The thesis, "Sound Health for Sound Tribes," examined how risk assessments of salmon recovery actions treat effects on the culture and well-being of Puget Sound tribes, and offered a Community Sustenance Dynamics model centered on accessible, high-quality local resources.

Shima, a professor in the School of Biological Sciences at Victoria University of Wellington, is listed with Nicole Phillips as doctoral advisor of Sonja Lee Miller, whose 2008 thesis assessed ra'ui in Rarotonga, Cook Islands. Shima earned a PhD at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and studied reef fish ecology, including how moonlight shapes reef life histories.

name: Jeffrey Wright
text: Jeffrey Wright worked with Susan Lynn Williams at Bodega Marine Laboratory, where a 2004 Marine Biology paper with Williams and Megan N. Dethier of Friday Harbor Laboratories compared Fucus gardneri embryos, juveniles and adults across tidal zones and seasons. Earlier papers (1997-2000) covered sponge assemblages and the red alga Delisea pulchra. At the University of Wollongong, Wright studied fragmentation in invasive Caulerpa taxifolia (2005). A 2014 Ecology paper on an invasive seaweed, with James E. Byers and Jayna DeVore, gave a University of Tasmania affiliation, and Wright was working on kelp at its Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies as of 2026.

name: Jenn Huber
text: Jenn Huber was an MS student of Billie J. Swalla at Penn State from 1997 to 1999, with a degree in biology. Huber was first author, with K. Burke da Silva, W. R. Bates and Swalla, of a 2000 paper in Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology on the evolution of tailless (anural) larvae in molgulid ascidians, drawing on 18S and 28S ribosomal phylogenies.

name: Jenna C. Rolf
text: Jenna C. Rolf was a master's student of Terrie Klinger at the University of Washington, with a 2022 thesis in marine affairs. Rolf used video transects from five sites in the western Strait of Juan de Fuca, 2011 to 2019, to test for shifts from kelp-dominated reefs to urchin barrens after sea star wasting disease. One site, where sea otters were routinely present, changed little.

name: Jenna Judge
text: Jenna Judge, of the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, advised Jessica M. Kendall-Bar's undergraduate research on deep-sea wood falls in 2013 and 2014. With James P. Barry of the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, Judge published a 2016 Ecology paper showing that wood type strongly influenced macroinvertebrate communities on wood falls in Monterey Bay.

name: Jenna Rackovan
text: Jenna Rackovan was an MS student at the University of New Hampshire, with a 2016 thesis listing William H. Howell as first advisor, Elizabeth A. Fairchild as second and Winsor H. Watson as third. Rackovan measured how salinity affects oxygen consumption in juvenile lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) and studied their timing and distribution in the Great Bay Estuary, published with Howell in Regional Studies in Marine Science (2017).

name: Jenna Sullivan
text: Jenna Sullivan was a student in the Friday Harbor Laboratories Larval Biology course, summer 2014, taught by Daniel Grünbaum and Richard B. Emlet, while in Oregon State University's Department of Integrative Biology. With Silke Bachhuber, Sullivan measured swimming and sinking of Pisaster ochraceus larvae and modeled their stability in shear. As Jenna Sullivan-Stack, Sullivan completed an Oregon State PhD (2019), publishing on whelks after Pisaster declines and on marine protected areas.

name: Jenna Valley
text: Jenna Valley earned a 2016 University of Oregon PhD with Richard B. Emlet as advisor, based at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology. The dissertation examined phenotypic plasticity: veliger larvae of the snail Littorina scutulata changed shell and velum form in response to cues from predatory crab larvae, food and gravity, and juvenile Strongylocentrotus purpuratus urchins turned from green to purple with sunlight. A 2018 Marine Ecology Progress Series paper with Emlet reported the predator work. Valley had earlier taken a 2011 MS at Appalachian State University. Later work at the institute included microinjection methods with George von Dassow (2019).

name: Jennafer Malek
text: Jennafer Malek was a PhD student of James E. Byers at the University of Georgia, finishing in 2015. In summer 2012 Malek took the Ecology of Infectious Marine Disease course at Friday Harbor Laboratories and co-wrote, as Jenna Malek, a report on whether acidification alters the susceptibility of Crassostrea gigas larvae to Vibrio tubiashii. With a Smithsonian Environmental Research Center affiliation, Malek published with Denise Breitburg on Perkinsus marinus infection in eastern oysters (2016) and joined a 2012 paper on ocean sprawl and jellyfish blooms. Papers with Byers covered predators, tidal elevation and air temperature in oyster-parasite interactions (2016-2018). Malek held a 2016 NOAA Knauss Marine Policy Fellowship.

name: Jennie Beltrán
text: Jennie Beltrán was an MS student of Adam P. Summers. A 2006 Journal of Experimental Biology study with Marianne E. Porter, Thomas J. Koob and Summers, from the University of California, Irvine, tested mineralized vertebral cartilage from seven elasmobranch species and found it as stiff and strong as mammalian trabecular bone. A 2013 PeerJ preprint with Porter, Stephen M. Kajiura, Koob and Summers examined material properties and biochemical components of jaws and chondrocrania in sharks, skates and rays, and gives a Santa Ana College affiliation. Beltrán was an assistant professor of biology at that California college in 2016.

text: Jennifer Ann German was an MS student in marine biology at the University of Oregon (2001), advised by Nora B. Terwilliger, with Alan Shanks and Richard B. Emlet on the committee. German's thesis examined hemocyanin polymorphism in the red rock crab Cancer productus, testing whether oligomers and subunits shifted with temperature or salinity, which they did not significantly, and measuring oxygen binding.

Sebens, on the feeding biology of anthozoans. The three wrote a 2004 Coral Reefs paper on near-reef zooplankton in Jamaica. Purcell was at Western Washington University's Shannon Point Marine Center in 2012.

name: Jennifer Hempelmann
text: Jennifer Hempelmann carried out a Puget Sound rockfish (Sebastes emphaeus) project in the spring 2003 marine molecular ecology research apprenticeship at FHL, taught by Erik Sotka and Christiane H. Biermann. It led to a 2005 Marine Biotechnology paper with both instructors: mitochondrial sequences from 128 adults at five sites showed no significant genetic differentiation and pointed to population expansion. Later papers by Jennifer A. Hempelmann concern resident killer whales: prey species and stocks (2009), paternity inferred from microsatellites (2011) and diet estimated by DNA sequencing of feces (2016), the last from NOAA's Northwest Fisheries Science Center in Seattle.

name: Jennifer Israel
text: Jennifer Israel, on earlier papers Jennifer A. Wygoda, earned a PhD at Duke University (2010 to 2015) and was a member of Gregory A. Wray's lab. name: Jennifer R. Hoffman
text:
Jennifer R. Hoffman is a marine ecologist who later turned to climate-change adaptation. The census papers appear to belong to Jennifer Hoffman, an affiliate of EcoAdapt. Its listing says she has an undergraduate degree in geology from Brown University and a Ph.D. in marine ecology from the University of Washington, began studying the effects of global change as a toxicologist in 1992, co-founded EcoAdapt, and now works independently through Adaptation Insight. She co-wrote Climate Savvy: Adapting Conservation and Resource Management to a Changing World with Lara Hansen, who also co-authored her 2003 FHL paper. Bibliographic records give her addresses at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (1995), at FHL (2000 to 2004) and at the National Wildlife Federation (2012). The report's network lists Terrie Klinger, her co-author, as a teacher.

Her FHL work examined how ultraviolet radiation, alone and with temperature, affects the early life stages of marine organisms. With Benjamin Miner and Steven Morgan she tested whether chromatophores in decapod crustacean postlarvae collected from the FHL docks are an adaptation to UV radiation (2000). With Hansen and Klinger she exposed early stages of the brown algae Alaria marginata and Fucus gardneri to combinations of UV and temperature. Each factor changed the effect of the other, which limits what single-factor experiments can show (2003). With Miles Lamare she studied natural variation of carotenoids in the eggs and gonads of Strongylocentrotus sea urchins and its bearing on UV protection (2004). She also co-authored papers on risk and the evolution of embryonic cell-cycle durations (with Richard Strathmann, 2002) and on thyroxine and non-feeding development in echinoids (2001). Her 2007 popular book Ocean Science thanks the 2005 FHL Invertebrate Zoology students.

name: Jennifer Ruesink
text:
Jennifer L. Ruesink is an estuarine ecologist and a professor of biology at the University of Washington as of 2026, an assistant professor from 1999 and full professor from 2012. She studied ecology and systematics at Cornell (BA 1989), botany at Cambridge (MPhil 1990) and zoology at Washington (PhD 1996), then held a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of British Columbia from 1996 to 1999. She advised the dissertations of Sarah Alexandra Hart (2014), Katie A. Dobkowski (2017), whose field work on bull kelp and kelp crabs took place at FHL, Alexander T. Lowe (2018) and Mo Turner (2022), who studied sea stars around San Juan Island, and served on Kathryn A. McDonald's graduate committee.

Her early papers include a 1990 study with C. Drew Harvell of predation by the snail Cyphoma signatum on Caribbean gorgonians, and field-container experiments on hermit crabs grazing the diatom Isthmia nervosa (1998) and on intertidal mesograzers in field microcosms (2000). The Ruesink lab emphasized field experimental approaches, primarily in estuarine soft sediment systems, and many of its studies were in Willapa Bay. A 2010 paper with Ruesink as first author compared native and introduced eelgrass there. The lab's research areas include restoration strategies for native oysters and environmental impacts of shellfish aquaculture. Ruesink was also a co-author of a 2007 paper, first-authored by N. S. Banas, that used CTD transects and a 3D circulation model to examine tidal exchange and bivalve grazing in Willapa Bay. With Megan N. Dethier, Ruesink worked on clam recruitment and estuarine gradients in Washington. Work reported in 2026 asked what triggers eelgrass flowering and tested vibration and surface pressure as a control for burrowing shrimp on oyster ground. Ruesink was among the authors of the 2016 resolution of respect for Robert T. Paine.

text: Jennifer Sunday was an MSc student of Michael W. Hart at Simon Fraser University from 2005, arriving from UBC and the Vancouver Aquarium. Sunday studied genetic and reproductive differentiation among populations of the bat star Patiria miniata, with papers on selection at the bindin locus (2013) and ocean-circulation models of gene flow (2014). Sunday became an associate professor of biology at McGill University, working on species distributions under climate change.

name: Jennifer Wang
text: Jennifer Wang, of the University of Washington's Department of Biology, worked at FHL in the spring 2014 Aquatic Animal Research Experience, with Petra Ditsche and Russel Barsh as mentors. Wang's report asked whether particulate matter from town-dock sewage helps explain the abundance of white plumose anemones (Metridium farcimen) under docks in Friday Harbor and at FHL, since their zooplankton prey may feed on it. Anemones from both sites were held in controlled tanks and offered zooplankton of different sizes. They showed no overall preference for particle size, with a slight preference for 0.3 mm over 0.5 mm particles.

name: Jenny Sider
text: Jenny Sider, publishing as Jenny R. Sider, worked as a technician in William M. Bement's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Sider was first author of a 1999 Journal of Cell Science paper that used Xenopus egg extracts and fluorescent probes to show f-actin colocalizing with microtubules of asters. A 2009 Journal of Cell Biology paper with George von Dassow and Bement, listing Sider at FHL's Center for Cell Dynamics, used live imaging of urchin and frog embryos and concluded that asters give accuracy and precision to a furrow-inducing signal. A 2012 Cytoskeleton paper screened 1,990 compounds for inhibitors of cytokinesis in sand dollar embryos and wound repair in Xenopus.

name: Jenny Tung
text: Jenny Tung was a member of Gregory A. Wray's lab at Duke University, where she earned a PhD in 2010 on the genetics of a wild baboon population. A 2009 Nature paper with Susan C. Alberts and Wray examined variation at the malaria-related FY (DARC) gene in yellow baboons of Amboseli National Park, Kenya. After a postdoctoral fellowship in human genetics at the University of Chicago, she returned to the Duke faculty in 2012. In 2022 she founded the Department of Primate Behavior and Evolution at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology. Honors include a MacArthur Fellowship (2019) and election to the US National Academy of Sciences (2024).

name: Jeremy Cooper
text: Jeremy Cooper was a graduate student in Linda G. Wordeman's lab at the University of Washington, taking a PhD in physiology and biophysics (2002 to 2009) after an MS in physics there. The work concerned how the kinesin-13 MCAK depolymerizes microtubules. A 2008 Journal of Cell Biology paper described a mutant that catalytically depolymerizes microtubules in ADP, and a 2010 Nature Structural & Molecular Biology paper showed that MCAK's positively charged neck speeds its association with microtubules rather than tethering it during diffusion. Cooper also co-wrote a 2009 review with Wordeman on diffusive microtubule binding proteins and a 2010 methods chapter on kinetochore subcomplexes.

name: Jessica A. Masterman
text: Jessica A. Masterman, also listed as Jessie Masterman, was a PhD student of Aaron W. E. Galloway at the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, advised for the first part by Kelly Sutherland, and defended in 2025. The dissertation used fatty acid analysis to examine gelatinous zooplankton in the Northern California Current: paired gut content and fatty acid work on the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei, published with Sutherland and Galloway in the Journal of Plankton Research (2025), comparison across co-occurring gelatinous taxa, and a test of how storage degrades fatty acids. Masterman earlier took BS degrees in geology and chemistry at the University of Wisconsin (2010) and an MS in marine science at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (2012) under Michael Berumen.

text: Jessica E. Spiewak was a PhD student in biology at the University of Washington (2020), with Billie J. Swalla as committee chair. text: Jessica Kimber was an undergraduate in the Marine Environmental Research Experience at Friday Harbor Laboratories in autumn 2012, mentored by David O. Duggins and Megan N. Dethier. text: Jessica M. Kendall-Bar did a summer 2014 Research Experience for Undergraduates at FHL with Vikram K. Iyengar, while an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley (BA 2016). name: Jessica Palmeri
text: Jessica Palmeri was an undergraduate in Mackenzie E. Gerringer's lab at SUNY Geneseo, class of 2021. With Gerringer, Palmeri co-wrote two 2025 papers: descriptions of three new abyssal snailfishes from the eastern Pacific, collected at 3,268 to 4,119 m, and a study of swimming kinematics that compared in situ video of bony fishes across a 6,000 m depth gradient with tank recordings of shallow relatives from Puget Sound. A 2021 paper tested knotweed rhizome toxicity on mosses. Palmeri went on to a DVM program at Cornell University (2022 to 2026) and co-wrote a 2026 study of maternal antibody transfer in dogs from Cornell's Baker Institute for Animal Health.

name: Jessica Ward
text: Jessica Ward is listed among the graduate student alumni, with a PhD, of C. Drew Harvell's lab at Cornell University. Publishing as Jessica R. Ward from Cornell's Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Ward studied disease in corals and other marine life. A 2004 PLoS Biology paper with Kevin D. text: Jessie Andino is listed among the undergraduate students (honors, REU and similar) of Emily Carrington's lab in the University of Washington Department of Biology. Andino co-authored a 2019 Journal of Shellfish Research paper with Matthew N. George, Jonathan M. Huie and Carrington. The study measured pH and dissolved oxygen inside mussel aggregations at a mussel farm in Washington state, then applied those conditions to the adhesive plaques of byssal threads. Extreme pH delayed plaque strengthening early in curing, extreme hypoxia weakened mature plaques, and strength recovered after return to open-ocean seawater.

name: Jim Cushing
text: Jim Cushing earned a PhD in applied mathematics at the University of Maryland in 1968 under Monroe H. Martin, who also advised Simon Levin. Cushing joined the University of Arizona in 1968, was a professor there from 1979 to 2021, and then became emeritus. Early papers treated Volterra integral equations. Later work modeled structured population dynamics and tested the models against experimental populations (Science, 2001, on lattice effects in chaotic dynamics) and seabird colonies (2007, 2018). Cushing was co-editor-in-chief of the Journal of Biological Dynamics, an inaugural American Mathematical Society Fellow (2013), and Bernd Aulbach Prize recipient (2021).

name: Joann J. Otto
text:
Joann J. Otto (died 2024) was a cell and developmental biologist whose papers deal with the cytoskeleton of eggs and oocytes. Her earliest FHL-connected paper, a 1976 chapter in Coelenterate Ecology and Behavior, gives addresses in developmental and cell biology at the University of California, Irvine, and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. From the early 1980s into the early 2000s her papers list the Department of Biological Sciences at Purdue University; her 1984 papers give both Purdue and FHL addresses. The census counts four FHL-address papers between 1976 and 1984, written alone or with Thomas E. Schroeder of FHL, and the FHL research bibliography lists further papers of hers through 1996. In the report's network, Richard A. Heil-Chapdelaine, her co-author at Purdue, is listed as her student.

Otto's papers concern how actin filaments and microtubules are organized and remodeled during oocyte maturation and early cleavage. The 1976 chapter described early development and planula movement in the stalked jellyfish Haliclystus. Three 1984 papers with Schroeder analyzed actin bundles and actin-associated proteins in the isolated cortex of starfish oocytes, the cyclic assembly and disassembly of cortical microtubules during maturation and early development, and microtubule arrays near the germinal vesicle. Later papers with Schroeder examined actin and myosin in the contractile ring of dividing sea urchin eggs (1990) and described 'snoods', a periodic network containing cytokeratin in the starfish oocyte cortex (1991). She also worked on the actin-bundling protein fascin, reviewing actin-bundling proteins (1994) and helping to clone a mouse fascin (1995). With Heil-Chapdelaine she measured changes in F-actin during starfish oocyte maturation and during the first cell cycle of the sea urchin egg (1996).

name: Johanna Taylor Cannon
text:
Johanna Taylor Cannon is an evolutionary biologist who uses molecular phylogenetics and phylogenomics to work out relationships among animal groups, especially hemichordates. Her ORCID record lists a B.A. in biology from Bryn Mawr College (2004) and work as a neuroscience laboratory technician at the University of Virginia (2004–2006). It also lists a Ph.D. in biological sciences from Auburn University (2013) and, from 2014, a postdoctoral post in the Department of Zoology at the Swedish Museum of Natural History (Naturhistoriska riksmuseet) in Stockholm. Her papers from 2018 to 2024 give an address in the Department of Ecology, Evolution and Marine Biology at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Her FHL link came through her doctoral research on hemichordates. She held an FHL Patricia L. Dudley Fellowship, and several papers from 2009 to 2016 with Billie J. Swalla list the laboratories among the authors' addresses.

Her doctoral research, co-authored with Kenneth M. Halanych at Auburn and with Swalla, built molecular phylogenies of the Hemichordata, the acorn worms and their relatives. A 2009 paper updated the status of deep-sea acorn worms (enteropneusts). A 2013 study, supported by her FHL fellowship, identified a cold-water clade of harrimaniid acorn worms, and a 2013 paper reported that modern Antarctic acorn worms build tubes. In 2014 she led a phylogenomic analysis that resolved the hemichordate and echinoderm clade. She also contributed to studies of opsin evolution in that group (2015), global hemichordate diversity (2016) and lophotrochozoan phylogenomics (2016). In Stockholm she worked on the place of the Xenacoelomorpha in the animal tree (2016) and contributed to a 2017 study of nerve-cord evolution that used brachiopods collected near FHL. Her later papers deal with eye and opsin evolution in cnidarians, hemichordate mitochondrial genomes and the Mesozoa.

name: John Currey
text:
John D. Currey (died 2018) was a British zoologist and professor of biology at the University of York who studied the mechanics of bone and other mineralized tissues. His tie to FHL core scientists runs through M. A. R. Koehl, whose Berkeley page lists a postdoctoral fellowship at York with Currey as advisor, alongside a postdoctoral fellowship at FHL with Richard Strathmann. Koehl's doctoral advisor at Duke, Stephen A. Wainwright, was also Currey's coauthor on Mechanical Design in Organisms, first published in 1976.

Currey read zoology at Brasenose College, Oxford, graduating in 1956, served as a whaling inspector on an Antarctic voyage, and was a demonstrator in Oxford's zoology department. His 1961 DPhil thesis dealt with functional aspects of bone structure, with special reference to Haversian systems. He joined the new University of York in 1964, helped set up its biology department, spent 1969 in Cleveland at Case Western Reserve University and a Veterans Administration hospital, and became a York professor in 1970. He headed the department from 1984 to 1990, then served as deputy vice chancellor, and retired in 1999. His books include Animal Skeletons (1970), The Mechanical Adaptations of Bones (1984) and Bones: Structure and Mechanics (2002). The European Society of Biomechanics awarded him its Huiskes Medal in 2013.

name: John Edsall
text:
John Tileston Edsall (1902–2002) was a protein chemist at Harvard University. Edsall's tie to Friday Harbor scientists runs through Lynn M. Riddiford, who took a Cornell PhD (1961) co-advised by Harold A. Scheraga, spent two years as a postdoctoral fellow in Edsall's laboratory at Harvard, moved to the University of Washington zoology department in 1973 and later set up a laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories. Scheraga had spent a postdoctoral year with Edsall at Harvard Medical School after a 1946 PhD. As a Harvard medical student Edsall did research under the physiology professor Alfred C. Redfield, on how pH change and lack of oxygen affect contraction of tortoise heart muscle. Redfield then pointed him to Edwin Cohn's Department of Physical Chemistry at the medical school, which Edsall joined full time after graduating.

In Cohn's laboratory Edsall isolated a muscle globulin, later recognized as actomyosin, and with Alexander von Muralt used flow birefringence to show that it was an elongated molecule. He used Raman spectroscopy to show that amino acids are dipolar ions, and wrote Proteins, Amino Acids and Peptides (1943) with Cohn. After wartime work on plasma proteins he studied mercaptalbumin by light scattering, then human red-cell carbonic anhydrases after moving to Harvard's Cambridge campus, where he chaired the committee that became the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology. His postdoctoral fellows included Scheraga, Geoffrey Gilbert, Charles Tanford and Joseph Foster. He co-founded Advances in Protein Chemistry (1944) and was chief editor of the Journal of Biological Chemistry (1958–1967).

text: John Ewer was a postdoctoral fellow with James W. name: John Gosline
text:
John M. Gosline (1943–2016) was a comparative biomechanist and professor of zoology at the University of British Columbia from 1973 to 2008. Emily Carrington, later of the University of Washington, was a Killam Postdoctoral Fellow with Gosline in the UBC Department of Zoology from 1992 to 1995. Their work on mussel attachment included papers on byssus design (1996) and on dislodgment of two Mytilus species (1997), and a 2004 paper on load cycle and strain rate in the byssus. Carrington gave the 2017 Gosline Memorial Lecture. Gosline and Carrington were also coauthors of Demes and others (2011) on foliose red macroalgae and of Horton and others (2022) on the gut mechanics of the stomachless shiner perch Cymatogaster aggregata.

Gosline earned a BA at the University of California, Berkeley (1966) and a PhD at Duke University (1970), publishing papers in 1971 on the connective tissue mechanics of the sea anemone Metridium senile. Postdoctoral work at the University of Cambridge preceded the move to UBC. He co-wrote Mechanical Design in Organisms (1976) with Stephen A. Wainwright, W. D. Biggs and J. D. Currey; Wainwright co-taught a biomechanics summer course at FHL in 1980. Gosline's research concerned elasticity in structural proteins such as spider silk, elastin, resilin, collagen and keratin, across animals from cnidarians and cephalopods to hagfish and cetaceans. His book Mechanical Design of Structural Materials in Animals appeared in 2018. UBC credits him with more than 35 trainees.

name: John H. Henson
text:
John H. Henson is a cell biologist and the Charles A. Dana Professor of Biology at Dickinson College in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, where he has been on the faculty since 1989. He received a B.A. from the University of Virginia (1979), an M.S. from Florida State University (1983) and a Ph.D. from Harvard University (1989). His research uses marine organisms as experimental systems to study how cells move, change shape and divide. His papers from 2017 to 2024 list Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) as an affiliation alongside Dickinson and describe work carried out during summer residence at FHL, with sea urchins kept in the laboratory's seawater systems and in subtidal cages. Much of this work is a collaboration with Charles B. Shuster of New Mexico State University, supported by collaborative research grants from the National Science Foundation.

Henson's FHL-connected papers center on cytokinesis, the final step of cell division, in sea urchin eggs and embryos. Using platinum-replica electron microscopy, a 2017 paper described the arrangement of actin and myosin II filaments in the contractile ring and offered new support for a long-standing model of cytokinesis. Papers in 2021 and 2024, which also used super-resolution light microscopy, traced how the ring is assembled: from early clusters of myosin II, anillin and septin, through a septin filament network, to the recruitment of α-actinin, and how inhibiting myosin II alters the process. Related work examined the control of primary mesenchyme cell shape by the GTPase Cdc42 (2018), polar lobe formation in embryos of mollusks collected around San Juan Island (2019), the nanoscale arrangement of the Wnt signaling protein Dishevelled in the egg's vegetal cortex (2021), and methods for high-resolution imaging of the isolated cortex (2019).

text: John J. Meyer was an MS student of James E. Byers, then at the University of New Hampshire, and finished in 2005. Meyer also co-authored a 2006 Marine Biology paper with Jennifer Griffiths, Megan N. Dethier and others on invertebrate community responses to recreational clam digging. Meyer was a NOAA John A. Knauss Marine Policy Fellow in 2006.

name: John P. Geyman
text:
John P. Geyman is a family physician and professor emeritus of family medicine at the University of Washington School of Medicine. He earned an A.B. in geology at Princeton (1952) and an M.D. at the University of California, San Francisco (1960), and practiced in rural northern California. He was among the first family practice residency directors, beginning at Santa Rosa, California, in 1969. After working in the University of Utah's Division of Family Practice (1971–72), he developed a network of residency programs in northern California at the University of California, Davis. He chaired the University of Washington's Department of Family Medicine from 1976 to 1990. He was the founding editor of The Journal of Family Practice and edited the Journal of the American Board of Family Practice from 1990 to 2003. He was elected to the Institute of Medicine, now the National Academy of Medicine.

Geyman's work concerns primary care and how health care in the United States is organized and paid for. By 2007 he had published more than 160 journal articles and 10 books; his ORCID record lists 18 books. He served as president of Physicians for a National Health Program in the mid-2000s. His four census papers (2011–2022) are of this kind: a 2011 festschrift for G. Gayle Stephens, two 2021 articles in the International Journal of Health Services on investor-owned health care and on privatized Medicare Advantage, and a 2022 article on private equity ownership in U.S. health care. They entered the census through their author affiliation lines. None reports research at the laboratories, and none of the sources describes any work by him at FHL, so they are not FHL research.

name: John R. Blinks
text:
John R. Blinks was a physician-trained pharmacologist and muscle physiologist. His curriculum vitae in FHL's 2002 program review records a B.A. from Stanford University (1951) and an M.D. from Harvard Medical School (1955). He taught pharmacology at Harvard Medical School (1958-1968), including a year at University College London with A. F. Huxley and D. R. Wilkie, then chaired the Department of Pharmacology at the Mayo Foundation (1968-1988) and was professor of pharmacology at Mayo Medical School (1973-1990). In 1990 he became Professor of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington. His honors include the 1987 Otto Krayer Award of the American Society for Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics. FHL describes him as spending summers and his retirement years at the laboratories. In 1996 he co-founded the Anne Hof Blinks Fellowship Endowment, which supports FHL's Blinks program for students from diverse backgrounds, and he served on the FHL Advisory Board.

Blinks's research concerned how calcium ions control muscle contraction, especially in heart muscle. To measure free calcium inside living cells he used aequorin, the calcium-sensitive light-emitting protein of the local hydromedusa Aequorea victoria, which he purified from very large numbers of jellyfish. Census papers from 1974, 1980 and 1991 that mention FHL in their text used aequorin to follow calcium in invertebrate photoreceptors, amoeboid cells and muscle. His FHL-address papers (1993-2003) include the cloning of mitrocomin (1993), a method for correcting imbalance in calcium-EGTA buffer solutions (1996) and, with Eugene Vysotski, Boris Illarionov, John Lee and colleagues, studies of obelin from the hydroid Obelia geniculata, covering its cloning, the roles of its calcium-binding sites and how its light emission is triggered (2001-2003). FHL's 2002 review describes his search for photoproteins better suited than aequorin as intracellular calcium indicators. FHL's autumn 2012 newsletter carried a memorial tribute to him by Dennis Willows.

name: John W. Brookbank
text:
John W. Brookbank worked on the biochemistry and development of sea urchin eggs and embryos. His 1954 paper, written with Arthur H. Whiteley, gives the Department of Zoology and the Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) of the University of Washington. His two 1959 papers give the Department of Biology at the University of Florida in Gainesville together with FHL, and his 1984 paper gives the Department of Microbiology and Cell Science in the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, again with FHL. His 1970, 1972 and 1980 papers give FHL alone. All seven of his census papers, from 1954 to 1984, name FHL, and the 1984 paper thanks the laboratories for research space in the summer of 1982 and used adult sea urchins from the FHL live tanks.

Brookbank's papers use the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, and a sand dollar to study the biochemistry of eggs and the replication and packaging of DNA in early development. The 1954 study with Whiteley measured urease in sea urchin eggs and embryos. Two 1959 papers used antisera against fertilizin to detect fertilizin haptens inside unfertilized eggs and to test how the antisera affect egg respiration. In 1970 and 1972 he followed DNA synthesis and development in reciprocal hybrids between a sea urchin and a sand dollar, measuring the DNA of individual nuclei by microspectrophotometry (the 1972 paper with Joseph E. Cummins). His later papers turned to H1 histones: how the drug cordycepin and the dissociation of embryos into single cells affect H1 synthesis (1980), and the H1 histones of adult sea urchin tissues, with embryos for comparison (1984).

name: Joleah Lamb
text: Joleah Lamb was a postdoctoral associate in C. Drew Harvell's lab in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at Cornell University, where Lamb was a research fellow from 2014 to 2019. Lamb earned a PhD at James Cook University in 2014. Coral disease work includes a 2015 Ecology paper with Bette L. Willis and others on protected areas reducing fishing damage and disease. Two Science papers with Harvell came from Cornell: a 2017 study of seagrass ecosystems reducing exposure to bacterial pathogens, and a 2018 study linking plastic waste to coral disease. Lamb became an assistant professor at the University of California, Irvine, in 2019 and an associate professor at the University of Bristol in 2026.

name: Jonathan B. Alberts
text:
Jonathan B. Alberts is a computational biologist who builds simulations of the cell's cytoskeleton. His FHL-connected papers, from 2004 to 2014, came out of the Center for Cell Dynamics, a National Institutes of Health center that Garrett Odell directed at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 2002 to 2010 and that worked on modeling cell and developmental processes. His 2004 paper with Odell lists both authors at the Center in Friday Harbor. It credits Alberts's Alfred P. Sloan Foundation postdoctoral fellowship in computational biology for the start of the work, with further support from an NIH grant to both authors. His papers of 2009 and 2011 also list the Center, and those of 2012 and 2014 give the University of Washington at Friday Harbor.

Alberts writes agent-based simulations, in which individual filaments and proteins are tracked and interact through explicit biochemical and mechanical rules. His 2004 PLoS Biology paper with Odell simulated the actin-based propulsion of the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes. The simulated bacterium moved with realistic speed and tail shape, in nanometer-scale runs and pauses ("nano-saltation") that arose as links between actin filaments and the bacterial surface protein ActA formed and broke together. A 2009 study with Susanne Rafelski and Odell combined experiments and models and found that speed rose with the amount and polarity of ActA. A 2009 PLoS ONE paper set out a method for modeling filament bending in such simulations. Later papers analyzed the motion of centrin foci in living cells (2011, with Rafelski, Lani Keller and Wallace Marshall) and how flexibly bonded, low-valence particles form finite clusters (2012 and 2014, with Olga Markova, Edwin Munro and Pierre-François Lenne).

text: Jonathan Chapman was a student in the 2020 research apprenticeship Pelagic Ecosystem Function in the San Juan Archipelago at Friday Harbor Laboratories, with a project on diel vertical migration patterns and stereocamera analysis of Pacific sand lance. text: Jonathan Cowart was listed among Larry R. McEdward's PhD students and marked as a student in 2001; McEdward taught at the University of Florida. Miner and McEdward revisited egg energetics in the facultative planktotroph Clypeaster rosaceus. A 2005 paper in the Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology, with Adam M. Reitzel, Cecelia M. Miles, Andreas Heyland and McEdward, compared how the facultative feeding period contributes to larval development and size at metamorphosis across echinoids.

name: Jonathan Frommeyer
text: Jonathan Frommeyer was a PhD student co-advised by Matthew A. Kolmann and Andrew Mehring in biology at the University of Louisville, graduating in August 2025. The dissertation, on fish hosts and freshwater mussel conservation in Kentucky rivers, ran infestation trials on host specificity in two common mussel species and found that host susceptibility followed fish evolutionary relationships. It compared mussel and fish communities at nine sites across five river systems, where the two groups aligned only weakly. It also modeled population structure in two common species and the federally endangered Cyprogenia stegaria, finding multiple size cohorts and evidence of ongoing recruitment.

name: Jonathan M. Huie
text:
Jonathan M. Huie is a comparative organismal biologist who studies form and function in fishes and salamanders, and was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, Irvine as of 2025, working on tooth evolution in deep-sea fishes. Huie's ties to FHL began as a University of Washington undergraduate (BS 2019, Aquatic and Fishery Sciences and Marine Biology), with FHL financial aid in 2016 and an FHL student presentation award in 2017. Huie then worked as Micro-CT Lab Technician at FHL (2019–2020), was a visiting researcher there from 2021 through at least 2025, and in 2024 lectured in the FHL fish functional morphology course and co-mentored three course theses.

As an undergraduate Huie presented and published with Adam P. Summers and Matthew A. Kolmann on ontogeny of feeding mechanics in scale-feeding fishes (2018) and presented with undergraduate advisor Luke Tornabene on cleaner gobies at the University of Washington Undergraduate Research Symposium (2019). Papers followed on body shape in herbivorous serrasalmids with Summers and Kolmann (2019) and, with Tornabene and Christine Thacker, on cleaning and feeding morphology in gobies (2020). Suction-based adhesion followed: one 2022 paper tested soft and rough substrates, and another compared clingfish, lumpsuckers and snailfish, using micro-CT and scanning electron microscopy to study their adhesive discs. SegmentGeometry (2022), written with Summers and Sandy Kawano, measures second moment of area in 3D Slicer. Huie's PhD at George Washington University (2020–2025, advisor Kawano, NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) concerned climbing salamanders, and a 2026 paper with Kawano treated salamander limb bone diversity.

name: Jonathan Michaux
text: Jonathan Michaux was a graduate student of Edwin Munro at the University of Chicago, in the Cellular and Molecular Biology program, with a PhD in Molecular Genetics and Cell Biology (2010 to 2017). Donoughe and Munro showed how modulating RhoA effectors shifts zygotes toward oscillatory and wavelike RhoA dynamics. Michaux entered graduate study in robotics at the University of Michigan in 2019.

name: Jordan Omoto
text: Jordan Omoto was a University of Washington School of Oceanography student whose 2016 senior thesis was advised by Kathy Newell and Daniel Grünbaum. The thesis counted Alexandrium cysts in sediment collected near fish farms and towns in Nootka Sound in December 2015, with higher counts, 275 to 575 cysts per cubic centimeter, at the stations closest to farms and towns. It adapted a larval transport model devised by Grünbaum to predict where cysts might gather. A 2016 Friday Harbor Laboratories student paper by Omoto examined zooplankton grazing on phytoplankton in San Juan Channel, reading high phaeopigment concentrations at the North station as a sign of strong grazing.

text: Jose Tavera was a Fulbright Fellow and visiting scholar with Adam P. Summers in 2023, from the Universidad del Valle in Cali, Colombia, where he joined the biology faculty in 2014 (listed as profesor titular). A PLOS ONE paper with Klinger and Kelly followed in 2023.

name: Joseph J. Bizzarro
text:
Joseph J. Bizzarro is an ichthyologist and fisheries ecologist studying the trophic ecology and spatial associations of bottom-dwelling sharks, skates, rays and groundfishes; NOAA Fisheries has listed Bizzarro as an Assistant Project Scientist on the Habitat and Groundfish Ecology Team at the Southwest Fisheries Science Center. The tie to FHL is Adam P. Summers, advisor of Bizzarro's University of Washington PhD (School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences, 2015). The dissertation found that space mattered more than food in structuring eastern North Pacific skate assemblages: species and life stages segregated spatially but overlapped heavily in diet. Bizzarro's papers include Paig-Tran and others (2011) on filtering in fishes and a 2016 study of burrowing in Pacific sand lance with Summers and H. Gary Greene.

Bizzarro took a BA in biology at Dartmouth College (1992). At the Center for Habitat Studies at Moss Landing Marine Laboratories, whose personnel page lists Bizzarro as Ichthyologist/Fisheries Biologist and Greene as Geologist, Bizzarro managed seafloor mapping and groundfish projects from 1997 to 2004 and took part in six submersible research projects. An MS at Moss Landing (2006) concerned the fishery biology and feeding ecology of rays from Bahía Almejas, Mexico. From 2002 to 2009 Bizzarro was staff scientist and project manager at the Pacific Shark Research Center, mentoring six of its MS students. In late 2015 Bizzarro became a postdoctoral fellow with Mary Yoklavich's Habitat Ecology Team at the Southwest Fisheries Science Center in Santa Cruz, building a Major Prey Index from diets of 18 Pacific Coast groundfish species.

name: Joseph K. Gaydos
text:
Joseph K. Gaydos is a wildlife veterinarian and research scientist and the Science Director of the SeaDoc Society, a marine conservation program of the UC Davis Karen C. Drayer Wildlife Health Center, based in Eastsound, Washington. He has worked on wildlife and ecosystem conservation in the Pacific Northwest for about two decades, has advised policymakers from Washington State to Washington, D.C., and has published more than 75 peer-reviewed papers. He co-wrote the books The Salish Sea: Jewel of the Pacific Northwest and Explore the Salish Sea, and he hosts the video series Salish Sea Wild. His six census papers (2014–2022) are connected to FHL through co-authors with FHL addresses, an FHL course, an FHL student intern, FHL dive support and advice from an FHL core scientist.

Gaydos studies diseases that affect both wildlife and human health, and works on seabirds, harbor seals, river otters, porpoises and killer whales. A 2014 paper from FHL's Ecology of Marine Infectious Disease course found that older eelgrass leaves and shallower beds in the San Juan Archipelago are more prone to wasting disease, and a 2016 paper examines Labyrinthula, the agents of seagrass wasting disease. Volunteer and scientific dive surveys showed that sea star wasting disease severely depleted sunflower sea stars in the Salish Sea (2016). With Elizabeth Ashley of SeaDoc he analyzed 882 harbor seal strandings in San Juan County from 2002 to 2018, finding that most pup deaths had nutritional causes (2020), and about 13,000 volunteer diver surveys that recorded 138 of the 261 fish species known from the Salish Sea (2022). A 2020 review of 30 river otter carcasses found trauma the main cause of death.

name: Josh Sandquist
text: Josh Sandquist was a postdoctoral fellow with William M. Bement in the Department of Zoology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison from 2008 to 2012, studying the unconventional myosin, myosin-10, in mitotic spindle structure. A 2018 Journal of Cell Biology paper with Bement and others reported an interaction between myosin-10 and the cell cycle regulator Wee1 linking spindle dynamics to mitotic progression in epithelia. Earlier, Joshua C. Sandquist completed a PhD in Pharmacology and Cancer Biology at Duke University in 2008 under Anthony R. Means, on nonmuscle myosin II isoforms in cell migration. Sandquist joined the biology faculty at Grinnell College in 2012, studying spindle orientation and the timing of cell division in frog embryos.

name: Julia N. Kobelt
text:
Julia N. Kobelt is a marine ecologist whose papers deal with nearshore food webs, clams and shoreline habitats in Washington State. Her FHL-connected papers date from 2017 to 2025, and all but one were written with Megan N. Dethier of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Papers from 2017 and 2018 list her at FHL. Papers from 2018 and 2019 give her address as the Department of Biology at Montclair State University in New Jersey, and Aaron W. E. Galloway's CV marks her as a student co-author on two of them. Her 2023 and 2025 shoreline papers list her at the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences, and her first-authored 2024 paper on clam recruitment lists her at FHL. An FHL newsletter column from January 2026 thanks her among the laboratories' staff and researchers.

Kobelt's work combines feeding experiments, biochemical tracers and field surveys. A 2017 paper examined how the kelp crab Pugettia chooses between two kelps. A 2018 study followed how two sea urchin species digest, excrete and build tissue from the fatty acids of brown, red and green seaweeds, and a 2019 paper measured the nutritional value of urchin feces for other bottom-dwelling animals. With Dethier and Jennifer Ruesink she studied juvenile clams: the physical and biological factors affecting their performance (2019), and recruitment of Manila and soft-shell clams to collectors at eight Washington beaches in 2016 and 2017 (2024). With Galloway and others she measured how many purple urchins sunflower sea stars eat and modeled whether their recovery could help kelp forests return (2023). Her shoreline papers compare beaches where armor was removed with natural reference beaches (2023) and armored with unarmored beaches below eroding feeder bluffs (2025).

name: Julia S. Miles
text: Julia S. Miles was a PhD student of Kenneth P. Sebens at Northeastern University from 1985 to 1992, working on coelenterate agonistic behavior and energetics. With Sebens, Miles described sweeper tentacles in a gorgonian octocoral as morphological modifications for interference competition (Biological Bulletin, 1988). A 1991 paper in the same journal showed that the tropical corallimorpharian Discosoma sanctithomae used modified marginal tentacles and mesenterial filaments to damage neighboring scleractinian corals in the laboratory and field. All transplanted colonies of Agaricia agaricites were damaged, and 67 percent of the corallimorpharians first wounded by Meandrina meandrites recovered and retaliated within one to six months.

name: Julia Skowronski
text: Julia Skowronski was an MS student of Colette J. Feehan at Montclair State University (2024). The thesis used settlement plates at nine Florida Keys reef sites to map settlement of the long-spined sea urchin Diadema antillarum, finding more settlers offshore and in the middle and upper Keys, with no seasonal pattern. The results can help managers choose sites for urchin habitat restoration.

name: Julia Wulfkuhle
text: Julia Wulfkuhle was a graduate student of Joann J. Otto at Purdue University, listed among the lab's past graduate students on its 2000 page. With Otto, Wulfkuhle worked on the actin cytoskeleton: mapping a vinculin binding site on talin (1992), sea urchin fascin as a homolog of the Drosophila singed gene product (1993), and F-actin changes during Drosophila bristle development (1998). Work on the membrane protein supervillin with E. J. Luna at the University of Massachusetts Medical School followed (1999). Wulfkuhle then turned to cancer proteomics in the NCI/FDA Clinical Proteomics Program (2003) and became a research professor at George Mason University's Center for Applied Proteomics and Molecular Medicine.

name: Julian Sachs
text: Julian P. Sachs became professor of chemical oceanography at the University of Washington School of Oceanography in 2013. He guided Colton Skavicus's 2015 senior thesis, which tested Nootka Sound sediments for traces of pulp mill effluent. His research applies organic geochemistry and stable isotopes to past climate, especially tropical climate over the last 2,000 years.

name: Julie Ann Koehlinger
text: Julie Ann Koehlinger was an MS student of Terrie Klinger at the University of Washington (marine affairs, 2018). Using mooring records from the Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary, the thesis built a nearshore temperature climatology and related anomalies during the 2013-14 marine heat wave and 2015 El Niño to winds and currents. A related paper with Klinger appeared in PLOS ONE in 2023.

name: Julie Canman
text: Julie Canman was a technician in William M. Bement's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where Canman and Bement reported that microtubules suppress actomyosin-based cortical flow in Xenopus oocytes (1997). Canman later became an associate professor of pathology and cell biology at Columbia University.

name: Julie Schram
text:
Julie B. Schram is an integrative marine biologist and, as of 2026, Assistant Professor of Animal Physiology at the University of Alaska Southeast, using fatty acids and stable isotopes as biomarkers of how consumers use primary producers. From 2016 to 2020 Schram was a postdoctoral scholar with Aaron W. E. Galloway at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology. Papers from that period include fatty acid transfer in two urchin species (2018) and urchin feces as food (2019), both with Megan N. Dethier. Schram's earlier tie to FHL was a student report from summer 2011 on experimental approaches to ocean acidification, written with Emily E. Bockmon, on how biomass and flow-through rate shift carbonate chemistry in aquaria.

Schram earned a BS at Western Washington University (2004) and an MS (2010) and PhD (2015) at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, the PhD under James B. McClintock. The dissertation measured seawater pH and temperature near Palmer Station, Antarctica, then tested two gastropods, Nacella concinna and Margarella antarctica, and two amphipods, Gondogeneia antarctica and Paradexamine fissicauda, under predicted conditions. Lower pH and higher temperature changed gastropod behavior more than growth or calcification, while a three-month exposure reduced survival of both amphipods. Later papers treat sea otter effects on seagrass food webs in southeast Alaska (2021), a rhizocephalan parasite of shrimp (2023) and long-term resistance of Antarctic amphipod assemblages to acidification (2025).

name: Julie Sexton
text: Julie Sexton was a curator at the National Center for Marine Algae and Microbiota at Bigelow Laboratory, on the center's staff list for 1989 to 2018, overlapping Robert A. Andersen's term as director from 1989 to 2009. As J. P. Sexton, the curator coauthored the center's strain catalogs with Andersen (1991, 1997), the description of the alga Pelagomonas calceolata and a new algal class (Journal of Phycology, 1993), and phylogenies of the Eustigmatophyceae, including Nannochloropsis (Protist, 1998), and the Chrysophyceae (1999). A 2018 Frontiers in Microbiology paper on carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus ratios in marine eukaryotic phytoplankton lists Sexton at the center.

text: Julie Van De Weghe was a postdoctoral fellow in Dan Doherty's University of Washington laboratory, listed as a valued guest of Linda G. Wordeman's lab. text: Julio A. Rivera was a postdoctoral scholar with Emília P. Martins at Arizona State University from 2017 to 2021, after a biology PhD at the University of Hawai'i at Manoa (2017). name: Julius Bauschinger
text:
Julius Bauschinger (1860–1934) was a German astronomer who specialized in orbit determination, including the orbits of comets and minor planets. He studied at Munich and Berlin and took his doctorate at Munich in 1884 under Hugo von Seeliger, with a dissertation on the motion of Mercury. In 1882 he joined the German expedition to Hartford, Connecticut, that observed the transit of Venus. From 1883 he was assistant and observer at the Munich observatory. From 1896 to 1909 he directed the Astronomisches Rechen-Institut in Berlin and was professor of theoretical astronomy. He then directed the Strasbourg observatory (1909–1918) and the Leipzig observatory (1920–1930). He was a member of the Bavarian, Saxon and Prussian academies of sciences. He has no papers in the census; he appears in the report at the root of a mentoring line that reaches FHL.

Much of Bauschinger's work was computational. His Bahnbestimmung der Himmelskörper (1906; second edition 1928) treated the determination of orbits. He published Tafeln zur theoretischen Astronomie (1901) and, with Jean Peters, eight-place logarithmic-trigonometric tables (1910–1911) that were reissued in 1936 and 1958. He wrote articles for the Enzyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften on least-squares adjustment, interpolation, astronomical constants and the rotation of celestial bodies, and his 1888 habilitation thesis dealt with the bending of meridian telescopes. His doctoral students in Berlin, Strasbourg and Leipzig included Alfred Wegener (1905) and Aurel Wintner, whose Leipzig dissertation on convergence questions in lunar theory he supervised with Leon Lichtenstein. Wintner's Johns Hopkins student Monroe H. Martin advised Simon A. Levin (Maryland, 1964), whose Cornell student Daniel Grünbaum is a University of Washington scientist with FHL-connected papers from 2010 to 2020.

name: Justin Decarreau
text: Justin Decarreau was a postdoctoral fellow in Linda G. Wordeman's University of Washington laboratory. Decarreau earlier published on smooth muscle myosin structure and kinetics with Christopher L. Berger at the University of Vermont (2011). In the Wordeman lab, Decarreau coauthored work on MCAK at microtubule tips and spindle length (2012) and was first author of a study showing that the kinesin Kif25 suppresses pre-mitotic centrosome separation to set spindle orientation (Nature Cell Biology, 2017). Later papers concern computational protein design, including self-assembling helical filaments (Science, 2018) and modular hydrogels (PNAS, 2024). The Wordeman lab page places Decarreau afterward in the Structural Biology Core of the university's Institute for Protein Design.

name: Justin Schaefer
text: Justin Schaefer was a doctoral student of Adam P. Summers, who chaired the committee, at the University of California, Irvine, working on batoid wing structure. With Summers, Schaefer used high-resolution radiography to show that calcification and fin-ray organization in skate and ray wings varied between families and predicted locomotor strategy (Journal of Morphology, 2005). Schaefer also coauthored a study of tooth reorientation during prey processing in the lesser electric ray Narcine brasiliensis (Zoology, 2008) and a shark-inspired biomimetic skeleton for the tail of an aquatic robot (Marine Technology Society Journal, 2011).

name: K. M. Pos
text: K. M. Pos is Kelsie M. Pos, an undergraduate at Knox College who worked with Nicholas J. Gidmark and was mentored by Stacy C. Farina. Pos led a 2019 paper that used micro-computed tomography scans of 165 leuciscid minnow species to measure pharyngeal jaw, muscle attachment and tooth traits, testing phylogenetic signal and correlation with diet. A 2018 abstract with Matthew A. Kolmann and Gidmark compared evolutionary history and dietary niche in shaping these jaws in cyprinid fishes. Pos also coauthored a 2019 book chapter on feeding biomechanics in fishes and was first author of a 2021 abstract on fish gizzards with Kolmann and L. P. Hernandez.

name: Kaddee A. Lawrence
text:
Kaddee A. Lawrence worked on the behavior and neurobiology of the nudibranch Melibe leonina with a University of New Hampshire group that studied the animal at Friday Harbor Laboratories. The census counts three FHL-address papers by her, from 2001 to 2004; all list the Zoology Department and Center for Marine Biology at the University of New Hampshire together with FHL. All three were written with Winsor H. Watson, and two also with James M. Newcomb. A footnote in the 2002 paper gives her a later address at Highline Community College in Des Moines, Washington.

Lawrence's papers concern the swimming behavior of Melibe leonina and its neural control. A 2001 paper led by Watson in American Zoologist summarized the swim circuit. About 15 swim motoneurons in each pedal ganglion are driven by a central pattern generator of four interneurons, and swimming is inhibited by light and by nitric oxide donors. Her 2002 paper with Watson in the Biological Bulletin broke swimming into a fixed sequence of five movements. It showed that swimming can be set off reliably by contact with the predatory sea star Pycnopodia helianthoides, by pinching or by potassium chloride, which makes it suitable for neuroethological study. A 2004 paper led by Newcomb found that Melibe is more active at night and that constant light suppresses its locomotion. In isolated brains, light acting through the eyes quickly inhibited the swim motor program.

text: Kaelan Yao completed a master's degree at Brown University in ecology, evolution, and organismal biology in 2022, with Elizabeth L. name: Karen Vedder
text:
Karen Vedder is a co-author of four papers on the reproduction, larvae and settlement of marine invertebrates, all carrying a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. Three papers, from 1977 to 1982, give her address as FHL; the fourth, from 2014, lists all three authors at "Friday Harbor Laboratories and Department of Biology, University of Washington." Each was written with Richard R. Strathmann of the University of Washington and FHL, with E. Sanford Branscomb, or with both.

The papers deal with how invertebrates provision and release their young and what happens to larvae at settlement. The 1977 Marine Biology paper with Strathmann related the size and organic content of eggs of echinoderms and other invertebrates to their developmental strategies and to egg eating. A 1981 Oecologia paper treated fatal settlement errors by barnacle larvae as a cost of dispersal and examined the influence of intertidal flora on barnacle settlement. A 1982 Crustaceana paper with Branscomb described the naupliar larval stages of three Puget Sound barnacles, Balanus glandula, B. cariosus and B. crenatus, the first two not described before. The 2014 Invertebrate Biology paper returned to B. glandula: broods ready to hatch at different times in winter all hatched within about two weeks in spring, breaking up brood masses triggered hatching, and crabs that broke open barnacles released many larvae while whelks released few.

name: Karl Banse
text:
Karl Banse (1929–2025) was an oceanographer at the University of Washington, where he became an assistant professor in 1960 and a full professor in 1966, and later professor emeritus. He moved from zoology to oceanography at the University of Kiel and took his PhD there in 1955. His tie to FHL runs through Richard R. Strathmann, resident associate director at FHL from 1973 to 2008, who named Banse and Alan J. Kohn as his thesis advisors at UW, where Strathmann earned an MS in oceanography in 1966 and a PhD in zoology in 1970. Banse's papers at UW Libraries Special Collections hold folders on FHL (1974 to 1984), a Friday Harbor planning committee (1952 to 1968) and Friday Harbor courses (1966 to 1984).

His research ranged from upwelling during the southwest monsoon off India's west coast to phytoplankton blooms in the northern Arabian Sea and the seasonality of satellite-derived chlorophyll. He argued that grazing, rather than cell division rate, regulates phytoplankton abundance. He also studied benthic polychaetes of the northeast Pacific, including a 1968 paper with Hobson on species from Puget Sound and a 1972 Pacific Science paper on six polychaete families. With Winter and Anderson he published on phytoplankton blooms in Puget Sound in 1975. He chaired SCOR Working Group 33 on phytoplankton methods and received the Lifetime Achievement Award of ASLO, the Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography, in 1998; the award was renamed for Alfred C. Redfield in 2004.

name: Karly Elizabeth Cohen
text:
Karly E. Cohen is a comparative biologist who studies the evolution, development and mechanics of hard skeletal tissues in fishes, particularly teeth, scales and armor. She completed a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington in 2022 with a thesis on homodont and heterodont dentitions. The mentoring network links her to Adam P. Summers through that thesis, to L. Patricia Hernandez of George Washington University as MS advisor, and to Gareth J. Fraser as postdoctoral supervisor. She moved to Friday Harbor Laboratories in 2018. UW News described her as a doctoral student in 2019 and as a postdoctoral researcher at FHL in 2025. The Save Our Seas Foundation, which supports her work on spotted ratfish, says she developed research and mentorship programs at FHL and lists her as a postdoctoral fellow in the University of Florida Department of Biology. The census counts 25 FHL-address papers from 2019 to 2026.

Cohen combines CT scanning, histology, gene expression and mechanical testing to relate skeletal form to function. Early papers dealt with filter feeding in silver carp (2018) and tooth replacement in piranhas and pacus (2019), and during her doctoral years she examined tooth shape and replacement in wrasses and Pacific lingcod (2020-2021). Many FHL-connected papers use local species: armor, fluorescence and drag reduction in the Pacific spiny lumpsucker, adhesion in clingfishes, lumpsuckers and snailfishes, vertebral shape across habitats, poacher armor and prickleback jaws. A 2025 PNAS paper with Michael Coates and Fraser, based on spotted ratfish caught around FHL, showed that the forehead clasper (tenaculum) of male ratfish carries teeth rooted in a dental lamina, a tissue previously known only from the jaw. She has also reported a possible ratfish nursery in San Juan Channel (2025) and co-authored papers on biological armor and bioinspired design.

name: Kassandra L. Ford
text:
Kassandra L. Ford is an evolutionary morphologist, an assistant professor of fisheries, wildlife and conservation biology at the University of Minnesota and curator of fishes and mollusks at the Bell Museum as of 2025. She earned a BS in genetics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in 2015 and a PhD in biology at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette in 2021, supervised by James S. Albert, with Adam P. Summers on her committee. Her FHL tie came through Summers: skulls for her 2022 comparative study were CT-scanned at FHL with support from the laboratories, Summers and the Scan All Fishes project.

Her work uses CT imaging and 3D geometric morphometrics to study skull shape in teleost fishes. The 2022 study of 391 specimens from 78 species of South American Apteronotidae and African Mormyridae found no overlap between the two families in skull-shape morphospace, and so no complete convergence. Related papers treat ghost electric fishes (2022) and mormyrids (2026), and a 2023 review with Summers and others covers methods for comparative anatomy. A 2026 Journal of Morphology paper, led by R.C. Hoover, examines jaws and teeth in prickleback fishes. Earlier she did undergraduate zebrafish research under Mary Halloran and spent a year under Frank Pezold at Texas A&M University–Corpus Christi; postdoctoral positions followed in Ole Seehausen's lab at Bern and at George Washington University.

name: Katharine R. Hind
text:
Katharine R. Hind, known as Katy Hind, is a phycologist and teaching professor of biology at the University of New Brunswick, where she joined the faculty in 2022. She studies the diversity and ecology of coralline red algae. She was a PhD student at UNB in G. W. Saunders's lab, publishing a molecular phylogeny of the coralline tribe Corallineae with him, then a postdoctoral Hakai Scholar in Patrick T. Martone's lab at the University of British Columbia. Part of her coralline work with Martone and Paul W. Gabrielson, including a 2014 Journal of Phycology paper, was done while Gabrielson was a visiting professor at FHL. She worked at the University of Victoria from 2017 to 2022 and has taught seaweed biodiversity courses there and at Bamfield Marine Sciences Centre.

Much of her work with Martone and Gabrielson used DNA from type and historical specimens to fix coralline names. A 2014 paper sequenced a 296 base pair chloroplast fragment from a 187-year-old specimen of Pachyarthron cretaceum and showed it to be Corallina officinalis. A 2015 paper separated cryptic species of Bossiella, a 2016 paper described the crustose genus Crusticorallina, and a 2018 paper reported a genus with both jointed and crustose species. In a 2019 PNAS paper from the Hakai Institute and UBC, surveys of four reef sites on the central British Columbia coast showed that urchin barrens had more coralline cover than kelp forests but less diverse coralline assemblages. At UNB she also works on teaching in large first-year biology courses.

name: Katherine A. Corn
text:
Katherine A. Corn is an evolutionary biologist and functional morphologist of fishes, assistant professor in the School of Biological Sciences at Washington State University and director of its Conner Museum of Vertebrates since 2024. Her tie to FHL began in summer 2014, when, as a Cornell undergraduate, she took the FHL fish course taught by Adam P. Summers and E. W. Misty Paig-Tran, with Stacy C. Farina as teaching assistant. There she glued shark teeth to reciprocating saw blades to mimic head-shaking, published in Royal Society Open Science in 2016 with Farina, Jeffrey Brash and Summers. A 2015 FHL report with Summers on burial in English sole preceded a 2018 Journal of Experimental Biology paper. She took FHL's quantitative genetics course in 2019 and guest lectured there in 2020.

At Cornell she worked with William E. Bemis, her honors thesis advisor, on the development of sevengill shark teeth, and took a BSc in 2016. She completed a PhD in population biology at the University of California, Davis in 2022 with Peter C. Wainwright, with a thesis on the evolution of form and function in teleost fishes, then held a postdoctoral position with Josef C. Uyeda at Virginia Tech from 2022 to 2024. Her research combines biomechanical studies, museum specimen data and phylogenetic comparative models. A 2022 PNAS paper with Wainwright and others linked the rise of biting during the Cenozoic to diversification of reef fish body shape.
