name: Katherine Graubard
text:
Katherine Graubard is a neurobiologist who worked on small motor circuits in crustaceans in the Department of Zoology, later Biology, at the University of Washington, in a group listed as The Crab Lab. A directory of stomatogastric research groups gives Graubard's interests as non-spiking transmission, cellular properties, functional morphology and calcium, and names Andrew E. Christie as an associate. Graubard coauthored with Christie a 2003 paper that mapped nitric oxide and carbon monoxide neurons in the crayfish Cherax quadricarinatus. A 2004 paper on the crab Cancer productus described a neurosecretory site, the anterior cardiac plexus, and gave FHL as an address for Graubard, Christie, Shaun D. Cain and most other authors.

Graubard's earlier work concerned how neurons of the stomatogastric ganglion signal without action potentials. A 1978 paper treated a non-spiking presynaptic neuron in the spiny lobster Panulirus interruptus, and a 1980 PNAS paper with J. A. Raper and D. K. Hartline showed graded transmission between spiking neurons in the lobster. With W. N. Ross, Graubard used optical methods to record calcium changes in crab neurons, in PNAS papers of 1985 and 1989. Later papers with colleagues in the group treated the fine branching of stomatogastric neurons in Cancer borealis with D. H. Baldwin (1995), calcium currents with L. M. Hurley (1998), and nitric oxide and cGMP signaling with N. L. Scholz (1996 to 2002).

name: Kathleen M. T. Grosicki
text: Kathleen M. T. Grosicki completed a Bachelor of Science with honors thesis at St. Francis Xavier University in 2014, co-supervised by Russell C. Wyeth and Cory D. Bishop. The thesis tested five surfaces for inhibiting settlement or metamorphosis of larvae of Ciona intestinalis, a tunicate that fouls mussel farms in Atlantic Canada. Polyvinyl siloxane, a material used in dental molds, bent larval tails and killed larvae through a substance leaching into water, likely a surfactant. Grosicki coauthored a 2016 paper in Marine Environmental Research from the same group, which reported that a siloxane-based elastomeric impression material leached alkylphenol ethoxylates toxic to C. intestinalis larvae.

name: Kathleen Rankin
text: Kathleen E. Rankin was a graduate student in Linda G. Wordeman's lab in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington. Rankin's work concerned the kinesin-13 microtubule depolymerizer MCAK. A 2005 paper in Journal of Cell Biology, with George von Dassow among the coauthors, showed MCAK tracking the tips of polymerizing microtubules in living cells. A 2010 paper with Wordeman depleted MCAK from HeLa cells to produce ultra-long astral microtubules, which caused the mitotic spindle to rock along its axis in early anaphase, driven by oscillations of cortical nonmuscle myosin II.

name: Kathryn A. McDonald
text:
Kathryn A. McDonald is a marine invertebrate biologist whose papers deal with the swimming and development of echinoderm embryos and larvae. She did graduate research in the University of Washington's Department of Biology while based at the Friday Harbor Laboratories, which her papers from 2003 to 2011 give as her address. Her graduate advisory committee was Richard R. Strathmann, Danny Grünbaum, Tom Daniel and Jennifer Ruesink. Her turbulence study was supported by an FHL Wainwright Fellowship and by a National Science Foundation grant to Strathmann. By 2010 her papers gave a present address at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in Panama, and a 2014 paper on development in the gastropod Calyptraea lichen, with Rachel Collin and Maryna Lesoway, lists her at Humboldt State University in California and at STRI.

Her FHL research asked how the earliest swimming stages of sea urchins and sand dollars move in the water and respond to their surroundings. A 2004 paper measured swimming and sinking of blastulae of four eastern Pacific echinoids. Sinking speeds equaled or exceeded swimming speeds, smaller embryos swam faster, and sinking was faster at 10 °C than at 14 °C. In the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus the temperature effect disappeared in killed embryos, suggesting active density regulation. With Dawn Vaughn (2010) she found that a sudden increase in food induced cloning in D. excentricus plutei, possibly by anterior autotomy. A later paper used a grid-stirred turbulence tank and shear flows: swimming increased upward transport of D. excentricus blastulae but reduced it in the purple urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus. A 2003 paper with Megan N. Dethier and Strathmann compared the seaweeds and animals of an isolated Washington jetty with distant source sites.

name: Kathryn L. Van Alstyne
text:
Kathryn L. Van Alstyne is a marine chemical ecologist and phycologist. She received a B.S. in zoology from the University of Rhode Island in 1983 and a Ph.D. in zoology from the University of Washington in 1988. Her papers list addresses at the University of Guam Marine Laboratory (1992 to 1994), the Department of Biology at Kenyon College in Ohio (1993 and 1995) and the Department of Zoology at Oregon State University (1999). From 1997 to 2025 she was a marine scientist at Western Washington University's Shannon Point Marine Center. The FHL-connected papers begin in 1988-1990, from the UW Department of Zoology; the 1989 and 1990 papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as a second address. Later census papers, from 2016 to 2023, come from collaborations on eelgrass, kelp crabs and ocean acidification with co-authors including Maya Groner, Megan Dethier and Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria.

Van Alstyne has studied how seaweeds and other attached marine organisms defend themselves against herbivores, predators and environmental stress. The FHL-era papers showed that grazing increased polyphenolic levels and induced adventitious branching in the intertidal rockweed Fucus distichus, measured how wounding by Littorina snails affects its growth and reproduction, and, with Valerie Paul, tested whether polyphenolic defenses of temperate brown algae deter tropical herbivorous fishes. Papers with Guam addresses examined chemical and structural defenses in Halimeda green algae, sea fans and soft corals. Later studies cover phlorotannins in Northeast Pacific kelps and rockweeds, DMSP cleavage as an activated defense, nutrients and DMSP in green-tide Ulva, and contaminants in edible Salish Sea seaweeds. The census papers from 2016 to 2023 deal with eelgrass wasting disease and its pathogen Labyrinthula zosterae, oysters and eelgrass in a high-CO2 ocean, and food choice between two kelps by the kelp crab Pugettia (2017).

name: Kathryn Lawrence
text: Kathryn Lawrence completed a PhD in zoology at the University of New Hampshire in 1997 under Winsor H. Watson III, with a dissertation on the neuroethology of swimming in the Pacific nudibranch Melibe leonina. The work described swimming as a stereotyped five-phase sequence that could be elicited by potassium chloride or the tube feet of a predatory sea star, and located the driving motor neurons in the pedal ganglion. Animals swam more in darkness, low-level light disrupted fictive swimming in isolated brains, and removing the eyes reversed the effect. A 2002 paper with Watson in Biological Bulletin, using Pycnopodia helianthoides, reported the behavioral findings.

name: Katie A. Dobkowski
text:
Katie A. Dobkowski is a marine ecologist whose work centers on bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) and the crabs that graze it in the Salish Sea. She joined the Ruesink laboratory in UW Biology in 2012 to pursue a PhD and completed a dissertation in 2017 on the biological and physical factors that influence bull kelp abundance and distribution. Her doctoral fieldwork was based at Friday Harbor Laboratories, and she was a UW scientific diver. Her 2023 paper on the graceful kelp crab lists her at Bates College, FHL and Woodbury University in California, and Woodbury reported in 2023 on her talks about kelp and kelp crabs. In summer 2020 Bates College students did research projects with her at FHL. Her FHL-connected papers run from 2017 to 2024, and she appears on FHL student reports from 2011, when she wrote a course report on cormorant diving, to 2025.

Dobkowski asks how species interactions and physical conditions control the abundance of bull kelp. Her 2017 study of northern and graceful kelp crabs (Pugettia producta and P. gracilis) combined laboratory feeding trials, in which P. producta preferred fresh bull kelp but also ate snails, with field enclosures in which only protected juvenile kelp grew. Further papers compared crab preferences between two kelps (2017), examined what influences bull kelp recruitment (2018) and described the scaling and structure of juvenile kelp (2021); with Megan Dethier she also studied shore crab predation on juvenile clams (2019). Recent papers (2023–2024) test how warming affects feeding by kelp crabs and the graceful kelp crab's choice between bull kelp and the invasive Sargassum muticum. Her annual snorkel surveys in the San Juan Islands suggest that bull kelp is declining overall. Student projects she co-authored at FHL range from kelp grazing and breakage to river otter diets.

name: Kayla C. Hall
text:
Kayla C. Hall is a biologist who studies the form, movement and life history of cartilaginous fishes. Hall's first papers, in 2018, came from the Department of Biology at San Francisco State University, in work with Karen Crow, Peter Hundt, John Swenson and Adam Summers of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Hall then completed a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington in 2023, with Summers as advisor. Papers from 2025 and 2026 give the Friday Harbor Laboratories and the UW Department of Biology as affiliations. Hall's FHL-connected papers in the census run from 2018 to 2026 and include fieldwork in the San Juan Channel near the laboratories, laboratory studies of sharks, skates and chimaeras, and a 2026 preprint, with Summers and others, on clingfish adhesive discs and skull shape.

Hall's research asks how skeletal design, swimming style and reproduction relate to where sharks, skates, rays and chimaeras live. Using radiography, CT scanning and dissection, the 2018 study showed that rays that swim by flapping, such as manta rays, have pectoral fin rays shifted toward the rear of the fin, and that fin-ray number and distribution are set early in development. The dissertation reviewed chondrichthyan life-history traits, compared the hydrodynamics of egg cases from several skate species, and described how spotted ratfish (Hydrolagus colliei) use their pectoral and pelvic fins in swimming. Later papers report the first identified potential ratfish nursery in the San Juan Islands, found in trawls from FHL (2025), and the shape and orientation of denticles around the nostrils of the Pacific spiny dogfish (2025). A 2026 paper used model chimaera fins to test how fin-ray diameter and packing affect fin motion.

text: Kelly Dorgan was a postdoctoral researcher in M. A. R. text: Kelly Druzisky earned an MS in 2001 in the Organismic and Evolutionary Biology graduate program at the University of Massachusetts Amherst under Elizabeth Brainerd. Her thesis examined buccal oscillation in the semi-aquatic turtle Platysternon megacephalum, using x-ray video and airflow measurements to test whether hyobranchial movements contribute to lung ventilation. name: Kenneth Lohmann
text:
Kenneth J. Lohmann is a biologist who studies animal navigation and magnetic sensing; Lohmann's papers give the Department of Biology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill as the address from at least 2000. He was a PhD student in A. O. Dennis Willows's lab at the University of Washington. A 1987 Science paper with Willows, giving Zoology and FHL as addresses, reported that the sea slug Tritonia diomedea orients to Earth's magnetic field, in patterns that varied with lunar phase. A 1991 paper with Willows and Robert B. Pinter identified a Tritonia neuron that responds to Earth-strength fields. In an account of Willows's work, W. N. Frost and P. S. Katz trace Lohmann's later sea turtle work to this discovery.

He had published on geomagnetic field detection in the spiny lobster Panulirus argus in 1985, and a 1991 paper on magnetic orientation in hatchling loggerhead turtles carried a University of Illinois address. At UNC he continued the Tritonia work with John H. Wang and Shaun D. Cain; their 2003 and 2004 Journal of Experimental Biology papers identified further neurons excited or inhibited by magnetic stimuli, and Cain's address on the second was FHL. A 2011 paper with Michael J. Baltzley, Allison Sherman and Cain treated a pedal peptide network across gastropods. Nature papers treat true navigation in spiny lobsters (2003, with L. C. Boles) and learned magnetic map cues in turtles (2025, with K. M. Goforth and others).

name: Kenneth M. Halanych
text:
Kenneth M. Halanych is an evolutionary biologist who studies the relationships and evolution of marine invertebrates. He holds a BS in biology from Wake Forest University and a PhD in zoology from the University of Texas (1994). After postdoctoral work at Rutgers University and the University of Pretoria, he was a scientist at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution from 1998 to 2002. He was then a professor at Auburn University from 2003 to 2021, where he held the Stewart Schneller Endowed Chair and was curator of marine invertebrates at the university museum from 2014. He is now executive director of the Center for Marine Science at the University of North Carolina Wilmington. He has edited the Biological Bulletin since 2016 and was elected an AAAS Fellow in 2018. He has taught at FHL several times as a visiting instructor, in courses on metazoan evolution and development and on deep-sea biology.

Halanych uses molecular systematics and genome-scale phylogenetics to work out the relationships of major animal groups. He also works on Antarctic fauna and on chemosynthetic animals. His 1995 Science paper used 18S ribosomal DNA to argue that lophophorates are protostomes. The census lists 29 FHL-connected items by him from 1995 to 2023, several written with the FHL-based Billie J. Swalla. Two papers concern hemichordate phylogeny, including deep-sea enteropneusts (2009) and a cold-water clade of harrimaniid acorn worms (2013). Two 2011 papers cover the spionid polychaete Boccardia proboscidea, whose reproduction varies along the West Coast, and the compact, fast-evolving mitochondrial genome of the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei. Later phylogenomic papers resolve the hemichordate–echinoderm clade (2014), major tunicate relationships (2017) and the aplacophoran mollusks (2019). Kevin M. Kocot and Johanna Taylor Cannon, linked to him in the report's network, are co-authors on several of these studies.

name: Kenneth P. Sebens
text:
Kenneth P. Sebens is a marine benthic ecologist and Professor in the Department of Biology and the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences at the University of Washington, resident at Friday Harbor Laboratories since 2005. He received a BA from the University of Connecticut (1972) and a PhD from the University of Washington (1977). He was on the Harvard faculty from 1977 to 1985, and from 1979 a curator of invertebrates at the Museum of Comparative Zoology. He then directed Northeastern University's Marine Science Center (1985–1991) and the University of Maryland system's Marine-Estuarine-Environmental Sciences graduate program (1991–1997), and was the first dean of the College of Science and Mathematics at the University of Massachusetts Boston (2003–2005). He was Director of FHL from 2005 to 2013, holding the Dennis Willows Director's Endowed Professorship from 2011. The census counts 16 FHL-address papers by him, from 2005 to 2021.

Sebens studies subtidal populations and communities in temperate and tropical seas. He has spent six missions living in the Hydrolab and Aquarius underwater laboratories on Caribbean reefs. His coral research concerned coral nutrition and how water flow affects particle capture, nutrient uptake and growth; a 2005 paper measured nitrate uptake by a reef coral. His paper on indeterminate growth and optimal size in marine invertebrates received the Ecological Society of America's 1983 Mercer Award. In 2006 he began studying rocky subtidal communities of the San Juan Islands. His FHL-connected papers cover grazer removal and four decades of change in subtidal communities (2013), ocean warming and coral body size (2016), mussel mechanics, energetics and byssal threads (2014–2021), giant Pacific octopus along an urbanization gradient (2018) and seawater data from the FHL Ocean Observatory (2020–2025). The mentoring network lists many of his students, including Robin Elahi and Eliza Heery.

name: Kerry J. Kim
text:
Kerry J. Kim is a biologist whose published work spans retinal physiology, computer models of gene networks and biology education research. Papers under his name from 2001 and 2003 give the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington as his address. From 2009 to 2011 his papers list the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories; the census counts four FHL-address papers from those years among five FHL-connected papers. His papers from 2017 to 2023 give SimBiotic Software in Missoula, Montana, as his address. The link between his earlier, FHL-era and later papers rests on bibliographic author matching.

At the Center for Cell Dynamics Kim worked with computer models of gene regulatory networks, describing Ingeneue, a software tool for simulating and exploring them (2009). With Vilaiwan Fernandes he used a model of the segment polarity network, a gene network essential to development in many insects, to simulate evolution in haploid and diploid, sexual and asexual populations; robustness rose in all four, most in diploid sexual populations (2009). He wrote the 2009 Science commentary 'Sizing up the cell' with Bruce Edgar and co-authored a 2011 Nature study of how E2F and CRL4Cdt2 control endocycles in Drosophila and a 2011 Current Biology paper, with Marie-Anne Félix and Edwin Munro, on quantitative variation in signaling in the Caenorhabditis vulval network. Earlier papers with Fred Rieke studied adaptation in salamander retinal ganglion cells. His SimBiotic papers test question formats, assessments and feedback for teaching biology, including neurophysiology and experimental design.

name: Kerry Walton
text: Kerry Walton was co-supervised by Nicole E. Phillips for a 2017 thesis at Victoria University of Wellington on the phylogeography of the New Zealand rocky-shore whelks Cominella maculosa and C. virgata. Using mitochondrial CO1 and 16S and nuclear 18S sequences, the work found considerable phylogeographic structure in both species and synonymized the purported subspecies C. virgata brookesi. A 2018 Biological Journal of the Linnean Society paper with Phillips, Bruce A. Marshall and others followed. Walton later applied paleogenetic techniques to historic abalone shells (Molecular Ecology Resources, 2023) and became curator of invertebrates at the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa in 2023.

name: Kevin H. Britton‐Simmons
text:
Kevin H. Britton-Simmons is a marine community ecologist whose published work concerns subtidal habitats of the San Juan Islands, Washington. With Timothy Wootton and support from the SeaDoc Society, he ran three years of field and laboratory experiments on the introduced brown seaweed Sargassum muticum. The census counts ten FHL-address papers by him, from 2004 to 2014; several from 2004 to 2010 also list the University of Chicago. His co-authors include H. L. Stewart, K. C. Abbott, T. Klinger, D. K. Padilla, D. O. Duggins and A. W. Galloway.

Much of his work tested how Sargassum muticum, introduced to Washington's inland waters with oysters imported from Asia, affects native communities. A 2004 paper reported its direct and indirect effects on subtidal communities; SeaDoc's summary says the seaweed outcompetes native kelp for light and indirectly harms green urchins, and that native communities recovered within about a year of its removal. Later papers examined how disturbance and propagule supply shape invasion success (2007), invaders in marine reserves (2006) and effects on a native herbivorous snail (2010). He also studied the nonnative seagrass Zostera japonica (2010) and how tidal currents bias estimates of kelp bed size (2008). A second line of work followed seaweed drifting below the zone where it grows: drift algae as food for a deep subtidal sea urchin (2009), drift macrophytes and their invertebrates (2011), fatty-acid signatures of macrophytes (2012) and sedentary urchins below the macroalgal zone (2014).

name: Kevin Houston
text: Kevin D. Houston is a professor of biochemistry in New Mexico State University's Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry and co-mentored Taylor Landfair with Charles Shuster in the university's G-RISE program (2025-2026). The Houston laboratory studies how breast cancer cells develop resistance to anti-estrogen therapies such as tamoxifen.

name: Kevin Leempoel
text: Kevin Leempoel is listed as a postdoctoral researcher of Sarah Cohen at San Francisco State University. Leempoel earned a PhD at the Environmental Engineering Institute of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (2011-2015), and landscape genomics work there included multiscale models for detecting selection in the alpine plant Biscutella laevigata (Ecology and Evolution, 2018). As a Stanford University postdoctoral fellow (2017-2020), Leempoel compared environmental DNA with camera trapping for assessing terrestrial mammal diversity (Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2020, with Trevor Hebert and Elizabeth A. Hadly). From 2020 Leempoel was a bioinformatician at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, and coauthored a 2024 Nature paper on angiosperm phylogenomics.

name: Kevin M. Kocot
text:
Kevin M. Kocot is an invertebrate zoologist and systematist who joined the University of Alabama in 2016 as an assistant professor and curator of invertebrate zoology at the Alabama Museum of Natural History, and later became professor. His PhD at Auburn University (2013) was chaired by Kenneth M. Halanych, who also supervised a short postdoc. At FHL he took Marine Invertebrate Zoology in 2007, the year he began at Auburn, and Evolution and Development of the Metazoans in 2008, and served as a teaching assistant in Marine Genomics (2010) and Evolution and Development (2011). He taught Marine Invertebrate Zoology in 2016 and 2018, co-taught Biodiversity and Integrative Taxonomy of Invertebrates in 2022 with Gustav Paulay, and chaired the FHL Illg Lecture Committee from 2021.

His dissertation used phylogenomics to resolve the molluscan tree; a 2011 Nature paper placed chitons with worm-like aplacophorans in Aculifera, sister to the shelled mollusks. He was then a postdoc with Bernie Degnan at the University of Queensland (2014-2015), on an NSF fellowship. His lab concentrates on mollusks, particularly aplacophorans. Local work includes three new meiofaunal solenogasters from Friday Harbor (2014, with Christiane Todt) and a new kinorhynch from the San Juan Islands (2019), led by Rebecca Varney, his PhD student from 2017 to 2021, who took the FHL invertebrate course in 2017. With Billie J. Swalla he co-wrote phylogenomic papers on hemichordates and echinoderms (2014) and tunicates (2017).

name: Kevin Miklasz
text: Kevin Miklasz was a postdoctoral researcher with Emily Carrington at the University of Washington, listed on the Carrington lab's alumni page (2012), and gave Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address on a 2018 Journal of Phycology paper with Rebecca Guenther, Carrington and Patrick T. Martone showing that ocean acidification delays and weakens macroalgal spore adhesion. A 2015 Phycologia paper with Elizabeth van der Merwe, Paul W. Gabrielson and others used DNA sequencing to resolve Spongites species in the Northeast Pacific and South Africa. Miklasz, listed among alumni of Mark Denny's lab at Stanford University, wrote with Denny on diatom sinking speeds using a modified Stokes' law (Limnology and Oceanography, 2010).

name: Kevin Peteroy
text: Kevin Peteroy earned an MS in marine biology and coastal sciences at Montclair State University in 2024, with Matt Schuler as thesis sponsor and Colette J. Feehan on the committee. The thesis followed zooplankton and water quality in 20 vernal pools in Wayne, New Jersey, through two floods. Diversity fell after the August flood and rose after the October flood.

name: Kevin Richard Turner
text: Kevin R. Turner completed a PhD in Biology at the University of Washington in 2015 with Kenneth P. Sebens; Megan N. Dethier, Daniel E. Schindler and Terrie Klinger served on his committee, and he taught at Friday Harbor Laboratories. The dissertation tested how rockfish and other predatory fishes shape rocky subtidal communities in the San Juan Archipelago. Gastric lavage showed copper rockfish ate mostly shrimp and other demersal crustaceans (Turner, Rung and Sebens 2017). Exclusion experiments and surveys linked predators to fewer shrimp and small fish but gave little evidence of a fish-driven trophic cascade. He co-authored a 2013 paper on four decades of subtidal community change (Elahi et al.).

name: Kevin Sonnemann
text: Kevin Sonnemann was listed as an independent scientist in William M. Bement's laboratory at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. K. J. Sonnemann's earlier papers with J. M. Ervasti addressed actin and dystrophin in muscle: a 2006 study of mice lacking cytoplasmic gamma-actin in skeletal muscle, from Madison's Program in Cellular and Molecular Biology, and a 2009 test of TAT-utrophin in dystrophin-deficient mice, from the University of Minnesota. With Bement, Sonnemann co-wrote a 2011 review of wound repair, a 2016 study of membrane dynamics in wounded Xenopus laevis oocytes, and a 2026 preprint on the Rho GAP RGA-3/4 and F-actin.

text: Kieran J. Murphy is listed as an MSc student on the Russell C. Wyeth lab page. name: Kiho Kim
text: Kiho Kim was a postdoctoral associate in C. Drew Harvell's laboratory, working on coral disease. Papers with Harvell include a 1999 Science paper on emerging marine diseases, a six-year record of the fungal disease aspergillosis in sea fans, Gorgonia ventalina, in the Florida Keys (Kim and Harvell 2004), and a longitudinal study of the same disease (2006). The Harvell lab lists Kim as an associate professor at American University, where Kim's affiliation was the Department of Biology in 2004 and the Department of Environmental Science by 2017. Later papers used a coral skeleton record of sewage nitrogen on Guam (2017) and tracked fecal indicator bacteria in Saipan reef waters (2020).

text: Kimberly K. Fong earned a PhD in biochemistry at UW in 2016 in the lab of Trisha N. Davis, with Linda G. Wordeman on the supervisory committee. name: Kimberly Quillin
text: Kimberly J. Quillin was a graduate student in M. A. R. Koehl's laboratory at UC Berkeley and earned a PhD in integrative biology there in 1999. Three sole-authored Journal of Experimental Biology papers examined how the hydrostatic skeleton of the earthworm Lumbricus terrestris scales during growth: stress scaling (1998), peristaltic crawling (1999) and burrowing forces (2000). Quillin also wrote with Koehl and C. A. Pell on the stiffening of embryonic notochords (2000). Salisbury University lists Quillin as professor of the practice in biological sciences. Quillin co-authored the textbook Biological Science and co-wrote a 2015 framework on drawing as a tool for learning biology.

text: Kimya Nourbakhsh earned a PhD in pharmacology at UW in 2021, with Smita Yadav as doctoral advisor and Linda G. Wordeman on the reading committee. The work appeared in Developmental Cell (2021).

name: Kindall Murie
text:
Kindall Murie is a marine ecologist who studies how kelp and mussels change the chemistry of the water around them, and a postdoctoral scholar in the Oceans Department at Stanford University as of 2026, listed in Brooke L. Weigel's lab at Hopkins Marine Station. She earned a PhD at the University of Washington (thesis dated 2025) with Emily Carrington as advisor, doing much of the work at FHL. There she first measured how strong tidal currents in the San Juan Islands limit the effect of bull kelp, Nereocystis luetkeana, on pH and dissolved oxygen; kelp-driven oxygen gains occurred mainly at daytime slack tides. She then moved to mussels, within a collaborative NSF project led by Carrington, Matt Reidenbach and Mike Nishizaki.

In the large flume in FHL's Lab 6, she paired magnetic gape sensors with oxygen sensors in single-layer mussel beds. Oxygen depletion fell exponentially as flow increased, while gaping stayed largely static across three Mytilus species. Field outplants then showed oxygen falling sharply as aggregation density rose. Earlier, at Humboldt State University, she completed an MS (2020) with Paul Bourdeau as committee chair, showing that fragmented kelp patches in northern California still altered seawater chemistry much as large forests did (Scientific Reports, 2020). She also mentored Nina Michael in the FHL 470 course in spring 2023 and co-authored a 2022 NSF REU-Blinks intern report by Hana Larkins.

name: Kirk Parmenter
text: Kirk Parmenter earned a PhD in biological sciences at Clemson University in 2012, with Michael J. Childress as advisor and Amy L. Moran on the committee. The dissertation asked whether drought and rising salinity explain falling blue crab (Callinectes sapidus) abundance in South Carolina's ACE Basin, sampling 27 stations from 2008 to 2012. Higher salinity improved survival but increased infection by the parasite Hematodinium.

name: Kirk S. Zigler
text:
Kirk S. Zigler is an invertebrate zoologist and professor of biology at Sewanee: The University of the South, whose work moved from sea urchin evolution to cave biodiversity. He held an NSF International Research Fellowship (2002-2005) to work with H. A. Lessios at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama and Rudolf A. Raff at Indiana University. The project asked how development evolves, using Clypeaster rosaceus, a sea urchin with a facultatively feeding larva, as a step between indirect and direct development. He published on egg energetics in C. rosaceus and Brisaster latifrons and gamete incompatibility between C. rosaceus and C. subdepressus (2008), and on germ layer allocation in C. rosaceus (2013).

Much of his marine work followed the sperm protein bindin, which mediates sperm-egg attachment and species recognition. With Lessios he traced 250 million years of bindin evolution (2003) and speciation in Lytechinus along the coasts of the Americas (2004). A 2005 paper with Lessios and others, showing that bindin divergence predicts gamete compatibility, lists FHL among his addresses, and before Sewanee he collected sea urchins around the San Juan Islands. By 2008 his address was Sewanee, where he turned to cave-dwelling animals of Tennessee, Alabama and Georgia, surveying caves with undergraduates. Studies include cave biodiversity and endemism in Tennessee (2013, with Matthew Niemiller) and two new Nesticus spiders from Georgia caves (2022). A National Park Service grant funded study of caves at Cumberland Gap.

name: Kirsten Copren
text: Kirsten Copren was a postdoctoral researcher in Sarah Cohen's laboratory at San Francisco State University, after a PhD in population biology at UC Davis (2004). Copren's termite research used cuticular hydrocarbons, mitochondrial DNA and microsatellites to examine cryptic species and social structure in California subterranean termites, Reticulitermes, including a 2005 phylogenetic study and a 2007 paper on microsatellite loci. Copren was technical director of the Genome Analysis Core at UCSF's comprehensive cancer center from 2006 to 2017. The Cohen lab lists a later post as director of nucleic acid technology in the University of Pennsylvania's Gene Therapy Program.

text: Kirsten Marie Nelsen earned a Master of Marine Affairs at UW in 2015, with David Fluharty as committee chair and Terrie Klinger on the reading committee. The thesis assessed three decision support tools used in marine spatial planning (InVEST, Marxan and MIMES). It identified heavy data demands, thin documentation and hard-to-interpret outputs as barriers to their use in tradeoff analysis.

text: Kirsten Martina Feifel earned a PhD at UW in oceanography in 2015, with Evelyn Lessard as chair of the supervisory committee and Terrie Klinger among the committee members. The dissertation used sediment cores to study the survival of Alexandrium cysts and their use in reconstructing harmful algal blooms in the Pacific Northwest. With S. K. Moore and R. A. Horner, Feifel published a 2012 cyst record from Sequim Bay, Washington, and its relation to past climate variability.

name: Kit Yu Karen Chan
text:
Kit Yu Karen Chan is a biological oceanographer who studies larval swimming and feeding under ocean change, and an associate professor in the School of Oceanography at the University of Washington as of 2026. She took a BSc at the University of Hong Kong (2006), then an MSc and PhD (2012) in oceanography at UW under Daniel Grünbaum. Her thesis used video motion analysis to show that larval sand dollars, Dendraster excentricus, reared at elevated pCO2 kept swimming but fed less well. Purple urchin and heart urchin larvae showed similar tradeoffs and budded asexually under acidification. She also built three-dimensional larval models from confocal images and finite-element meshes. In 2012 she co-authored a report by FHL summer intern Cristina Villalobos, with Grünbaum, on fertilization of sand dollars at low pH.

After the PhD she held a Croucher Foundation fellowship at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, working on interactions between fluids and organisms under climate change. A 2013 paper with Houshuo Jiang and Dianna K. Padilla found that swimming speed in larval snails did not track size or ciliary beat frequency. She also held an assistant professorship in the Division of Life Science at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and worked in the Biology Department of Swarthmore College from 2019 to 2024. Her collaboration with Grünbaum continued in a 2020 study of echinoid larvae in pH-stratified water columns. Later papers cover microplastics and larval urchin feeding (2022), modeling fertilization (2024) and flow around barnacle nauplii (2026).

name: Kiyoshi Hiruma
text: Kiyoshi Hiruma was a research scientist in Lynn M. Riddiford's laboratory at the University of Washington, with affiliations in the Department of Zoology and later the Department of Biology, and the two published together from 1984 to 2013. The work concerned hormonal control of molting and metamorphosis in the tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta: cuticular melanization (1984), dopa decarboxylase regulation (1985, 1990), and control of the transcription factor MHR3 by ecdysone receptor isoforms (2004). By 2007 Hiruma's papers, including those with Riddiford, gave an affiliation at Hirosaki University's Faculty of Agriculture and Life Sciences; later work there treated juvenile hormone biosynthesis in the silkworm Bombyx mori (Kaneko and Hiruma 2014).

name: Kjell Johansen
text:
Kjell Johansen was a comparative physiologist who studied respiration and circulation in a wide range of animals. His papers from 1958 to the mid-1960s carry addresses at the Institute for Experimental Medical Research and the University of Oslo in Norway. From 1962 into the mid-1970s he published from the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington, and from 1972 his papers list the Department of Zoophysiology at Aarhus University in Denmark; his publications continue to the late 1980s. His FHL-connected papers date from 1967 to 1973. A 1967 study of the hepatic veins of elasmobranchs, written with David Hanson, gives both the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as addresses and states that its physiological experiments on dogfish and skates were made at FHL. The report's mentoring network links him to Hans Jørgen Fyhn as a student.

Johansen's research concerned how animals take up, transport and deliver oxygen, often comparing water and air breathing. His publications cover air breathing in fishes, including the African, South American and Australian lungfishes, the bowfin Amia calva and the electric eel; blood distribution in ducks during submersion; oxygen storage in pinnipeds and the sea otter; circulation and hemocyanin oxygen transport in the octopus Octopus dofleini; gravitational hemodynamics in the giraffe; and shifts in hemoglobin-oxygen affinity as an adaptation to hypoxia. His FHL-connected papers apply these questions to local marine animals: muscular sphincters that control hepatic blood flow in the Pacific dogfish and a skate (1967), oxygen uptake and responses to respiratory stress in sea urchins, with Robert Vadas (1967), and gas exchange in the sea star Pteraster tesselatus (1971) and the giant chiton Cryptochiton stelleri (1973), both with J. A. Petersen.

name: Koen Verbrugghe
text: Koen J. C. Verbrugghe was a postdoctoral fellow in William M. Bement's laboratory at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Earlier work in the university's Laboratory of Genetics with J. G. White examined cytokinesis in C. elegans embryos: SPD-1 and spindle midzone formation (2004), and the parallel roles of cortical centralspindlin and G alpha in furrow initiation (2007). With the Bement group, Verbrugghe co-wrote a 2009 study led by George von Dassow that used live imaging in urchin and frog embryos to relate microtubule organization to furrow position; the paper carried an FHL affiliation. A 2011 methods paper on imaging C. elegans embryos came from University of Michigan human genetics.

name: Kory M. Evans
text:
Kory M. Evans is an evolutionary morphologist of fishes at Rice University, which he joined as an assistant professor of biosciences in 2020. He earned a BS at Nova Southeastern University (2013) and a PhD at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette (2017), where he published on Neotropical electric fishes with James S. Albert. Elizabeth L. Brainerd's lab at Brown University lists him among its postdoctoral alumni, and papers from 2018 and 2019 give his address at the University of Minnesota. He came to FHL on a Wainwright Fellowship and, with Matthew A. Kolmann, conceived a 2018 study of scale-feeding fishes with Adam P. Summers that used CT scans made at FHL's Karel F. Liem Bio-Imaging Center.

His work asks how the fish skull diversifies and which parts evolve together. Two 2017 papers examined how shifts in integration and developmental disintegration shaped skulls in electric fishes, and a 2018 study treated sexually dimorphic phenotypes in the same group. A 2019 paper with Mark W. Westneat tested whether coral reefs promote diversification of the labrid pharyngeal jaw. At Rice he and his co-authors have studied flatfishes (2021), beaked wrasses (2023), parrotfish growth and diet (2024), and carangarian fishes (2026). In 2023 he received a five-year NSF CAREER award to study skull shape across about 300 million years of evolution in spiny ray-finned fishes, using CT scans and a method, developed with a University of Chicago lab, that analyzes the whole skull at once.

name: Kristian Fauchald
text:
Kristian Fauchald (1935–2015) was a Norwegian-born zoologist who specialized in polychaete worms. He took his first degrees at the University of Bergen and moved to California in 1965 for doctoral work with Olga Hartman at the University of Southern California. He became assistant professor of biology there in 1969 and was curator of marine annelids at the Allan Hancock Foundation until 1979. In 1979 he moved to the Department of Invertebrate Zoology at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History, where he stayed for the rest of his career and was latterly an emeritus research zoologist. He was a founding editor of the Polychaeta section of the World Register of Marine Species. At Friday Harbor he taught polychaete biology classes with Peter Jumars and later with Sally Woodin and Herb Wilson. The census holds three of his papers, from 2008 to 2014.

Fauchald worked on the classification of polychaetes. His 1977 definitions and keys to the orders, families and genera of polychaetes (the 'Pink Book') and his 1979 study of polychaete feeding guilds with Jumars, 'The diet of worms', had each been cited more than a thousand times by 2015. Much of his work concerned the order Eunicida, including revisionary monographs such as a 1982 revision of the onuphid genera Onuphis, Nothria and Paradiopatra based on type material, and he took part in early cladistic analyses of annelids. His census papers continue this line: a 2008 description of a new Diopatra from Belize and a 2014 study with Joana Zanol and Kenneth Halanych that reconciled taxonomy and phylogeny in the Eunicidae. The 2009 paper, with Nataliya Budaeva, described the larval development of the onuphid Mooreonuphis stigmatis from the north-east Pacific, using specimens collected and preserved with help from FHL staff.

name: Kristin Stover
text: Kristin Stover was a PhD student of Elizabeth Brainerd in Brown University's Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology (PhD 2017). name: Kristina Mead
text: Kristina S. Mead was a postdoc in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley, working on the hydrodynamics of stomatopod olfactory antennules. Papers from that work measured antennule flicking and sampling efficiency, and odor encounter by mantis shrimp tracking turbulent plumes (2000, 2003). Earlier work from Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station with Mark Denny and David Epel examined how water motion affects sea urchin fertilization (1995). By 2003 Mead was in the Biology Department at Denison University, publishing on crayfish antennules (2008) and on neuroscience teaching for undergraduates (2005-2012).

text: Krystal L. Rypien was a PhD student of C. Drew Harvell in Cornell University's Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology. text: Kyra Amacker was a PhD student of Stacy Farina at Howard University, as listed on Farina's 2023 curriculum vitae. The study used sonomicrometry crystals on the opercle bones and pressure transducers in the gill chambers to follow breathing above and below sediment and during burial. name: L. D. Partridge
text:
L. D. Partridge, who signs most of his papers L. Donald Partridge, is a neurophysiologist. His FHL-connected papers date from 1973 to 1979. A 1976 paper with Charles F. Stevens gives his address as the Department of Physiology and Biophysics, University of Washington School of Medicine, with a present address at Friday Harbor Laboratories. His 1975 and 1979 papers in Brain Research give FHL as his address. A 1973 note in The Veliger, under the name L. D. Partridge Jr., thanks R. L. Fernald, then FHL director, for use of the laboratories. Papers under the same name, continuing the same lines of work, give addresses at the University of New Mexico School of Medicine, first in physiology from 1980 and later in neurosciences, into the 2010s. Some bibliographic databases wrongly merge his papers with those of Linda Partridge, a different scientist.

His FHL-connected papers concern the anatomy and electrical behavior of molluscan neurons. The 1973 note described the circumesophageal ganglion complex of several dorid nudibranchs. A 1975 paper reported that bursting induced by the convulsant pentylenetetrazol can occur without a negative-conductance characteristic. In 1976 he published two papers in The Journal of Physiology. One, with Stevens, traced spike-frequency adaptation in neurons of the nudibranchs Archidoris montereyensis and Anisodoris nobilis to a slow current and added it to a model of repetitive firing. The other, with R. C. Thomas, showed that lithium injected into snail neurones raised their resting potassium permeability. A 1979 paper with S. H. Thompson, S. J. Smith and J. A. Connor analyzed current-voltage relationships of repetitively firing neurons. His later New Mexico papers continued this work, then turned to calcium-activated cation channels and synaptic transmission in mammalian neurons.

name: L. Patricia Hernandez
text:
L. Patricia Hernandez is Professor of Biology in the Department of Biological Sciences at the George Washington University, where her listed field of expertise is functional morphology. She received a BS in biology from Eckerd College (1987), an MS in zoology from the University of South Florida (1994) and a PhD in organismic and evolutionary biology from Harvard University (1999). Her connection to FHL in the census comes through co-authors with FHL addresses, chiefly Karly Cohen, who came to FHL from George Washington University, and Adam Summers of FHL. The census lists six papers with her name, from 2018 to 2022, on fish feeding, teeth, attachment and development.

Hernandez studies how the fish head develops and evolves. Her group has examined craniofacial development in zebrafish, including the role of the Hedgehog pathway in the differentiation of branchial cartilages. It has also studied the proportion and distribution of muscle fiber types in cranial muscles, neurocranial shape in cyprinids, and the evolution of the Weberian apparatus in otophysan fishes. Her FHL-connected papers use anatomy, micro-CT imaging and flow measurement. They include a 2018 model of filter feeding in silver carp built from micro-CT and 3D particle image velocimetry, a 2019 study of heterodonty and tooth replacement in piranhas and pacus, and a 2020 study of the soft tissues behind the viscoelastic grip of the remora's sucker. A 2022 paper examined how shifts in developmental position and timing shaped the epibranchial organs of otocephalan fishes. She also co-signed a 2018 editorial on the aims of the journal Integrative Organismal Biology.

name: Larry R. McEdward
text:
Larry R. McEdward was a marine biologist who studied the ecology, physiology and evolution of invertebrate larvae and life histories, especially in echinoderms. He completed his PhD with Richard R. Strathmann of the University of Washington, whose CV lists him among his doctoral students. His papers from the early 1990s give his address as the Department of Zoology at the University of Florida in Gainesville. He edited Ecology of Marine Invertebrate Larvae (CRC Press, 1995), a 13-chapter review of larval diversity, feeding, mortality, behavior, dispersal, recruitment and evolution. He died unexpectedly in 2001, and the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology held a symposium in his honor on life histories of benthic marine invertebrates. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 1984 to 1991. Later papers appear in the FHL bibliography or mention FHL in their text.

McEdward asked how egg size, larval form and feeding shape the development and evolution of marine life cycles. His FHL-era papers measured the growth, shape and metabolism of an echinoid pluteus larva and how temperature affects its form and development rate (1984–1985). Comparative studies of echinoid larvae related egg size to larval form, feeding and metabolism (1986). With Strathmann he argued that the ciliary sieve of the cyphonautes larva breaks a biological rule of inference (1986). Other papers showed that egg volume and energy content are not correlated among sibling starfish eggs (1987), tested the developmental effects of reduced egg size with Barry Sinervo (1988), and measured eggs of echinoderms with non-feeding pelagic larvae (1991). At Florida he proposed that the starfish Pteraster tesselatus had re-evolved pelagic larval development from brooding (1992), a theme he pursued with Daniel Janies, and later modeled fecundity and development time (2003–2004).

name: Laura Newcomb
text:
Laura Newcomb is a marine biologist whose ORCID record now lists her as a program analyst in the Office of Science Support of NOAA's Oceanic and Atmospheric Research. She received a PhD in biology from the University of Washington in 2015, supported by a National Science Foundation IGERT Program on Ocean Change fellowship, FHL's Strathmann and Wainwright fellowships and UW Biology's Edmondson Award. The report's mentoring network lists Emily Carrington as her thesis advisor. Her doctoral experiments used mussels held at Friday Harbor Laboratories, which appears as an address on her papers from 2015 to 2022. Earlier co-authored papers concern the sea crossings of migrating griffon vultures (2009) and coral mortality from low-temperature stress in the Florida Keys (2011). At NOAA she has co-authored analyses of research transition and a 2023 Philosophy of Science paper on how institutional values shape the evaluation of NOAA funding proposals.

Newcomb's FHL-connected work asks how ocean warming and acidification affect mussels' byssal threads. Her dissertation combined laboratory crosses of seawater pH and temperature (10 to 25 °C) with a field study at a mussel farm. Warm water produced fewer and weaker threads in Mytilus trossulus, and low pH strengthened the plaque but not the whole thread. Above about 18 °C the warm-adapted M. galloprovincialis attached more strongly while M. trossulus attached more weakly. Papers from this work analyzed thread structure under combined temperature and CO2 stress (2019) and the divergent responses of the two species to warming (2022). With Emily Roberts and others she showed that induced thread production reduces mussel growth (2021). She was first author, with Jason Hall-Spencer and others, of a 2015 study of ocean acidification and the alga called the mermaid's wineglass, and co-authored FHL student reports on tide-pool carbonate chemistry (2011) and thread production (2012).

text: Laura A. Romano was a postdoctoral research associate in Gregory Wray's lab at Duke University (2000-2003), after a PhD at the University of Arizona, where papers with R. B. Runyan showed Slug acting in epithelial-mesenchymal transformation in the developing chicken heart (1999, 2000). At Duke, Romano studied the sea urchin gene Endo16: conservation of its expression despite regulatory divergence (Development, 2003) and its requirement in gastrulation of Lytechinus variegatus (2006). At Denison University, as assistant professor from 2003 and associate professor from 2010, Romano published on the cis-regulatory region of SM50 in sea urchins (Developmental Biology, 2008) and worked on environmental effects on aquatic invertebrate embryos.

name: Laura S. Corley
text: Laura S. Corley was a PhD student in Billie J. Swalla's lab at Vanderbilt University in 1995 and 1996, then finished the PhD at the University of Kentucky with Allen J. Moore and was a postdoctoral fellow with Michael R. Strand at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. name: Lauren E. Vandepas
text:
Lauren E. Vandepas is a marine invertebrate biologist who has studied development and immunity in early-branching animals and in bivalves. A 2012 student paper from the Marine Invertebrate Zoology course at FHL compared meiofaunal communities at three sites on the Eagle Cove beach. Vandepas completed a University of Washington Biology PhD in 2018 under Chris T. Amemiya, with Kenneth P. Sebens on the graduate committee from 2012. A 2016 study of Nautilus pompilius phylogeography with Billie J. Swalla and Peter D. Ward lists Vandepas under Friday Harbor Laboratories and the Biology Department.

The dissertation traced chitin synthase genes across Cnidaria and used the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis to examine chitin in soft tissues and spirocysts. Other graduate work included the biogeography of the sea squirt Phallusia nigra (2015) and a 2016 Current Biology paper on the ctenophore through-gut. On a National Research Council postdoctoral fellowship, with an affiliation at NOAA's Northwest Fisheries Science Center, Vandepas was co-first author of a 2024 Nature Communications paper on extracellular DNA traps in the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi and the oyster Crassostrea gigas. Papers from 2023 to 2025 add a University of Miami affiliation, including work on transmissible neoplasia in the basket cockle. A 2025 single-cell study of Pacific oyster embryos, with Vandepas as co-first author, traced primordial germ cells to a distinct cluster at gastrulation; that paper lists Vandepas at the University of Washington School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences.

name: Lauren Eve Simonitis
text:
Lauren Eve Simonitis is a comparative morphologist who studies the anatomy of fishes, especially the olfactory organs of sharks and their relatives. Her papers from 2018 to 2022 give the Department of Marine Biology of Texas A&M University at Galveston as her address. She then held a National Science Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship in Biology (2022 to 2024), hosted by Florida Atlantic University and the University of Washington, and an FHL Calvin Postdoctoral Fellowship. Her papers from 2023 to 2025 list Friday Harbor Laboratories, often together with Florida Atlantic University; the census counts four FHL-address papers in those years, and the report lists her as still at FHL. These papers acknowledge the laboratories' Karl F. Liem Memorial Bioimaging Facility and micro-CT scanner. In 2022 she was co-author, with Ayi Ajavon, of an FHL student research paper comparing the olfactory organs of three intertidal gunnel species.

Simonitis asks how the structure of the olfactory organ relates to water flow and smell. She has described the microstructure of the bonnethead shark's olfactory rosette (2022) and the denticles of shark nostrils and their hydrodynamic implications (2025). Using contrast-enhanced micro-CT and scanning electron microscopy, she studied the rosettes of Pacific spiny dogfish and spotted ratfish trawled near Friday Harbor, finding larger, more folded lamellae at the center of the rosette but no difference in sensory surface area among lamellar positions (2024). Her NSF fellowship project asked whether ink from animals such as California sea hares and common cuttlefish deters sharks, whether sharks can smell it, and how it moves through the shark nostril. Other FHL-connected papers compare the anatomy and evolution of gizzards across fishes (2023) and reconstruct the history of shell-boring polychaetes in the native oyster Ostrea lurida in the Salish Sea, to inform its restoration (2025).

text: Lauren Gentry completed a 2016 Auburn University master's thesis under advisor Anthony Moss, with Kenneth M. Halanych on the committee. The thesis tested in the laboratory how the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi behaves in low oxygen, finding that animals gathered at an artificial oxycline and around an artificial oxygen source. Gentry became a research associate in marine ecology at the Fish and Wildlife Research Institute's Center for Spatial Analysis in 2018.

text: Lauren Pintor was a postdoc in James E. Byers's lab at the University of Georgia in 2010. Earlier papers with Andrew Sih compared aggression, boldness, growth and foraging in native and introduced populations of an invasive crayfish (2008). The Byers lab page lists Pintor later as an associate professor in the School of Environment and Natural Resources at Ohio State University; later papers with Suzanne Gray addressed behavior in African cichlids (2018, 2025).

text: Laurie Raymundo was a graduate student in C. Drew Harvell's lab at Cornell University, with Charles H. text: Lawrence Small was a PhD student of Adriana T. Dawes in Molecular Genetics at Ohio State University, listed in the lab from 2011 to 2016. Small earned a BA in molecular and cellular biology at Vanderbilt University in 2007 and held a research associate post in Ohio State's Molecular Genetics department from 2016.

name: Leda Gerber
text: Leda Gerber was a postdoc with Charles H. Greene at Cornell University from 2013 to 2015, working on marine microalgae as a source of fuel and feed. Gerber was first author of a 2016 modeling study, combining process design, techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment, that identified target algal productivity and financing values for biocrude from microalgae. Gerber also contributed to a 2016 report on geothermal heat for hydrothermal liquefaction of algae and, with Greene, a 2018 paper on replacing fishmeal and fish oil with microalgal products. Related work applied life cycle assessment to bioenergy systems (2011) and to designing renewable energy systems in a 2014 book.

name: Leon Lichtenstein
text:
Leon Lichtenstein (1878–1933) was a Polish-German mathematician, born in Warsaw, who came to mathematics from engineering. He graduated in mechanical engineering from the Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenburg in 1901 and worked as an electrical engineer for Siemens & Halske from 1902 to 1920, heading its cable factory from 1906. During those years he took a doctorate in engineering at the Technische Hochschule (1908) and a doctorate in mathematics at the University of Berlin (1909), and he habilitated at the Technische Hochschule in 1910. He became professor at Münster in 1920 and held the chair of mathematics at Leipzig from 1921 or 1922 until 1933. He co-founded Mathematische Zeitschrift in 1918 and edited the Jahrbuch über die Fortschritte der Mathematik from 1919 until the late 1920s. He has no papers in the census; he appears in the report at the root of a mentoring line that reaches FHL.

Lichtenstein worked in potential theory, integral equations, the calculus of variations, differential equations and conformal mapping. He applied these methods to hydrodynamics and to celestial mechanics, especially the equilibrium figures of rotating fluids. His books include Astronomie und Mathematik in ihrer Wechselwirkung (1922), Grundlagen der Hydromechanik (1929) and Gleichgewichtsfiguren rotierender Flüssigkeiten (1933). At Leipzig his doctoral students included Ernst Hölder, Erich Kähler and Aurel Wintner. Wintner was his assistant from 1927 to 1929, helping to edit Mathematische Zeitschrift and the Jahrbuch, and wrote his Leipzig dissertation on convergence questions in lunar theory under Lichtenstein and the astronomer Julius Bauschinger. Wintner later taught at Johns Hopkins, where Monroe H. Martin was his student. Martin advised Simon A. Levin (Maryland, 1964), and Levin's Cornell student Daniel Grünbaum is a University of Washington scientist with FHL-connected papers from 2010 to 2020.

name: Leonid L. Moroz
text:
Leonid L. Moroz is a neuroscientist at the University of Florida, where he is Distinguished Professor of Neuroscience, Genetics, Biology and Chemistry, based at the Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience. He received a B.S. in animal and human physiology from Belarus University in Minsk (1982) and a Ph.D. from the Institute of Developmental Biology in Moscow (1989), with Dmitry Sakharov as mentor. After research posts in Leeds, at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, in Lund and in Calgary, including a Royal Society fellowship at Leeds (1993-94), he worked at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (1994-98). He joined UF's neuroscience faculty in 1998, becoming professor in 2006 and Distinguished Professor in 2014. His FHL connection is collaborative: with Billie Swalla he directed UW research apprenticeships at FHL in 2008, 2010 and 2012 whose students contributed to sequencing the genome of the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei.

Moroz studies how neurons and their chemical signals arose and evolved, working mainly on ctenophores (comb jellies), placozoans and mollusks and combining neuroscience, microchemistry and genomics. His FHL-connected work centers on the sea gooseberry Pleurobrachia bachei, many specimens of which were collected in FHL waters: a 2011 study of its compact, fast-evolving mitochondrial genome; 2012 apprenticeship reports on its Wnt, LIM-homeobox, collagen and glutamate-signaling genes and candidate secretory peptides; and the 2014 Nature genome paper, which placed ctenophores on the first branch of the animal tree and argued that their neural systems evolved independently. With Tigran Norekian he mapped neural and muscular systems in Pleurobrachia, Beroe abyssicola, Euplokamis dunlapae and the hydromedusa Aglantha digitale (2015-2019), and found that nitric oxide suppresses ciliary activity in ctenophores collected from the FHL dock (2023). Earlier census papers treat nitric oxide signaling in Clione and Aglantha and, with Andreas Heyland, thyroid hormone signaling in invertebrates (2006).

name: Lillian Aoki
text:
Lillian R. Aoki is a coastal ecosystem ecologist who became an assistant professor in the University of Oregon Environmental Studies Program in 2023, after serving as a research scientist in the university's Data Science Initiative (2021-2023). Her tie to FHL came through C. Drew Harvell's group at Cornell, where she was a postdoctoral associate from 2019 to 2021. A Cornell call for 2020 applications names her coordinator of the CORALS program, designed to bring Cornell undergraduates to FHL for a field research semester. In summer 2020 she traveled with Harvell and Olivia Graham to the San Juan Islands and led the July eelgrass surveys. The team worked from Friday Harbor, with sites that included the intertidal meadow at False Bay.

Aoki took a BA in chemistry at Cornell (2012) and a PhD in Environmental Sciences at the University of Virginia (2018), advised by Karen McGlathery, with a dissertation on seagrass meadows as nitrogen filters in shallow coastal lagoons. She stayed as a postdoctoral associate until 2019 and later published on how a marine heat wave affected seagrass sediment carbon (2021). Her later work centers on eelgrass wasting disease, caused by Labyrinthula zosterae. A 2022 paper she led combined satellite ocean temperatures with 2019 surveys of 32 meadows across 3,500 km of the Pacific coast. A 2025 Ecology paper she led linked disease prevalence and lesion area to invertebrate grazing, and a 2025 Biology Letters paper she led connected community interactions to disease dynamics.

name: Linda G. Wordeman
text:
Linda G. Wordeman is a cell biologist and professor in the Department of Neurobiology & Biophysics at the University of Washington, where her ORCID record lists her employment from 1994. She received a BA in molecular biology (1982) and a PhD in zoology (1988) from the University of California, Berkeley, and was a postdoctoral fellow in pharmacology at the University of California, San Francisco, until 1993. She received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2009, has been an adjunct professor of biology at UW since 2015, and joined the Board of Scientific Counselors of the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIH) in 2019. Her FHL connection runs through the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories. Eight of her census papers are FHL-connected; four, from 2008 to 2012, carry an FHL address, and a 2007 paper thanks center staff for help with live imaging.

Wordeman studies how kinesin-related motor proteins control microtubules, the dynamic filaments that shape cells and separate chromosomes during division. Her work centers on the kinesin-13 microtubule depolymerizers, especially MCAK, and the kinesin-8 family, and uses single-molecule TIRF microscopy and high-resolution live-cell imaging. Her FHL-connected papers, several with George von Dassow, showed that MCAK associates with the tips of growing microtubules (2005), promotes turnover of kinetochore microtubules to aid chromosome movement (2007) and acts at microtubule tips to control spindle microtubule length and kinetochore attachment (2012). Others report a kinesin-13 mutant that depolymerizes microtubules in ADP (2008), the kinesin-8 Kif18A suppressing kinetochore movements to align chromosomes (2008, with Jason Stumpff), and long astral microtubules uncoupling the spindle from the cleavage furrow (2010). A 2011 review considers MCAK as a potential cancer drug target.

name: Lindsay Waldrop
text: Lindsay Waldrop was a graduate student of M. A. R. Koehl at the University of California, Berkeley, completing a PhD in integrative biology in 2012 on olfaction in marine crustaceans. Waldrop and Koehl studied how crabs sniff by flicking antennules bearing chemosensory hairs, including the shore crab Hemigrapsus oregonensis during growth (2015) and terrestrial hermit crabs (2016). Postdoctoral posts in mathematics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (2012-2015) and UC Merced (2015-2016) came with modeling of tunicate hearts. After a faculty post at New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Waldrop joined Chapman University in 2019, later as associate professor.

name: Linsey Haram
text: Linsey Haram was a PhD student of James E. Byers at the University of Georgia, finishing in 2018. With Byers, Haram studied how the introduced red seaweed Gracilaria vermiculophylla, which had spread across intertidal mudflats in the southeastern United States that historically lacked seaweeds, changes shorebird foraging and habitat use (Ecology, 2018). At the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, Haram then worked on coastal invertebrates rafting on plastic debris in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, where they survive and reproduce on the high seas (Nature Communications, 2021; Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023). Haram became assistant professor of marine policy in the Coastal and Ocean Studies Program of Williams College in 2025.

name: Liqun Luo
text: Liqun Luo is a professor of biology at Stanford University and an investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Jalal K Baruni's postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford, from 2021, was with Luo and Mark Krasnow. The Luo laboratory studies the development and organization of neural circuits and built the mosaic-analysis tools MARCM and MADM. Luo wrote the textbook Principles of Neurobiology and belongs to the National Academy of Sciences.

text: Lisa Truong was an intern with Petra Ditsche at Friday Harbor Laboratories in the Blinks NSF REU BEACON program, summer 2014, while at Wellesley College. name: Louis Graf
text:
Louis Graf is an algal systematist and genomicist, a postdoctoral fellow from 2024 at the Laboratoire de Biologie Computationnelle et Quantitative in Paris, after a 2023-2024 fellowship at the Institut de Biologie de l'École Normale Supérieure. Graf's tie to FHL is through Robert A. Andersen of Friday Harbor Laboratories, a co-author with Graf and Hwan Su Yoon. Graf earned a bachelor's degree at Université Paris Diderot (2011), then a PhD in Yoon's Evolutionary Genomics Laboratory at Sungkyunkwan University in Korea (2013-2019), staying there as a postdoctoral fellow until 2023.

With Andersen and Yoon, Graf worked on the classification of heterokont algae using multigene phylogenies and morphology. Their papers include the new pelagophyte genus Aureoscheda from the Bahamas (2014), the rediscovery of the Ochromonas type species at its type locality in Ukraine (2017), and five new species in the Phaeothamniophyceae (2019). In 2020 Graf was first author on the description of a new class, Phaeosacciophyceae, with four new species. A 2024 Current Biology paper, with Graf as second author, used plastid genomes from 138 species to date true multicellularity in brown algae to about 450 million years ago. Later work includes a 2026 preprint, with Graf as first author, proposing a marine mixotrophic ancestor for the Chrysophyceae.

name: Louise McGarry
text:
Louise P. McGarry is a marine acoustician whose work has covered fish and zooplankton, using echosounders and acoustic telemetry. McGarry's tie to FHL is through Charles H. Greene of Cornell, who with C. Drew Harvell used FHL as the home base for field research programs. McGarry completed a Cornell PhD in 2014 with Greene as committee chair, after working as a research support specialist in Cornell's Ocean Resources and Ecosystems Program (1997-1999), and stayed for postdoctoral work with Greene until 2016. Their 2014 Oceanography paper proposed using Wave Gliders for fisheries acoustics; Greene, as first author, acknowledged FHL's Whiteley Center as the setting for preparing it.

The dissertation examined blue whale foraging and its krill prey in the Monterey Bay Submarine Canyon, using 120 and 200 kHz echosounder data with zooplankton net tows. It found that rare gas-bearing siphonophores can produce more backscatter than krill, so ignoring them would overestimate krill abundance. It also tracked one whale's foraging dives against the mapped prey field. With Greene and others, McGarry co-authored a 2013 paper on climate-forced regime shifts in Northwest Atlantic shelf ecosystems, and with Ian G. Brosnan, papers on three-dimensional fish tracking (2015) and transmitter implantation training (2018). McGarry then worked on tidal energy and ecosystems at the University of Maine (2017-2019) and at the Fundy Ocean Research Centre for Energy (2021-2023), publishing on acoustic detection efficiency for estimating fish encounters (2023).

name: Lucília S. Miranda
text:
Lucília S. Miranda is a zoologist specializing in stalked jellyfishes (Staurozoa), in the Department of Zoology at the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais from 2017. Miranda's tie to FHL is through Claudia E. Mills of Friday Harbor Laboratories, a co-author on papers from 2012 to 2023. A 2012 Zootaxa paper recorded Lucernariopsis capensis in Brazil, the first record outside its South African type locality. A 2023 paper, led by Mills, formally described Haliclystus sanjuanensis, the most common staurozoan on the west coast of the United States and Canada, whose name dates to a 1926 master's thesis by Gellermann, a student at FHL.

Miranda took a biological sciences degree at the Universidade de São Paulo (2006), a master's in zoology on Staurozoa (2010), and a São Paulo PhD (2014) on the evolution of Staurozoa, advised by Antonio C. Marques. The thesis combined molecular, morphological and cnidome data. Published results include a 2016 PeerJ classification that divided Staurozoa into Amyostaurida and Myostaurida by the absence or presence of interradial longitudinal muscles in the peduncle, a comparative study of internal anatomy in nine species (2016), and a global review of diversity and natural history (2017). From 2016 to 2017 Miranda held a FAPESP postdoctoral scholarship at São Paulo with André C. Morandini, comparing anatomy across medusozoan life-cycle stages. Later work extends to the invasive hydroid Cordylophora caspia and western Atlantic biodiversity.

name: Ludwik Gąsiorowski
text:
Ludwik Gąsiorowski is an evolutionary biologist working on Spiralia, the animal clade that includes flatworms, annelids and mollusks, an assistant professor in the University of Warsaw Faculty of Biology from 2024. The tie to FHL comes from doctoral and later work in Andreas Hejnol's lab at the University of Bergen. A 2019 EvoDevo paper on Hox gene expression in juveniles of the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa thanked FHL staff and the crew of the vessel Centennial for help collecting adults; Gąsiorowski conducted the in situ hybridizations and confocal work. A 2022 paper on brachiopod biomineralization gave the same acknowledgment.

Gąsiorowski took a bachelor's degree at Warsaw (2014) and a master's at the University of Copenhagen (2016) in Katrine Worsaae's lab. Papers from these years covered microscopic animals, including the gnathostomulid nervous system (2017) and kinorhynchs from Singapore (2016). In Bergen, from 2017, the work moved to brachiopods, phoronids and nemerteans. A 2021 Current Biology paper reported molecular evidence for a single origin of ultrafiltration-based excretory organs. In April 2021 Gąsiorowski joined Jochen C. Rink's lab at the Max Planck Institute in Göttingen to study head regeneration in catenulid flatworms, supported by a Humboldt postdoctoral fellowship. A 2025 Nature Communications paper showed that Stenostomum brevipharyngium regenerates its whole body without conventional neoblasts.

name: Lyda S.T. Harris
text:
Lyda S. T. Harris is a marine biologist who works on microplastic pollution and environmental policy. She received a PhD in biology from the University of Washington in 2020, and her website adds a concentration in public policy from UW's Evans School of Public Policy. The report's mentoring network lists Emily Carrington as her thesis advisor. Her doctoral research was supported by FHL's Strathmann Fellowship, an FHL research award, an FHL travel grant and UW Biology's Edmondson Award. Her papers from 2019 to 2023 give Friday Harbor Laboratories as an address. Her website describes more than a decade of work on sustainability and marine debris prevention in academic, NGO and corporate settings, including corporate sustainability strategy, international marine debris program management and a NOAA Marine Debris Program grant. The website also lists recognition from the American Institute of Biological Sciences for emerging public policy leadership.

Harris's FHL work used the mussel Mytilus trossulus to ask how microplastics affect filter feeders and the habitats they connect. In laboratory experiments she found that high concentrations of microplastic, but not natural silt, reduced mussel clearance rates (2019). With mussels held in FHL seawater tables, she found that biodeposits from mussels fed microplastic contained fewer algal cells, sank more slowly and resuspended at lower water velocities, which could carry particles farther from mussel beds (2021). Her dissertation added a scientometric and diffusion analysis of marine microplastic research and of national plastic policies. It found that both had grown exponentially and that the amount of research was not a good indicator of national policy adoption (2021). Other papers surveyed microparticles in mussels at regional and local scales across the Salish Sea (2023) and tracked microparticles beneath the Seattle Aquarium during the COVID-19 pandemic (2021).

The other described three new abyssal snailfishes (Liparidae) from the eastern Pacific at depths of 3,268-4,119 m, among them Careproctus colliculi and C. yanceyi (Ichthyology & Herpetology, 2025).

name: Lynn M. Riddiford
text:
Lynn M. Riddiford is an insect developmental biologist and endocrinologist and Professor Emerita of Biology at the University of Washington. She received a BA in biochemical sciences from Radcliffe College (1958) and a PhD in zoology from Cornell University (1961). After postdoctoral work, teaching at Wellesley College and a fellowship in Carroll Williams's laboratory, she joined Harvard's biology faculty in 1966. She moved to the UW Department of Zoology in 1973, became professor in 1975 and was the first Virginia and Prentice Bloedel University Professor (2000–2005). After retiring in 2007 she spent about nine years as a Senior Fellow at HHMI's Janelia Research Campus; in 2016 she set up her laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She is a member of the National Academy of Sciences (2010) and was president of the American Society of Zoologists (1991–92). The census counts 13 FHL-address papers by her, from 2017 to 2026.

Riddiford's research asks how juvenile hormone (JH) controls molting, metamorphosis and development in insects. Much of her earlier work used the tobacco hornworm, Manduca sexta, and bore on the use of JH as an insect growth regulator in pest control. At Janelia she studied hormonal control of nervous system development and behavior in Drosophila. Her FHL-connected papers, partly from work with James Truman on the evolution of complete metamorphosis, include genetic tools for studying JH action in Drosophila (2017), JH and the developing optic lobe during metamorphosis (2018), the gene chinmo as the larval member of a three-part molecular system directing metamorphosis (2022) and the embryonic role of JH in the firebrat Thermobia domestica (2023). She has also written reviews of the evolution of insect metamorphosis (2019, 2026), a history of JH research (2020) and an autobiographical review (2019). At FHL she is extending the work to metamorphosis in crustaceans.

name: M. A. R. Koehl
text:
Mimi A. R. Koehl is a biomechanist and professor in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. She earned a B.A. in biology at Gettysburg College and a Ph.D. in zoology at Duke University with S. A. Wainwright. She then held postdoctoral fellowships at Friday Harbor Laboratories with Richard Strathmann (1976–1977) and at the University of York with John Currey. Her honors include a MacArthur Fellowship (1990), election to the National Academy of Sciences (2001) and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2002), the Borelli Award of the American Society of Biomechanics (2002) and the John Martin Award of ASLO. The census counts three FHL-address papers, all from 1977, and later papers of hers acknowledge FHL and its Helen R. Whiteley Center.

Koehl studies how the structure of organisms and their physical environment together determine mechanical function, using methods from fluid and solid mechanics and from field ecology. Her 1977 FHL papers treated sea anemones as cantilever-like sessile animals, examining the flow forces they meet and the mechanics of their body-wall connective tissue. They compared the short, wide, wave-swept Anthopleura xanthogrammica with the tall, calm-water Metridium senile. A 1977 paper with Wainwright found that high extensibility helps the kelp Nereocystis luetkeana avoid breaking in waves. A 1988 study with R. S. Alberte compared flapping and photosynthesis in undulate and flat Nereocystis blades. With Michael Hadfield she measured larval recruitment of the nudibranch Phestilla sibogae (2007) and asked whether larvae of the tubeworm Hydroides elegans must touch a biofilm to settle (2014). A 2022 study with Thomas Daniel examined flow interactions between the seaweed Mazzaella splendens and an epibiotic bryozoan at the FHL breakwater.
