name: M. W. Jacobs
text:
Molly W. Jacobs is a marine invertebrate biologist who studies larval development, metamorphosis and life histories, mainly in ascidians (sea squirts). Her papers of 2006 and 2008 give the Friday Harbor Laboratories as her address. There she published with Richard Strathmann of FHL and with Bernard Degnan's group at the University of Queensland. From 2010 her papers give the Department of Biology at McDaniel College in Westminster, Maryland, and a 2016 paper gives both McDaniel and FHL. Papers from 2012 to 2017 on American lobsters list the University of Connecticut and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, and a 2019 paper on long-term change in eastern Long Island Sound lists Project Oceanology in Groton, Connecticut. The census counts three FHL-address papers, all from 2006, within FHL-connected work from 2003 to 2016.

Jacobs's FHL research asked what happens when ascidian larvae delay metamorphosis. A 2006 study with Degnan's group found that older larvae of Herdmania momus change in shape and gene expression. A 2008 paper with Degnan, John Bishop and Strathmann found that three of six solitary species begin forming postlarval structures during the delay, and that delays of up to three days did not slow juvenile growth. With Kristin Sherrard she reported in 2010 that offspring size did not predict juvenile growth or survival in seven ascidian species. The FHL bibliography also lists a 2004 book chapter on solitary-to-colonial transitions in animal evolution. Other FHL-connected papers cover non-native species in marinas on England's south coast (2006), local adaptation in the colonial ascidian Botrylloides violaceus in the San Juan Islands (2013), and decorator crabs, Oregonia gracilis, which begin decorating at the first juvenile stage (2016).

name: Mackenzie E. Gerringer
text:
Mackenzie E. Gerringer is a deep-sea biologist who studies fishes of the abyssal and hadal (ocean-trench) zones. She earned a B.A. in biology and German studies at Whitman College, spent 2012–2013 as a Fulbright English teaching assistant in Bremen, Germany, and completed a Ph.D. in marine biology at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where she held an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship from 2015. From 2017 to 2019 she was a postdoctoral research fellow at FHL, working on the functional morphology and physiology of fishes. She was instructor of record for FHL's Integrative Oceans course in 2017 and 2019 and for Seminars in Marine Science in 2017. She joined SUNY Geneseo as assistant professor of biology in 2019, became associate professor in 2024, and in 2026 moved to Whitman College as assistant professor of biology. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 2017 to 2022.

Gerringer studies how fishes live under the high pressure, cold and darkness of the deep sea. Her papers include species descriptions, diet studies from stomach contents and isotopes, life histories from otoliths, measurements of metabolic enzymes and micro-CT scans of skeletons. Her CV lists more than 200 days at sea, including expeditions to the Kermadec, Mariana, New Hebrides and Peru-Chile trenches and a 2022 Alvin submersible expedition to the Puerto Rico Trench. Her FHL-connected work, partly with Adam Summers, includes a 2014 FHL student report on the gelatinous tissue under the skin of a hadal snailfish, a 2017 survey of gelatinous tissues in deep-sea fishes, a 2019 review of why snailfishes dominate the fish fauna of the deepest trenches, and micro-CT studies relating bone density to habitat depth in snailfishes (2021) and rattails (2022). Later papers describe otoliths of the deepest fishes (2023) and three new abyssal snailfishes (2025).

text: Marcela Figueroa Campos appears in James E. Byers's CV for a 2023 project at the Universidad Austral de Chile in Valdivia, with Byers as co-sponsor, on a possible spillback effect in the intestinal parasites of Chinook salmon at Toltén, La Araucanía. The work appeared in NeoBiota in 2025, with Sara Rodríguez, Mario George-Nascimento and Byers, crediting Figueroa with data curation and methodology. The authors examined the digestive tracts of 114 adult Chinook salmon from the Toltén River estuary and counted 12,277 parasite larvae. Adult Hysterothylacium, Lecithaster and Lampritrema suggested that the invasive salmon is a competent non-native host for those genera.

name: Marcus Singer
text:
Marcus Singer (1914–1994) was a biologist who worked experimentally on regeneration. The institutions on his papers place him at Harvard University in the 1940s and early 1950s, at Cornell University from about 1953 into the early 1960s, and from the early 1960s at Case Western Reserve University. He held a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1966. At Cornell he and Harold Scheraga advised the doctoral work of Lynn Riddiford, who received her PhD in zoology in 1961 with a thesis on the structure of paramyosin. Singer has no papers in the census. He appears in the report as Riddiford's teacher; in 2016 she and James Truman set up their laboratory at FHL, where she has carried out her later insect research.

Singer's main question was how nerves control the regrowth of amputated limbs. In a series of papers from 1942 to 1949 on forelimb regeneration in the adult newt Triturus, he tested the roles of the sympathetic, sensory and motor nerve supplies and related regenerative ability to the number of nerve fibers in the limb. He reported that augmenting the nerve supply could induce forelimb regeneration in frogs (1951, 1954), and he reviewed the subject in The Quarterly Review of Biology in 1952. Later papers extended the question to taste buds, catfish barbels, lizard tails and mouse limbs, and measured acetylcholine and acetylcholinesterase in the regenerating newt limb. A 1964 paper set out theoretical considerations on the trophic role of the neuron. He also published histochemical studies of dye binding by tissues and works on the human brain in sagittal section (1955) and the dog brain in section (1962).

name: Marianne E. Porter
text:
Marianne E. Porter is a biomechanist who studies skeletons and swimming in sharks and other fishes. Porter held an assistant professorship at Florida Atlantic University from 2014 to 2021 and was a professor of biological sciences there as of 2026. Porter's BS and MS were at Northern Arizona University, and the first research, by Porter's own account, was in plant ecology: a study of pinyon-juniper woodland in northern Arizona and a plant survey along the Colorado River in Grand Canyon National Park. The move to biomechanics and sharks came with a PhD at the University of California, Irvine (2002-2007), where Adam P. Summers chaired the graduate committee. The Summers lab roster gives the topic as shark vertebral columns.

With Blinks fellow Cassandra Donatelli, Porter wrote an FHL report (2013) testing 3-D printed models of vertebrae and intervertebral joints. A 2018 study with Sarah Hoffmann and others measured three-dimensional pectoral fin rotation during yaw turns in Pacific spiny dogfish, Squalus suckleyi, collected at Friday Harbor. With Danielle Ingle, Porter compared vertebral trabecular bone across cetaceans (2020), using microCT scans made at FHL. Papers with John H. Long Jr. include a biomimetic skeleton for a robot's flapping tail (2011) and a study of strain in shark vertebral columns (2014), the latter listing Vassar College among Porter's affiliations. A later project tracks migrating blacktip sharks off South Florida with drones and accelerometer tags.

text: Maris Daleo was an undergraduate researcher from Carleton College in the lab of Michael T. Nishizaki, listed as a 2020 FHL REU participant. Daleo coauthored a 2022 PLOS ONE paper, with a companion Dryad dataset, on how temperature and pH affect sperm swimming and fertilization in the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus and the sea urchin Mesocentrotus franciscanus. Daleo started veterinary school at the University of Illinois in 2021 and later coauthored papers on quantitative PCR assays for wildlife pathogens, including Sulawesi tortoise adenovirus (2024) and a multiplex assay for chelonian pathogens (2025).

text: Mark Christopher Tierney earned a PhD in biology at the University of Louisville in December 2025 under committee chair Andrew Mehring, with Matthew A. Kolmann on the committee. The dissertation examined greenhouse gas fluxes from small ponds, asking how Chironomus riparius larvae and duckweed affect methane and comparing two satellite atmospheric corrections for estimating chlorophyll-a in small water bodies.

name: Mark Denny
text:
Mark W. Denny is a marine biomechanist and John B. and Jean De Nault Professor of Marine Science, emeritus, at Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station, which he directed from 2017 to 2020. He entered biomechanics as an undergraduate at Duke University, recruited by Steve Wainwright and Steve Vogel. His doctoral work at the University of British Columbia, with John Gosline, concerned the mechanics of gastropod locomotion; his 1980 papers treated pedal mucus (Nature) and the cost of crawling in a terrestrial slug (Science). Two years as a postdoc with Robert T. Paine at the University of Washington introduced him to the ecology of wave-swept shores. He also held a postdoctoral position at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute.

His ties to FHL run through people he trained: Emily Carrington took a PhD with him at Stanford (1992), and Brian Helmuth was his postdoc at Hopkins (1997-1999). A 2011 paper with Jonathon Stillman and others on grand challenges in organismal animal biology cites a September 2009 workshop at FHL on ecomechanics, the joining of ecology and biomechanics. His lab applies physics and engineering to the size, shape and materials of organisms on wave-swept rocky shores, with physiology added to study metabolism, growth and reproduction. His books include Biology and the Mechanics of the Wave-Swept Environment (1988), Air and Water (1993) and Ecological Mechanics (2015).

text: Mark S. Fonseca is listed among the graduate students on the lab publication page of M. A. R. Koehl at UC Berkeley, with work on flow and seagrass. Kopp), and a 2019 flume study of eelgrass, Zostera marina, at three current speeds with James W. Fourqurean, in which shoot density did not affect flow reduction or drag. text: Mark L. Lupisella is listed as a Ph.D. student of Kenneth P. Sebens at the University of Maryland (2000-06), with the topic models of community structure. A NASA contributor note gives his Ph.D. in biology there, in the program in behavior, ecology, evolution, and systematics, with a dissertation on microbial contamination of Mars from a human mission. He worked for NASA as an engineer and scientist on the Hubble Space Telescope, Mars planning, and astrobiology topics such as planetary protection and artificial life. text: Mark Q. Martindale was a PhD student of Gary Freeman at the University of Texas at Austin (1981-1985), working on ctenophore development, after undergraduate study with John B. Morrill at New College. He held postdoctoral posts with Stephen Meier on medaka and with Marty Shankland at Harvard on leech. He joined the University of Chicago in 1990 and the University of Hawaii in 1998, directed its Kewalo Marine Laboratory from 2005, and became professor and director at the Whitney Laboratory in 2012. He led the Comparative Embryology course at FHL and received the 2009 Kowalevsky Medal. A 2002 paper with Freeman treated the origin of mesoderm in phoronids.

name: Mark R. Patterson
text: Mark R. Patterson was a Ph.D. student of Kenneth P. Sebens at Harvard University (1979-85), with T. McMahon as co-advisor, working on the biomechanics of benthic marine organisms, and a postdoctoral researcher with Sebens in 1984-85. Later papers include in situ measurements of flow effects on production and respiration in reef corals (1991, with Sebens) and wave-induced lightflecks and photosynthesis in the macroalgae Postelsia palmaeformis and Hedophyllum sessile (1993, with Stephen Richard Wing). As of 2026 Patterson was a professor at Northeastern University, directing the Field Robotics Laboratory, which builds autonomous underwater vehicles and sensors, and applying fluid transport theory to metabolic scaling in aquatic invertebrates and algae.

name: Marlene Martinez
text: Marlene M. Martinez is listed among the graduate students on the lab publication page of M. A. R. Koehl at UC Berkeley, with work on how crabs walk and run under water. With R. J. Full and Koehl, Martinez compared pedestrian locomotion in air and water and described underwater punting, a novel gait of an intertidal crab (1998). A single-author 2001 paper measured hydrodynamic forces on the shore crab Grapsus tenuicrustatus; a non-moving crab could withstand 200% faster flow in the aquatic posture than in the terrestrial one. Martinez also wrote on aquatic pedestrian locomotion (1996) and, with Winnie W. Y. Lau, on dislodgement of the crab Pachygrapsus crassipes (2003).

text: Mary Chow worked in the lab of M. W. Jacobs at McDaniel College in summer 2013, supervised by Jacobs and Brett McMillan, with Xi Huang and Shirley Mancia. The team asked whether trails at Hashawha act as a barrier to soil invertebrate communities. They collected soil samples at path and non-path sites at set distances from a creek, and buried 48 mesh traps at six sites, near and away from the path, to compare rates of recolonization by soil invertebrates.

text: Mary Groesch is listed as a past graduate student on the Purdue University lab page of Joann J. Otto (2000). Groesch and Otto published a 1990 paper on the adhesion plaque proteins vinculin and talin. They cut vinculin with Staphylococcus aureus V8 protease, purified the 85 kDa and 30 kDa fragments, and localized the talin-binding domain to the 85 kDa fragment, which bound four times more talin than intact vinculin. The Otto lab studied the actin cytoskeleton in cytokinesis and in microvilli and filopodia, using sea urchin eggs and Tetrahymena.

text: Mary Ruckelshaus was a graduate student of Susan Lynn Williams and earned a master's in fisheries and a doctorate in botany at the University of Washington. name: Mason N. Dean
text:
Mason N. Dean studies skeletal structure and mechanics in sharks, rays and ratfishes, in particular the tessellated cartilage of these fishes. Dean was appointed associate professor at City University of Hong Kong in 2021. After an A.B. in biology at Duke University (1997), Dean took an MS in zoology at the University of South Florida (2003) under Philip J. Motta. Two 2004 papers with Motta showed the lesser electric ray Narcine brasiliensis protruding its jaws beneath the substrate and sucking worms into its mouth. Dean then completed a PhD in ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of California, Irvine (2009) with Adam P. Summers, whose roster lists the topic as tessellated skeletons.

Several of Dean's papers use the spotted ratfish Hydrolagus colliei. A 2008 study of its bite forces and feeding mechanics used animals trawled in the San Juan Islands and housed at FHL, and a paper on very low ventilatory pressures in chimaeroid fishes followed in 2011. Others cover skeletal growth in the round stingray Urobatis halleri (2009) and, with Xiaoxi Liu and James C. Earthman, a composite model of the shark skeleton in bending (2010) and stress relaxation in blue shark jaw cartilage (2013). After the PhD, Dean was a Humboldt postdoctoral fellow with Peter Fratzl at the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces (2009-2011), an independent researcher there with a Human Frontier Science Program Young Investigator grant, and a group leader (2017-2021).

name: Mathew Leibold
text: Mathew A. Leibold, of the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of Texas at Austin, supervised Emlyn Resetarits's 2013-2019 PhD there together with Daniel Bolnick and Shalene Jha. Leibold and Resetarits were coauthors on a 2018 test of the keystone community concept in metacommunities. Leibold is a professor of biology at the University of Florida.

name: Matt Hahn
text: Matt Hahn is listed as a former lab member of Gregory A. Wray at Duke University, earned a Ph.D. at Duke in 2003, and was a postdoctoral fellow at the University of California, Davis (2003-2005). In Wray's group Hahn worked on the evolution of gene regulation, including a first-authored 2004 Genetics paper on positive selection on regulatory mutations at the human factor VII locus and a coauthored 2003 review of transcriptional regulation in eukaryotes. The Hahn Lab page lists Matthew Hahn as Distinguished Professor of Biology and Computer Science at Indiana University. The lab uses genomic data to study gene gain and loss, population genomics, speciation, and mutation rates.

name: Matt Larson
text: Matt Larson is listed as a former graduate student, M.D.-Ph.D., of William M. Bement at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where Larson was in the Medical Scientist Training Program. Larson and Bement (2017) developed automated spindle-tracking software and used it to describe mitotic spindle dynamics in the Xenopus laevis embryonic epithelium, where metaphase spindles rotate into position and then oscillate before anaphase. Larson also coauthored a 2018 paper linking myosin-10 and the cell cycle regulator Wee1 to spindle dynamics and mitotic progression, and a 2015 paper on Rho signaling and actin assembly as an excitable system in the cell cortex.

name: Matt Pierce
text: Matt Pierce was an MS student of James E. Byers at the University of Georgia's Odum School of Ecology, finishing in 2026. The work addressed disturbance, invasion and predator-prey ecology in saltmarshes and mudflats, including the range-expanding fiddler crab Leptuca thayeri and marsh periwinkles. A 2026 Estuaries and Coasts paper by Pierce and colleagues scaled the effects of wrack disturbance across a saltmarsh landscape.

name: Matt Rockman
text: Matt Rockman was a member of Gregory A. Wray's lab at Duke University, where Rockman earned a PhD in biology in 2004. With Wray, Rockman tested for positive selection on cis-regulatory variation in humans, with papers on a transcription factor binding site regulating IL4 (2003), MMP3 regulation and heart disease risk (2004), and regulation of the opioid precursor prodynorphin (2005). Rockman became Professor of Biology at New York University, using the nematode C. elegans as the main system for studying how heritable variation is generated and maintained, including selection at linked sites (2010). Rockman also published on the marine annelid Streblospio benedicti, including larval genetics (2021) and its genome (2022).

name: Matthew A. Kolmann
text:
Matthew A. Kolmann is an evolutionary biologist and functional morphologist who studies fishes. He received a BSc in biology from the University of Tampa (2008) and an MSc from Florida State University (2012), where he worked with Dean Grubbs on the feeding biomechanics and fisheries ecology of cownose rays. His PhD at the University of Toronto produced a 2016 thesis on the evolution of the feeding mechanism in stingrays. His papers from 2016 to 2020 list Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, several jointly with George Washington University or the Royal Ontario Museum, and he held an NSF Postdoctoral Research Fellowship in Biology from 2018 to 2020. Since 2022 he has been an assistant professor of biology at the University of Louisville. The census counts 11 FHL-address papers by him, from 2017 to 2020, and also includes a 2014 report in UW ResearchWorks on stingray jaws and shell crushing.

Kolmann studies how anatomy, mechanics and ecology shape the evolution of feeding in fishes, using CT scanning, measurements of bite force and jaw stiffness, museum specimens and phylogenetic comparisons. His stingray work covers jaw curvature and shell crushing (2015), chewing of insect prey (2016) and changes in jaw stiffness with growth in mollusk-eating stingrays (2019). His FHL-connected papers range across fish groups: sexual dimorphism in Neotropical electric fishes (2018), the armored keel (2018) and tooth replacement (2019) of piranhas and pacus, diet specialization in scale-eating fishes (2018), diet and form in freshwater sculpins (2019), habitat transitions in needlefishes (2020), trade-offs between swimming and armor in poachers (2020) and a step-by-step guide to CT data with open software (2020). Later papers treat fish gizzards (2023), tooth mechanics of fruit-eating fishes (2025), stingray spines (2026) and a new freshwater stingray species (2026).

name: Matthew Brown
text: Matthew Brown was an MS student at the University of Guelph from 2015 to 2018, advised by Andreas Heyland and Frédéric Laberge. The thesis, in integrative biology, tested conditioned prey avoidance in the fire-bellied toad Bombina orientalis. Toads learned to avoid mealworms paired with copper sulfate, and the study weighed avoidance intensity, sex and body size as predictors.

name: Matthew Connelly
text: Matthew Connelly completed an MS in geological sciences at Cornell University under Charles H. Greene, with C. Drew Harvell on the committee; the thesis was issued in January 2012. It evaluated an empirical model that predicts northwest Atlantic slope water temperature from North Atlantic Oscillation forcing, and predicted a modal shift like that of 1998 after the negative phases that began in 2009.

name: Matthew Curry Kay
text: Matthew Curry Kay completed an MS in biology at the University of Oregon in 2001 under Richard B. Emlet, and was a graduate teaching fellow at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology. The thesis studied spawning, larval development and settlement in the limpets Lottia digitalis and L. asmi and the flat abalone Haliotis walallensis. Papers appeared with Emlet in Invertebrate Biology (2002) and as sole author in Marine Biology (2002).

name: Matthew Galaska
text: Matthew Galaska was a PhD student of Kenneth M. Halanych at Auburn University, finishing in 2017 with a dissertation on the phylogeography and biodiversity of brittle stars in the Southern Ocean. Using mitochondrial markers and SNPs, Galaska found four geographically distinct populations of Ophionotus victoriae and genetic connectivity across the Antarctic Polar Front in Astrotoma agassizii (2017). Later work covered metapopulation connectivity in the deep-sea octocoral Paramuricea biscaya in the Gulf of Mexico (2021) and the effect of aquaculture on the annelid Diopatra biscayensis (2021). Galaska was a research scientist at the University of Washington (2019-2022) and a research biologist at NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory (2022-2024), publishing on Arctic environmental DNA monitoring (2023).

name: Matthew L. Aardema
text: Matthew L. Aardema, an associate professor of biology at Montclair State University, sponsored Nathan Martin Klunk's 2022 master's thesis on parasites of the invasive rusty crayfish in northern New Jersey. Aardema's research covers molecular evolution, population genetics and comparative genomics, with work on mosquitoes of the Culex pipiens complex and on the tick-transmitted bacterium Anaplasma phagocytophilum. Aardema earned a PhD in ecology and evolutionary biology at Princeton University.

name: Matthew McHenry
text: Matthew McHenry was a graduate student in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley, with a PhD in integrative biology in 2002. McHenry studied how small aquatic animals swim, including helical swimming in larvae of the ascidian Distaplia occidentalis (2001), scaling of hydrodynamics in the jellyfish Aurelia aurita (2003), and biomechanics of ascidian larvae (2005). After postdoctoral posts at Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology (2002-2004) and the University of Groningen (2004-2005), McHenry joined the University of California, Irvine, in 2005, becoming professor in 2016. Later papers include work with Adam Summers on force and speed (2011) and with Olaf Ellers and Amy Johnson on tube feet (2025).

name: Matthew Mills
text: Matthew Mills was a PhD student of Kenneth P. Sebens at the University of Maryland (1993-2000), working on suspension feeding by corals. Papers from this line of work measured how corals take up nitrogen from food: particulate matter ingestion and nitrogen uptake in four scleractinian species, with Fredric Lipschultz and Sebens (2004), and ingestion and assimilation of nitrogen from benthic sediments in three coral species, with Sebens (2004). Mills joined Stanford University's Earth System Science department as a research associate in 2005, moving to phytoplankton and nitrogen cycling, including a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria/haptophyte symbiosis (2020) and a summertime Arctic bloom linked to wildfire aerosols (2022).

name: Matthew N. George
text:
Matthew N. George is a marine biologist who studies how shellfish respond to changing ocean conditions. After a B.S. in biology from Gonzaga University (2010), he worked as a research technologist at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) in 2011–2012. He then earned a Ph.D. in biology at the University of Washington (2018) in Emily Carrington's laboratory, with a dissertation on mussel attachment from an ecomechanical perspective. He was then a research fellow in physiology and biomedical engineering at the Mayo Clinic (2018–2019), a postdoctoral fellow at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (2019–2020) and a research scientist in the University of Washington's School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (2020–2023). In 2023 he became Coastal Shellfish Manager in the Fish Program of the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. His FHL-address papers date from 2013 to 2022.

Most of George's FHL work concerns the byssus, the protein threads and adhesive plaques that anchor mussels to rocks and aquaculture lines. He co-authored a 2013 Nature Climate Change paper reporting that ocean acidification weakens byssal attachment. His later papers examined how seawater conditions after secretion strengthen the adhesive (2018), how low oxygen interrupts DOPA cross-linking as plaques cure (2018), how warming and elevated carbon dioxide together affect thread structure (2019), and how pH and oxygen fluctuate within mussel clumps, with implications for raft aquaculture (2019). Experiments used mussels from San Juan Island held at FHL and mesocosms in the laboratory's ocean acidification facility. A 2022 paper found that mussels repair shell damage despite limits imposed by acidification. With Carrington he also studied how sea urchins reorient their spines to capture drifting particles (2014), and at UW he later co-authored work on heatwave mortality in triploid Pacific oysters (2023).

name: Matthew R. Baker
text:
Matthew R. Baker is a fisheries ecologist who works on North Pacific fishes and their habitats. Since 2014 he has been Science Director of the North Pacific Research Board, a marine research organization in Anchorage, Alaska, created by Congress in 1997. He previously worked at NOAA's Alaska Fisheries Science Center and with the University of Washington's Alaska Salmon Program, and his ORCID record lists him as a research affiliate of the Center from 2010. At Friday Harbor Laboratories he is an instructor in Pelagic Ecosystem Function, an autumn research apprenticeship in which students study the oceanography, plankton, forage fish and predators of the San Juan Archipelago. A 2016 conference abstract gives his affiliation as UW Friday Harbor Labs. The census counts 15 FHL-address papers by him, from 2016 to 2026.

Baker's FHL research centers on the Pacific sand lance (Ammodytes personatus), a forage fish of sandy seabeds. With apprenticeship students he built a six-year time series (2010–2015) on sand lance in the San Juan Archipelago, covering abundance, diet, condition, movements and sediment association. Papers from this work report seasonal abundance and demographics (2016), feeding ecology (2017), gonad maturation (2022) and diel vertical migration (2023). In 2018 he led the sand lance team in a SeaDoc Society submersible project headed by Gary Greene of the Tombolo Mapping Laboratory, which filmed the fish over sand waves with a stereo-camera array. Papers on this sand-wave habitat followed (2019–2025). Others assess threats to the species (2024), microplastics in forage fish and sediments (2023, 2025), and climate and noise effects on condition, overwinter survival and anti-predator behavior (2025–2026). A 2020 paper compares age and growth at the latitudinal extremes of the Gulf of Alaska.

name: Matthew Reidenbach
text: Matthew Reidenbach was a postdoc in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley, using the spiny lobster Panulirus argus to study odor tracking. Using a flume, laser Doppler anemometry and planar laser-induced fluorescence imaging of odor fields, Reidenbach reported on antennule flicking (2008) and odors sampled in turbulent plumes (2011). Other work with Koehl examined hydrodynamic forces on settling coral reef larvae (2009). Reidenbach joined Environmental Sciences at the University of Virginia in 2007. An NSF award from 2021 supported work on mussels and flow, including 2023 experiments in the FHL Flume Lab.

text: Matthew S. Schuler, an associate professor of biology at Montclair State University, sponsored Emily Jin Searles Stone's 2021 master's thesis on bacterial communities along a nutrient gradient in Overpeck Creek and Kevin Peteroy's 2024 thesis on zooplankton in flooded vernal pools. Schuler's research addresses freshwater and coastal ecology, including wetland resilience and road-salt pollution.

text: Matthew Walker, a professor of neuroscience and psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, advised Jessica M. Kendall-Bar's undergraduate research on sleep deprivation in 2015-2016. Walker founded and directs Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science, which studies how sleep affects human health and disease, and wrote the 2017 book Why We Sleep.

name: Maureen Keller
text: Maureen Keller was Assistant Curator from 1981 to 1992 at the Culture Collection of Marine Phytoplankton, which moved to Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences in 1981, under directors Robert R. L. Guillard (1981-1989) and Robert A. Andersen (from 1989). Publishing as Maureen D. Keller, Keller worked on culturing marine phytoplankton, with a chapter on culturing dinoflagellates with Guillard (1984) and media for oceanic ultraphytoplankton (1987). Glover, Keller and Guillard reported on light quality and oceanic ultraphytoplankters in Nature (1986). Later work addressed dimethyl sulfide production (1989), intracellular dimethylsulfoniopropionate with P. A. Matrai (1994), and glycine betaine production in batch and chemostat cultures (1999).

name: Megan L Vandenberg
text:
Megan L. Vandenberg is a doctoral student in Biology at the University of Washington, working in Adam Summers' laboratory at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL), where she began her PhD research in autumn 2023. She earned a B.S. in Biology from UW in 2022. Her connection to FHL began in autumn 2021 with the Bio Imaging research apprenticeship led by Summers, followed the next summer by the Functional Morphology and Ecology of Marine Fishes course. In July 2022 she gave an FHL talk on poacher armor, and in 2023 she worked at FHL as a research technician in CT scanning, particle image velocimetry and SEM imaging. Her research has been supported by FHL's Stephen and Ruth Wainwright Endowed Fellowship (2023) and Research Endowment Fellowship (2025), and she wrote FHL's March 2025 Tide Bite column. Her FHL-connected papers date from 2023 to 2026.

Poachers (family Agonidae) are bottom-dwelling fishes covered in overlapping bony plates. Her research asks what this armor does besides protection, testing functions such as reducing drag and adding bending stiffness. She combines CT scanning, scanning electron microscopy and histology with 3D-printed models, flume experiments, particle image velocimetry and materials testing. A 2024 paper in the Biological Journal of the Linnean Society found that larger spines on poacher armor reduce boundary-layer separation and drag. Papers from 2026 address the phylogenomics of poachers and the evolution of armor across cottoid fishes, and the mechanical strengths and weaknesses of poacher armor. Her first paper (2023), from her apprenticeship project, showed how the keratin plates of whale baleen break away to expose the hair-like fringe that filters food. Other work covers the neck vertebrae of plunge-diving seabirds (2026), bioinspiration research shared between biologists and engineers (2025) and FHL undergraduate research reports she co-authored (2025).

name: Megan N. Dethier
text:
Megan N. Dethier is a marine ecologist and research professor in the University of Washington Department of Biology, in full-time residence at Friday Harbor Laboratories. She received a BA in biology from Carleton College (1975) and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington (1981), working with Robert Paine on the community structure of Washington tidepools, and held an FHL postdoctoral fellowship in 1983. After research positions at UW's Institute for Environmental Studies and in Zoology and Biology, she became research professor in 2006. At FHL she taught the spring Marine Biology (invertebrate zoology) course from 1987 to 2019, became associate director for academics and the environment in 2014, and was interim director from July 2019 and director from 2020. She was president of the Western Society of Naturalists in 1991 and its Naturalist of the Year in 2011. The census lists 59 FHL-connected papers, 1981–2026.

Her research concerns the community ecology of Pacific Northwest shorelines, first rocky shores and later mud, gravel and salt marsh, and how physical conditions, stress, disturbance and herbivory shape them. Early work covered tidepool algae, algal crusts and the effects of desiccation on seaweeds. She later designed a marine and estuarine habitat classification for Washington, co-wrote the book Monitoring Rocky Shores (2006) and worked with the National Park Service on intertidal monitoring. In Puget Sound and the Salish Sea she has studied how shoreline armoring, and its removal, affect beach biota (2016–2024). Other FHL-connected papers examine the food value of kelp detritus and urchin feces in nearshore food webs (2014–2019), kelp crab feeding (2017), growth and predation of juvenile clams (2019), native and invasive macrophytes as nurseries for juvenile salmon (2020), kelp responses to temperature and nitrogen (2023) and the effects of the 2021 heatwave on intertidal communities (2025).

name: Megumi F. Strathmann
text:
Megumi F. Strathmann is a marine invertebrate embryologist and larval biologist associated with the University of Washington's Friday Harbor Laboratories. Her papers of 1992 and 2007 give FHL as her address, the first jointly with the UW Department of Zoology. She is the author of Reproduction and Development of Marine Invertebrates of the Northern Pacific Coast (University of Washington Press, 1987), a 670-page volume of data and methods for studying eggs, embryos and larvae, prepared with text contributions and advice from colleagues and students of Robert L. Fernald. Many of her papers are co-authored with Richard R. Strathmann. FHL's Richard and Megumi Strathmann Fellowship supports graduate students working on natural and physical science problems in the Pacific Northwest. The census counts 12 FHL-address papers by her, from 1984 to 2020.

Her papers deal mainly with how development responds to conditions and how larval life histories evolve. With co-authors she examined developmental plasticity in sea urchin larvae and its implications for the evolution of nonfeeding larvae (1992), used rates of development and form of sea urchin larvae to test whether larvae in coastal waters are food-limited (1994), and compared food effects on a molluscan veliger (1993) and across echinoderm classes (2020). Other papers concern suspension feeding in the tube worm Spirobranchus giganteus (1984), shells and pelagic development in trochoidean snails (1990), oxygen supply to masses of embryos (1995), nurse eggs, cannibalism and brood reduction in a vermetid gastropod (2005, 2018), a 4.5-year larval period in the snail Fusitriton oregonensis (2007), hatching plasticity in the nudibranch Phestilla sibogae (2010), a new brooding sea star, Henricia pumila (2010), and coelom development in a brittle star (2020).

text:
Michael A. Harkey is a biologist whose publications move from sea urchin developmental biology to transplantation research, all in Seattle. From 1980 to the early 1990s he published with Arthur H. Whiteley of the University of Washington's Department of Zoology on the cells that build the sea urchin larval skeleton; his 1988 and 1992 papers, with H. R. Whiteley as well, list the Department of Microbiology. His 1980 paper lists both the Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and his census papers span 1980 to 1989. He also collaborated with R. A. Raff's group at Indiana University on skeletal genes (1987–1997). A 1995 paper lists the UW Department of Orthopaedics, and he co-authored collagen studies with D. R. Eyre's group (1997, 2007). From the early 2000s his papers are associated with the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, which his ORCID record gives as his employer.

Harkey's FHL-connected work focused on primary mesenchyme cells, the descendants of the micromeres that secrete the skeleton of the sea urchin larva. He developed methods to isolate and culture primary mesenchyme cells (1980) and to isolate micromeres in bulk (1985), and used two-dimensional gel electrophoresis to follow cell-specific programs of protein synthesis as these cells differentiate (1982, 1983). Later papers showed that five transcripts accumulate together in primary mesenchyme during skeleton formation (1988) and that embryonic primary mesenchyme genes are also expressed in adult skeletal tissues of several echinoderms (1989). Others examined the skeletal proteins msp130 and PM27 (1992, 1995). At Fred Hutch his publications concern gene transfer into blood-forming stem cells, canine models of marrow and cord blood transplantation, and variation in the canine leukocyte antigen (DLA) genes.

text: Michael Boller was a PhD student of Emily Carrington at the University of Rhode Island, finishing in 2005 with a dissertation on the biotic and physical determinants of drag in marine macroalgae. Boller appears among alumni of Mark Denny's Stanford lab and became associate professor and sustainability program director at St. John Fisher University, Rochester, New York.

name: Michael G. Hadfield
text:
Michael G. Hadfield is an invertebrate biologist and professor emeritus at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. He earned BA and MS degrees in zoology at the University of Washington. On a Fulbright fellowship he studied with the larval biologist Gunnar Thorson at the University of Copenhagen's marine laboratory, and he completed a PhD in biological sciences at Stanford University in 1966. After teaching at Pomona College until 1968 he joined the University of Hawaiʻi faculty. There he was among the first faculty of the Kewalo Marine Laboratory, which he directed from 1996 to 2007; he retired in 2013. His FHL connection is through collaboration. The census lists nine papers from 1985 to 2018; three were written with Megumi Strathmann of FHL (two also with Richard Strathmann), and a 2014 paper thanks FHL's Helen R. Whiteley Center as a place to analyze data and write.

Hadfield studies the reproduction and development of marine gastropods and worms, and how their larvae settle and metamorphose. For about thirty years his group has examined the bacterial signals that induce larvae of the polychaete Hydroides elegans to settle. He has also worked on Hawaiian tree snails (Achatinella) and set up a captive breeding program for them in 1989. His FHL-connected papers center on larvae. Several concern the coral-eating nudibranch Phestilla sibogae: feeding by its yolk-supplied (lecithotrophic) larvae (1985), its recruitment in the field (2007), nitric-oxide signaling at metamorphosis (2008), and plasticity in hatching (2010). Others treat larval shells and torsion in trochoidean snails (1990, 2001), whether Hydroides larvae must touch a biofilm to settle (2014), and brood reduction in a vermetid snail (2018). In 2014 he was the first recipient of the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology's M. Patricia Morse Award for Excellence and Innovation in Science Education.

name: Michael G. Tassia
text: Michael G. Tassia was a PhD student of Kenneth M. Halanych at Auburn University (2021), after a BS at the University of Washington (2014) and work as a laboratory technician at the university and FHL (2014-2015). Tassia's dissertation credits Billie J. Swalla with the introduction to hemichordates, and Tassia's 2014 FHL student report treated benthic macrofauna along a transect from False Bay, San Juan Island. The dissertation examined the evolution of deuterostome immune systems, centered on hemichordates such as the acorn worm Saccoglossus kowalevskii. Papers cover the global diversity of Hemichordata (2016, with Swalla and Halanych), Toll-like receptor pathway evolution in deuterostomes (2017), and the TIAMMAt protein-domain tool (2021). Tassia became a postdoctoral fellow at Johns Hopkins University in 2022.

name: Michael J. Baca
text: Michael J. Baca was a PhD student of L. D. (Lloyd Donald) Partridge Jr. at the University of New Mexico, finishing in biomedical sciences in 2013. Baca's dissertation asked how a genetic factor, heterozygous deficiency of the SNARE protein SNAP-25, and an environmental one, prenatal nicotine exposure, jointly affect striatal long-term depression in mice. The combination weakened this form of synaptic plasticity and lowered dopamine D2 receptor agonist affinity without changing receptor number. The work, framed around ADHD and schizophrenia, appeared in Brain Research in 2013 with Andrea M. Allan, Partridge and Michael C. Wilson; the paper gave Baca's affiliations as the university's Department of Neurosciences and Sandia National Laboratories.

name: Michael J. O’Donnell
text:
Michael J. O'Donnell describes himself in his ORCID record as a biomechanist, with interests in marine ecology, ocean acidification, biomechanics and translational medicine. His 2006 study of wave exposure on rocky shores lists Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station and the Marine Science Institute of the University of California, Santa Barbara. From 2008 to 2013 he was a postdoctoral researcher with Emily Carrington at the University of Washington and Friday Harbor Laboratories. He was also key senior personnel (co-investigator) on her National Science Foundation project 'Effects of ocean acidification on coastal organisms: an ecomaterials perspective'. A 2019 paper lists him at the Department of Bioengineering, University of California, Berkeley. Carrington's 2020 CV gives him as executive director of the Master of Translational Medicine program of UC Berkeley and UCSF. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 2008 to 2022.

O'Donnell applies mechanics and physiology to how marine invertebrates fare as seawater warms and acidifies. A 2008 study with Gretchen Hofmann's group found that elevated CO2 alters the response of sea urchin larvae to heat stress, and a 2010 paper described a system for rearing larvae under controlled pCO2. Co-authored FHL studies showed that acidification changes the shape of sand dollar larvae, affecting swimming and feeding (2011), and delays early development of Pacific oyster larvae (2012). As lead author of a 2013 Nature Climate Change paper, he found that bay mussels (Mytilus trossulus) from San Juan Island held at low pH made weaker byssal threads, which most often broke at the adhesive plaque; at pH 7.5 they lost up to 40 percent of their attachment strength. Later papers examined temperature and pCO2 together on mussel attachment (2019), shell repair under acidification (2022) and, by radio tracking, thermoregulation in snails (2017).

name: Michael LaBarbera
text:
Michael LaBarbera is a biologist who works on biomechanics and functional form. A University of Chicago Press author note describes him as professor emeritus in the Department of Organismal Biology and Anatomy at the University of Chicago. Publication records link his papers of the mid-1970s to Duke University and his later papers to Chicago from 1979 to 2010; his papers of the mid-1980s give the university's Department of Anatomy. He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists, but a 2004 editorial in Palaios, written with Michał Kowalewski, says he had returned to FHL every two to three years for about 30 years to do research, to teach a course, or both. The census holds seven of his FHL-connected papers, from 1985 to 2008. In the mentoring network he is linked as doctoral advisor to Kristin Sherrard, whose two 2005 papers with him give FHL as her address.

LaBarbera's census papers all concern mechanics and form in marine animals. With Drew Harvell (1985) he examined flexibility as a way for hydroid colonies to control local water velocities, and a 1985 study with Richard Satterlie and Andrew Spencer, much of it carried out at FHL, described swimming behavior and morphology in the pteropod Clione limacina. With Elizabeth Boulding (1986) he showed that repeated loading, which causes fatigue damage, lets crabs open larger bivalves, and with Rachel Merz (1992) he measured how gastropod shells lose strength after death, with consequences for hermit crabs, snails and their predators. With Sherrard (2005) he studied how the form of newly settled ascidians affects their performance and how their pumping rates scale with growth. With Adam Tomašových and Sandra Carlson (2008) he related the loss of rotation ability in the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa to allometric growth.

text: Michael O'Toole was a laboratory Assistant III and safety coordinator in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley. O'Toole worked on the hydrodynamics of microscopic organisms: dynamically scaled physical models of barnacle nauplius larvae, testing how spines affect swimming, sinking, feeding and surface attachment, and videomicrography of protozoan predators and choanoflagellates. A 2023 Journal of Eukaryotic Microbiology paper found that colony formation increases choanoflagellates' susceptibility to capture by amoeboid predators.

name: Michael P. Hannam
text: Michael P. Hannam was a PhD graduate of the University of Washington School of Environmental and Forest Sciences (2013), with Kern Ewing as chair and Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria on the reading committee. Hannam's dissertation examined how environmental context at several spatial scales shapes the distribution of invasive Zostera japonica and native Z. marina; terrestrial laser scanning and transplants showed that centimeter-scale relief altered competition and supported coexistence (Biological Invasions, 2014, with Wyllie-Echeverria). Later papers covered submersed aquatic vegetation in Chesapeake Bay (2017, 2018, 2023). By 2023 Hannam was with the National Park Service's Southwest Alaska Inventory and Monitoring Network, publishing on coastal marsh vegetation and lake-ice phenology.

name: Michael Stierwald
text: Michael Stierwald was a doctoral student at the University of Basel, with a 2004 thesis on the evolution of cnidarian eyes, working with Volker Schmid at the Institute of Zoology. Studying hydrozoan jellyfish, including Cladonema, Stierwald traced muscle and eye formation through developmental genes, identifying a jellyfish MyoD homolog and a Pax gene active during eye maintenance and regeneration, possibly upstream of Six genes. The thesis supported a single origin of eyes and a more complex common ancestor of cnidarians and bilaterians. A 2004 Developmental Biology paper with Schmid treated Sine oculis/Six genes in jellyfish with and without eyes; Stierwald also coauthored work on BMP genes (2006) and Pax genes (2010).

text: Michael Stuart Roberts was an MS student of Robert C. Terwilliger in the University of Oregon Department of Biology (1980). The thesis purified and compared hemoglobins from five holothurian species and found them dimeric, with native molecular weights of 32,000 to 35,000 daltons: heterodimers in Cucumaria and a homodimer in Sclerodactyla. Roberts held a BA in biology from The Colorado College (1974).

name: Michael T. Brett
text:
Michael T. Brett is a limnologist and professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Washington. He studied fisheries at Humboldt State University (BSc 1983) and zoology at the University of Maine (MSc 1985), and earned a PhD in limnology at Uppsala University in Sweden. He was a research associate at the University of California, Davis, from 1991 to 1997 and joined the UW department as an assistant professor in December 1997; a 2019 department news item names him its associate chair. He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists. His three FHL-connected papers, from 2012 to 2014, came from collaborations with researchers based at the laboratories. In the mentoring network he is linked as co-advisor to Aaron Galloway, an FHL core scientist who completed a UW thesis in 2013 under Kenneth Sebens.

Brett's research follows nutrients and food quality through aquatic food webs: eutrophication and the regulation of algal biomass and secondary production in lakes, nutrient bioavailability, the production and bioaccumulation of essential fatty acids such as omega-3s, zooplankton ecology, and links between aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. His FHL-connected papers use fatty acids as dietary markers. A 2012 study led by Galloway, with Kevin Britton-Simmons and David Duggins of FHL and Paul Gabrielson of the University of North Carolina Herbarium, showed that fatty acid profiles separate marine seaweeds and seagrasses at the level of order and family. A 2013 paper led by Sami Taipale profiled 37 strains of freshwater microalgae as fatty acid biomarkers, and a 2014 study with Galloway, Morgan Eisenlord and Megan Dethier at FHL and Gordon Holtgrieve used a Bayesian fatty acid mixing model to estimate what marine isopods eat.

name: Michael T. Nishizaki
text:
Michael T. Nishizaki is a marine physiological ecologist who studies how temperature and water flow affect intertidal invertebrates. His first papers (2005, 2007), on how juvenile red sea urchins associate with adults, are linked in the census to the University of Northern British Columbia, and in 2008 and 2011 he co-authored mathematical models of swarming and helical swimming with Daniel Grünbaum. He received a PhD in biology from the University of Washington in 2013, with a thesis on barnacles in Emily Carrington's group, based on work at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 2010 to 2013. He then worked at Bowdoin College (visiting instructor, 2012–2013), the University of Guelph (postdoctoral researcher, 2013–2015), Williams College (visiting assistant professor of maritime studies, 2015–2017) and Harvard University (teaching fellow, 2018), and became an assistant professor of biology at Carleton College in 2018. His census papers and datasets with an FHL address span 2014 to 2026.

Nishizaki uses the acorn barnacle Balanus glandula and intertidal mussels to study how environmental stressors combine. His thesis and 2014–2015 papers with Carrington measured how water temperature and flow speed alter barnacle feeding, respiration and growth. Modeling suggested that respiration is limited by mass transfer in slow, warm water and by uptake kinetics in fast, cold water. The barnacle data, from Cantilever Point at FHL, are archived at BCO-DMO. A 2022 Carleton study, also listing FHL, tested how temperature and pH affect sperm swimming and fertilization in sand dollars and sea urchins. As principal investigator of a collaborative project on mussels and their fluid environment, he recorded temperatures inside a mussel bed at Argyle Creek on San Juan Island from 2019 to 2024 and measured mussel respiration in experiments at FHL from 2020 to 2023. A 2026 paper showed that realistic temperature fluctuations alter mussel respiration and thermal performance.

name: Michael W. Hart
text:
Michael W. Hart is an evolutionary biologist who works on marine invertebrates, chiefly echinoderms. The addresses on his papers trace his career. His first papers, of 1987 and 1988, give the University of Alberta's Department of Zoology with the Bamfield Marine Station, and Dalhousie University. From 1989 to 1996 they give the University of Washington's Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the census counts four FHL-connected papers from these years. Papers of 1996 and 1997 give the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry at Simon Fraser University, and those of 1997 to 1999 the University of California, Davis. From 2000 to 2005 his papers give Dalhousie's Department of Biology, and from 2004 the Department of Biological Sciences at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia, which publication records list as his most recent institution.

At FHL Hart studied how echinoderm larvae feed and how larval form evolves. A 1989 paper with Lauren Dickie and Richard Helling found that the time Strongylocentrotus sea urchin larvae take to begin feeding is not correlated with egg size. A 1991 paper examined how echinoderm larvae capture particles when suspension feeding, and a 1994 study with Richard R. Strathmann tested the functional consequences of phenotypic plasticity in echinoid larvae. With Richard L. Miller and Laurence P. Madin he described the form and feeding of a living specimen of the hemichordate Planctosphaera pelagica (1994). A 1996 paper treated the facultatively feeding larva of the echinoid Brisaster latifrons as a case of evolutionary loss of larval feeding. His later work turned to molecular evolution: life-history evolution in asterinid sea stars, speciation, and selection on sperm-egg recognition genes in sea stars and in mammals, including humans and other primates.

name: Michelle Hodgson
text: Michelle Hodgson was an honors undergraduate at St. Francis Xavier University, Nova Scotia, co-supervised by Russell C. Wyeth and Jim Williams, with a BSc Honours thesis dated April 2020. The thesis tested for behavioral innovation in the American lobster, Homarus americanus, in the fishing district around Antigonish, using baited, solvable containers on a seafloor tripod filmed by an overhead camera. Hodgson built an ethogram of foraging behaviors; the results supported innovation, with larger lobsters showing a broader repertoire. Hodgson also coauthored a 2021 Aquaculture paper with Wyeth on commercial non-toxic netting against mussel biofouling at a trout aquaculture operation in the Bras d'Or Lakes.

text: Mike McCay (Michael G. McCay) was a graduate student of M. A. R. Koehl in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. McCay studied how tree frogs glide. A 2003 Biotropica paper addressed winds under the rain forest canopy, the setting in which these frogs glide. McCay also coauthored Koehl's 2001 Science paper on how lobster antennules capture odors from turbulent plumes.

name: Miles D. Lamare
text:
Miles D. Lamare is a marine biologist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, where his ORCID record lists him as professor and head of the Department of Marine Science. He received a PhD from Otago's Department of Marine Science in 1997 with a thesis on the population biology and recruitment of the sea urchin Evechinus chloroticus. A 1998 paper on its larvae in a New Zealand fiord gives his address as Otago's Portobello Marine Laboratory, with a present address at Friday Harbor Laboratories. His papers from 1999 to 2004 give FHL as an address. Most report New Zealand studies, written with co-authors including M. F. Barker, Paul E. Brewin, Philip V. Mladenov and Stephen R. Wing; the last, from 2004, concerns sea urchins of the genus Strongylocentrotus. Publication records link nearly all of his later work to the University of Otago.

Lamare's research centers on sea urchins and other echinoderms: their reproduction, larval biology and responses to environmental stress. His FHL-connected papers trace the origin and transport of Evechinus chloroticus larvae in a fiord (1998) and estimate their development and mortality in situ (1999). Two 2000 papers compare four years of reproductive variation among habitats and model the urchin's growth. A 2001 paper with Wing measured the calorific content of New Zealand marine macrophytes. A 2004 study with Jennifer R. Hoffman examined natural variation of carotenoids in the eggs and gonads of Strongylocentrotus and their possible role in protection from ultraviolet radiation. That theme continued in his later work on ultraviolet damage to the DNA of Antarctic sea urchin embryos, including the protection given by sea ice, and in studies of the effects of ocean acidification and warming on echinoderm larvae from Antarctica to the tropics.

name: Min Zhong
text: Min Zhong completed a PhD in biological sciences at Auburn University in 2009 under Kenneth M. Halanych, who chaired the committee. The dissertation used mitochondrial genomes to examine annelid phylogeny, focusing on the tube-dwelling Terebelliformia, and reported two group II introns in a partial mitochondrial genome of the myzostomid Endomyzostoma. Analyses placed Pectinariidae as the earliest-diverging terebelliform family. Related papers include a 2008 Gene article on three terebelliform mitochondrial genomes with T. H. Struck and Halanych, a 2009 BMC Evolutionary Biology paper on the position of Myzostomida, and a 2011 multigene analysis of terebelliform annelids in the same journal.

name: Minako S. Vickery
text:
Minako S. Vickery is an echinoderm larval biologist and instructor in the Department of Biology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB). Vickery took BS and MS degrees at Toyama University in Japan under Mieko Komatsu, with theses on development in the starfish genus Astropecten, and a PhD at UAB under James B. McClintock on regeneration and cloning in the planktotrophic larvae of echinoderms. By Vickery's own account, most of the research was conducted at Friday Harbor Laboratories. After the PhD, Vickery was a postdoctoral fellow at Dauphin Island Sea Lab, then returned to UAB to teach microbiology, genetics, physiology and introductory biology.

The work showed that echinoderm larvae can regrow whole bodies after being cut in two. Vickery and McClintock reported on regeneration in metazoan larvae in Nature (1998). A 2002 paper in The Biological Bulletin described complete regeneration, with organogenesis, after surgical bisection in larvae of the asteroids Luidia foliolata and Pisaster ochraceus and the echinoids Lytechinus variegatus and Dendraster excentricus, with aggregations of mesenchyme cells forming at the cut within 48 hours. A 2001 paper in Gene identified nine novel cDNAs from genes differentially expressed early in larval sea star regeneration. A separate line of work compared tube-foot morphology across the Asteroidea as a phylogenetic character (American Zoologist, 2000).

name: Ming Wei Aaron Toh
text: Ming Wei Aaron Toh completed a PhD in the Zoology Program at the University of Hawai'i at Mānoa in May 2025, in Amy L. Moran's lab, defending the dissertation on April 22, 2025. Toh's research concerned the larval and visual ecology of Antarctic invertebrates, particularly sea spiders and nudibranchs, with field experience in Antarctica. Toh coauthored a 2019 Proceedings of the Royal Society B paper on polar gigantism in pycnogonids, a 2024 Ecology paper on spawning and larval development of Colossendeis megalonyx, and a 2026 preprint on seasonal temperature, oxygen and conductivity around McMurdo Sound. name: Miranda Winningham
text: Miranda Winningham (Cornell class of 2017) was an undergraduate researcher in C. Drew Harvell's lab. The work concerned eelgrass wasting disease and its pathogen Labyrinthula zosterae, with co-authored papers on how environment, dose, and isolate shape virulence (2018), warming and summer epidemics (2021), and waterborne transmission (2024).

name: Miriam Hauer-Jensen
text: Miriam Hauer-Jensen wrote a 2022 senior thesis in organismal biology at Scripps College, with Angela Sremba as first reader and Sarah E. Gilman as second. Using passive acoustic recordings from the western Ross Sea, the thesis documented marine mammal vocalizations through 2016, including leopard seal and humpback whale calls, alongside environmental and anthropogenic sound.

name: Mitch Anderson
text: Mitch Anderson completed a University of Chicago PhD in development, regeneration, and stem cell biology in 2025, advised by Sally Horne-Badovinac, with Edwin Munro on the committee. The dissertation used the Drosophila egg chamber to study how the basement membrane and semaphorin signaling (Sema5c and PlexA) guide tissue elongation. A 2025 paper with Horne-Badovinac examined basement membrane architecture and mechanics.

name: Mo Armstrong
text: Mo Armstrong is listed among past students of Michael T. Nishizaki as a Carleton College undergraduate in the 2021 Friday Harbor Laboratories REU program. Armstrong coauthored a 2026 Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B paper with Nishizaki, Sara Leuchtenberger and Wanying Na, with Carleton and Friday Harbor affiliations. The study compared mussel respiration under alternating temperature cycles and under a field-based regime built from continuous temperature records at the study site. Thermal performance curves differed between the treatments, which pointed to heating rate and exposure duration as influences on thermal performance.

text: Mogens Lesner Glass (died 2018) completed an MSc in zoophysiology at Aarhus University in 1977, supervised by Kjell Johansen, studying lung ventilation and breathing pattern in the aquatic snake Acrochordus javanicus. He went on to study ventilatory control and pulmonary gas exchange in reptiles and amphibians, including a 1983 review with Steve Wood, and became a full professor of physiology at Universidade de São Paulo in Ribeirão Preto.

name: Molly Grear
text: Molly Grear earned a PhD in civil and environmental engineering at the University of Washington in 2018, with Michael R. Motley as advisor and Adam P. Summers and Andrea E. Copping on the reading committee. The dissertation tested skin and blubber of marine mammals, including harbor seals, harbor porpoises and killer whales, to build material models and finite element simulations of tidal turbine strikes, with support from Friday Harbor Laboratories. A 2018 Zoology paper with Summers tested anisotropy in harbor seal skin and blubber. Grear joined the Marine Sciences Laboratory of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory as an environmental engineer in 2012, with later reports on marine energy for kelp farming.

name: Monica V. Orellana
text:
Mónica V. Orellana is a biological oceanographer who works on phytoplankton and marine polymer gels, with a principal investigator position from 2010 at the University of Washington's Polar Science Center, Applied Physics Laboratory, and the Institute for Systems Biology. She studied zoology at the Universidad de Concepción in Chile, then took MS and PhD degrees at the University of Washington. A 1992 paper with M. J. Perry, from the School of Oceanography, described an immunoprobe for measuring Rubisco in individual phytoplankton cells. As a postdoctoral fellow she co-authored a 1998 Nature paper with Wei-Chun Chin and Pedro Verdugo reporting that dissolved organic polymers in seawater spontaneously assemble into microgels.

Papers with Verdugo cover ultraviolet radiation blocking carbon exchange between the dissolved and gel phases of seawater (2003), blue light triggering regulated exocytosis of gels from Phaeocystis globosa (2004), optical and proteomic fingerprints of marine microgels, with Ger van den Engh (2007), and the self-assembly of marine biopolymers in carbon cycling (2008). By her 2014 account, she used systems biology at the Institute for Systems Biology to study phytoplankton responses to ocean acidification, and at the Polar Science Center she examined how phytoplankton influence cloud formation. A 2021 review with D. A. Hansell and others treats marine gels as a source of aerosols and cloud condensation nuclei.

name: Monroe H. Martin
text:
Monroe Harnish Martin (1907–2007) was an American mathematician who spent most of his career at the University of Maryland. He graduated from Lebanon Valley College in 1928 and earned a PhD at Johns Hopkins University in 1932 under Aurel Wintner, with a dissertation on infinite orthogonal matrices. After a National Research Council fellowship at Harvard and, from 1933, an instructorship at Trinity College in Hartford, he joined Maryland in 1936, became full professor in 1942, and headed the mathematics department from 1943 to 1954. In 1949 he became the first director of the university's Institute of Fluid Dynamics and Applied Mathematics, and he became emeritus in 1972. He has no FHL papers; he appears in the report as an early link in an academic lineage.

Martin's research centered on fluid dynamics, and he also worked on partial differential equations, including a 1952 study with J. B. Diaz of Riemann's method for equations of hyperbolic, parabolic and elliptic type, and a 1969 paper on inequalities for Hermitian functionals. He held a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1959, when he lectured at the University of St Andrews and the University of Rome, and the University of Maryland later named the Monroe H. Martin Prize after him. The Mathematics Genealogy Project lists three Maryland doctoral students: Simon Levin (1964), Dennis Dunninger (1966) and Jim Cushing (1968). The tie to FHL runs through the ecologist Simon Levin, whose own student Daniel Grünbaum is in the report's table of FHL core scientists; both links in this lineage come from Wikidata.

name: Morgan D. Linney
text: Morgan D. Linney held a Blinks-REU-Beacon Fellowship at Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2013, working with James A. Murray of California State University, East Bay, while at Mount Holyoke College. Their joint report on the nudibranch Tritonia tetraquetra described search-like behavior after loss of an odor plume, some evidence of reliance on geomagnetic cues, and changes in cerebral nerve spiking after magnetic field rotation. Linney earned a PhD in oceanography at the University of Hawai'i at Mānoa in 2021 and published with David M. Karl on dissolved DNA in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (2021) and microbial sources of exocellular DNA (2022). A postdoctoral position at MIT began in 2021.

name: Morgan Eisenlord
text:
Morgan E. Eisenlord is a marine disease ecologist who was a postdoctoral researcher at Western Washington University as of 2025. Eisenlord took a BS in biology at the University of Washington (2010-2013), and the undergraduate research was at FHL: a summer 2011 course project on how tidal current phase affects Rhinoceros Auklets in Cattle Pass, and a fall 2012 Pelagic Ecosystems Function apprenticeship on tides, water masses and seabirds. Eisenlord co-authored the 2014 kelp detritus study by Megan Dethier, David Duggins and others, a paper with six undergraduate authors, and a 2014 fatty acid study of isopod diets. Two spring 2014 FHL student reports on sea star wasting disease carry Eisenlord's name with Dethier's, and one lists Eisenlord as primary mentor to undergraduate Zhongran Ni.

At Cornell University Eisenlord completed a PhD in ecology and evolutionary biology (2024). Eisenlord is listed as a graduate student in the lab of C. Drew Harvell, who sat on the thesis committee, chaired by Andre Dhondt. The thesis examined two temperature-sensitive diseases, sea star wasting disease in Pisaster ochraceus and seagrass wasting disease in Zostera marina. A 2016 paper combined field monitoring with an FHL experiment, linking disease risk to size and temperature and reporting adult populations at one quarter of pre-outbreak abundance. A 2024 paper in Royal Society Open Science used field outplants and laboratory exposures, with shoots brought to FHL, and implicated waterborne transmission of Labyrinthula zosterae.

name: Morgan Mouchka
text: Morgan Mouchka earned a PhD in ecology at Cornell University in 2014 with C. Drew Harvell as committee chair. The dissertation, on how cnidarians respond to pathogenic and mutualistic microbes, used the sea anemone Aiptasia pallida; after exposure to the bacterium Serratia marcescens, anemones with dinoflagellate symbionts differed in gene expression from those without and had lower survival. Mouchka first-authored a 2010 Integrative and Comparative Biology review of coral-associated bacteria with I. Hewson and Harvell, and coauthored a 2014 G3 paper on gene expression in symbiotic and aposymbiotic cnidarians. The Harvell lab alumni page lists Mouchka as a postdoctoral researcher in the Schlenke lab at Reed College.

name: Nadjejda Espinel Velasco
text: Nadjejda Espinel Velasco earned a PhD in marine science at the University of Otago in 2020, supervised by Miles D. Lamare with Linn Hoffmann and Sergio Morales. The thesis asked whether ocean acidification affects larval settlement in the urchin Evechinus chloroticus, the abalone Haliotis iris and the polychaete Galeolaria hystrix, directly, indirectly through settlement surfaces, or as carry-over effects, concluding that effects likely vary by species. A 2018 Marine Ecology Progress Series review covered the question in invertebrate and fish larvae. Espinel Velasco then held postdoctoral posts at the Norwegian Polar Institute and UiT The Arctic University of Norway, and joined the University of Gothenburg as a researcher in 2023.

name: Nancy Beckage
text: Nancy Beckage (died 2012) earned a PhD at the University of Washington in 1980, starting under Arthur Martin and finishing with Lynn M. Riddiford, then held a postdoctoral position in Riddiford's laboratory. Her thesis covered developmental interactions between the tobacco hornworm Manduca sexta and its endoparasite Apanteles congregatus, work published with Riddiford in 1978, 1982 and 1983. Later work centered on the wasp Cotesia congregata and the same hornworm. She established a lab at the Issaquah Biomedical Research Institute in 1982, joined the USDA at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, in 1987 and moved to the University of California, Riverside, in 1990. She was elected an AAAS fellow in 2004.

name: Nancy Douglas
text: Nancy Douglas, listed with a PhD among past staff of C. Drew Harvell's lab at Cornell University, worked on the health of Caribbean sea fans and corals. Douglas was lead author, with Kerri Mullen, Stephanie Talmage and Harvell, of a 2006 Marine Biology paper on chitinolytic enzymes in the sea fan Gorgonia ventalina. Coauthored papers from the same group followed on sea fan immunocompetence in the Florida Keys (2008), Labyrinthulomycetes associated with G. ventalina (2012), and persistent shifts in coral microbiota linked to the 2010 Caribbean warm anomaly (2015), the last listing Douglas in Cornell's Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.

name: Nancy Papalopulu
text: Nancy Papalopulu, a professor of developmental neuroscience at the University of Manchester, hosted Sarah Woolner's postdoctoral project there on a Beit Memorial Fellowship awarded in 2008. The two published on spindle position in symmetric cell divisions in 2012. Papalopulu's research examines how oscillating gene expression times neurogenesis, and Papalopulu was elected a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences in 2013.

name: Nancy Sealover
text: Nancy Sealover completed a 2016 project in the Friday Harbor Laboratories Research Apprenticeship "Pelagic Ecosystem Function in the San Juan Archipelago," on the distribution and sediment associations of Pacific sand lance in the San Juan Archipelago. Listed at Friday Harbor Laboratories, Sealover later shared authorship with M. R. Baker and others on a 2024 Marine Environmental Research paper, an atlas of benthic habitat for Ammodytes personatus. That study combined multibeam echosounder maps with multiyear sediment sampling to identify subtidal substrates suited to the fish, which relies on specific sediments for rest and refuge from predators.

name: Natalia Kravtsova
text: Natalia Kravtsova was a doctoral student in mathematics at The Ohio State University in the group of Adriana T. Dawes, listed as a Graduate Research Associate, after earning a BS (2012) and a master's degree there. She built mathematical models of cell polarization in the early Caenorhabditis elegans embryo, including a 2014 Bulletin of Mathematical Biology paper with Dawes on actomyosin regulation and symmetry breaking. Later papers with Dawes treated parameter sampling for constrained models using Markov chain Monte Carlo (2023), a Gromov-Wasserstein distance for comparing biological time series (2023), and AIR-1 dynamics in centrosome maturation (2025).

name: Natalia Taft
text: Natalia Taft, of the University of Wisconsin-Parkside, was a sabbatical visitor with Adam P. Summers in 2021. Taft's research has addressed the form and function of fish fin rays. Papers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst compared pectoral fin ray morphology between fishes that use their fins differently (2011) and related fin ray specializations in the longhorn sculpin, Myoxocephalus octodecimspinosus, to function (2012). Work from Parkside measured flexural stiffness of yellow perch fin rays under different preservation techniques (2018) and contributed to a computed tomography study of fin rays in Tiktaalik and other tetrapodomorphs (2020). A 2023 paper described the muscles controlling pectoral free rays in scorpaenoid fishes.

name: Natalie Rivlin
text: Natalie Rivlin appears among both undergraduate alumni and past staff of C. Drew Harvell's lab at Cornell University. Listed at Cornell, Rivlin coauthored a 2016 study of ochre star (Pisaster ochraceus) mortality during the 2014 wasting disease epizootic, which related disease risk to size and temperature at sites including the San Juan Islands. As Natalie D. Rivlin, the same author contributed to a 2018 Ecology paper on co-culturing eelgrass and Pacific oysters under raised pCO2 and a 2021 paper, with Harvell, linking warm sea surface temperatures to eelgrass wasting disease. Both listed the University of Maryland Baltimore County's Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology.

She joined through the 2018 REU, mentored by Julie Schram, with a project on isopod behavior and color, then worked as a lab technician and on Dungeness crab projects funded by Oregon Sea Grant. She coauthored a 2023 paper on juvenile Dungeness crab foraging and lipid composition.

name: Nataliya Budaeva
text: Nataliya Budaeva was listed as a Smithsonian fellow at the National Museum of Natural History, with Kristian Fauchald as host, in 2008-2009. Budaeva had taken a master's degree at Lomonosov Moscow State University (2004) and done doctoral work at the Shirshov Institute of Oceanology (PhD 2008). With Fauchald, Budaeva described Diopatra tuberculantennata from Belize (2008) and the larval development of Mooreonuphis stigmatis from the northeast Pacific (2010). Budaeva later coauthored work on that species' developing jaws with Elena Vortsepneva and Alexander Tzetlin (2017). After a Marie Curie fellowship at the University Museum of Bergen (2012-2017), Budaeva became an associate professor there, working on annelid systematics, including an Onuphidae phylogeny (2016) and deep-sea quill worm dispersal (2024).

name: Nathan Churches
text: Nathan Churches was an undergraduate mentee of Billie J. Swalla in 2012, listed as a Mary Gates Undergraduate Research Fellow and in the Friday Harbor Laboratories Blinks/BEACON/REU program. Two 2012 FHL student reports, written with Swalla, Andrea B. Kohn and Leonid L. Moroz, examined collagens of the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei; a genome search found six distinct collagen type IV alpha chains on three scaffolds. Churches then entered a PhD program at the University of Southern California. Later papers covered the fecal microbiome of Pacific oysters on shifting algal diets (2018) and selection during larval development in the mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis (2023), the latter listing San Francisco State University's biology department.

name: Nathan Kley
text: Nathan Kley was a doctoral student of Elizabeth L. Brainerd, publishing from the University of Massachusetts Amherst on how snakes feed. Their work included mandibular raking in a snake (Nature, 1999) and an x-ray video study of prey transport in the black pinesnake (2002), followed by a study of ophiophagy in the California kingsnake (2004). Publishing from the Department of Anatomical Sciences at Stony Brook University from 2006, Kley described jaw and skull morphology of blindsnakes, including the Texas blindsnake (2006) and Liotyphlops albirostris (2009). With Paul Gignac, Kley refined iodine-enhanced micro-CT imaging of soft tissue (2014), and later coauthored a study of caecilian head muscles (2023).

name: Nathan Martin Klunk
text: Nathan Martin Klunk was an MS student in biology at Montclair State University (2022), sponsored by Matthew Aardema, with Colette Feehan and Meiyin Wu as committee members. The thesis surveyed the invasive rusty crayfish, Faxonius rusticus, in northern New Jersey and dissected samples for parasites. Parasitism was more likely on cobble than on mud, and most observed signs were primary indicators of the fungal plague.

name: Nathan Whelan
text: Nathan Whelan was a member of Kenneth Halanych's lab at Auburn University, where Whelan held a postdoctoral fellowship (2014-2016) after a 2013 PhD at the University of Alabama. A 2017 paper with Halanych placed ctenophores as sister to all other animals. Whelan directed the US Fish and Wildlife Service Southeast Conservation Genetics Lab (2016-2025) and, as of 2025, was associate professor and director of the Museum of Biological Diversity at Ohio State.

Durham coauthored a 2001 American Zoologist paper with Leise on serotonin and nitric oxide in metamorphosis.

text: Neil T. Umbreit was a University of Washington biochemistry PhD student of Trisha Davis (2014), with Linda Wordeman on the advisory committee. text: Nicholas B. Colvard received a PhD in 2016 from Northeastern University's Department of Marine and Environmental Sciences, advised by Brian Helmuth, with Emily Carrington as an external committee member. With Carrington and Helmuth, Colvard measured temperature-dependent photosynthesis in the intertidal alga Fucus gardneri and its sensitivity to climate change (2014). A 2017 Ecological Applications paper with Helmuth tested how nutrients alter the thermal ecophysiology of an intertidal macroalga.
