name: Nicholas Burnett
text: Nicholas P. Burnett, known as Nick, was a PhD student in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley (2012-2017), after a BS at the University of South Carolina. The research examined biomechanics of the kelp Egregia menziesii and its invertebrate grazers on wave-exposed shores of northern California, including a 2019 paper with Koehl on how kelp mechanical properties change with season, growth rate and herbivore wounds. As a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, Davis, from 2017, Burnett studied bee flight with S. A. Combes and macroalgal biomechanics with Brian Gaylord, including a 2024 paper on bull kelp spore release heights.

name: Nicholas J. Gidmark
text:
Nicholas J. Gidmark is a comparative biomechanist who studies how fishes capture and process food. He received a B.A. from the University of Minnesota in 2006 and a Ph.D. from Brown University in 2012. He has taught at Knox College in Galesburg, Illinois, since 2016 and is associate professor of biology there. His papers from Brown were co-authored with Elizabeth Brainerd, who appears as his teacher in the report's mentoring network. His FHL connection runs from 2011 to 2020. A 2011 study of sand lances had FHL co-authors, including Adam Summers. He co-authored a series of FHL student research papers in 2014 and 2015, and his papers of 2016 to 2020 give FHL as an address, from 2018 alongside Knox. The census counts three FHL-address papers in that period.

Gidmark links the properties of muscles to skeletal mechanics and whole-animal performance. His methods include CT scanning, 3D biomechanical modeling, electromyography, high-speed light and X-ray video, and XROMM (X-ray reconstruction of moving morphology). His Brown-era work examined how sand lances move from water into sand (2011) and how the throat (pharyngeal) jaws of grass carp chew food and those of black carp crush hard prey (2014, 2015). At FHL he turned to local sculpins and Pacific salmon. Student papers he co-authored, with Nina Finley and others, compared jaw muscles, bite and suction forces and jaw leverage in Salish Sea sculpins and in salmon. Published results include a 2016 paper with Daniel Geldof on developmental timing in two Psychrolutes sculpins, a 2018 study of jaw-closing muscles and bones across sculpins and their relatives, and a 2020 paper with Elska Kaczmarek on the bite force–gape relationship in two salmonid fishes.

name: Nick Davenport
text: Nick Davenport earned a PhD in William M. Bement's lab, listed among its former graduate students, in the Cellular and Molecular Biology program at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The work asked how cells reseal after damage. A 2016 Molecular Biology of the Cell paper with Bement imaged membrane dynamics in wounded Xenopus laevis oocytes at high resolution, finding that damage triggers fusion of intracellular compartments, which form a barrier limiting influx of extracellular dextrans, consistent with the patch hypothesis. A second 2016 paper with Bement revisited that hypothesis, and a 2023 paper with L. A. Sepaniac and Bement used wounding to examine cortical and epithelial excitability in Xenopus embryos.

name: Nick Schuh
text: Nicholas W. Schuh worked with Andreas Heyland of the University of Guelph and Jonathan P. Rast on immunity and development in larvae of the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus. Adults for its natural microbiota experiments, collected at Clallam Bay, Washington, were held in cages off the Friday Harbor Laboratories dock. Coauthored work included chapters on urchin larvae as a model for postembryonic development (2018) and on larval immune response (2019).

name: Nicolai Truemper
text: Nicolai Truemper is listed as a PhD student of Nicole E. Phillips at Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand (2012). The thesis examined the spatial dynamics and life history of the New Zealand half crab Petrolisthes elongatus on Wellington cobble beaches. Cobble size predicted crab density and mean carapace width at most scales of observation, and densities were about sixfold higher inside Wellington Harbour than on the south coast. Reproductive traits varied across sites, with the highest fecundity at Island Bay. Larvae responded strongly to waterborne settlement cues from adults in both laboratory and field trials.

name: Nicole E. Phillips
text:
Nicole E. Phillips is a marine ecologist in the School of Biological Sciences at Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. Her work centers on the early life stages of marine invertebrates. Her papers of 1996 and 1997 give the Friday Harbor Laboratories and the University of Washington Department of Zoology as her address. There she co-authored a study of polychaete larvae with Bruno Pernet and studies of molluscan neuropeptides with A. O. Dennis Willows. She completed a Ph.D. in ecology, evolution and marine biology at the University of California, Santa Barbara, in 2002. A paper of that year gives Victoria University's School of Biological Sciences as her new address, and from 2008 her papers also name its Coastal Ecology Laboratory. The census records three FHL-address papers from 1996 and 1997, and a 2009 paper co-authored with Richard Strathmann of FHL.

Her FHL-era papers cover two subjects. With Pernet she showed that larvae of the scaleworm Arctonoe vittata, which lack the feeding structures most polychaete larvae use, capture particles up to 60 micrometers across (1996). With Willows and colleagues she helped purify and sequence neuropeptides from identified neurons of the sea slug Tritonia (1996), and a 1997 follow-up showed that these peptides speed the beating of the cilia that drive crawling. The 2009 paper with Douglas Bertram and Strathmann found that larger eggs did not speed development of the juvenile rudiment relative to the larval body in Strongylocentrotus sea urchins. Her later work, listed on her ORCID record, follows larvae through settlement into juvenile life: larval nutrition and size at settlement in mussels, maternal provisioning in whelks, ultraviolet and low-tide stress on egg masses, copper effects on sea urchin larvae, and recruitment on New Zealand shores and reefs.

name: Nicole L. Hack
text: Nicole L. Hack was a Blinks/NSF REU/BEACON participant at Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2013, working with Vikram K. Iyengar while at the University of California Santa Cruz. The project tested how size, sex and shelter shape cohabitation in the maritime earwig Anisolabis maritima from San Juan Island beaches, published in PLoS ONE in 2017. Females tolerated cohabitation less than males, and earwigs mismatched in size shared shelter less often. Hack then earned an MS at California Polytechnic State University (2017) with Sean C. Lema, testing plasma Igf1 as a growth biomarker in olive and blue rockfish, with a 2018 paper on olive rockfish.

With Emlet, Nakata described facultative larval feeding in an undescribed brittle star, Amphiodia sp. opaque (Ecology and Evolution, 2023): fed larvae developed faster and metamorphosed at higher rates. The pair also published descriptions and a key for northeastern Pacific brittle star larvae (Invertebrate Biology, 2025). text: Niels Van Steenkiste was a postdoctoral fellow (2015-2021) and then research associate (2021-2025) in Brian S. text: Nina Lester Finley was a Blinks-NSF REU-BEACON participant at Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2014, working with Nicholas J. Gidmark while at Whitman College. name: Noa Shenkar
text:
Noa Shenkar is a marine invertebrate zoologist who studies ascidians (sea squirts) at Tel Aviv University, where the Steinhardt Museum of Natural History lists her as curator of marine invertebrates and as an associate professor in the School of Zoology. She completed a PhD in zoology at Tel Aviv under Yossi Loya. Papers with Loya from 2008 compared native Red Sea and non-indigenous Mediterranean populations of Herdmania momus and followed ascidian recruitment on an artificial reef at Eilat. She then did postdoctoral work at the University of Washington, and Billie J. Swalla's lab page lists her in December 2010 as a postdoctoral fellow of NSF and the Israel Taxonomy Initiative.

With Swalla and Gretchen Lambert of Friday Harbor Laboratories, Shenkar reported the first Pacific record of the Atlantic ascidian Molgula citrina (2010), from floating docks at Seldovia, Alaska, in a paper prepared with space and support from FHL and its Whiteley Center. With Swalla she also published a 2011 review of global ascidian diversity that listed 2,815 valid species, and with Lambert a new Red Sea species of Boltenia (2010). After returning to Israel in 2012 she established a laboratory at the Steinhardt Museum, working on marine bioinvasion, ascidian ecology, phylogeny and regeneration, and ascidians as indicators in ecotoxicology. Later work includes central nervous system regeneration in Polycarpa mytiligera (2022).

text: Noah Jaffe earned an MS in biology in 2020 in Sarah Cohen's lab at San Francisco State University's Estuary and Ocean Science Center, after a BA at Pitzer College. Jaffe was first author, with Cohen, of a 2019 PLOS ONE study of sea star wasting disease demography and etiology in the brooding sea star Leptasterias.

name: Noah R. Bressman
text: Noah R. Bressman was a Blinks/NSF REU/BEACON intern at Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2015, a Cornell University student working with Stacy C. Farina and Alice Gibb. The project described an "army crawl" overland gait in the tidepool sculpin Oligocottus maculosus, published in Zoology in 2018. Bressman took a PhD in biology at Wake Forest University (2020), publishing on terrestrial movement and orientation in mangrove rivulus, northern snakehead and walking catfish, and was then a postdoctoral fellow at Chapman University. As of 2026 Bressman was at Salisbury University, an assistant professor of physiology studying amphibious behavior in invasive fishes and the biology of blue catfish.

name: Nora B. Terwilliger
text: Nora B. Terwilliger, a biologist at the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, advised Anne Christine Brown's 1991 PhD and chaired the committees for master's theses by Karen Lynn Dumler (1996) and Jennifer Ann German (2001). The Brown and Dumler theses were on the Dungeness crab, and the German thesis on hemocyanin in the red rock crab. Terwilliger worked on crustacean hemocyanins, including a 2007 paper on hemocyanins and the immune response, and published with Brown in 1992 on ionic and osmotic regulation in the Dungeness crab.

name: Noraly Van Meer
text: Noraly Van Meer is listed among visiting graduate students on Elizabeth L. Brainerd's lab page. Working from Wageningen University's Experimental Zoology Group, van Meer used XROMM with Brainerd and others to track food transport and swallowing in white-spotted bamboo sharks (Journal of Experimental Biology, 2019), and co-authored a 2024 XROMM study of forelimb function in loggerhead sea turtles and river cooters. The Wageningen doctoral thesis (2024), with Johan van Leeuwen and Martin Lankheet, covered the structure and activity of swimming muscles in larval zebrafish. Van Meer then held a postdoctoral post in entomology and nematology at the University of Florida (2025-2026), working on weapon-bearing insects.

text: Ole Seehausen, a professor at the University of Bern's Institute of Ecology and Evolution since 2004, also works in the Department of Fish Ecology and Evolution at Eawag in Switzerland. Kassandra L. Ford was a postdoctoral researcher in Seehausen's Bern lab. Seehausen studies speciation and adaptive radiation in cichlid fishes and Alpine whitefish; Ford and Seehausen coauthored a 2023 PLOS ONE paper on cichlid microtomography.

name: Olga Hartman
text:
Olga Hartman (1900-1974) was a polychaete taxonomist at the Allan Hancock Foundation of the University of Southern California. Her tie to Friday Harbor runs through Kristian Fauchald, who moved to California in 1965 for doctoral study with her, completed the PhD in 1969, later followed her as curator of polychaetes, and taught polychaete biology classes at Friday Harbor. Hartman earned an MA (1933) and a PhD (1936) at the University of California, Berkeley, with a dissertation under S. F. Light on the polychaetes of the California littoral zone. She worked at Scripps Institution of Oceanography in 1937, studied annelid collections in Europe and the United States on a Sarah Berliner fellowship in 1939-40, and spent summer 1940 at the U.S. Fisheries Biological Laboratory in Beaufort, North Carolina.

Hartman joined the Hancock Foundation as a research associate in 1940 and described material from its 1932-1937 expeditions off Mexico, Central America, South America and the Galápagos Islands. From the early 1950s, bottom samplers on the research vessel Velero IV gave her many new species and the collections for a quantitative study. Her works include The Marine Annelids of North Carolina (1945), the Catalogue of the Polychaetous Annelids of the World (1959) and its 1965 supplement, and atlases of the errantiate and sedentariate polychaetes of California (1968, 1969). She is credited with describing 473 species. She became associate professor in 1961 and professor in 1967, curated the marine annelids, retired formally in 1969, and stayed at the foundation until her death.

name: Olivia J. Graham
text:
Olivia J. Graham studies seagrass wasting disease in eelgrass (Zostera marina). FHL's people pages list Graham among postdoctoral fellows in January 2024 and January 2026, and Graham's ORCID record lists a research scientist position at Friday Harbor Laboratories beginning in June 2026. After a biology BA at Claremont McKenna College (2013), Graham was a post-baccalaureate student at the University of Washington in 2014-15. In the fall 2014 Pelagic Ecosystem Function Research Apprenticeship at FHL, Graham studied Pacific sand lance in San Juan Channel, examining foraging in relation to tides, abundance, condition and year-class structure. The report thanks Matt Baker, W. Breck Tyler, Jan Newton and Becca Guenther as advisors and teaching assistant. Graham later coauthored sand lance work led by Baker (2016, 2019).

Graham was a PhD student in C. Drew Harvell's lab at Cornell University (2016-2022), with a dissertation on climate, communities and seagrass wasting disease, and then a postdoctoral research associate there. Papers from this work tracked disease effects on eelgrass growth and belowground sugar (2021), and surveyed 5,761 leaves from Alaska to Washington, finding prevalence 16% lower in subtidal than intertidal leaves (2023). Experiments showed that reducing the leaf microbiome with antibiotics and bleach lowered disease severity (2024), and that grazing scars from isopods and snails increased it (2025). A 2025 paper treated deeper San Juan Islands meadows as refugia. Graham also coauthored a 2023 FHL REU-Blinks report by Baylen Ratliff on subtidal meadows.

name: Olivia L. George
text: Olivia L. George earned an MS (2003) and a PhD (2007) in the Molecular Biology program at New Mexico State University, both listed with Charles Bradley Shuster as advisor. The dissertation was "Using Chemical Biology to Probe the Regulation of Cell Division." With Shuster, George showed that Aurora B kinase maintains chromatin organization between meiosis I and II in oocytes of the surf clam Spisula solidissima (Cell Cycle, 2006). A 2008 ACS Chemical Biology paper reported that Bisphenol A causes multipolar spindles in fertilized eggs of the sea urchin Lytechinus pictus, and identified tubulin as a candidate binding protein.

name: Olivia Turnross
text: Olivia Turnross, who published as O. R. Turnross, was an undergraduate researcher in Emily Carrington's lab at the University of Washington. In the Blinks/REU program at Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2011, while at the College of Creative Studies, University of California Santa Barbara, Turnross worked with Dawn Vaughn and Carrington on how raised low-tide air temperature affects the predatory snail Nucella ostrina feeding on the barnacle Balanus glandula. Heating did not change the timing or size of a foraging bout, though males and females fed out of step. A related paper with the same coauthors, on sex-specific temperature dependence of foraging and growth in intertidal snails, appeared in Marine Biology in 2013. Hilary A. Hayford thanked Turnross among former undergraduates who helped collect data for Hayford's 2016 dissertation on thermal risk in Nucella ostrina.

name: Olivier Fedrigo
text: Olivier Fedrigo is listed among former members of Gregory A. Wray's lab at Duke University, with a later post as research scientist at Rockefeller University. Earlier work with Gavin Naylor at Iowa State University included a gene-specific DNA sequencing chip for studying molecular evolution (2004). At Duke, Fedrigo studied primate genome evolution, including positive selection in promoters of neural and nutrition-related genes (Nature Genetics, 2007) and glucose transporters and human brain size (2011). From Rockefeller's Vertebrate Genome Lab, Fedrigo co-authored the 2021 Nature paper on complete, error-free assemblies of vertebrate genomes, along with reference genomes of species such as the vaquita.

name: Oluchi L. Aroh
text: Oluchi L. Aroh earned a PhD in biological sciences at Auburn University in 2023 with Kenneth M. Halanych. The dissertation used bioinformatics to study associations between marine invertebrates and microbes. It covered LTR retrotransposons in the deep-sea tubeworm Lamellibrachia luymesi (BMC Genomics, 2021, with Halanych); a new symbiont, "Candidatus Mycoplasma mahonii," from the basket star Gorgonocephalus chilensis, with a broad Pacific range (PLoS ONE, 2023, with Mark R. Liles and Halanych); and microbial communities of farmed and wild oysters. Aroh also co-authored a 2023 Molecular Biology and Evolution study of the epigenome in three deep-sea polychaetes.

name: Ondrej Maxian
text: Ondrej Maxian was a postdoctoral fellow in Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago from 2023 to 2025, after a 2023 PhD at New York University, where Maxian worked at the Courant Institute, and degrees in mathematics and chemical engineering from Case Western Reserve University. Maxian built mathematical models of how large-scale order arises in cells, coupling biochemistry and mechanics in the C. elegans embryo. Representative papers cover cross-linked actin network simulations (2021, PLOS Computational Biology) and actin heterogeneity in activator-inhibitor dynamics at the cell cortex (2025, PNAS, with A. R. Dinner and Munro). Maxian was an assistant professor at the University of Notre Dame as of 2026.

name: Osamu Shimomura
text:
Osamu Shimomura (1928–2018) was a Japanese organic chemist who studied bioluminescence. He graduated from the pharmacy course of Nagasaki Medical College in 1951 and received his PhD from Nagoya University in 1960 under Yoshimasa Hirata, working on the luciferin of the sea firefly Cypridina. From 1960 he worked with Frank H. Johnson at Princeton University, returned to Nagoya as an associate professor in 1963, and was a senior research associate at Princeton from 1965 to 1982 and at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole from 1982 to 2001; he was also a visiting professor at Boston University. With Johnson he collected the jellyfish Aequorea victoria over many summers at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where in 1962 they discovered aequorin and green fluorescent protein (GFP). He shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien for the discovery and development of GFP.

The census lists four papers with an FHL address, from 1962 and 1963, written with Johnson and Yo Saiga. They describe the extraction and purification of aequorin from Aequorea, a related photoprotein, halistaurin, from the hydromedusa Halistaura, and the use of aequorin's light emission to measure small amounts of calcium (Science, 1963). Later census papers mention FHL in their text or are listed in its research bibliography: work with Johnson on the chemistry of coelenterate bioluminescence (1975) and on peroxidized coelenterazine as the active group of aequorin (1978), the structure of the GFP chromophore (1979), and a series in the Biochemical Journal (1981 to 1990) on the stability and molecular forms of aequorin, the effect of calcium chelators on its luminescence, and semi-synthetic and recombinant aequorins, made with Yoshito Kishi and colleagues, as improved calcium indicators for cells. He recounted the work in 'A short story of aequorin' (1995).

name: Oscar D. Pérez
text: Oscar D. Pérez is listed among former doctoral members of Federico D. Brown's evolutionary developmental biology lab at the Universidade de São Paulo. Pérez's published work with Brown concerns embryology. A 2017 paper in the Journal of Experimental Zoology Part B, with Y. E. Chávez-Viteri and Brown, followed early cleavage in Aplysia cf. californica using embryos cultured in vitro and tubulin staining of mitotic spindles, with Pérez at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador in Quito. A 2021 paper in the International Journal of Developmental Biology, with Pérez and Brown at São Paulo, described molecular identity, embryology and planktotrophy in the sea slug Elysia diomedea in Ecuador.

name: Owen M. Woodward
text:
Owen M. Woodward is a physiologist who studies urate transport and polycystic kidney disease, listed by the University of Maryland School of Medicine as an associate professor of pharmacology and physiology. Woodward's tie to FHL is predoctoral work at the University of Washington, where Woodward earned a PhD in zoology, on the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea. An NIH predoctoral fellowship (2004-2005) supported a study of its crawling circuit and ciliated motor cells. A 2006 paper with A. O. Dennis Willows, with addresses at UW Biology and FHL, showed that dopamine suppresses a calcium-dependent chloride current in ciliated pedal epithelial cells and raises ciliary beat frequency. A second paper with Willows and a third with Willows and Russell C. Wyeth covered nervous control of cilia and navigation.

After a BA in biology at the University of Virginia and the UW doctorate, Woodward was a research fellow in physiology at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. There Woodward was first author of a 2009 paper in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences identifying ABCG2 as a urate efflux transporter and showing that the common Q141K mutation, linked to gout, reduced urate transport by 53%. A 2013 paper in the same journal, again with Woodward as first author, reported that the mutation destabilizes the nucleotide-binding domain and that small molecules can correct the defect. Woodward's Maryland lab has also studied the first stages of cyst formation after loss of the PKD2 gene product, using a three-dimensional kidney tubule culture model.

name: Pamela Roe
text:
Pamela Roe (died 2019) was an invertebrate zoologist who worked on nemerteans (ribbon worms). Her 1970 and 1976 papers on the nemertean Paranemertes peregrina give the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington as her address. The 1976 paper acknowledges support from FHL. From 1981 to at least 2001 her papers give the Department of Biological Sciences at California State College (later California State University), Stanislaus, in Turlock. Papers of 1981 and 1982 written with John and Lois Crowe and Daniel Wickham also list FHL, and the 1982 paper lists the University of California, Davis and the Bodega Marine Laboratory. The census counts three FHL-address papers from 1976 to 1982. A 2020 column, first published in FHL's Tide Bite newsletter, lists a Pamela Roe Graduate Student Endowed Fund among the awards supporting graduate students' summers at FHL.

Roe's research concerned the feeding, life histories and reproduction of nemerteans. Her first papers described the food and feeding behavior of Paranemertes peregrina (1970) and its life history and predator–prey interactions on Washington mud flats (1976). There it feeds only on polychaete worms and returns to its burrow by following its own mucus trail. She also wrote on territorial behavior in young nereid polychaetes (1975). With the Crowes and Wickham she showed that juveniles of Carcinonemertes errans, an egg-eating nemertean that lives on crabs, take up dissolved amino acids (1981, 1982). Later papers dealt with transmission between crab hosts, mating and parthenogenesis in Carcinonemertes, and the high-intertidal Pantinonemertes californiensis. With Jon Norenburg she studied pelagic nemerteans off California and Hawaii, and with Norenburg and Svetlana Maslakova she wrote the Nemertea chapter of the Light and Smith Manual (2007).

text: Patrick Flannery, class of 2021 at SUNY Geneseo, is listed among undergraduate alumni of Mackenzie E. Gerringer's lab there. name: Patrick T. Martone
text:
Patrick T. Martone is a phycologist and professor in the Department of Botany at the University of British Columbia, where his lab studies the biomechanics, evolution and ecophysiology of marine macroalgae. He received a BS from Duke University in 1998 and a PhD from Stanford University in 2007, followed by a year as a postdoctoral scholar at Stanford. He joined UBC as an assistant professor in 2008, became associate professor in 2013 and professor in 2019. He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists; his FHL connection comes through collaborators. Several of his coralline papers note work done while co-author Paul Gabrielson was a visiting professor at FHL, and others came from projects with Emily Carrington and colleagues at the laboratories. In the mentoring network he is linked to Katharine Hind as postdoctoral supervisor.

Martone's lab asks how intertidal seaweeds withstand wave forces and other stresses, using flumes and breakage tests. It uses DNA barcoding to sort out coralline algal diversity and evolution, including cryptic species, and studies kelp development, the evolution of algal cell walls and seaweed physiology on the British Columbia coast. Most of his FHL-connected papers are coralline systematics with Gabrielson and Hind: two species of Calliarthron (2011), Chiharaea and Yamadaia as reduced, recently derived articulated forms (2012), sequencing of type specimens (2014, 2023), cryptic Bossiella species resolved with historical DNA (2015), the new crustose genus Crusticorallina (2016), and Bossiella as a genus with both jointed and unjointed species (2018). Others treat the hydrodynamic performance of foliose red algae (2011), ocean acidification delaying and weakening spore adhesion (2017), and whether calcification protects corallines from urchin grazing (2021) or lowers their caloric value (2023).

name: Patsy S. Dickinson
text:
Patsy S. Dickinson is a neurobiologist and is Josiah Little Professor of Natural Sciences Emerita and adjunct professor of biology at Bowdoin College. She received a BA from Pomona College and MS and PhD degrees from the University of Washington. From 1979 to 1981 she was a postdoctoral researcher at the Laboratoire de Neurobiologie Comparée (CNRS and Université de Bordeaux I) in Arcachon, France. Her FHL-connected work falls into two periods. Her single-authored papers of 1978 to 1980 list FHL as an address. From 2006 to 2010 she co-authored papers on crustacean neuropeptides, mostly with Andrew E. Christie and Elizabeth A. Stemmler, that are linked to FHL through an author address or the text. The census lists ten FHL-connected papers by her from 1978 to 2014, including a multi-author 2014 BioScience article on synthesis in organismal biology.

Dickinson studies how the nervous system produces flexible patterned movements, such as the change between walking and running. Her Bowdoin laboratory uses two simple neural circuits in the lobster, combining recordings of neuronal activity and heart contractions with immunohistochemistry and molecular methods. Her first FHL paper described the conduction systems that control expansion and contraction in the sea pen Ptilosarcus gurneyi (1978). Papers in 1979 and 1980 examined the neurons that control gill movements in nudibranchs, Pleurobranchaea and several Aplysia species, and proposed that they are homologous across these groups. Her later FHL-connected papers identified crustacean neuropeptides, among them a SIFamide peptide in the stomatogastric nervous system of the American lobster (2006) and a C-type allatostatin-like peptide that acts on both neural circuits and the heart (2009). A 2008 paper found that the pyloric circuit of the herbivorous crab Pugettia producta responds only weakly to several neuromodulators that act strongly in more opportunistic feeders.

name: Paul K. Dayton
text:
Paul K. Dayton is a benthic marine ecologist and emeritus member of the Integrative Oceanography Division at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego, where he spent a 35-year career. He earned a BS at the University of Arizona in 1963 and a PhD in zoology at the University of Washington (1970, per Wikidata) under Robert T. Paine. His FHL connection rests on subtidal work in the San Juan Islands from his Washington years: a 1982 paper with Charles Birkeland and Norman Engstrom gives FHL as the authors' address, thanks Robert Fernald for facilities there and credits a National Science Foundation grant to the UW Department of Zoology. He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists, but Wikidata lists Terrie Klinger, who is, as his doctoral student. His honors include the Ecological Society of America's Mercer (1974) and Cooper (2000) awards and the first Ramon Margalef Prize in Ecology.

Dayton's research covers benthic ecology, natural history and marine conservation, including coastal Antarctic habitats, Washington's rocky shores, and the effects of overfishing and El Niño on coastal ecosystems; a 1971 paper treated competition and disturbance in a rocky intertidal community. The 1982 FHL paper describes a subtidal food web in the San Juan Islands, where the small sea cucumber Cucumaria lubrica lives at about 4,400 per square meter. Seven sea star species eat it, yet together they take only about 3% of the population each year. The authors argued that the top predator, Solaster dawsoni, probably keeps the sea cucumber's most abundant predator, Solaster stimpsoni, from building up, while refuges in size and behavior let S. stimpsoni persist. None of the three trophic levels changed significantly from 1965 to 1976. His other census paper (1999) is a multi-author case for networks of no-take marine reserves.

name: Paul Nival
text:
Paul Nival is a biological oceanographer and plankton ecologist. France's national library lists Nival as emeritus professor of biological oceanography at Université Pierre et Marie Curie (2016) and at the Laboratoire d'océanographie de Villefranche of Sorbonne Université (2021). Nival's tie to the FHL network is through Sophie B. George, whose 1990 Paris 6 doctoral thesis Nival directed. It tested reproductive responses to reduced food in two sea urchins, Arbacia lixula and Paracentrotus lividus, and the sea star Luidia clathrata, with consequences for larval development. The French thesis catalog lists Nival as director of 47 doctoral theses from 1986 to 2008, among them those of Hervé Claustre (1987), Frédéric Partensky (1989), François Carlotti (1990) and Sami Souissi (1998).

Nival's own work centered on plankton of the Ligurian Sea and the Bay of Villefranche. With S. Nival, Nival described a device for sorting live planktonic copepods (1971) and measured particle retention in the copepod Acartia clausi and its effects on grazing (1976), and with S. Nival and I. Palazzoli reported the respiration of common plankton organisms at Villefranche-sur-Mer (1972). Modeling followed: plankton in the Bay of Villefranche (1976), salp population dynamics in Ligurian coastal waters (1986), and a pelagic ecosystem model of biogenic particle production and sedimentation that weighed the roles of salps and copepods (1988). Later coauthored papers linked long-term changes in northwestern Mediterranean zooplankton and copepod phenology to climate (2005, 2008).

text: Paula Bucko earned a PhD in pharmacology at the University of Washington in 2020, with John D. Scott as thesis advisor; Linda G. Wordeman's CV lists Bucko as a student supervised with Scott. The thesis examined mitotic kinase signaling, focusing on Aurora A and polo-like kinase 1: the scaffold protein Gravin held active kinase pools at mitotic centrosomes, and a system called LoKI directed inhibitors to chosen subcellular sites. Papers include a 2019 eLife study of subcellular drug targeting and a 2020 Journal of Biological Chemistry study of gravin-associated kinase networks, both with Wordeman and Scott, and a 2021 Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology article on AKAP targeting.

text: Paula Pappalardo was a postdoctoral research associate in James E. name: Pedro Verdugo
text:
Pedro Verdugo is a biophysicist and professor emeritus of bioengineering at the University of Washington. He studied chemistry and medicine at the University of Chile, trained in pediatric cardiology in Santiago, and came to the University of Washington as an NIH Fogarty International senior postdoctoral fellow (1969-1973). He joined UW Bioengineering in 1974, chaired its graduate curriculum committee and, from 1982, as assistant director, led the development of a pilot undergraduate program. He later moved his research to Friday Harbor Laboratories, where he launched a research program in 2001 with a National Science Foundation grant; over the following 17 years more than 80 undergraduates worked in his laboratory. His honors include a fellowship of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge (1988) and a UW award for contributions to undergraduate education (2004). The census counts 26 FHL-address papers from 2003 to 2022.

Verdugo's research applies polymer physics to biological gels. His group found that secreted mucus is stored in vesicles as a condensed polymer network that undergoes a gel phase transition on release, a model since used to study airway disease, and that intracellular calcium is released in periodic pulses; FHL-connected papers on mast-cell granules, airway ciliated cells and mucus continue this line (2003-2012). In 1998, with graduate student Wei-Chun Chin and postdoctoral fellow Monica Orellana, he reported in Nature that dissolved organic matter in seawater can assemble spontaneously into polymer gels, and proposed a role for these microgels in ocean carbon cycling. His FHL papers develop this idea: regulated secretion in the phytoplankter Phaeocystis globosa, effects of ultraviolet light and lower pH on gel formation, bacterial exopolymers that promote assembly, and reviews of marine microgels (2011, 2021). Iván Quesada is also among his students in the mentoring network.

name: Peter A. Getting
text: Peter A. Getting (died 2006) joined A. O. Dennis Willows's lab as a postdoc in the early 1970s and published Burst formation in electrically coupled neurons with Willows in Brain Research (1973), carrying a Friday Harbor Laboratories affiliation. With colleagues, Getting identified the neurons of the central pattern generator for the Tritonia escape swim, concluded that its rhythm emerges from synaptic interactions as a network oscillator, and tested those neurons in realistic network simulations. Positions included Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station and the University of Iowa's Department of Physiology and Biophysics. His former postdoc William N. Frost continued this work, including a 1994 Nature paper with Paul S. Katz and Getting.

name: Peter A. Jumars
text:
Peter A. Jumars is a marine benthic ecologist. He received a BA in biological sciences from the University of Delaware in 1969 and a PhD from Scripps Institution of Oceanography in 1974. Publication records link his papers to the University of Washington mainly from the mid-1970s to the late 1990s and to the University of Maine from the late 1990s; papers from 2001 and 2003 give his address as Maine's Darling Marine Center. He is now professor emeritus in Maine's School of Marine Sciences; his teaching of biological fluid dynamics at the Darling Marine Center was the basis of his 2019 book on viscous flow environments. He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists. The census lists 22 FHL-connected papers by him from 1986 to 2003; most appear in FHL's research bibliography, and a few mention FHL in the text or give the FHL address of his co-author Robert Self.

Jumars has studied how animals that live in sediments obtain food, and how water flow and sediment transport shape that supply. His 1979 review with Fauchald of polychaete feeding guilds was updated in 2015. With Deborah Penry, linked to him as a doctoral student in the report's network, he modeled animal guts as chemical reactors (1986, 1987) and related gut architecture to diet in polychaetes (1990). Other FHL-connected papers measured bacterial growth and chemical conditions inside deposit-feeder guts (1989, 1992), the availability of sedimentary amino acids and contaminants to digestion (1995 to 1997), and particle selection by deposit feeders (1988). Flume studies with Arthur Nowell examined suspended sediment, the erosion and deposition of grains, and flow in eelgrass beds (1988 to 1990). Later papers used acoustics, including field manipulations in West Sound, Orcas Island (2001), and a record of mysids rising nightly from the seabed (2003).

Corn's 2022 PhD in population biology. name: Peter D. Ward
text:
Peter D. Ward is a paleontologist at the University of Washington in Seattle; his ORCID record lists him as a professor in Biology and Earth and Space Sciences since 1985. He received his PhD from McMaster University in 1976. He has also held teaching posts and other connections with Ohio State University, the University of California, Caltech and the NASA Astrobiology Institute, and is associated with the Sprigg Institute of Geobiology at the University of Adelaide. He was elected a fellow of the California Academy of Sciences in 1984, and his book On Methuselah's Trail (1992) received the Paleontological Society's Golden Trilobite Award. He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists. The census lists four FHL-connected papers by him from 2012 to 2016, and the 2016 paper gives his address as FHL and the university's Biology Department.

Ward's research centers on mass extinctions, especially the Cretaceous-Paleogene and Permian-Triassic events. He wrote In Search of Nautilus (1988) about the living cephalopod and published on Late Permian land vertebrates of South Africa's Karoo Basin (2005). He co-wrote Rare Earth (2000) with Donald Brownlee and proposed the Medea hypothesis, that multicellular life may be self-destructive. His FHL-connected papers are experimental and genetic. A 2012 study led by Loren Ballanti, which thanks FHL staff, compared oxygen consumption in the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa and two bivalves for clues to survival through mass extinctions. Papers led by Frederick Dooley in 2012 and 2015 tested how seedlings of the seagrasses Zostera marina and Phyllospadix scouleri tolerate hydrogen sulfide, and the census records Dooley's 2015 University of Washington doctoral thesis on seagrasses and hydrogen sulfide, with Ward as advisor. A 2016 paper revisited the phylogeography of Nautilus pompilius.

name: Peter Edmunds
text: Peter Edmunds was a postdoctoral researcher in Kenneth P. Sebens's lab in 1989 and 1990 and is listed there with a PhD from Glasgow University. From Glasgow, Edmunds published energy budgets for the coral Porites porites with P. S. Davies (1986, Marine Biology; 1989, Coral Reefs). A 1991 paper with J. D. Witman examined Hurricane Hugo's effect on a reef at St. John in the US Virgin Islands. Later work at California State University, Northridge, covers coral reef ecology and ecophysiology: long-term coral monitoring at St. John, elevated pCO2 and massive Porites in Moorea (2012), and hurricane effects on Caribbean reefs (2019, Ecology).

name: Peter Gullickson
text: Peter Gullickson was an undergraduate in Michael T. Nishizaki's lab at Carleton College. With Nishizaki and other students, Gullickson worked on the reproductive ecology of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus and the sea urchin Mesocentrotus franciscanus, animals collected near FHL in the summers of 2020 and 2021 and held at the station. The 2022 PLOS ONE paper measured thermal performance curves for sperm swimming and fertilization and tested temperature and pH together in the sand dollar; a companion dataset is in Dryad. From 2021 to 2023 Gullickson held a research support position in Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics at the University of Minnesota.

text: Peter Nilsson was a student of Bruno Pernet at California State University, Long Beach, earning an MS (2019-2022) while raising echinoid larvae of Dendraster excentricus and Lytechinus pictus at three culture densities on two food rations. Nilsson and Pernet (2022, Marine Ecology Progress Series) reported food-conditioned morphological plasticity at ecologically relevant densities. Brown the research of Luiza Saad and colleagues on eye reduction in cave planarians, published in 2025. He studies regeneration in planarian flatworms and neoblasts, the adult stem cells that produce their tissues.

name: Peter Walker
text: Peter Walker, a professor of geography and environmental studies at the University of Oregon, co-supervised Rhodalyn Tetteh's PhD with Aaron Galloway; Tetteh approached marine trophic ecology from a political ecology perspective. Walker's research areas include political ecology, environmental politics and climate change adaptation. Peter A. Walker, of the university's Department of Geography, wrote on political ecology in Progress in Human Geography in 2005 and 2007.

name: Peter X. Wu
text: Peter X. Wu appears as an undergraduate in a December 2010 photo caption from Billie J. Swalla's lab at the University of Washington. With Daniel W. Seufert and Swalla, Wu studied how molgulid ascidians repeatedly lost the tadpole tail, describing an unusual arrangement of the SSNA1, Manx and Bobcat genes in these sea squirts and comparing it with Oikopleura dioica. The work came from a summer 2011 BEACON Research Fellowship, used FHL facilities and was reported in September 2011 among FHL student research papers. A June 2011 version with the same title won a UW Library Research Award for Undergraduates in the senior non-thesis division.

name: Petra Ditsche
text:
Petra Ditsche is a biologist trained in Germany who studies how aquatic animals attach to surfaces and cope with water flow. She earned undergraduate degrees in biology and hydrobiology at the University of Düsseldorf and the Technical University of Dresden and a PhD at the University of Bonn on how surface roughness affects attachment in running-water insects. Postdoctoral work followed at Bonn with Wilhelm Barthlott on air-retaining superhydrophobic surfaces and at the University of Kiel with Stanislav Gorb on underwater attachment and biomimetics. She came to Friday Harbor Laboratories in 2012 on a German Academic Exchange Service postdoctoral scholarship and returned a year later to work with Adam Summers on an NSF project on sticky intertidal fishes. Some 2017 papers also list the University of Alaska Anchorage. By 2019 she was based in Germany, where she founded ClingTech Bionics to develop a bionic suction cup.

Ditsche's research asks how organisms hold on in wet, moving environments and how engineers can borrow their solutions. At FHL she worked mainly on the northern clingfish, Gobiesox maeandricus, whose suction disc attaches to rough and fouled surfaces. Papers measured its attachment on fouled and rough substrates (2014) and described its intertidal habitat (2017). A 2019 paper with Summers used the disc as a model for artificial suction cups, the best of which outperformed the fish in pull-off tests on every surface. Related papers examined how biofilm affects attachment of mayfly larvae (2013), compared attachment in water and on land (2014) and tested harbor seal skin and blubber for direction-dependent properties (2017). A 2023 paper showed that the widened legs of stream mayfly larvae work like hydrofoils that hold them on the bottom. She also co-authored 2014 FHL student reports on attachment in chitons, anemones, sculpins and clingfish.

name: Philip F. Copenhaver
text: Philip F. Copenhaver earned his Ph.D. with James W. Truman in the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington in 1985, working on the neuroendocrine system of the moth Manduca sexta; papers from 1986 identified the cerebral neurosecretory cells that contain eclosion hormone and followed that system through metamorphosis. Postdoctoral work followed with Paul Taghert at Washington University in St. Louis and William Moody at the University of Washington. He joined Oregon Health & Science University in 1990 and became professor in 2011. Research from his lab has addressed neuronal migration in the Manduca enteric nervous system and the normal role of the Amyloid Precursor Protein.

text: Philip J. Motta, a professor emeritus of integrative biology at the University of South Florida, advised Mason N. Dean's 2003 master's degree in zoology there. Motta studied feeding in sharks and rays. The two published on the feeding behavior and kinematics of the lesser electric ray in 2004, and Motta was first author of a 2010 study of filter feeding by whale sharks off the Yucatan Peninsula.

name: Philip Maini
text: Philip Maini, a mathematician and professor of mathematical biology at the University of Oxford, supervised Dan Nicolau's DPhil in mathematics there. He has directed Oxford's Wolfson Centre for Mathematical Biology since 1998 and builds mathematical models of tumors, wound healing and embryonic pattern formation. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2015.

name: Philip S. Lobel
text: Philip S. Lobel, who publishes as Phillip S. Lobel, is listed by Kenneth P. Sebens among former graduate students at Harvard University (Ph.D., 1977-79), with the subject coral reef fish ecology. Papers from that period include one with John C. Ogden on herbivorous fishes and urchins in coral reef communities (1978) and one on alimentary pH and digestion in herbivorous reef fishes (1981). Lobel became professor of biology at Boston University. The main field site from 1983 to 2003 was Johnston Atoll, under a US Army marine monitoring program; work in Belize from 2003 centered on fish bioacoustics and new species.

name: Phillip Davidson
text: Phillip Davidson was a PhD student of Gregory A. Wray in biology at Duke University (2016-2021), after a BS at the University of Miami. In the Wray lab, Davidson compared sea urchins with different life histories: egg provisioning (2019), a chromosome-level genome of Lytechinus variegatus (2020), and changes in chromatin and developmental gene networks during rapid life history evolution in Heliocidaris (2022). Davidson then went to Indiana University as a postdoctoral researcher, holding an NSF Postdoctoral Research Fellowship in Biology (2022-2024), and published with Armin P. Moczek on cis-regulatory evolution in horned dung beetles (2024).

name: Phoebe D. Dawkins
text: Phoebe D. Dawkins was a graduate student of C. Drew Harvell at Cornell University, completing an MS in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology in 2019 with Harvell as chair and Charles H. Greene on the committee. The thesis used dosage-controlled inoculations to study eelgrass wasting disease in Zostera marina, following lesion onset, host genotype and phenol response, and testing pathogen isolate, dose, temperature and light (paper, 2018). Dawkins also coauthored papers on warming and summer eelgrass epidemics (2021) and on manipulating the seagrass microbiome (2024), and was first author of a 2024 protocol from the University of California, Irvine, on collecting and culturing giant kelp for restoration.

name: Rachel A. Merz
text:
Rachel A. Merz is an invertebrate biomechanist and the Walter Kemp Professor Emerita of Natural Science at Swarthmore College. Publication records associate her early papers with the University of Chicago and Northeastern University in the 1980s and her later work with Swarthmore from 1991. She is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists, but her FHL-connected work runs from 1984 to 2023. Her 1984 paper on the feeding currents of a sabellid worm thanks FHL's director and staff, and a 2023 paper lists her at FHL. From 2011 to 2014 she co-wrote project reports with undergraduates in FHL's Blinks/BEACON/NSF REU summer internship program; the census includes these reports. One of those interns, Rachel Crane, became her co-author on a 2017 paper funded through FHL's REU program.

Merz's laboratory borrows theory and techniques from engineering to address ecological and evolutionary questions about invertebrates. Much of her work concerns the chaetae (bristles) of polychaete worms. With Sarah Woodin she tested whether hooked chaetae anchor tube-dwelling worms (1987, 2000) and reviewed the mechanical functions of chaetae (2003). With Deirdre Edwards she examined the role of jointed chaetae in locomotion and gait changes (1998). She has also studied how flow shapes feeding posture and predator avoidance in black fly larvae, and the strength of empty snail shells used by hermit crabs (1992). Later FHL-connected papers showed that overturned sand dollars orient in flow to help them right themselves (2013) and examined how tube textures give polychaetes traction (2015). Others related sediment mechanics to lugworm burrowing and distribution (2017), work that began as a 2012 intern project in False Bay, and to eelgrass seed burial (2023).

name: Rachel Assink
text: Rachel Assink was an MS student of Terrie Klinger in Marine Affairs at the University of Washington, finishing in 2019. The thesis examined humpback whale entanglements in commercial fishing gear on the US West Coast, comparing mortality and serious injury across Distinct Population Segments and estimating the reductions needed if stock boundaries under the Marine Mammal Protection Act were redrawn to match them.

name: Rachel Crane
text: Rachel L. Crane was an undergraduate research mentee of Rachel A. Merz of Swarthmore College and worked at False Bay in the 2012 Blinks/BEACON/NSF REU program at FHL. They measured sediment stiffness and grain size and timed burrowing by the lugworms Abarenicola pacifica and A. claparedi vagabunda, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology (2017). After a BA at Swarthmore (2013), Crane managed the Patek Lab at Duke University (2013-2015) and earned a PhD at Hopkins Marine Station of Stanford University (2021), publishing with Mark W. Denny on fatigue damage and repair in bivalve shells (2021, 2022). A postdoctoral fellowship at the University of California, Davis began in 2021.

text: Rachel Fawcett was a student in the Nearshore Ecology Research Experience at Friday Harbor Laboratories in spring 2014, with David O. Duggins assisting on data analysis. With Megan N. Dethier and Alex Lowe, Fawcett compared fresh Nereocystis luetkeana and Saccharina latissima with feces of urchins fed those algae as food for the copepod Tigriopus californicus. The copepods preferred feces, suggesting urchins may carry nutrient-rich detritus to deeper habitats.

name: Rachel Fleming
text: Rachel Fleming is listed as a doctoral student of Elizabeth L. Brainerd in the Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology at Brown University, in Brainerd's curriculum vitae of December 2024 and on the lab's website. A 2026 paper by Fleming with C. Other papers from the same department concern hearing in a Permian stem reptile (2025) and muscle marker placement (2026).

name: Rachel Kadzik
text: Rachel Kadzik is listed as a staff researcher in Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago, working on actin network assembly and disassembly in C. elegans. Kadzik's PhD is from the University of Pennsylvania; a 2014 PNAS paper from there with E. E. Morrisey examined Wnt/Frizzled 2 signaling in the shape and branching of lung tubes. Later papers with S. Petry at Princeton University concerned microtubule nucleation (2018), and those with D. R. Kovar at Chicago concerned actin (2020, 2024). Preprints with Munro (2025, 2026) address cortical flow and rapid actin filament turnover in C. elegans zygotes.

name: Rachel Menegaz
text: Rachel Menegaz was a postdoctoral teaching and research associate with Elizabeth L. Brainerd at Brown University (2013-2015), after a PhD in the University of Missouri's Pathobiology Area Program (2013). At Brown, Menegaz used XROMM, which combines CT-based morphology with biplanar videofluoroscopy, to quantify tooth occlusion and temporomandibular joint movement in feeding juvenile miniature pigs (2015). After a visiting post at Indiana University School of Dentistry (2015-2017), Menegaz joined the University of North Texas Health Science Center in 2017 and became associate professor in 2023. Later papers address craniofacial growth in mice with osteogenesis imperfecta and skeletal changes after lower-limb amputation.

name: Rachel Pepper
text: Rachel E. Pepper was a postdoctoral researcher with M. A. R. Koehl at the University of California, Berkeley, a Miller Fellow also working with Evan Variano and examining how marine larvae interact with turbulence. Her Harvard physics PhD was done in Howard Stone's group. With Koehl she coauthored papers on flows that supply fresh fluid to choanoflagellate colonies (2013) and the velocity gradients zooplankton encounter near benthic communities (2015). She also held a postdoctoral fellowship in physics education research at the University of Colorado. She became Professor of Physics at the University of Puget Sound, working on flow around sessile microscopic organisms and seed dispersal from splash-cup plants.

name: Rachel Sanford
text: Rachel S. Sanford was a University of Washington undergraduate in the Marine Genomics Research Apprenticeship at Friday Harbor Laboratories in spring 2012, working under Billie Swalla and Leonid Moroz. Sanford's student paper, with Swalla, Moroz and Andrea Kohn, searched the ctenophore Pleurobrachia bachei for LIM homeobox genes, finding four subfamilies and cloning two from an embryonic cDNA library. Sanford coauthored the 2014 Nature paper on the ctenophore genome. name: Ralf Sommer
text:
Ralf J. Sommer is an evolutionary developmental biologist who has directed the Department of Integrative Evolutionary Biology at the Max Planck Institute in Tübingen since 1999 and has been an adjunct professor at the University of Tübingen since 2002. His tie to scientists at FHL runs through Federico D. Brown, who studied zoology at the University of Washington from 2002 to 2008 and worked on ascidians. The Sommer lab's alumni page lists Brown (as Frederico) among former postdoctoral fellows, with the working field nematode mutation behavior. Their 2011 paper in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, with Isabella D'Anna, disrupted nictation by forward genetics in Pristionchus pacificus and related the behavior to attachment to a laboratory insect host.

Sommer earned a diploma at Tübingen (1989) and a PhD at Ludwig-Maximilians University Munich (1992) in Diethard Tautz's lab, on the evolution of segmentation genes in insects. He was an EMBO research fellow in Paul W. Sternberg's lab at the California Institute of Technology from 1993 to 1995, then a young investigator at the Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology from 1995 to 1999. He and colleagues described P. pacificus in 1996, and he developed it as a model for studying evolutionary change, combining forward genetics, CRISPR engineering and genomics with field work, including on La Réunion. Developmental plasticity is a central theme. His honors include the FALCON Prize (1996), EMBO membership (2015) and fellowship of the Society of Nematologists (2026).

name: Rebecca Guenther
text:
Rebecca Guenther studied the ecophysiology of calcified coralline algae under environmental stress and climate change. The alumni list of Patrick Martone's lab in Botany at the University of British Columbia gives Guenther an MSc in 2012 and a PhD in 2016. In summer 2011 Guenther took the Ocean Acidification class at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL), with financial support from Emily Carrington, and co-wrote student reports with Roberta Challener, Rosaleen Gilmore, Laura Newcomb and Karen Rickards on carbonate chemistry in two tide pools on San Juan Island. Carrington served as an external member of Guenther's PhD committee, and FHL appears as a second affiliation on Guenther's 2018 and 2022 papers.

A 2014 paper with Martone (Journal of Phycology) measured the physiological performance of intertidal corallines during a simulated tidal cycle. The 2016 thesis addressed temperature, pH, growth and biomechanics in coralline algae. Two papers with Carrington and Martone followed. Using algae collected at Deadman Bay on San Juan Island, with spores released and settled in FHL's Ocean Acidification Environmental Laboratory, the team used a shear flume to show that lower pH delayed spore attachment by 40 to 52 percent in Corallina vancouveriensis and in the uncalcified Polyostea robusta, and weakened attachment in Corallina (2018). A later study (2022, Marine Ecology Progress Series) found that warming and lower pH cut growth by 30 to 89 percent in C. vancouveriensis and Calliarthron tuberculosum, with little change in calcium carbonate content or joint biomechanics.

name: Rebecca L. Maher
text:
Rebecca L. Maher is a microbiologist who studies microbial communities associated with hosts and habitats, including the eelgrass microbiome and its role in disease. Her ORCID record lists her as a graduate fellow in microbiology at Oregon State University from 2016 and as a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Oregon's Institute of Ecology and Evolution. She then held FHL's William Calvin Postdoctoral Fellowship, which is credited in her 2025 and 2026 eelgrass papers. FHL is also her address on 2024 training materials and presentations for the National Microbiome Data Collaborative's ambassador program, and on her other papers from 2025 and 2026. The census lists eleven FHL-connected items by her from 2024 to 2026, including datasets and preprints.

At FHL she studied eelgrass (Zostera marina) and wasting disease, which is caused by Labyrinthula zosterae. Her 2025 paper with C. Drew Harvell and others infected eelgrass in the laboratory with two local pathogen strains at ambient and raised temperatures. It also sampled blades at Fourth of July Beach on San Juan Island around unusually hot low tides in May 2024. Heat increased disease severity and lowered microbiome diversity in the laboratory, and in the field the heat event damaged blades, slowed growth and reduced microbiome diversity. A 2025 Biology Letters paper links wasting disease to community interactions, and a 2026 paper examines the distribution of L. zosterae and the emergence of a new seagrass pathogen. Her other recent work covers the genomics of predatory Pseudobdellovibrionaceae bacteria (2025 preprint), microeukaryotes in the coral Acropora hyacinthus during an extreme bleaching event (2025), and microbial patchiness in stream beds at a subcontinental scale (2025–2026).

name: Reginald McGee
text: Reginald L. McGee II was a postdoctoral fellow with Adriana T. Dawes from 2016 to 2018, at the Mathematical Biosciences Institute of the Ohio State University. Earlier work from Purdue University's Department of Mathematics modeled Syk activity in B cell receptor signaling (2015), and a 2018 paper with Gregery Buzzard treated the choice of maximally informative next experiments for nonlinear models. With Natalia Kravtsova and Dawes, McGee published an optimal transport distance for comparing biological time series (2023). An associate professor of mathematics and statistics at Haverford College as of 2026, McGee has analyzed single-cell data in acute myeloid leukemia and patient structure in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

name: Reyn Yoshioka
text:
Reyn Yoshioka is a marine disease and trophic ecologist, a research scientist at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences as of 2026. Yoshioka took a BS at Cornell in 2014 and worked in Drew Harvell's lab as a research aide from fall 2014 through summer 2016, on coral growth anomalies at Puako, Hawaii (2016), and on sea star wasting disease, including ochre star mortality during the 2014 epizootic (Eisenlord et al. 2016). Three of the sea star papers are among publications connected to Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL). Yoshioka's dissertation names Harvell as a mentor through graduate school and calls FHL home to one of its chapters.

Yoshioka earned a PhD at the University of Oregon in 2021, based at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology with Aaron Galloway as advisor. The dissertation asked how parasites alter food webs by changing their hosts rather than killing them. Two chapters showed that the eelgrass pathogen Labyrinthula zosterae synthesizes the fatty acid DHA (2019) and that diseased eelgrass produced more of the copepod Tisbe than healthy eelgrass did. Another examined the rhizocephalan Sylon hippolytes in the shrimp Pandalus danae, collected from the FHL docks in 2020 and published in 2023. FHL awarded Yoshioka fellowships in 2018, 2019 and 2020. Yoshioka also taught at the University of Oregon's Honors College. Work at Bigelow has included black eye syndrome in Bering Sea snow crab (2026) and eelgrass wasting disease (2025).

name: Richard A. Cloney
text:
Richard A. Cloney, of the Department of Zoology at the University of Washington, used electron microscopy to study the fine structure of marine invertebrate cells, tissues and larvae. His papers run from 1961 to 1996, and the census lists ten of them, from 1973 to 1996. Those with an FHL address include a 1973 study of ascidian metamorphosis and five papers from 1981 to 1983, and a 1983 paper gives both the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as addresses. Stephen A. Stricker, on nemertean worms (1981 to 1985), appears as his student in the report's mentoring network; Christopher G. Reed was a co-author on brachiopod tentacles (1977) and bryozoan larvae (1982). Other frequent co-authors included Michael J. Cavey, on ascidian muscle and the larval tunic.

Cloney's main subject was the metamorphosis of ascidian (sea squirt) tadpole larvae. Papers from 1961 into the early 1970s examined tail resorption and the role of cytoplasmic filaments in the epidermis and notochord, and a 1973 study tested the effect of cytochalasin B on tail resorption and metamorphosis in ten ascidian species. Later papers covered larval adhesive papillae, sensory neurons, sperm and the larval tunic, the effect of tunichrome on tunic and fin formation in Ascidia callosa embryos (1986), and the role of test cells in keeping larvae from becoming hydrophobic (1996). He also studied cephalopod chromatophores and reflector cells, polychaete setae and chiton sensory hairs. His FHL-address papers from 1981 to 1983 describe the nemertean Paranemertes peregrina, its stylet apparatus and role in prey capture (1981), stylet formation (1982) and venom-producing cells (1983), and the larval structure, settlement and metamorphosis of the bryozoan Bowerbankia gracilis (1982).

name: Richard A. Satterlie
text:
Richard A. Satterlie is an invertebrate neurobiologist who studies the neural and muscular control of swimming in marine animals. His papers from 1993 to 1997 give his address as the Department of Zoology at Arizona State University, and those from 2000 to 2004 as the university's Department of Biology; from 2005 they give the Department of Biology and Marine Biology and the Center for Marine Science at the University of North Carolina Wilmington. His FHL connection came through summer fieldwork on the pteropod mollusk Clione limacina: an ASU outreach article notes that he went to Washington State every summer to collect the animals, and papers with Tigran P. Norekian in 1993 and 1994 carry a Friday Harbor Laboratories address. The census credits him with 17 FHL-connected papers between 1985 and 2010, and the report's mentoring network links him to Norekian and Thomas J. Pirtle, frequent co-authors on the Clione work.

Satterlie's work asks how simple nervous systems generate and adjust rhythmic locomotion. In Clione, which swims by beating a pair of wings, he described swimming behavior and wing musculature (1985, 1989-1991), showed that reciprocal inhibition and postinhibitory rebound produce reverberation in the swim pattern generator (Science, 1985), and found two types of striated muscle that suggest two-geared swimming (1990). Later papers analyzed fast-strike prey capture, in which buccal cones are inflated hydraulically by co-activated antagonistic motoneurons (1992-1995), serotonergic and nitric oxide modulation of swim speed (1996-2001, 2020), startle and escape swimming (1997), and a hyperpolarization-activated current that alters swim frequency (2010). A second line of work examines how jellyfish nerve nets and pacemakers control swimming, from the hydromedusa Aequorea (1985, 2008) to box jellyfish (2001) and scyphomedusae (2014-2015).

name: Richard Aronson
text: Richard B. Aronson was a Harvard graduate student of Kenneth P. Sebens (1979-85), working on the ecology and behavior of octopus and ophiuroids, and took a PhD in 1985 after an AB at Dartmouth. Aronson later held posts at Dauphin Island Sea Lab (1999-2008) and the University of South Alabama, then headed the Department of Ocean Engineering and Marine Sciences at Florida Institute of Technology. Later work addressed eastern Pacific coral-reef collapse (2012) and shell-crushing crabs returning to Antarctica (2015).

name: Richard B. Emlet
text:
Richard B. Emlet is a marine invertebrate biologist and professor emeritus of biology at the University of Oregon, based at the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (OIMB) in Charleston, Oregon. He received a BS in zoology from Duke University in 1977 and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington in 1985. His FHL-connected papers from 1982 to 1986 give the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address and include a 1985 Science paper with Richard Strathmann. He later joined the University of Oregon faculty at OIMB, where his research group studied marine invertebrate larvae and how larval history affects juveniles. From 2022 to 2025 he was a research associate of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute. FHL is also named in the text of several of his later papers, up to 2025.

Emlet studies the functional morphology, biomechanics, ecology and evolution of marine invertebrates, especially echinoderm larvae. His methods include video micrography, motion analysis, dynamically scaled mechanical models, and laboratory and field experiments. His early FHL-connected papers examined the mechanics of calcite in sea urchin larval spicules (1982) and showed that crystal axes in living and fossil adult sea urchins indicate whether their larvae fed (1985). Others analyzed how gravity and drag shape the feeding currents of small zooplankton (1985) and followed larvae of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus in a fjord, including their vertical migrations (1986). Later papers in the census cover swimming in nonfeeding echinoderm larvae (1994), offspring size in a marine snail (2001, with Amy Moran), barnacle survival after settlement along an estuarine gradient (2006) and chiton eggs and larvae (2015). With Nicole Nakata he described brittle star larvae of the northeast Pacific (2023, 2025).

name: Richard E. Norris
text:
Richard Earl Norris (1926–2013) was a phycologist who studied marine algae, especially small flagellates, in the Pacific Northwest and South Africa. The Harvard University Herbaria's Index of Botanists associates him with the University of Washington, the University of Natal and the University of Hawaii. It records him as a collector of algae mainly in the Puget Sound area from 1948 to 1955 and in Minnesota from 1956, with specimens in herbaria including FHL's. His census papers with an FHL address date from 1977 to 1984. The 1977 to 1979 papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, and the 1978 paper also lists the Department of Botany of the University of Natal in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa. A biography with a photograph appeared in Phycologia in 2001.

Norris's FHL-connected papers use electron microscopy to work out the structure, life histories and classification of small marine algae. A 1977 paper described flagellate cells in the life history of the chrysophyte Stichogloea. With Richard N. Pienaar of the University of Natal he compared the fine structure of five marine species of the green flagellate Pyramimonas (1978) and described scale production in the flagellate Chrysochromulina spinifera (1979). An earlier study with Barbara R. Pearson (1975) followed cell division in Pyramimonas parkeae, a species named by the two of them. With Terumitsu Hori and Mitsuo Chihara he revised the prasinophyte genus Tetraselmis (1980). With David J. Hibberd he described the cytology and ultrastructure of the amoeboid alga Chlorarachnion reptans and placed it in a new division and class, the Chlorarachniophyta and Chlorarachniophyceae (1984). Names he authored include Gelidiocolax lyndae.

name: Richard Lloyd Miller
text:
Richard L. Miller worked on sperm chemotaxis, the guidance of swimming sperm by substances released from eggs; his 1983 paper gives his address as the Department of Biology at Temple University in Philadelphia. His earlier papers dealt with chemotaxis during fertilization in the hydroids Campanularia (1966) and Gonothyrea (1970), and a 1975 paper in Nature reported sperm chemotaxis in the ascidian Ciona intestinalis. A 2012 review of the field in the Journal of General Physiology states that his experiments of the late 1960s and 1970s firmly established chemotaxis in animal sperm. His papers connected with Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) run from 1979 to 1994. Most give FHL as an address, and the 1983 paper, written with Kenneth King of the University of Washington's Department of Oceanography and FHL, thanks the FHL staff for their hospitality during the authors' residence.

Miller's FHL papers extend sperm chemotaxis studies across the local fauna. Two 1979 papers on hydromedusae covered the species-specificity of sperm attraction, sperm behavior and the attractants' chemical properties. Hybridization tests with the medusa Sarsia (1982) revealed at least three species within the 'Sarsia tubulosa complex' at Friday Harbor, and work with Gary Freeman showed that hydrozoan eggs can be fertilized only at the site of polar body formation. With King he showed chemotaxis in the larvacean Oikopleura dioica, collected at the FHL dock (1983). Later papers showed sperm chemotaxis in sea stars, sea cucumbers and brittle stars (1985), detected sperm attractant in the FHL seawater system in the spring and summer of 1986 (1989), and partially purified the attractant of the sunflower star Pycnopodia helianthoides (1992). He also co-authored papers on a ctenophore eating a medusa (1984, with Claudia Mills) and on a living Planctosphaera pelagica, a hemichordate (1994).

name: Richard N. Mariscal
text:
Richard N. Mariscal, a cnidarian biologist, became professor emeritus of biological science at Florida State University, with a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley (1966). A tie to Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) runs through Claudia E. Mills, later an independent research scientist at FHL, who took an MS in zoology at Florida State in 1976 with Mariscal as advisor, and who took summer classes at FHL in 1974 and 1976. Mills's 1976 description of the hydroid Podocoryne selena from the Gulf of Mexico dates from those years. Mariscal's "The control of nematocyst discharge during feeding by sea anemones," in Publications of the Seto Marine Biological Laboratory (1973), used the anemones Calliactis tricolor from the Florida Gulf Coast and Epiactis prolifera from the Friday Harbor region and acknowledged the use of facilities at FHL.

Mariscal's research concerned cnidae, the everting organelles of cnidarians that include stinging nematocysts, and the animals that live among the tentacles of sea anemones without being stung. Early papers (1969, 1970) tested how anemonefishes such as Amphiprion xanthurus avoid being stung by host anemones, a line continued with J. K. Elliott in studies of anemonefish protection (1994, 1997) and of nine coexisting species (2001). With colleagues Mariscal reported inhibited nematocyst discharge in fed Calliactis tricolor (1971, Nature) and described the ptychocyst, a category of cnida used in tube building by a cerianthid anemone (1977). Work with Glen Watson covered the ultrastructure and nematocyst development of catch tentacles in the anemone Haliplanella (1983 to 1985).

name: Richard R. Olson
text: Richard Randolph Olson was a Harvard graduate student of Kenneth P. Sebens (PhD, 1978-84), working on the larval ecology of ascidians. Papers examined larval photoadaptation and midday release in the ascidian-Prochloron symbiosis (1983), photoadaptation in the Caribbean ascidian Trididemnum solidum (1986), the consequences of short-distance larval dispersal (1985), and fish predation on larvae of Lissoclinum patella (1987, with Ross McPherson). Olson also wrote a 1989 Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics article with M. H. Olson on whether food limitation controls larval recruitment. Two 1993 papers treated larval dispersal in Caribbean reef corals, with David B. Carlon, and larval development of the pencil urchin Phyllacanthus imperialis.

name: Richard R. Strathmann
text:
Richard R. Strathmann is a marine invertebrate biologist and professor emeritus in the University of Washington Department of Biology, based at Friday Harbor Laboratories. He earned a BA in zoology and chemistry at Pomona College (1963), then an MS in oceanography (1966) and a PhD in zoology (1970) at the University of Washington, advised by K. Banse and A. J. Kohn. After postdoctoral work at UCLA and the Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology and two years as an assistant professor at the University of Maryland, he joined the UW Zoology Department in 1973 and was professor from 1982 to 2008. From 1973 to 2008 he was also Resident Associate Director of FHL, facilitating research and instruction by visitors from many institutions. He was a Guggenheim Fellow in 1980–81 and received the Western Society of Naturalists' Lifetime Achievement Award in 2012. The census lists 86 FHL-connected papers by him, 1975–2025.

His research asks why patterns of development evolved as they did, by working out the functional demands and limits on marine embryos, larvae and juveniles. He has studied how larvae capture food with cilia, trade-offs between feeding and swimming, plasticity of larval feeding structures, how long embryos and larvae spend in the plankton and the risks they face there, and limits on brooding and on benthic egg masses. His subjects include echinoderm and bryozoan larvae, gastropod veligers, and annelid, brachiopod and ascidian larvae. FHL-connected papers report a 4.5-year larval period in the snail Fusitriton oregonensis (2007), predator-induced cloning in echinoderm larvae (2008), a new brooding sea star, Henricia pumila (2010), kelp detritus as food for urchin larvae (2017) and hazards to drifting periwinkle embryos (2022). He has also written reviews on multicellularity, dispersal and the origin of feeding larvae. His PhD students include Richard Emlet, Larry McEdward and Michael Hart.

name: Robert A. Andersen
text:
Robert A. Andersen is a phycologist who works on the systematics and culture of algae. He holds a BS in botany from North Dakota State University, an MA in aquatic biology from St. Cloud State College and a PhD in botany and phycology from the University of Arkansas. He directed the Provasoli-Guillard National Center for Culture of Marine Phytoplankton (CCMP) at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences until he retired from the post in 2009, and is emeritus director of the center, now the National Center for Marine Algae and Microbiota. He edited Algal Culturing Techniques (Elsevier, 2005), sponsored by the Phycological Society of America. He is listed as a senior research scientist at the University of Washington and an adjunct professor at Michigan Technological University, and Wikispecies gives Friday Harbor Laboratories as his affiliation. The census lists 43 FHL-connected papers, 2011–2026.

His listed research interests are chrysophyte algae, algal systematics and algal culturing, and in 1987 he named the class Synurophyceae. His FHL-connected papers combine cultures, microscopy and multigene or plastid-genome data to describe new taxa and revise old ones, mostly among heterokont algae (chrysophytes, pelagophytes, xanthophytes and related classes) and haptophytes. Examples include a re-examination of the haptophyte Chrysotila from its type locality (2014–15), new pelagophytes from the Bahamas (2014) and the Great Barrier Reef (2025), a new class, Phaeosacciophyceae (2020–21), the perforated theca that defines the Pelagophyceae (2022) and a revised classification of the Cyanidiophyceae (2023). He also co-authored work on alkenone-producing haptophytes used in paleoclimate reconstruction (2015, 2019), a study placing the origin of brown algae in the Ordovician (2024), and reports of the Nomenclature Committee for Algae (2018–2023).

name: Robert Allison Graham
text: Robert Allison Graham completed a PhD in biology at the University of Oregon in 1983 under Robert C. Terwilliger, working in Eugene and Charleston from 1979. The thesis examined the structure and function of hemocyanin from the crab Cancer magister, proposing a model of how L-lactate binds an allosteric site to raise oxygen affinity and testing how different subunits contribute to oxygen binding. Papers include a 1983 study with Charlotte P. Mangum and the Terwilligers on organic acids and oxygen binding, and a 1985 model of L-lactate binding. Graham held earlier degrees from William and Mary (1969) and North Carolina (1977) and taught at North Carolina State (1975-79).
