name: Robert C. Terwilliger
text:
Robert C. Terwilliger is a comparative biochemist whose papers, from 1964 to 1988, concern the oxygen-binding proteins of marine invertebrates and fishes. His papers of 1966 to 1972 give Boston University as his address, several also the New England Aquarium. From the early 1970s through 1988 they give the University of Oregon's Department of Biology and its Oregon Institute of Marine Biology at Charleston. The census records three FHL-address papers, all from 1970 and written with Kenneth R. H. Read of Boston University, on sea cucumbers, chitons and marine snails. It also includes papers of 1987 and 1988 on chiton and bivalve respiratory proteins that are listed in the FHL bibliography. In 1988 he also wrote on teaching and research at marine stations.

Terwilliger described the structure and oxygen binding of hemoglobins, myoglobins, chlorocruorins and hemocyanins across many animal groups. His earliest papers concern fiddler crab responses to ionizing radiation (1964) and, with Frank Belamarich, neurosecretory substances and a heart-stimulating peptide in crabs (1966, 1970). His 1970 FHL papers characterized the hemoglobins of the sea cucumbers Cucumaria miniata, C. piperata and Molpadia intermedia, and the radular muscle myoglobins of chitons such as Katharina tunicata and of gastropods including a limpet, an abalone and Tegula. At Oregon he and co-authors, often Nora B. Terwilliger, studied giant extracellular hemoglobins of polychaetes and clams, hemoglobins of hydrothermal-vent animals and vestimentiferan tubeworms, changes in crab hemocyanin during development, and maternal–fetal oxygen transfer in the viviparous seaperch Embiotoca lateralis. The FHL-listed papers of 1987–1988 cover Katharina hemocyanin, bivalve hemocyanins and tissue hemoglobins in a lepidopleurid chiton.

name: Robert G. Chuinard
text:
Robert G. Chuinard appears in the census as a co-author, with Sefton R. Wellings, of three papers on skin tumors in flatfishes published in 1964 and 1965. The papers give a joint address: the Department of Pathology, University of Oregon Medical School, Portland, and Friday Harbor Laboratories. The bibliographic database behind the census links the same name to later papers on orthopedic surgery, with addresses at the University of California, Davis (1976) and Louisiana State University, including its Health Sciences Center in New Orleans (from 1977). The census's Louisiana State University destination comes from these records, but whether they are by the same person has not been confirmed.

The FHL-connected papers with Wellings concern epidermal papillomas in the flathead sole, Hippoglossoides elassodon, from waters around the San Juan Islands. A 1964 paper in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, with R. T. Gourley and R. A. Cooper, reported tumors in 281 of 4,364 flathead sole collected between July 1963 and July 1964. The growths began in first-year fish as small nodules, some of which later became papillomas, and similar neoplasms appeared occasionally in other pleuronectid flatfishes. A 1964 report in Science described virus-like particles, and granular bodies that may also be viral, in the tumor cells but not in normal epidermis. A 1965 paper with M. Bens in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences compared skin neoplasms in four pleuronectid species.

name: Robert Hendrickson
text: Robert Hendrickson was a summer 2022 participant in the NSF REU-Blinks program at Friday Harbor Laboratories, coming from the School of Biological Sciences at the University of California San Diego. Working with Chelsea Bergman, Colleen Burge, Maya Groner and C. Drew Harvell, Hendrickson tested in the laboratory whether Pacific oysters, Crassostrea gigas, can carry seagrass wasting disease to eelgrass, Zostera marina. Oysters exposed to Labyrinthula zosterae and then held in tanks with healthy eelgrass transmitted the disease at a prevalence similar to direct inoculation. The authors concluded that moving oysters from infected to uninfected waters can spread the disease and should be considered in aquaculture management.

name: Robert Paul Wolf
text: Robert Paul Wolf was listed as a PhD student of Nicole E. Phillips at Victoria University of Wellington, with a thesis dated 2020 on recruitment, settlement and ontogeny of the New Zealand intertidal serpulid tubeworm Spirobranchus cariniferus. The thesis found that abiotic factors such as sunlight and wave disturbance affected recruitment more than the presence of adults, and reported possible hermaphroditism in the species. Wolf's 2024 paper in Marine Environmental Research, from the university's Coastal Ecology Laboratory and School of Biological Sciences, asked what this species gains and loses by settling in aggregations or alone, weighing protection from physical stress and reproductive benefit against competition for food, space and oxygen.

name: Robert T. Paine
text:
Robert T. Paine (1933-2016) was a marine community ecologist on the University of Washington zoology faculty from 1962 to 1998, chairing the department from 1990 to 1998. He took an AB at Harvard (1954) and a PhD at Michigan (1961) with Frederick E. Smith as advisor and a thesis on living brachiopods, then held a postdoctoral fellowship at Scripps. His 1966 paper described a rocky shore at Mukkaw Bay where removing the sea star Pisaster ochraceus let the mussel Mytilus californianus take over, and a 1969 paper proposed the keystone species concept. He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1986 and received the International Cosmos Prize in 2013.

Paine worked near Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) for a 1969 paper with Robert Vadas. They set up subtidal plots in the San Juan Islands, caging rocks or removing the urchin Strongylocentrotus franciscanus at 7 to 8 meters' depth, and paired them with tide pool removals at Mukkaw Bay; a National Science Foundation grant to FHL helped fund it. Later papers with FHL ties include one on the crustose alga Petrocelis middendorffii with Carol Slocum and David Duggins (1979) and one on encrusting corallines with Robert Steneck (1986). Paul Dayton took his doctorate under Paine, and Megan Dethier, later in full-time residence at FHL, did her PhD work under him. Dethier, Duggins and Kenneth Sebens were among the authors of a 2016 resolution of respect for him.

name: Robin B. Kodner
text:
Robin B. Kodner is a biologist whose work spans algal evolution, microbial ecology and geobiology. Her first papers (2000–2002) give the Department of Botany at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and concern fossil fungi and early land plants. From 2004 to 2008 her papers give Harvard University's Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, where she published with Andrew Knoll and Roger Summons. Her papers of 2009 and 2010 give FHL, and those of 2009 to 2013 the University of Washington School of Oceanography, where she published with E. Virginia Armbrust. A 2011 news report gave her affiliations as FHL and the Beam Reach Marine Science and Sustainability School. Her ORCID record lists her as professor in the Department of Environmental Science at Western Washington University from 2012. It also lists a visiting researcher post at the Laboratoire d'Écologie Alpine, Université Grenoble Alpes, for 2026–2028.

Kodner studies how algae and other single-celled eukaryotes evolved and how their communities respond to the environment. With Knoll and Summons she traced sterols (2008) and the resistant biopolymer algaenan (2009) across algal lineages, to help interpret molecular fossils in ancient rocks. Her other FHL-connected work includes a 2009 PNAS paper with Phoebe Cohen and Knoll interpreting large spiny Ediacaran microfossils as resting stages of early animals, and pplacer (2010), software developed with Frederick Matsen and Armbrust that places DNA sequences on a fixed reference tree. A 2011 FHL student report she co-authored dealt with growth and domoic acid (toxin) production by the diatom Pseudo-nitzschia, and in 2011 she presented work on toxin-producing Pseudo-nitzschia blooms in East Sound, Washington. At Western Washington University she studies snow algae in the Cascade Mountains, including through the Living Snow Project, a citizen-science program, and has worked on plankton in Bellingham Bay.

name: Robin Elahi
text:
Robin Elahi is a marine ecologist and advanced lecturer at Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station as of 2026, on the teaching staff there since 2018. Elahi took a PhD in biology at the University of Washington in 2012 with Kenneth Sebens as advisor, working on subtidal rock walls in the Salish Sea. Field experiments on these walls showed that urchins, by grazing clonal ascidians, set the relationship between prey richness and space use, and that removing both urchins and chitons changed communities in non-additive ways (2012, 2013). A survey of 18 sites linked diversity to water retention (2014). A comparison with surveys from the 1970s, with Charles Birkeland, found limited change over four decades but lower urchin densities (2013).

Elahi took an MS at California State University, Northridge (2003 to 2005), with coral papers alongside Peter Edmunds, among them a 15-year decline in Montastraea annularis (2007). In 2011 Elahi was a teaching assistant in the Ocean Acidification class at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) and co-wrote reports on carbonate chemistry in the San Juan Archipelago with Kirk Sato, Lydia Kapsenberg, Jenn Phillips, Carlie Pietsch and Chelsea Vaughn. An NSF postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford and the University of British Columbia (2014 to 2016) produced an analysis of local-scale marine biodiversity trends (2015, Current Biology), then postdoctoral work at Stanford to 2018. A 2016 paper with Sebens addressed warming and coral body size. Elahi was a visiting lecturer in the Historical Marine Ecology Research Experience at FHL in 2018.

name: Robin J. Fales
text:
Robin J. Fales is a marine ecologist who studies how kelps and other intertidal organisms respond to climate change. Fales earned a B.S. at the University of California, Irvine (2016) and an M.S. in biology at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona (2019), while working as a technician for the Multi-Agency Rocky Intertidal Network (MARINe). Fales then completed a Ph.D. in the University of Washington Department of Biology (2019–2023), with Emily Carrington as committee chair, and held a position in UC Irvine's Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology in 2023–2024. Since 2024 Fales has been Assistant Professor of Marine Ecology in Environmental Studies at Soka University of America. Fales's FHL-connected papers date from 2021 to 2026. Several list FHL as an affiliation, the doctoral experiments used FHL facilities, and the dissertation thanks reading-committee member Megan Dethier for supporting the work at FHL.

Fales's dissertation asked how warming and nutrient supply affect kelp physiology across habitats, species and populations in the Salish Sea, measuring growth, bleaching, photosynthesis, respiration and nutrient uptake. It used the 2021 Western North American heatwave to study how Hedophyllum sessile survives through self-shading and protection of its meristem, and found that eight bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) populations shared a critical thermal maximum of 22 °C. A 2023 paper with Brooke Weigel, Carrington, Helen Berry and Dethier, run in FHL's Ocean Acidification Environmental Laboratory, crossed three temperatures with two nitrogen levels in bull kelp and Saccharina latissima: high temperature, not low nitrogen, was the main stressor. Other FHL-connected work covers warming and the bull kelp microbiome (2025), size-dependent mussel survival on the high and low shore at Cattle Point after the 2021 heat dome (a 2026 data set), and a 2021 analysis of microplastic research and national plastic policies.

name: Roger D. Longley
text:
Roger D. Longley is a neurobiologist who has studied the nervous systems of gastropod mollusks at Friday Harbor over several decades. A 2020 island newspaper item calls him a marine neurobiologist and a long-time researcher at FHL. In a 1984 paper in the Journal of Experimental Biology his address was the Pacific Sciences Institute in Friday Harbor, and he thanked the director of FHL for the use of its facilities. His papers from 2008 to 2014 give FHL as his address, and most are single-authored. The census matches six papers from 1997 to 2014 to his full name, and lists earlier work from 1981 to 1993 under 'R. D. Longley' that has an FHL address or appears in FHL's research bibliography.

His research asks how gastropod nervous systems are organized and how they control behavior. The earlier census items describe mating behavior in the nudibranch Aeolidia papillosa (1981, 1984, 1993), agonistic or mating behavior in Hermissenda (1982) and variation in a ganglion of the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea (1991). The 1984 paper related axon surface infolding to axon size in Tritonia and other gastropods. His later FHL papers focus on the ciliated sole of the foot. He traced the development of a serotonin-like immunoreactive nerve plexus in the foot of the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis appressa (2008), compared the neural control of pedal cilia in Lymnaea and Helisoma trivolvis (2010, 2012), and mapped immunoreactive axons in the sole of the land pulmonates Limax, Arion and Helix (2014). A 2011 paper measured neurogenesis in the procerebrum of the snail Helix aspersa. A 1997 co-authored paper on numerical least-squares methods also gives an FHL address.

name: Roger deRoos
text:
Roger McLean deRoos (1930–2015) was a comparative endocrinologist at the University of Missouri. He earned a bachelor's degree in wildlife conservation at the University of California, Berkeley, a master's degree in wildlife management at Utah State University and a doctorate in zoology at Berkeley, where he studied under the endocrinologist Howard Bern. He joined the Missouri faculty in 1961, taught undergraduate biology and graduate courses in anatomy, histology and endocrinology, and received the Purple Chalk award, given by students for teaching. After retiring in 1992 he taught biology at Skagit Valley Community College. His obituary records that he spent most summers at Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL), studying glucose regulation in the spiny dogfish with his research partner and co-author Carolyn C. deRoos; their papers with an FHL address appeared from 1967 to 1992.

The deRooses' FHL work asked how the pituitary–adrenal axis and other hormones regulate blood sugar in sharks and their relatives, using the spiny dogfish, Squalus acanthias, as the experimental animal. A 1967 paper reported corticotropin (ACTH) activity in the pituitary glands of chondrichthyan fishes. Later papers, all in General and Comparative Endocrinology, reported that mammalian ACTH (1973) and catecholamines (1978) raise plasma glucose in dogfish, described severe hypoglycemia induced by insulin (1979), and found that plasma glucose rises after partial removal of the pituitary and also after sham surgery (1980). Papers in 1985, with Carole and Harold Werner, and in 1992 measured glucose, alanine, lactate, β-hydroxybutyrate and other potential fuels and gluconeogenic substrates in the plasma of unfed dogfish after surgery, insulin infusion or ACTH treatment.

name: Ross Whippo
text:
Ross Whippo is a nearshore marine ecologist who joined NOAA's National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science as a research biologist at the Kasitsna Bay Laboratory in Alaska in 2023. His ties to Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) began as a University of Washington undergraduate (BS 2011, aquatic and fishery sciences). He assisted a rescue diving course at FHL in 2010, worked as a dive technician in the Duggins lab there in 2011, and returned in 2014 as a scientific diving assistant instructor. His early research examined how red sea urchins structure deep benthic communities in the San Juan Archipelago, published with Alexander Lowe, Aaron Galloway, Kevin Britton-Simmons and Megan Dethier (2014). He took an MSc at the University of British Columbia (2013) with Mary O'Connor on seagrass epifauna in Barkley Sound.

After a technical post with the Hakai Institute and a position as biologist with the Smithsonian's MarineGEO network (from 2015), Whippo completed a PhD at the University of Oregon's Oregon Institute of Marine Biology in 2023 with Galloway as advisor. His dissertation covered fatty acid and stable isotope profiles of 31 Antarctic macroalgae, kelp in marine reserves, and the feeding of the sunflower sea star Pycnopodia helianthoides. With Sarah Gravem, Ethan Porter-Hughes and Galloway, he showed that a waterborne Pycnopodia cue cut grazing by fed purple urchins by half, while starved urchins kept eating kelp (2024, Ecosphere). He also contributed to the 2023 study of Pycnopodia predation on urchins and kelp recovery, and co-wrote a 2021 student report on algal community change that revisited Neushul's work.

name: Rudolf A. Raff
text:
Rudolf A. Raff (1941-2019) was an evolutionary developmental biologist at Indiana University. He received a BS from Pennsylvania State University and a PhD in biochemistry from Duke University (1967). He then held postdoctoral posts at the National Naval Medical Center and, from 1969, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He joined Indiana's Department of Biology as an assistant professor in 1971 and was named James H. Rudy Professor in 2000 and Distinguished Professor in 2002. He directed the Indiana Molecular Biology Institute and retired in 2018. He founded and edited the journal Evolution & Development. His honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship (1987), the A. O. Kovalevsky Medal (2001), the Sewall Wright Award (2004) and election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2000). He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists; his five census papers, from 1991 to 2013, connect to FHL mainly through co-authors.

Raff studied how changes in development produce evolutionary change, working mainly with sea urchins. A 2017 tribute from his department credits him with arguing early that changes in form require changes in developmental processes, using DNA sequence data to show that genes and developmental pathways are conserved across distantly related animals, and showing that embryos evolve as readily as adults. His books include Embryos, Genes, and Evolution (1983, with Thomas Kaufman), The Shape of Life (1996) and Once We All Had Gills (2012). Two 1991 papers with Gregory Wray, then at FHL, described the wrinkled blastula of the sea urchin Heliocidaris erythrogramma and reviewed the evolution of developmental strategy in marine invertebrates. Later papers with Kirk Zigler, whose NSF postdoctoral fellowship (2002 to 2005) Raff co-hosted and who also held FHL fellowships, examined egg energetics and fertilization in echinoids with facultatively feeding larvae (2008) and germ-layer allocation in Clypeaster rosaceus (2013).

name: Russell C. Wyeth
text:
Russell C. Wyeth is a neuroethologist and professor in the Department of Biology at St. Francis Xavier University (StFX) in Antigonish, Nova Scotia. His earliest papers, on feeding in the glass sponge Rhabdocalyptus dawsoni (1996, 1999), began at the University of Victoria. From 1999 to 2006 his papers give the University of Washington as his address. By 2008 he was in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at Dalhousie University, and his StFX papers begin in 2010. His five FHL-address papers, from 2006 to 2008, were all co-authored with A. O. Dennis Willows. A 2006 press release described Wyeth and Willows as biologists at the University of Washington's Friday Harbor Laboratories. In 2026 he received a five-year NSERC Discovery Grant for research on chemical and flow-based navigation in aquatic gastropods.

Wyeth studies how gastropod mollusks use sensory cues, especially odors and water flow, to find their way. His FHL-connected work centered on the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea, a sea slug much used in studies of how nervous systems control behavior. With Willows he used SCUBA and time-lapse video to record its behavior in the field near Vargas Island, British Columbia, and in southern Puget Sound (2006). The slugs crawled upstream to feed and mate, and swam up into currents to escape predators. Related 2006 papers adapted underwater video to measure currents near the seabed, analyzed orientation to flow, prey, other slugs and predators, and showed that odors sensed by the rhinophores guide orientation to flow. A 2008 paper identified 1-phenoxy-2-propanol as a useful anesthetic for gastropod neurophysiology. His later work includes navigation in the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis and the use of ultraviolet-C light against marine biofouling.

name: Ryan S. Littlefield
text:
Ryan S. Littlefield is a cell biologist who studies the structure of muscle and has been an assistant professor of biology at the University of South Alabama since 2013. He received a BA in biophysics from Johns Hopkins University in 1994 and a PhD in cell biology from The Scripps Research Institute in La Jolla, California, in 2001. His papers from 2006 to 2010 give the University of Washington's Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address. He was corresponding author of a 2009 paper written there. His co-authors in this period included Velia Fowler, Richard Lieber and Ju Chen. The census does not record a teaching role or other formal position at FHL.

Littlefield's research asks how the lengths of the actin thin filaments in the sarcomeres of striated muscle are set and maintained. His FHL-connected papers center on nebulin, a protein proposed to act as a ruler for thin filament length. A 2006 study of nebulin-deficient mice found shorter thin filaments and reduced contractile function in skeletal muscle. A 2008 review with Fowler argued that dynamics at the filaments' pointed ends go beyond a simple nebulin ruler, and the 2009 Biophysical Journal paper reported that a nebulin ruler does not dictate thin filament lengths. Related papers examined nebulin's role in actin-myosin interactions (2009), tropomodulin isoforms that cap filament ends (2010) and the length-tension relationship of the external anal sphincter muscle (2008). A 2024 preprint on his record concerns actin assembly by FHOD-1 and profilin in the sarcomeres of the nematode C. elegans.

text: Sam Bashevkin was a Blinks NSF REU BEACON intern at FHL in 2012 and 2013, working with Sophie B. George during a BS at Tufts University (2014). name: Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria
text:
Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria is a seagrass biologist whose work centers on eelgrass (Zostera marina) in the northeast Pacific. A 1994 Alaska Sea Grant report on research needs for managing seagrass systems in western North America, begun while Wyllie-Echeverria was a graduate student at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, lists the author as a visiting scholar in the University of Washington School of Marine Affairs and a member of its Interdisciplinary Seagrass Working Group. Later School of Marine Affairs pages and a newspaper notice give the titles seagrass research coordinator and research scientist there. A 2022 Seacology article says Wyllie-Echeverria has worked at Friday Harbor Laboratories since the early 2000s, with students in the laboratories' Seagrass Lab. The census counts 28 FHL-address papers from 2007 to 2023.

Wyllie-Echeverria's research covers seagrass population biology, genetics, disease and restoration. FHL-connected papers compare native eelgrass with the introduced Zostera japonica, including desiccation tolerance and vertical zonation (2007), the role of climate in the distribution of Z. japonica in North America (2008) and how small-scale topography lets the two coexist (2014). Others treat the genetic structure of eelgrass beds in the San Juan Archipelago, San Francisco Bay and Alaska; seed size, long-term seed storage and seedling tolerance of hydrogen sulfide; water flow through eelgrass canopies; and eelgrass wasting disease, including its relation to host demography and whether migratory waterfowl carry seagrass pathogens (2020). A 2015 disturbance experiment modeled on traditional Indigenous harvesting of eelgrass, and the reseeding of Westcott Bay since 2020 with Seacology and the San Juan Islands Conservation District, connect the research to restoration.

name: Sanjay Shrestha
text: Sanjay Shrestha was a graduate student of Charles Bradley Shuster at New Mexico State University, taking an MS in 2008 with the thesis "Studying Human Mitotic Exit Network Using RNA Interference" and a PhD in 2011 with the dissertation "Insights into the Functions of Microtubule Bundling and Motor Proteins During Monopolar Cytokinesis." name: Sara M. Rolfe
text:
Sara M. Rolfe is an engineer who develops software for analyzing three-dimensional biological shape. She studied electrical engineering at Seattle Pacific University (BS, 2005) and electrical and computer engineering at the University of Washington (MS, 2007; PhD, 2014). She worked as a clinical research engineer at NeuroVista from 2007 to 2009. After a postdoctoral fellowship at the Center for Developmental Biology and Regenerative Medicine of Seattle Children's Research Institute (2014 to 2018), she became a research scientist there in 2021. Her ORCID record also lists a research scientist position at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 2018, and her FHL-connected papers, from 2021 and 2022, give FHL as an address. SlicerMorph, the platform whose software development she led, was funded by NSF Advances in Biological Informatics grants whose recipients included Adam Summers of FHL.

Rolfe's work applies image analysis and computer vision to morphometrics, the quantitative study of shape. She led software development for SlicerMorph (2021), an open extension of the 3D Slicer imaging platform. It lets biologists import image stacks, retrieve open-access 3D models, place landmarks, and run geometric morphometric analyses. With Arthur Porto and Murat Maga she developed ALPACA (2021), a fast computer-vision method for automatically placing landmarks on 3D specimens, and a 2022 paper extended it to multiple templates. A 2021 paper compared semi-landmarking approaches for 3D cranial morphology, and a 2022 study applied computational anatomy to craniofacial phenotypes in zebrafish. Her earlier work produced landmark-free tools for quantifying shape variation and asymmetry, including a 2019 study of facial skeletal asymmetry during fetal development. Later papers use deep learning to segment organs in mouse embryos (2023).

name: Sarah A. Woodin
text:
Sarah A. Woodin is an ecologist of marine soft-sediment communities and Carolina Distinguished Professor Emerita at the University of South Carolina. She received a BA in biology from Goucher College in 1967 and a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington in 1972. She was an assistant professor of zoology at the University of Maryland (1972 to 1975) and of earth and planetary sciences at Johns Hopkins University (1975 to 1980). At South Carolina she rose from research associate professor in 1980 to professor in 1987 and was Carolina Distinguished Professor of Biology and Marine Science from 1999 to 2013. She is an elected fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. She is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists. The census lists 15 FHL-connected papers by her from 1984 to 2012, several of which thank FHL or report experiments run there.

Woodin has studied how animals living in soft sediments interact, and how those interactions and sediment cues shape where larvae settle. A 1984 paper, which thanks FHL's then director Dennis Willows, examined how infaunal animals change their activity after browsing predators remove tissue. She continued this theme with Sara Lindsay in work on feeding-mode switching and sediment disturbance by browsed spionid polychaetes (1995, 1996). With Rachel Merz she tested whether hooked chaetae anchor worms in their tubes (1987, 2000) and reviewed chaetal mechanics (2003). Other papers reported brominated compounds in soft-bottom animals (1987) and sediment disturbance by the lugworm Abarenicola pacifica (1993). Others examined chemical and disturbance cues that inhibit or guide recruitment (1993, 1995, 1998), including experiments run at FHL in 1990. Later collaborations covered decorating by the spider crab Oregonia gracilis with Sarah Berke (2008, 2009) and intermittent bioirrigation by tellinid bivalves (2012).

name: Sarah Alexandra Hart
text: Sarah Alexandra Hart was a PhD student in biology at the University of Washington, advised by Jennifer Ruesink, with Terrie Klinger on the committee (dissertation 2014). Hart used mesocosm and field experiments on the rockweed Fucus distichus to test how the snail Littorina sitkana, epiphytes and tidal immersion affect the alga, and found that constant immersion slowed growth even without herbivores or epiphytes. Friday Harbor Laboratories provided space and equipment for part of the work.

name: Sarah Cohen
text:
C. Sarah Cohen is a marine biologist and professor of biology at San Francisco State University, where her ORCID record dates her appointment from 2003. Her papers since 2006 give the university's Romberg Tiburon Center for Environmental Studies and, from 2019, its Estuary and Ocean Science Center. ORCID lists studies in biology at Swarthmore College, a PhD in zoology from the University of Washington and a fellowship of the California Academy of Sciences. Her papers of 1988 to 1996 give the UW Department of Zoology and, from 1990, Friday Harbor Laboratories. Later addresses are Stanford University's Department of Developmental Biology and Hopkins Marine Station (1998) and Harvard University's Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology (2001-02). Her FHL-connected papers span 1988 to 2014. A 1996 study was written with Richard R. Strathmann, and the eelgrass papers of 2012 and 2014 with Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria of FHL.

Cohen uses genetic tools to study mating systems, population structure and self-recognition in marine invertebrates and plants. Her early FHL work concerned genetic differentiation in the brooding sea cucumber Leptosynapta clarki (1988, with several co-authors) and outcrossing in field populations of two self-fertile ascidians (1990). Two 1996 papers examined levels of inbreeding under contrasting modes of fertilization in the marine invertebrate genus Corella, and how environment and the structure of egg masses affect the supply of oxygen to embryos. Later papers address allorecognition and phylogeny in botryllid ascidians, a histocompatibility gene in an estuarine fish under pollution stress, the invasive tunicate Didemnum vexillum, and population genetics and wasting disease in brooding Leptasterias sea stars. The eelgrass studies measured genetic diversity among Zostera marina beds and depths in San Francisco Bay (2012) and its conservation in a mesocosm restoration experiment (2014).

name: Sarah D. Arnette
text: Sarah D. Arnette, who also published as S. D. Arnette, held Arizona State University and Friday Harbor Labs affiliations during a PhD with Stacy C. Farina of Howard University on the committee. Farina was lead mentor on a 2023 Zoology paper, with Jacob Saffarian and Lara A. Ferry, measuring pressures in the parabranchial chambers of the Pacific spiny dogfish (Squalus suckleyi) during ventilation. "True grit?" with Matthew A. Kolmann and others (Journal of Anatomy, 2023) found that gizzards evolved six times across 51 bony fishes sampled. A 2025 Integrative and Comparative Biology paper tested whether northern clingfish, Gobiesox maeandricus, actively modulate suction as flow speed rises. The Kolmann lab at the University of Louisville lists Arnette as a former postdoc and Assistant Professor (Term), working on comparative biomechanics and functional morphology of fishes.

name: Sarah Domnitz
text: Sarah B. Domnitz is listed as a graduate student on Linda G. Wordeman's page of former lab members at the University of Washington. Working in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics, Domnitz coauthored papers with Wordeman on the kinesin-13 MCAK and microtubule dynamics. A 2008 Journal of Cell Biology paper showed that a kinesin-13 mutant catalytically depolymerizes microtubules in ADP. A 2012 paper in the same journal, with Domnitz as first author, showed that MCAK tracking on polymerizing microtubule tips, through binding to end-binding proteins, limits microtubule length in the assembling bipolar spindle and promotes robust kinetochore attachment.

name: Sarah E. Gilman
text:
Sarah E. Gilman is an intertidal ecologist at the Claremont Colleges in California. ORCID lists a B.S. in Earth Systems from Stanford University, a PhD in population biology from the University of California, Davis, an associate professorship of biology at Scripps College from 2016 and a professorship of biology at Pitzer College. Her first papers, of 1995 and 1999, give Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station and the Center for Population Biology at UC Davis, and those of 2005 and 2006 the University of South Carolina. A 2017 paper acknowledges a postdoctoral fellowship from Friday Harbor Laboratories, and papers from 2006 to 2010 give FHL as her address. From 2009 her papers give the Joint Science Department of the Claremont Colleges and, from 2014, the W. M. Keck Science Department of Claremont McKenna, Pitzer and Scripps Colleges. She continued FHL-connected work with Hilary Hayford and Emily Carrington into the 2020s.

Gilman studies how temperature and other conditions on rocky shores shape the performance, distribution and interactions of intertidal animals under climate change. Her first papers documented climate-related change in a California intertidal community (1995, 1999). FHL-connected papers test the northern range limit of the limpet Collisella scabra (2006), evaluate effective shore level as a measure of wave exposure (2006) and, with many co-authors, map mosaic patterns of thermal stress on rocky shores (2006). A 2009 paper with Lauren Yamane found opposite responses of an intertidal predator to rising water and air temperatures, and a 2010 review with Mark Urban and others proposed a framework for community interactions under climate change. Work with Hayford and Carrington showed that a marine snail's foraging limits its heat exposure, aided by tidal cues (2014, 2021). Later studies concern the barnacle Balanus glandula and the effects of ocean and terrestrial warming on an intertidal crustacean (2024-2025).

name: Sarah Heerhartz
text:
Sarah M. Heerhartz is a nearshore ecologist who trained at the University of Washington, taking a PhD through the fisheries program in 2013. The university's ResearchWorks record names Charles A. Simenstad as advisor, and the CV of FHL's Megan N. Dethier lists Dethier as PhD co-supervisor. Dethier, Jason D. Toft, Jeffery R. Cordell and Andrea S. Ogston were coauthors on the journal papers on shoreline armoring. Before the dissertation was finished, Heerhartz also contributed to monitoring reports with Toft and Cordell on shoreline enhancements at the Olympic Sculpture Park (2008, 2010).

The dissertation, on how shoreline armoring disrupts marine-terrestrial connectivity, surveyed 29 paired armored and unarmored beaches in Puget Sound over three years, with observations of juvenile salmon and birds at six pairs. Armoring lowered the land-sea interface and narrowed the intertidal transition zone. Armored beaches held less wrack and fewer logs and had different invertebrate communities. Juvenile salmon distribution shifted while feeding rates stayed high, and song sparrows and other terrestrial birds foraged among wrack and logs on unarmored beaches and were largely absent from armored ones. Papers on wrack subsidies (2013) and wrack-associated invertebrates (2016) appeared in Estuaries and Coasts. A 2016 study led by Dethier on cumulative and threshold effects of armoring on Salish Sea shorelines appeared in Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science.

text: Sarah Schorno is listed as a PhD student (2013 to 2018) on the alumni page of Andreas Heyland's lab and among alumni of Douglas Fudge's lab. name: Sasha K. Seroy
text:
Sasha K. Seroy is an oceanographer whose work combines marine community ecology with oceanography education. As an undergraduate at Stony Brook University, Seroy was mentored by Dianna Padilla, who later also helped with Seroy's summer research at FHL. Seroy completed a Ph.D. in oceanography at the University of Washington in 2021, with Daniel Grünbaum as committee chair. Much of the experimental work was done at FHL, including its Ocean Acidification Environmental Laboratory, with support from FHL fellowships. Seroy's FHL-connected research papers run from 2018 to 2024 and list both FHL and the UW School of Oceanography as affiliations. Education papers from 2019 to 2025 describe student-built pH and acoustic sensors, an interactive 3D model of thermohaline circulation for introductory courses, and the Student Seaglider Center, a student-run laboratory.

Seroy's research uses inducible traits, such as defenses that prey grow when predators are present, to follow how species interactions shape responses to ocean acidification and warming. A 2018 paper with Grünbaum, from experiments at FHL, tested the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea and its nudibranch predator Corambe steinbergae across pH 7.0 to 7.9. Defensive spines still formed at every pH, and a model showed that competition for space amplifies the cost of defense at the population level. The dissertation also showed that the snail Lacuna vincta moves often between eelgrass and macroalgae, which shapes its response to warming. In later work with Katie Dobkowski and colleagues, graceful kelp crabs (Pugettia gracilis) preferred native bull kelp to the invasive Sargassum muticum and ate more at about 19.5 °C than at 11.5 °C (2023). In a 2024 study, warming did not change the feeding rate or diet of the omnivorous Pugettia producta.

name: Scott Smiley
text:
Scott Smiley's research began with sea cucumber reproduction at the Friday Harbor Laboratories and later turned to seafood and aquaculture-feed science in Alaska. Smiley's papers from 1985 to 1988 give FHL and the University of Washington Department of Zoology as addresses; the first was written with Richard A. Cloney. The 1986 paper also gives an address in the Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California, San Francisco, where Smiley co-authored a 1992 study of cytoskeleton reorganization during Drosophila oogenesis with William Theurkauf, Mei Lie Wong and Bruce Alberts. A 1990 review of echinoderm oogenesis carries addresses at the Institute of Arctic Biology and the Department of Biology and Wildlife of the University of Alaska Fairbanks. Papers from 2003 to 2013 place Smiley at the university's Fishery Industrial Technology Center in Kodiak, part of its School of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences.

The FHL-connected papers describe the reproductive biology and development of the sea cucumber Stichopus californicus (now Apostichopus californicus). A 1985 paper with Cloney described the fine structure of the ovarian tubules and ovulation. A 1986 paper described metamorphosis and discussed where it places holothurians among the echinoderms, and a 1988 paper traced oogenesis through the annual ovarian cycle. Two further census papers from the FHL bibliography concern classification: a 1987 study with V. S. Levin and colleagues of triterpene glycosides in two stichopodid species, and a 1988 cladistic analysis of holothurian relationships. In Kodiak the work turned to fishery byproducts: fish meals, hydrolysates, oils and testes meals tested as feeds for trout, tilapia, Pacific threadfin and shrimp, and salmon-based infant foods. A 2012 paper returned to the same sea cucumber, under the name Parastichopus californicus, analyzing the chemical composition of animals harvested commercially in Alaska.

name: Scottie Y. Henderson
text: Scottie Y. Henderson completed a PhD advised by Richard R. Strathmann, whose CV lists Henderson among completed PhD students. A 2000 Invertebrate Biology paper with Strathmann compared ciliary filters in fan worms: prototrochal cilia lengthened as larvae of the serpulid Hydroides elegans grew, while latero-frontal cilia did not lengthen during postlarval development and were only weakly correlated with body size across adults of five species. Henderson later joined the Department of Biology at Cerritos College and worked on intertidal kelp with Jennifer L. Burnaford, including a 2013 UW ResearchWorks report on low-tide exposure and a Journal of Phycology paper on Hedophyllum sessile performance, published online in 2020.

name: Seamus O'Mahony
text: Seamus O'Mahony wrote a 2021 thesis at Victoria University of Wellington, co-supervised by Nicole E. Phillips, on the phylogeny and phylogeography of the New Zealand oyster borers Haustrum scobina and H. albomarginatum, direct-developing intertidal dogwhelks. Using a nationwide collection, O'Mahony generated 277 new mitochondrial COI sequences toward a dataset of 654, which yielded 58 haplotypes from 31 sites. COI did not separate the expected species, but nuclear 28S sequences and shell morphology indicated two species within H. scobina in the broad sense, limiting what the COI data could show about geographic structure.

name: Sean Corcoran
text: Sean Corcoran is listed as a graduate student in Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago, studying the cellular and molecular mechanisms that control how morphogens spread through the tissues they pattern. As first author of a 2025 preprint with Munro, Corcoran examined Sonic Hedgehog dispersal in embryonic limb bud mesenchyme, using a synchronous release system to follow its trafficking through the exosome biogenesis pathway. Shh-bound exosomes diffused through extracellular space and could also travel along cytonemes, and a synthetic patterning assay showed that exosome secretion was essential for short-range Shh gradients in vitro.

name: Sean Grace
text: Sean Patrick Grace earned a PhD in biological sciences at the University of Rhode Island in 2004 with Emily Carrington as first advisor. The dissertation studied the temperate coral Astrangia poculata on reefs in Narragansett Bay, using surveys, field transplants and flume experiments to show that short colonies survived better and had less contact with macroalgae. Grace joined the biology faculty at Southern Connecticut State University in 2004. Later papers cover seasonal physiology of A. poculata (2021) and the replacement of kelp by algal turf at the southern edge of Northwest Atlantic kelp forests (2019).

name: Sebastian Kruppert
text:
Sebastian Kruppert is a zoologist whose work concerns the biomechanics of predators and prey. He received his doctorate from Ruhr University Bochum, with a 2016 dissertation on the form, function, structure and plasticity of the carapace of the water flea Daphnia, and his earlier papers dealt with predator-induced defenses and carapace mechanics in Daphnia. His papers from 2019 to 2022 give Friday Harbor Laboratories (FHL) as his address, and several were written with Adam Summers. His FHL work on poacher fishes was supported in part by the German Research Foundation (DFG). Papers from 2022 also give the Plant Biomechanics Group at the University of Freiburg's Botanic Garden as an address. His later papers, listed on his ORCID record, deal with latex coagulation in Campanula, a biomimetic speaking valve (2024) and the transfer of animal strides to a biomimetic soft walker (2025).

At FHL, Kruppert studied the bony armor of poachers (Agonidae). A 2020 paper in the Journal of Morphology used CT scans of 27 poacher species to compare the mineral invested in armor and skeleton, and recorded abrasion and impact damage, worsening with age, on the plates of the northern spearnose poacher, Agonopsis vulsa. A 2021 conference abstract with Summers and others used feeding trials and machined crab claws to test whether red rock crabs cause such damage. He also co-authored a 2021 study of swimming, body stiffness and vertebral counts in four elongate fishes of the genera Anoplarchus and Xiphister, and a 2019 Nature commentary with Summers on a paradox in fish feeding. With colleagues from Bochum and Freiburg he worked on carnivorous aquatic plants: prey spectra and prey capture of the waterwheel plant Aldrovanda vesiculosa (2019) and the defenses of the water flea Ceriodaphnia dubia against a bladderwort (2022).

name: Sebastian Logan
text: Sebastian Logan wrote a 2019 thesis at Victoria University of Wellington, co-supervised by Nicole E. Phillips, on the phylogeography of the oyster borer Haustrum scobina, a direct-developing New Zealand intertidal gastropod. Using 379 new mitochondrial COI sequences from the southern North Island, Logan found significant geographic structure and low haplotype diversity in the southeast. The contrast between northern and southern populations suggested recolonization of the south after a range contraction during the Last Glacial Maximum, and evidence of long-distance movement pointed to dispersal by rafting or human translocation. Sixteen sequences from H. albomarginatum supported treating it as a separate species.

name: Sefton R. Wellings
text:
The pathologist Sefton R. Wellings combined research on the mammary gland in mice and humans with research on tumors and disease in fishes. His papers of the late 1950s and early 1960s give the Department of Pathology of the University of California School of Medicine in San Francisco and the Department of Zoology and its Cancer Research Genetics Laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. From 1962 to 1969 they give the Department of Pathology of the University of Oregon Medical School in Portland, and from 1969 into the late 1980s the Department of Pathology of the University of California, Davis, School of Medicine. His four FHL-connected papers, from 1964 to 1969, give the Oregon department together with Friday Harbor Laboratories; the 1969 paper also lists UC Davis.

At Friday Harbor, Wellings and his co-workers, chiefly Robert G. Chuinard, studied epidermal papillomas of the flathead sole, Hippoglossoides elassodon. They reported virus-like particles in the tumors (1964), described similar growths in other flatfishes of the family Pleuronectidae (1964) and compared skin neoplasms in four pleuronectid species (1965). A 1969 paper with G. A. Brown described the larval skin of the flathead sole. Later papers treat skin tumors of English sole and starry flounder from Puget Sound (1968), flathead sole tumors in East Sound, Orcas Island (1971), fish diseases in the Bering Sea (1977) and liver tumors in fish from an urban estuary (1977-78). His earlier electron-microscope studies dealt with milk secretion in the mouse mammary gland and with human melanoma. At Davis he studied the human breast, including a 1975 atlas of its subgross pathology and a 1980 hypothesis tracing breast cancer to the terminal ductal lobular unit.

name: Sergio Antonio Carrasco Órdenes
text: Sergio Antonio Carrasco Órdenes was a PhD student of Nicole E. Phillips at Victoria University of Wellington from 2008 to 2013 (thesis 2012). The thesis compared maternal investment in three direct-developing whelks, Cominella virgata, C. maculosa and Haustrum scobina, tracing how single embryos, multiple embryos and nurse-embryo feeding shaped hatchling size, lipid provisioning and juvenile performance. A 2016 Biological Bulletin paper with Phillips and Mary A. Sewell treated maternal lipid provisioning. Carrasco then held postdoctoral posts at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile and Universidad Católica del Norte, and became an assistant professor of oceanography at the University of Concepción in 2023, with papers on cephalopods and Southeast Pacific island ecosystems.

text: Seung-won Lee is listed among past graduate students of Joann J. Otto on the Otto lab page at Purdue University (2000). text: Shannon E. Smith Wallace, who also published as Shannon E. Smith, joined Billie J. Swalla's University of Washington lab in January 2001 as an undergraduate Howard Hughes intern. Swalla's CV lists a Mary Gates fellowship and the 2002 Franco Award for best undergraduate research paper in the biological sciences. Smith Wallace graduated in March 2002 with a BS in Biology and a BA in Zoology and worked as a full-time research technician in the lab until February 2003, on the ascidian innate immunity project and on a hemichordate project. The hemichordate work became a 2003 Canadian Journal of Zoology paper identifying enteropneust worms of the Pacific Northwest. With Brad Davidson, Rebecca Howsmon and Swalla, Smith Wallace published a 2003 characterization of metamorphosis in the ascidian Boltenia villosa. Later coauthorships were a 2006 Molecular Biology and Evolution paper on collagen and pharyngeal cartilage in chordates and a 2007 study led by Brock Roberts proposing that a complement response may activate metamorphosis in Boltenia villosa.

name: Shaun D. Cain
text:
Shaun D. Cain is a neurobiologist and professor of biology at Eastern Oregon University (EOU). He holds a BS in biology with a marine biology concentration from Florida Atlantic University, an MS in biology from the University of North Carolina Wilmington and a PhD in biology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. His 2004 and 2005 papers give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address, and he joined EOU's biology faculty in 2005. A 2010–2011 EOU program report says he specializes in cellular and organismal neurobiology, teaches anatomy and physiology, cell biology, neurobiology and neuroethology, and involves undergraduates in research on neurotransmission in the slug. At FHL he has co-taught the summer Neuroethology course with James Murray. The census counts eight FHL-address papers from 2004 to 2011, plus later papers that mention FHL in their text.

Cain studies how invertebrate nervous systems detect sensory cues and control behavior. With Kenneth Lohmann's group at Chapel Hill he worked on the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea, in which three pairs of identifiable pedal neurons respond to magnetic fields of Earth strength. His FHL-address papers identified a pair of neurons that such fields inhibit (2004) and analyzed the neurochemistry and electrophysiology of the responsive cells (2005). He also co-wrote reviews of magnetic orientation in sea turtles, lobsters and mollusks (2005) and of the neural bases of orientation and navigation (2006). With Andrew Christie and colleagues he co-authored anatomical and mass-spectrometry studies of neuroendocrine sites in the crab Cancer productus (2004–2005). Later work traced a network of Tritonia pedal peptides across gastropods (2011). A 2014 study he co-authored, run in FHL's magnetic coil, found that four chiton species headed north-northwest in the natural field but at random in a rotated field.

name: Shawn M. Luttrell
text:
Shawn M. Luttrell received a PhD from the University of Washington in 2017 with a dissertation on regeneration in the acorn worm Ptychodera flava. The supervisory committee was chaired by Billie J. Swalla, then director of Friday Harbor Laboratories. Luttrell's papers from 2012 to 2018 give the UW Department of Biology and FHL as addresses. They include a 2012 conference paper with Swalla and others and a 2014 book chapter with Swalla; a 2011 abstract with Swalla and others concerned neural organization in the hemichordate Saccoglossus bromophenolosus. For the larval experiments, P. flava larvae were carried from Taipei, Taiwan, to FHL, and a 2018 paper on larval regeneration was written with Yi-Hsien Su and Swalla.

Luttrell's research asks how hemichordates, a sister group to the echinoderms that shares some features with chordates, build and rebuild their nervous system and anterior structures. The 2012 conference paper described neurulation in a ptychoderid hemichordate that lacks a notochord. The 2014 chapter reviewed genomic and evolutionary evidence on chordate origins. A 2016 paper in Developmental Dynamics, with Kirsten Gotting, Eric Ross, Alejandro Sanchez Alvarado and Swalla, concluded that head regeneration in hemichordates is not a strict recapitulation of embryonic development. The dissertation followed anterior regeneration over time and compared transcriptomes at eight stages. It and the 2018 paper extended the work to larvae, which regenerate after being cut in several planes and re-form serotonin-positive cells in the region of the eyespots and larval brain within two weeks. New cells are added both at the cut site and throughout the regenerating tissue.

name: Sheh May Tam
text: Sheh May Tam was a postdoctoral researcher at San Francisco State University in Sarah Cohen's lab, after a PhD at Cambridge University. Tam coauthored a 2014 PLoS ONE study with Brian Ort, Cohen and others that tested whether buoy-deployed seeding kept eelgrass (Zostera marina) genetic diversity comparable to San Francisco Bay source populations, using microsatellites in mesocosms. The Cohen lab page gives Tam's later post as associate professor at Taylor's University in Malaysia, where Tam's papers concern plant genetics and taxonomy: a new Begonia species (2018) and the leaf transcriptome and naphthoquinone biosynthesis of Impatiens balsamina (2019-2020).

name: Sheila Voon
text: Sheila Voon was an undergraduate at the University of Washington in the Ecology and Physiology of Nearshore Organisms research apprenticeship at Friday Harbor Laboratories in spring 2012, with David O. Duggins among those thanked for guidance. Voon set out to test water flow effects on Nereocystis fertilization and sporophyte growth; when diatoms overgrew the sporophytes, the analysis turned to the diatoms, which had more chlorophyll and biomass under high flow.

text: Shelby Burgess, an undergraduate from the University of Michigan, took part in the 2012 Blinks-REU/BEACON program at FHL, mentored by Megan Dethier and David O. Duggins. text: Shelby Ziegler is listed as a former postdoc (2024) in James E. Byers's lab at the University of Georgia, with a later post as assistant professor of biology at Villanova University. Ziegler's ORCID record gives a BS in biology from the College of William and Mary and a PhD in ecology from the University of North Carolina. text: Shelley Ann Edmundson earned a PhD in zoology at the University of New Hampshire in 2016, advised by Elizabeth A. Fairchild, with William H. Howell and Winsor H. Watson also advising. The dissertation covered channeled whelk (Busycotypus canaliculatus) biology and its fishery in Vineyard and Nantucket Sounds: egg incubation, juvenile survival, sperm storage, growth, movement and trap behavior. Edmundson coauthored whelk bait studies with Fairchild and Watson (2024, 2025).

name: Shigeki Mizuno
text:
Shigeki Mizuno, a molecular biologist, wrote four FHL-connected papers, from 1973 to 1981, that report work with Arthur H. Whiteley and Helen R. Whiteley in the University of Washington's Departments of Microbiology and Zoology and at Friday Harbor Laboratories. A 1968 paper with Helen Whiteley on RNA synthesis in Bacillus subtilis gives his address as the Department of Microbiology of the UW School of Medicine. Papers in one database record under his name give the University of Tokyo's Institute of Applied Microbiology in the 1960s and early 1970s, and the University of Leicester's Department of Zoology, in work with Herbert C. Macgregor, from 1974 to 1976. From 1984 to 2001 they give the Faculty of Agriculture of Tohoku University, and from 2001 to 2007 Nihon University. These later attributions rest on one bibliographic database record and are less certain than the UW and FHL papers.

Mizuno's research concerned how RNA populations, chromosomes and chromatin relate to gene expression and development. With the Whiteleys he studied embryos of the sand dollar Dendraster excentricus. They reported an enrichment of egg-type RNA in cleavage-stage embryos (1973) and examined how RNA populations are distributed among the cells of the 16-cell embryo (1974). A 1975 paper discussed transcripts of repeated DNA sequences in the determination of blastomeres and early differentiation of echinoid larvae. A 1981 paper with Arthur Whiteley used electron microscopy to visualize giant polysomes in sea urchin embryos. Earlier papers in the same record deal with RNA synthesis in bacteria, the silk gland of the silkworm and the salmon brain. Later ones cover repetitive DNA in salamander chromosomes, the chicken W sex chromosome and a protein that binds its repeated DNA, the silk fibroin genes of Bombyx mori, and DNA-based sexing of birds.

name: Shigeko Ooishi
text:
Shigeko Ooishi (1927–2014) was a taxonomist of copepods that live in ascidians (sea squirts). She was a professor at Mie University in Japan: the Japanese research database KAKEN lists her as a professor in the Faculty of Fisheries in 1986, and the E. S. Morse Institute at Friday Harbor Laboratories describes her as a professor on Mie's faculty of biosciences. According to the Morse Institute, she spent many summers at FHL working with Paul Illg on the systematics and biology of parasitic copepods, and after retiring she continued her copepod work at FHL for many years. She was inducted into the Morse Institute in 2013. Her 2006 description of a new copepod genus from Okinawa gives FHL as her address and thanks the laboratories for facilities and equipment. The census counts 29 FHL-address papers by her from 1994 to 2014.

Ooishi's research was the descriptive taxonomy of cyclopoid copepods of the families Ascidicolidae and Notodelphyidae, which live inside colonial and solitary ascidians, some of them in the host's intestine. The earliest papers in the census, from 1977 and 1980, treat haplostomine copepods from compound ascidians of the San Juan Archipelago and the larval development of these copepods, and mention FHL in their text. Later papers describe new species and redescribe little-known ones, often treating both females and males, from hosts collected in Hawaii, Florida, the Gulf of California, Vancouver Island, New Zealand, Okinawa, Madagascar and European sites such as Roscoff, Strangford Lough and the Clyde estuary. A series on species from Madagascar ran from 2008 to 2014. Most of this work appeared in the Journal of Crustacean Biology and the Proceedings of the Biological Society of Washington.

text: Shiree Palmer was an MS student of Nicole E. Phillips at Victoria University of Wellington, with a thesis dated 2010. The thesis examined the cushion star Patiriella spp. in intertidal cobble fields of Wellington Harbour and the Wellington South Coast, surveying density, size and feeding, and testing scavenging on mussel carrion in field and laboratory experiments.

name: Shirley Mancia
text: Shirley Mancia worked in summer 2013 in Molly Jacobs's lab at McDaniel College with Mary Chow and Xi Huang, under Jacobs and Brett McMillan. McDaniel's summer research blog describes the team's field study at Hashawha, which asked whether trails act as a barrier to the migration of soil invertebrate communities. The team collected soil samples at path and non-path sites at set distances from a creek, and placed mesh traps of topsoil near and away from the path to measure how quickly invertebrates recolonized.

name: Sima Jonusaite
text: Sima Jonusaite was a postdoctoral fellow in 2021-2022 in Andreas Heyland's lab at the University of Guelph, on an NSERC fellowship (2020-2022). Jonusaite completed a PhD at York University, with a dissertation dated December 2016 and supervised by Andrew Donini and Scott Kelly, on transepithelial transport in the freshwater larvae of Chironomus riparius and Aedes aegypti, then studied septate junctions in Drosophila Malpighian tubules as a postdoc at the University of Utah. A 2023 Developmental Biology paper with Heyland identified candidate septate junction genes in early sea urchin development. After postdoctoral work at Kiel University (2023-2024), Jonusaite became an assistant professor of biological sciences at the University of Tulsa in 2025.

name: Simon A. Levin
text:
Simon A. Levin is an ecologist trained in mathematics. Since 1992 he has been James S. McDonnell Distinguished University Professor in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at Princeton University, where he directs the Center for BioComplexity. He received a BA from Johns Hopkins University and a PhD in mathematics from the University of Maryland; Wikidata names Monroe H. Martin as his doctoral advisor. From 1965 to 1992 he was at Cornell University. There he chaired the Section of Ecology and Systematics, directed the Ecosystems Research Center, and was Charles A. Alexander Professor of Biological Sciences from 1985. He has been president of the Ecological Society of America and of the Society for Mathematical Biology. His honors include the Kyoto Prize (2005), the Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement (2014), the National Medal of Science, membership of the National Academy of Sciences and election as a Fellow of the Royal Society (2026).

Levin's research combines mathematical modeling with empirical study. It asks how large-scale patterns and processes in ecosystems and the biosphere are maintained by ecological and evolutionary mechanisms acting mainly at the level of organisms. He has also worked on infectious diseases and on links between basic and applied ecology. He is not in the report's table of FHL core scientists. The census lists two of his papers. One is a 2002 model, with William McFarland of FHL, of how water currents affect prey capture by plankton-feeding fishes. The other is a 2008 article with Jane Lubchenco on resilience, robustness and ecosystem-based management of marine systems. It thanks FHL's director and staff for use of the laboratories' Helen R. Whiteley Center. Wikidata lists many doctoral students for him, among them Daniel Grünbaum, who appears in the report's table of FHL core scientists for papers from 2010 to 2020.

name: Sofia Chang
text: Sofia W. Chang is listed as a graduate student in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley, working on the aerodynamics of load carrying by flying insects. With Koehl, R. Dudley and F. T. Muijres, Chang coauthored a 2017 Journal of Experimental Biology study of take-off in blood-fed malaria mosquitoes, Anopheles coluzzii, in which wing forces supplied 61% of push-off force, reducing force on the host's skin. In summer 2011, listed with Berkeley's Department of Integrative Biology, Chang took FHL's marine birds and mammals course and wrote a report on echolocation clicks of southern resident killer whales recorded at Lime Kiln State Park.

name: Song Kim
text: Song Kim, who publishes as Songeun Kim, is listed as a graduate student in William Bement's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The lab studies cortical excitability, the propagating waves of Rho activity and F-actin assembly seen during cytokinesis in amphibian and echinoderm embryos. She coauthored a 2022 Journal of Cell Biology paper on a pattern-forming circuit built from Rho, F-actin, Ect2 and RGA-3/4, and a 2024 Nature Physics paper on energy partitioning in the cell cortex. As first author of a 2026 preprint, she reported from Xenopus oocytes, purified protein and TIRF microscopy that the Rho GAP RGA-3/4 binds and bundles F-actin directly.

Miller coauthored a 2011 book chapter with Craig Osenberg, Shima and Adrian Stier on spatial confounding in marine protected area assessments.

name: Sophie B. George
text:
Sophie B. George is a marine biologist who studies the reproduction and larval biology of echinoderms. Her doctoral thesis (Université Paris 6, 1990, supervised by Paul Nival) examined how food affects reproduction and larval development in the sea urchins Arbacia lixula and Paracentrotus lividus and the sea star Luidia clathrata, and her first papers came from the Station Zoologique at Villefranche-sur-Mer. Later papers list the University of South Florida (1991), Friday Harbor Laboratories (1994) and Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution in Florida (1996-97); since the late 1990s she has published from the Biology Department of Georgia Southern University. Her FHL-connected census papers run from 1994 to 2025. Seven are reports from FHL's summer Blinks/NSF REU/BEACON internship program with student first authors, among them Sam Bashevkin (2012), whom she mentored as a fellow. In 2023 she was first author of a note in Oryx announcing the new IUCN Marine Star Specialist Group.

Her research asks how a parent's diet and condition, and the conditions larvae meet in the plankton, affect egg quality, larval growth and metamorphosis. At Georgia Southern she has also worked on diets for rearing the sea urchin Lytechinus variegatus and on shell use by juvenile fiddler crabs (2010). Her FHL-connected papers began with maternal size and offspring quality in populations of the sea star Leptasterias epichlora (1994). Papers from 2006 to 2008 examined how food and dietary lipids affect growth and fatty acid composition of sand dollar (Dendraster excentricus) larvae, and how short-term salinity fluctuations speed their development. Since 2012 most concern larvae of the ochre star Pisaster ochraceus: shape changes and vertical position in low-salinity layers (2012), the use of larval arms in swimming (2019, with Richard Strathmann of FHL), feeding under fluctuating temperature and salinity (2021), and development during temperature spikes and marine heatwaves (2025).

name: Stacy C. Farina
text:
Stacy C. Farina is a comparative biologist who studies the functional morphology and evolution of fishes. She earned a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology at Cornell University in 2015; William E. Bemis chaired the committee, which included Adam Summers of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. In summer 2012 she took Summers's course in functional morphology and ecology of marine fishes at FHL and used her course project data as the basis for a doctoral dissertation improvement grant proposal. The dissertation's sculpin ventilation study was carried out at FHL that summer, and she returned to the Summers lab for many later visits. Her FHL-connected work, from 2014 to 2023, includes student reports from the FHL fish course (2014) and the Blinks–NSF REU–BEACON internship program (2015) on which she is a co-author. Farina is on the biology faculty at Howard University in Washington, D.C.; her 2023 dogfish paper gives both Howard and FHL addresses.

Farina's research centers on how fishes pump water over their gills and how breathing is tied to feeding and locomotion. The dissertation found that restricted gill openings evolved at least 11 times among ray-finned fishes, described very slow ventilation in the goosefish Lophius americanus, and proposed adding a third pump, formed by the branchiostegal rays, to the usual two-pump model. A 2019 paper followed the coupled evolution of suction feeding and gill ventilation in sculpins. Other FHL-connected work covers burial by flatfishes (2015) and by English sole (2018), dynamic testing of shark teeth (2016), overland walking by the tidepool sculpin Oligocottus maculosus (2018), the evolution of sculpin jaw bones and muscles (2018), skeletal reduction with depth in snailfishes (2021), and a ventilatory shunt in the flatfish Isopsetta isolepis (2022). A 2023 paper measured pressures in the gill chambers of the Pacific spiny dogfish, Squalus suckleyi.

name: Stanislav Gorb
text:
Stanislav N. Gorb is a zoologist who works on the biomechanics of biological surfaces and attachment. Professor of Functional Morphology and Biomechanics at Kiel University since 2008, he was also director of its Zoological Institute as of 2025. The tie to FHL core scientists runs through Petra Ditsche, who worked with Gorb on underwater attachment during postdoctoral work at Kiel before coming to FHL, and through Adam P. Summers, a coauthor on the tessellated skeleton of the round stingray (2009) and suction adhesion in the northern clingfish (2013). With Ditsche, Gorb published on biofilm and attachment in mayfly larvae (2013), the elasticity of hairs on air-retaining Salvinia surfaces (2015) and the hydrofoil-like legs of stream mayfly larvae (2023).

Gorb studied biology at the University of Kiev (1982 to 1989) and took a PhD at the Zoological Institute of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences, the Schmalhausen Institute (1989 to 1991), under L. Frantsevich. Postdoctoral work followed in Kiev, in Vienna with F. G. Barth and at the Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology in Tübingen with U. Schwarz (1996 to 1998). After a post at the University of Jena, he led groups at Max Planck institutes in Tübingen (1999 to 2002) and Stuttgart (2002 to 2008). Papers include work on beetle tarsal claws (2002), gecko adhesion (2005) and ladybird setae (2013). Honors include the Karl-Ritter-von-Frisch Medal (2018) and Leopoldina membership (2011).

name: Stephan Froggett
text: Stephan Froggett earned an MS in 1997 as a graduate student of Esther Leise at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro. Working with larvae of the mud snail Ilyanassa obsoleta, Froggett ran pharmacological tests with nitrergic reagents, following histochemical work on nitric oxide synthase by an earlier student in the lab. Nitric oxide donors blocked pharmacologically induced metamorphosis, while injected inhibitors of nitric oxide synthase let competent larvae become juveniles. The results, published with Leise in Biological Bulletin (1999), described nitric oxide as an endogenous inhibitor of molluscan metamorphosis. Froggett also coauthored a 2009 paper on the differing effects of diatom cultures on metamorphosis in the same snail.

name: Stephanie B. Crofts
text:
Stephanie B. Crofts is a biomechanist and functional morphologist and an assistant professor of biology at the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester, Massachusetts, where she has worked since 2020. She completed her PhD at the University of Washington in 2015, working with Adam Summers on the functional morphology of teeth that crush hard prey. She then studied swimming in living and extinct reptiles with Brooke Flammang at the New Jersey Institute of Technology. Her papers from 2018 to 2020 give the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as her address. The census lists sixteen FHL-connected items by her from 2011 to 2025. Besides her doctoral papers, they include student research reports she co-authored in FHL's autumn research courses (2012, 2014), a 2014 summer fish course and its summer internship programs (2014, 2023), and later papers with FHL-based colleagues.

Crofts uses physical specimens, CT data and models to study how organisms match their structures to their ecology, with a particular interest in the evolution of specialized dentitions. Her FHL-era papers deal with durophagy, the eating of hard-shelled prey. A 2014 study measured how tooth shape affects the load needed to crush snail shells. Other papers built finite element models of occlusal variation in crushing teeth (2015), tested jaw curvature and prey crushing in stingrays (2015) and analyzed tooth shape in the extinct marine reptiles Placodontia (2016). She also contributed to studies of chiton morphology under ocean acidification (2015) and of harbor seal skin and blubber (2017). Later FHL-linked papers treat the scaling and structure of juvenile bull kelp (2021, with Katie Dobkowski) and tooth indentation in fruit-eating fishes (2025). At Illinois her papers turned to biological puncture, including snake fangs and cactus spines.

text: Stephanie Bilodeau is listed as a postdoctoral associate in James Byers's lab at the University of Georgia, where her research concerned how life history traits govern species distributions in the ocean. name: Stephen A. Stricker
text:
Stephen A. Stricker is a cell and developmental biologist and professor emeritus of biology at the University of New Mexico (UNM). He received his PhD in zoology from the University of Washington in 1983. His early papers give the UW Department of Zoology and Friday Harbor Laboratories as addresses. They include a 1982 study of stylet formation in nemertean worms co-authored with Richard A. Cloney, and a 1983 study of maturing starfish oocytes with Thomas E. Schroeder. Papers from 1985 list the University of Calgary and one from 1988 the University of Wisconsin–Madison; by 1990 he was in UNM's Department of Biology. The census counts eight FHL-address papers from 1981 to 1984, and later papers through 2016 that appear in the FHL bibliography or mention FHL. UNM lists his research as calcium dynamics during oocyte maturation, fertilization and early development, and the roles of kinases and cyclic nucleotides in eggs.

Stricker's early studies used electron and polarization microscopy to show how nemertean worms build the calcified stylets of their proboscis armature, and described venom-producing cells in Paranemertes peregrina (1982–1985). He described two new nemerteans from Washington: Paranemertes sanjuanensis (1982) and a Tetrastemma from San Juan Island (1985). Related work examined shell and pedicle formation in the brachiopod Terebratalia transversa (1984–1985) and calcareous ossicles of sea cucumbers (1985–1986). Other papers covered gametogenesis in nemerteans, including a crab symbiont (1986), and the cyphonautes larva and metamorphosis of the bryozoan Membranipora membranacea (1988). His later papers, largely on nemerteans such as Cerebratulus, imaged calcium signals at fertilization by confocal microscopy. They also tested the roles of cAMP, serotonin, MAP kinase, protein kinase C, Src-family kinases and AMP-activated kinase in oocyte maturation and aging, with comparative reviews in 1999, 2013 and 2015.

name: Stephen A. Wainwright
text:
Stephen A. Wainwright (died 2019) was a zoologist and biomechanist on the Duke University faculty from 1964. He took a B.S. at Duke in 1953, studied at the University of Hawaii and at Cambridge, earned a PhD at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1962, and did postdoctoral work at the Karolinska Institute and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. His tie to FHL came through teaching and students. In his own account, Dennis Willows invited him in 1979 to organize and teach the first biomechanics course for marine biologists at FHL, which he taught with M. A. R. Koehl and Steven Vogel. Of its thirteen students, Rachel A. Merz recalled, nine went on to dissertation projects inspired by that summer.

By his count Wainwright had 36 graduate students at Duke, many of whom took FHL summer courses and some of whom did dissertation research there. Koehl was his PhD student, and their 1977 paper examined the mechanical adaptations of a giant kelp. His own work asked how support systems in plants and animals resist impact and tearing, including helically wound fibers in body walls and, in a 1978 Science paper, crossed collagen fibers in shark skin. His books include Mechanical Design in Organisms (1976, with Biggs, Currey and Gosline) and Axis and Circumference (1988). He co-founded Duke's Bio-Design Studio in 1990 and served on FHL's Advancement Board. FHL's Stephen and Ruth Wainwright Endowed Fellowship supports graduate students in functional morphology.

name: Stephen Kajiura
text: Stephen Kajiura was a postdoctoral fellow with Adam Summers at the University of California, Irvine, from 2002 to 2004, after an MS at Florida Institute of Technology (1994) and a PhD in zoology at the University of Hawaii (2001). Their joint work asked whether the hammerhead head shape aids maneuvering (2003) and olfaction (2004); later papers with Summers covered hammerhead olfactory responses (2009) and elasmobranch jaw materials (2013). Kajiura moved to Florida Atlantic University in 2003, is listed as professor of biological sciences, and published from there on electroreception in sawfish and rays (2012), magnetic orientation in the yellow stingray (2017, 2020) and blacktip shark aggregations off southeast Florida (2016).

name: Stephen M. Bollens
text:
Stephen M. Bollens is a zooplankton ecologist who joined Washington State University Vancouver as a professor in 2004 and directed WSU's Meyer's Point Environmental Field Station from 2018. He took a B.A. at Oberlin College (1982) and an M.Sc. (1986) and PhD (1990) in biological oceanography at the University of Washington. Bollens was listed as a PhD student of Bruce W. Frost. In autumn 1991 he team-taught Ocean and Coastal Processes at FHL as visiting faculty in Northeastern University's East/West Marine Biology Program.

With Frost, Bollens studied what drives diel vertical migration in copepods: ultraviolet light in Acartia hudsonica (1990), rapid individual responses to predators (1991), field evidence for predator avoidance (1992), vulnerability of Metridia lucens and Calanus pacificus to vertebrate predators (1993), and chemical, mechanical and visual cues (1994). Bollens was a postdoctoral fellow and then assistant scientist at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (1990 to 1996), coauthored a 1996 paper on predation by planktonic hydroids, and was on the San Francisco State University faculty from 1996 to 2004. Later work addressed zooplankton invasions, including a 2019 global survey with Eric Dexter and a 2020 paper on 38 northeast Pacific estuaries. He was elected to the Washington State Academy of Sciences in 2022.

name: Steve Moore
text: Steve Moore, who published as Steven W. Moore, is listed among the postdocs on the lab page of M. A. R. Koehl at the University of California, Berkeley. Moore, R. E. Keller and Koehl miniaturized a stress-relaxation test to measure the viscoelastic properties of Xenopus laevis tissues during gastrulation. Their 1995 paper in Development showed that the dorsal involuting marginal zone stiffens during its convergent extension, more along the anteroposterior axis than the mediolateral one. A 1994 paper by Moore from the same Berkeley department, in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering, described a fiber optic system for measuring the dynamic mechanical properties of embryonic tissues.

name: Steve Morton
text: Steve Morton was a curator of the Provasoli-Guillard National Center for Culture of Marine Phytoplankton at Bigelow Laboratory from 1996 to 1998, during Robert Andersen's time as its director, and coauthored the center's 1997 list of strains with Andersen.
