name: Steven B. Roberts
text:
Steven B. Roberts is a Professor in the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (SAFS) at the University of Washington, where his laboratory studies the genomics, epigenetics and physiology of marine invertebrates. Earlier papers place him at the University of Notre Dame's Department of Biological Sciences (about 1999-2001), working on genes involved in fish ovulation and muscle growth, and at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole (about 2003-2007), working on aquaculture species and marine pathogens, including the hard clam parasite QPX. His SAFS papers begin in 2007. His FHL-connected census papers, from 2012 to 2026, draw on oysters spawned and held at Friday Harbor, a graduate course taught there and FHL-based co-authors. He chaired the doctoral committee of Emma Timmins-Schiffman (UW SAFS, PhD 2014), first author of his oyster papers in the census.

The Roberts lab studies how marine organisms carry a memory of past environmental conditions, linking molecular regulation to physiology across life stages and generations, in oysters, corals and sunflower sea stars. His FHL-connected papers follow two lines. The first concerns the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas and ocean acidification: a 2012 paper with FHL's Michael O'Donnell found that larvae from wild adults spawned at Friday Harbor developed more slowly under elevated carbon dioxide, a 2013 paper on oysters held at FHL tested shotgun proteomics of the gill, and a 2014 paper used it to describe responses to four weeks in acidified water. The second concerns disease. A 2013 genome-browser dataset for QPX came largely from a graduate course at Friday Harbor; a 2015 paper measured immune and nervous system gene expression in sunflower sea stars with wasting disease, and 2026 papers with FHL's C. Drew Harvell compare juvenile and adult responses.

name: Steven Jury
text: Steven Jury earned a PhD in zoology at the University of New Hampshire in 1999 with Winsor Watson, on the behavioral and physiological responses of the American lobster, Homarus americanus, to temperature. The dissertation found that lobsters prefer a narrow temperature range, avoid water above about 23.5 degrees C and appear to thermoregulate by behavior; a spatial model including temperature and salinity responses correlated with field data from coastal New Hampshire and the Great Bay Estuary. With Watson, Jury used a cardiac assay to measure lobster thermosensitivity (2000) and coauthored a study of salinity detection (2001) and work on metabolic responses to warming (2023).

Vogel wrote Life in Moving Fluids (1981) and studied flow in prairie dog burrows, flight in tiny insects and jet propulsion in squid.

name: Stuart H. Thompson
text:
Stuart H. Thompson is a neurobiologist and Professor of Biology at Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove, California, and a member of Stanford's Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute. Thompson's papers carry the Hopkins address from 1983 onward, and Thompson teaches courses on the physiology and sensory ecology of marine animals. The earliest FHL-connected papers date from the 1970s: a 1973 chapter on bursting mechanisms in mollusk locomotion, written with A. O. Dennis Willows and Peter Getting, carries FHL and UW Department of Zoology addresses, and a 1979 Brain Research paper with L. Donald Partridge, Stephen Smith and John Connor carries an FHL address. Later FHL-connected papers, from 2002 and 2005, came from a collaboration with Winsor Watson of the University of New Hampshire on the nudibranch Melibe leonina.

Thompson studies ion channels and the electrical behavior of nerve cells, mostly in marine animals. Work from the 1970s and 1980s on molluscan neurons identified three pharmacologically distinct potassium channels (1977), examined the slow currents behind bursting pacemaker activity in Tritonia and Aplysia, and used patch methods to map the uneven distribution of potassium and calcium channels over the cell body. In the 1990s Thompson used fura-2 imaging to study calcium signaling in neuroblastoma cells. Later work includes vision in juvenile rockfish, measured by electroretinogram, the spectral sensitivity of box jellyfish eyes (Tripedalia cystophora), bluefin tuna heart cells and the nervous system of the colonial tunicate Botryllus schlosseri. The FHL-connected Melibe papers link cell properties to behavior: a 2002 study showed that isolated Melibe brains still produce the swim rhythm, and a 2005 paper identified the two pairs of interneurons that form the swim central pattern generator.

name: Susan Lynn Williams
text:
Susan Lynn Williams (1951–2018) was a marine ecologist who studied seagrasses, seaweeds and coral reef algae. She received a B.S. in biology from the University of Michigan (1972), an M.S. in biological oceanography from the University of Alaska (1977) and a Ph.D. in botany and marine biology from the University of Maryland (1981). Several papers from 1983 to 1985 came from the Smithsonian Institution's Marine Systems Laboratory, and she was later science director of NOAA's National Undersea Research Program in the Virgin Islands. Her papers from 1988 to 1990 carry FHL addresses, with the UW Department of Botany in 1989 and San Diego State University in 1990. At San Diego State she was a professor of biology and directed the Coastal and Marine Institute. From 2000 she was at the University of California, Davis, where she directed the Bodega Marine Laboratory until 2010 and was Distinguished Professor of Evolution and Ecology.

Williams studied how light, nutrients, grazing and physical stress shape coastal seagrass and seaweed communities, and how human activity affects them. Her FHL-connected papers from 1988 to 1990 cover grazing by green turtles on the seagrass Thalassia testudinum in a disturbed bed, the photosynthetic response of nitrogen-starved brown algae (Petalonia fascia and Laminaria saccharina) to ammonium resupply (with Stephen Herbert), and photosynthesis-light relationships among components of coral reef algal turfs (with R. C. Carpenter). Later FHL-connected papers (2004–2008), with Megan Dethier and colleagues, concern the rockweed Fucus gardneri on San Juan Island: the performance of embryos, juveniles and adults across tidal heights and seasons, variation in net photosynthesis, and the effects of manipulated stress and herbivory. With Dianna Padilla she identified aquarium and ornamental trades as sources of aquatic invasive species (2004). She was president of the Coastal and Estuarine Research Federation (2009–2011) and a fellow of the AAAS (2006).

name: Susana Patino del Olmo
text: Susana Patino del Olmo began as a PhD student in Michael Hart's lab at Simon Fraser University in 2006, after a BSc at UNAM and an MSc at CINVESTAV, both in marine ecology. She studied the evolution of genes encoding proteins involved in gamete recognition and fertilization in sea stars. Publishing as Susana Patiño, she characterized the gene for the sperm protein bindin in Patiria miniata (2009), extending its known evolutionary history beyond sea urchins, and then compared bindin across 13 sea star species, finding more positive selection in outcrossing genera than in selfing hermaphrodites (2016).

name: Susanne M. Rafelski
text: Susanne M. Rafelski was a postdoc at the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories, working with Garrett M. Odell, after a PhD in biochemistry at Stanford University. name: Susanne Menden-Deuer
text: Susanne Menden-Deuer was a PhD student of Daniel Grünbaum in oceanography at the University of Washington, finishing in 2004 after a UW master's degree. She was a research fellow at Princeton University and a lecturer at Western Washington University, and became professor of oceanography at the University of Rhode Island. Her work includes plankton patches in East Sound, Orcas Island (2012). As president of ASLO she wrote President's messages from 2024 to 2026.

name: Suzanne Cooke
text: Suzanne M. Cooke was a PhD student of Winsor H. Watson III in zoology at the University of New Hampshire, finishing in 2004 with a dissertation on how temperature affects the physiology and locomotion of the American lobster, Homarus americanus. Heart rate in intact lobsters rose linearly with temperature, also after the cardioregulatory nerves were lesioned, while isolated hearts did not speed up. Summer-acclimated lobsters avoided water above about 22.3°C and winter-acclimated lobsters avoided about 14.3°C. Juveniles moved farther in the dark and in warmer water. Cooke related these results to the seasonal movement of lobsters into and out of the Great Bay estuary.

name: Tamara M. McGovern
text:
Tamara M. McGovern is a marine biologist whose papers concern reproduction and population genetics in marine invertebrates, seagrasses and sharks. McGovern's 2002 and 2003 papers on brittle stars give Florida State University's Department of Biological Science as an address. A 2003 paper with Michael Hellberg gives Louisiana State University's Department of Biological Sciences as an address and the Friday Harbor Laboratories as a present address. FHL also appears on a 2002 brittle star paper and on a 2004 coral study, so the FHL-connected work falls between 2002 and 2004. Later papers give addresses at the Dauphin Island Sea Lab in Alabama (2007, 2009) and in Clemson University's Department of Biological Sciences (2009, 2010). A 2010 paper gives a present address in the Natural Sciences Division of Limestone College in South Carolina.

McGovern's work at Florida State concerned the brittle star Ophiactis savignyi, which reproduces both sexually and by dividing in two. Two 2002 papers described sexual and asexual reproduction in Florida Keys populations and showed that males divide more often than females, enough to explain the excess of males. A 2003 study found that individuals divide less often when mates are present. With Hellberg, McGovern used mitochondrial COI sequences to show that regional differences in the chemical defenses of the western Atlantic bryozoan Bugula neritina follow two cryptic species; the bryostatin-producing bacterium Endobugula sertula was found only in the southern species (2003). A 2004 study led by Don Levitan, with McGovern as co-author, examined reproductive isolation among broadcast-spawning corals of the Montastraea annularis complex. Later papers address seagrass reproduction in the northern Gulf of Mexico, lemon shark phylogeography and rocky-shore phylogeography, and, with Levitan, Allee effects in the sea.

name: Tanya Lynn O'Reilly
text: Tanya Lynn O'Reilly completed a Master of Science in biology at St. Francis Xavier University in 2025, co-supervised by Russell C. Wyeth and David Garbary. The thesis examined ribbed mussels, Geukensia demissa, and cord grass, Sporobolus alterniflorus, in eroding salt marshes of the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence. O'Reilly surveyed 16 populations across three marsh elevation zones. Marshes with extensive dead zones had older mussels at lower density, and the most degraded sites lacked mussels under 3 cm, which suggested declining recruitment. A 12-month field experiment at Fox Harbour found no evidence for the mutualism described from New England, possibly because density, about 100 per square meter, is too low.

name: Teresa Audesirk
text:
Teresa Audesirk is a neurobiologist and an author of biology textbooks. Her papers of 1975 to 1978 give the University of Southern California, including its Catalina Marine Science Center, and the California Institute of Technology. Her four FHL-connected papers, of 1979 and 1980, give Friday Harbor Laboratories. Her papers of 1982 to 1984 give the University of Missouri-Columbia, and those of 1985 to 2004 the biology department of the University of Colorado at Denver. The FHL papers form two two-part series in the Journal of Comparative Physiology on the nudibranch Tritonia diomedea. The first is single-authored and the others were written with Gerald J. Audesirk, whose own FHL papers of 1978 and 1979 concern the neurons that control Tritonia's locomotory cilia. With Gerald Audesirk and Bruce E. Byers she is an author of the textbook Biology: Life on Earth (from 1986; eleventh edition 2016).

Her research has used mollusks and, later, cultured vertebrate neurons to study how animals sense their surroundings and how toxic substances affect nerve cells. Early papers examined distance chemoreception and evidence for pheromones in the sea hare Aplysia californica, and a 1979 field study followed its growth and reproduction. At FHL she recorded from oral mechanoreceptors of Tritonia, describing their electrophysiological properties, receptive fields and role in feeding (1979). The 1980 papers described complex mechanoreceptors, their responses to mechanical and chemical stimuli, and neuronal correlates of a change in the animal's behavioral responsiveness. Later work with freshwater snails, chiefly the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis, dealt with rapid and one-trial reward conditioning and with the effects of chronic lead exposure on identified neurons. From about 1990 she and colleagues studied how inorganic lead, nicotine and estradiol affect calcium channels, neurite growth and dendritic branching in cultured hippocampal and neuroblastoma cells.

name: Teris Oglesby
text: Teris Oglesby was a Blinks-REU-BEACON Fellow at Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2015, working with James A. Murray, from the marine science department at Savannah State University. Their paper asked how water flow interacts with the rhinophores of the nudibranch Tritonia tetraquetra. Particle image velocimetry on a fixed rhinophore model, used to measure boundary layer thickness at different speeds, gave inconclusive results. Dye studies in three nudibranch species showed cilia-driven currents along the rhinophore, and electron micrographs showed dense cilia on the inner folds of the tuft. The authors proposed that these cilia may clear the boundary layer, helping the animal respond faster to odor changes, much like sniffing.

name: Terra Hiebert
text: Terra Hiebert earned a PhD in biology at the University of Oregon in 2016, advised by Svetlana Maslakova, with Richard B. Emlet on the committee. The dissertation doubled the known nemertean species in one northeast Pacific region by surveying larvae as well as adults. A 2015 paper with Maslakova revised the Micrura alaskensis species complex; a 2023 paper with George von Dassow and others analyzed appendicularian tail pumping.

name: Terrie Klinger
text:
Terrie Klinger is a marine ecologist whose work spans seaweed biology, marine conservation and ocean governance. She received a BA from the University of California, Berkeley (1979), an MSc from the University of British Columbia (1984) and a PhD from the University of California, San Diego (1989), where her doctoral advisor was Paul K. Dayton. Wikidata records postdoctoral work at the University of California, Riverside (1989 to 1992), lecturing for Northeastern University (1991 to 1999) and a visiting position at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1992 to 2001. She joined the University of Washington faculty in 2001 as an assistant professor and became an associate professor in 2008. Her papers from 1993 to 2003 give FHL as an address. A 2018 ocean acidification study, papers on the San Juan Islands and a 2021 student report also name FHL.

Klinger's early FHL-connected work concerned algae: a 1993 review of why haplodiploid life cycles persist in algae, and 1999 studies with David Garbary, David Duggins and others of kelp gametophytes living inside red algae. With Duggins she did field work on how small grazers and current flow together affect kelp survival (2001), and on three understory kelps along a gradient of water motion (2003). With Jennifer Hoffman and Lara Hansen she showed that UV radiation and temperature interact, limiting what single-factor experiments can show (2003). She also wrote on biosafety assessment of genetically engineered organisms (1998, 1999). Later papers turned to marine reserves and ecosystem-based management: invaders in reserves (2006), the San Juan Archipelago (2007), dispersal among reserves (2007) and governance (2008). Her experiments on pteropod shell dissolution under ocean acidification were done at FHL during a graduate summer course (2018).

name: Terry Dial
text: Terry Dial was a doctoral student of Elizabeth L. Brainerd at Brown University and held a National Science Foundation dissertation improvement grant with Brainerd (2016-2018) on experimental miniaturization of guppy offspring. Their work asked how newborn size shapes maturity in Trinidadian guppies, including escape performance (2015) and oral jaw movement and morphology (2017). Dial earned an MS at the University of Utah (2010) and a PhD at Brown (2016). Earlier papers (2012) addressed limb development and aerodynamics in mallards, and a 2020 paper with G. V. Lauder at Harvard compared first feeding in zebrafish and guppies. Dial became an assistant professor of biology at Utah State University in 2022.

name: Theodore Y. Wu
text: Theodore Y. Wu (died 2023) was a fluid dynamicist and professor of engineering science at the California Institute of Technology. Thomas Daniel studied with Wu as a Bantrell Postdoctoral Fellow until 1984. Wu's research covered water waves and free-surface flows and the mechanics of fish swimming and of bird and insect flight. Wu was elected to the U.S. National Academy of Engineering in 1982.

name: Thomas Daniel
text:
Thomas L. Daniel is a biologist who studies the mechanics and neural control of animal movement and is professor emeritus of biology at the University of Washington, where he joined the faculty in 1984 and served as founding chair of the Department of Biology. He earned a BS and MS at the University of Wisconsin and a PhD at Duke in 1982, with a thesis on added mass in impulsive locomotion, especially in medusae, studying with Steven Vogel and Stephen Wainwright. He then held the Bantrell Postdoctoral Fellowship at Caltech. His ties to FHL run through Daniel Grünbaum, a postdoc in his lab, and Kathryn A. McDonald, on whose graduate advisory committee he sat. His lab also trained Brian Helmuth (PhD 1997).

His early papers treated swimming: medusan jet propulsion (1983), size limits in the escape locomotion of caridean shrimp with Edgar Meyhöfer (1989), and a 1992 chapter on swimming hydromechanics with Jordan and Grünbaum. By 1996 his research included coordinated locomotion in leeches and flying hawkmoths, and later papers took up insect wing mechanics, including wing flexural stiffness with Stacey Combes (2003). With M. A. R. Koehl he studied a blade-like red alga and an encrusting bryozoan on the floating breakwater at the FHL dock (2022), measuring how the bryozoan raised water forces on the alga and stiffened its blades. He was a MacArthur Fellow (1996), AAAS Fellow (2012) and Guggenheim Fellow (2013), and President and CEO of the Washington Research Foundation from 2022 to 2025.

name: Thomas E. Schroeder
text:
Thomas E. Schroeder, a cell biologist, studied cell division and the egg cortex using the eggs and oocytes of marine invertebrates. According to an FHL centennial timeline, he first came to Friday Harbor in 1965 as a University of Washington graduate student of Richard Cloney, to take the Comparative Invertebrate Embryology course. In 1971 he joined the UW Zoology Department and took up year-round residence at FHL, bringing an American Cancer Society grant with which he set up a transmission electron microscopy facility at the laboratories. His earliest papers (1970-1971) analyzed neurulation in the frog Xenopus laevis and the fine structure of dividing HeLa cells. The census credits him with 28 FHL-address papers from 1972 to 1991, and his papers of those years give Friday Harbor Laboratories as his address.

Much of Schroeder's work concerns the contractile ring, the band of filaments that pinches a dividing cell in two. His 1972 electron-microscope study of Arbacia sea urchin eggs found that the ring exists only from shortly after anaphase to the end of furrowing, that its volume decreases as it constricts, and that cytochalasin B removes its filaments and halts cleavage. A 1973 paper showed that ring filaments in dividing HeLa cells bind heavy meromyosin, indicating that they are closely related to muscle actin. From the late 1970s he turned to the egg surface and cortex: microvillus elongation after fertilization (1978), markers of egg polarity such as the jelly canal (1980), the "primitive" sea urchin Eucidaris (1981), actin and microtubule arrays in maturing starfish oocytes (1983-1985, several with J. J. Otto), unequal fourth cleavage in sea urchins (1987), and a periodic cytokeratin network in the starfish oocyte cortex called "snoods" (1991).

name: Thomas F. Mumford
text:
Thomas F. Mumford Jr. is a phycologist whose publications, from 1980 to 2024, deal mostly with seaweeds and seagrasses in Washington State. He received an A.B. in botany from Wabash College in 1966 and a Ph.D. in botany from the University of Washington in 1973. Papers from 1990 and 1997 give his address as the Washington State Department of Natural Resources, and papers from 2015 to 2023 list Marine Agronomics LLC. His ORCID record lists him as a visiting lecturer at Friday Harbor Laboratories since 1984, and his census papers with an FHL address date from 2016 to 2024. He co-authored FHL student papers, including a 2014 project with Megan Dethier on haptera growth in two kelps and a 2020 report with Chiko Meng on blade growth and erosion in the sugar kelp Saccharina latissima, based on a spring class project run at FHL over six years.

Mumford's work joins seaweed biology with resource management and aquaculture. Earlier publications deal with field cultivation of the red algae Iridaea cordata and Gigartina exasperata (1980), shellfish and seaweed harvests in Puget Sound (1988), the growth of nori farming in North America (1990), underwater video for estimating seagrass cover (1997), and kelp and eelgrass in Puget Sound (a 2007 report). Later papers report an introduced population of the brown alga Chorda asiatica (2015), reconstruct 145 years of bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) records in South Puget Sound, finding 63% less kelp in 2017 than in 1878 (2021), and model free-floating offshore seaweed farms (2019-2022). His FHL-connected papers are collaborations in red algal genetics and systematics: the organelle genomes of Mastocarpus papillatus (2016), DNA sequencing of the coralline genus Lithothamnion in the Arctic and Subarctic (2021), and the chloroplast genome of Rhodochorton tenue from San Juan Island (2024).

name: Thomas G. Dahlgren
text: Thomas G. Dahlgren was a member of Kenneth M. Halanych's lab at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution around 2000-2001, with interests in annelid phylogeny, especially chrysopetalids and Ophryotrocha, and in North Atlantic phylogeography under climate change. Papers with Halanych covered ocean quahog phylogeography (2000), Ophryotrocha phylogeny (2001) and deep-sea Chaceon crabs (2003). Later work, as a researcher at the University of Gothenburg from 2002 and at the Norwegian Research Centre NORCE from 2018, described a new Osedax whale worm from the North Atlantic (2005), surveyed abyssal fauna of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (2022-2023) and applied environmental DNA to monitoring around offshore wind farms (2023).

name: Thomas J. Pirtle
text:
Thomas J. Pirtle is a biologist whose research interests include comparative physiology, developmental biology and neuroethology. He earned a B.S. (1990) and an M.S. (1992) in biology at Abilene Christian University and a Ph.D. in biology at Arizona State University (2003). He taught at Abilene Christian University and Grand Canyon University before joining the biology faculty of The College of Idaho in 2014. His courses there include anatomy and physiology, developmental biology, and regional anatomy and histology for a physician assistant program run with Idaho State University. The census lists eight FHL-connected papers from 2000 to 2022, written from Arizona State, Abilene Christian, Grand Canyon and The College of Idaho, several also giving an FHL address. His 2022 review says the work depended on the continued support of the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Richard A. Satterlie, a co-author of six of the papers, is linked to him in the report's network.

Much of his research concerns the swimming pteropod mollusk Clione limacina and how its locomotor central pattern generator, the neural circuit that sets the swimming rhythm, speeds up. In 2000, with Satterlie and Tigran P. Norekian, he reported that serotonin narrows the spikes of the circuit's interneurons, permitting faster cycling. A second 2000 paper, led by Leonid L. Moroz, mapped NADPH-diaphorase reactivity, a putative marker of nitric oxide synthase, in the Clione nervous system and found that nitric oxide activates neurons in feeding and locomotor circuits. Later papers examined the pleural type 12 interneuron in swim acceleration (2006), postinhibitory rebound (2007) and a hyperpolarization-activated current that alters swim frequency (2010). A 2020 study of Pd-7 swim interneurons found that cGMP mediates acceleration induced by nitric oxide but not by serotonin, and a 2022 review brought the work together. His newer projects use chick embryos and the water flea Daphnia magna.

name: Thomas Kleinteich
text:
Thomas Kleinteich is a zoologist whose published research, from 2006 to 2022, concerns functional morphology and biomechanics, much of it in amphibians. He completed a doctoral dissertation at the Universität Hamburg in 2009 on the evolution of intrauterine feeding in caecilians (Gymnophiona). It compared the morphology, function and development of cranial muscles in egg-laying and live-bearing species. He then worked at Friday Harbor Laboratories as a postdoctoral researcher, a role named in a 2011 student report. His papers from 2010 to 2013 give FHL as an address, and several were co-authored with Adam Summers. From 2012 his papers also give the Functional Morphology and Biomechanics group of the Zoological Institute at Kiel University (Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel) as his address, and many of his Kiel papers were co-authored with Stanislav Gorb.

His research combines anatomy, micro-CT imaging, finite element analysis and performance testing. His FHL-connected papers extended his caecilian work: feeding biomechanics in egg-laying and live-bearing species (2010), the female cloaca (2011), larval throat muscles compared with those of salamanders (2011) and cranial performance in solid and fenestrated skulls (2012). At FHL he also took part in a finite element study of scorpion pincer shapes (2012) and a study of the filter pads of devil rays (2013). A 2011 report by Dylan Wainwright, an undergraduate in FHL's summer internship program, was followed by a 2013 paper with Kleinteich and Summers showing that the northern clingfish adheres about equally well across a wide range of surface roughness, while artificial suction cups hold only on the smoothest. Kiel papers treat adhesion by frog tongues and octopus suckers, insect mouthparts and legs, and, in 2021 and 2022, head shape, bite force, burrowing and vertebral shape in caecilians.

name: Thomas M. Leschine
text: Thomas M. Leschine, a professor emeritus in the University of Washington's School of Marine and Environmental Affairs, chaired Allison Morgan's 2024 master's thesis on passenger-only ferries and southern resident killer whales. Leschine's papers dealt with environmental decision making, including a 2004 pilot of the Hanford Decision Mapping System and a 2002 evaluation of the Columbia River Comprehensive Impact Assessment.

text: Tiffany Kim was a Northwestern University environmental sciences student in the Marine Environment Research Apprenticeship at Friday Harbor Laboratories in fall 2011, with Chris Neufeld as mentor and Michael T. Nishizaki as a teaching assistant. text: Tiffany Lu is listed as a graduate student in Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago, in the Cellular and Molecular Biology program. name: Tigran P. Norekian
text:
Tigran P. Norekian is a neurobiologist who studies the nervous systems and behavior of marine invertebrates. His 2020 and 2023 papers give joint affiliations with the Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience of the University of Florida and Friday Harbor Laboratories, and the 2020 paper also lists the Institute of Higher Nervous Activity and Neurophysiology in Moscow. Much of his ctenophore work is co-authored with Leonid L. Moroz of the Whitney Laboratory, and the animals for his 2020 siphonophore study and 2023 ctenophore study were collected at the FHL dock. The census counts 27 FHL-address papers from 1993 to 2024, and the mentoring network links him to Richard A. Satterlie through co-authorship from 1993 to 2019.

Norekian's earlier work, much of it with Satterlie, used the swimming pteropod mollusk Clione limacina to study how identified neurons produce behavior. These papers traced the cerebral neurons and motoneurons behind the hydraulic inflation of prey-capture appendages (1993-1995), control of startle and escape swimming (1997), serotonergic modulation of swimming speed, the roles of GABA, nitric oxide and peptides in feeding circuits, and control of heartbeat (1999, 2008). From 2014 he turned to ctenophores and cnidarians, contributing to the 2014 ctenophore genome paper and describing the neuromuscular systems of the ctenophores Pleurobrachia bachei, Beroe abyssicola and Euplokamis dunlapae and the trachymedusa Aglantha digitale (2015-2019). Later studies, one with Robert W. Meech, describe the nervous system of the siphonophore Nanomia (2020), nervous system development in larvae of Mnemiopsis leidyi (2021), the suppression of ciliary beating in ctenophores by nitric oxide (2023) and sensory networks in the sea slug Pleurobranchaea (2024).

text: Todd Maney is listed as a graduate student on the page of former members of Linda G. Wordeman's lab in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics, University of Washington School of Medicine. text: Tom Hata is listed as a postdoc in M. A. R. name: Tom Hunter
text: Tom Hunter is listed under graduate students on the publication list of M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley. Hunter's 1989 Biological Bulletin paper, from the Berkeley zoology department, tested plankton capture by the hydroid Obelia longissima in a flume and a wave tank. Feeding was more effective in oscillating than in unidirectional flow at the same velocity and particle flux. Bushier colonies fed less effectively except in high-frequency oscillating flow, and longer colonies less effectively than short ones. The paper mentions Friday Harbor Laboratories in its main text. An earlier paper with Steven Vogel (1986) showed that spinning embryos enhance diffusion through gelatinous egg masses.

name: Torsten Struck
text:
Torsten H. Struck is an evolutionary biologist working on annelid phylogeny and genomics, and from 2015 Professor of Evolutionary Genomics and Curator of the Helminth collection at the Natural History Museum, University of Oslo. Struck took a diploma (1999) and doctorate (2003) in biology at the University of Osnabrück, then worked from 2003 to 2005 as a postdoctoral fellow in the laboratory of Kenneth M. Halanych at Auburn University. Back at Osnabrück, Struck headed the phylogenomics laboratory in the working group of Prof. Paululat and completed a habilitation in 2008. A German Research Foundation Heisenberg fellowship followed at the Zoological Research Museum Alexander Koenig in Bonn, from 2011 to 2015. Halanych, in whose laboratory Struck was a postdoctoral fellow, has been a Visiting Instructor at FHL on multiple occasions.

Burnette, Struck and Halanych (2005) reported that holopelagic Poeobius meseres derives from benthic flabelligerid worms. Struck and colleagues (2007), acknowledging FHL support, placed Echiura as derived annelids with capitellids as their sister group and counted Sipuncula within Annelida. Kocot and colleagues (2016) addressed systematic error in the phylogenomics of Lophotrochozoa. A 2011 Nature paper led by Struck applied phylogenomics to annelid evolution. With José Cerca, Struck later studied the interstitial ghost worms Stygocapitella, reporting slowed morphological evolution in a cryptic species complex (2019) and much smaller geographic ranges once species were delimited (2020).

name: Trevor Bak
text: Trevor Bak is listed as a PhD student in Environmental Life Science in Alli N. Cramer's Integrative Marine Ecology Lab at Arizona State University. The lab studies how physical and eco-evolutionary processes shape the distribution and persistence of marine life, using field systems in Hawai'i and Bermuda and combining field observations, experiments, and computational approaches.

name: Trevor Gonzalinajec
text: Trevor Gonzalinajec was a graduate student in M. A. R. Koehl's lab at the University of California, Berkeley. Using dynamically scaled physical models, Gonzalinajec and Koehl measured drag, lift, side forces, and moments on a copepod, a veliger larva, and barnacle nauplius and cyprid larvae, finding that body shape, orientation, and proximity to a surface all affected them. The lab lists the paper as in press in the Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology (2014). A second project used high-speed video and physical models to study how powdery mildew sporocarps, including the shuttlecock-shaped sporocarps of Phyllactinia, are released from leaves and carried by wind.

name: Trevor M. O'Brien
text: Trevor M. O'Brien is listed among the staff alumni of the XROMM (X-ray Reconstruction of Moving Morphology) group of Elizabeth L. Brainerd at Brown University. O'Brien was also a PhD student in computer science at Brown, in David Laidlaw's Visualization Research Lab, working in scientific visualization and human-computer interaction. With D. F. Keefe, Brainerd, Laidlaw, and others, O'Brien published a 2008 Computer Graphics Forum paper on exploring high-speed animal kinematics data with instantaneous helical axes. With A. M. Ritz, B. J. Raphael, and Laidlaw, O'Brien published Gremlin (2010), an interactive visualization model for analyzing genomic rearrangements.

name: Tyler J. Carrier
text:
Tyler J. Carrier is a marine biologist who studies how marine invertebrates use microbial symbioses in reproduction and development. He holds a BS from the University of Maine and earned a PhD in 2020 at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, in the laboratory of Adam M. Reitzel, as an NSF Graduate Research Fellow. He and Andreas Heyland share papers from 2016 and 2020. He worked at FHL as a visiting graduate researcher in 2016 and 2019. He became a postdoctoral fellow in the Marine Symbioses unit at GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel in 2020. UNC Charlotte lists him as a postdoctoral researcher in Reitzel's lab, with an adjunct lectureship there and a visiting post at GEOMAR from 2024.

In summer 2016 he ran experiments at FHL and the Duke Marine Lab. He studied how larvae endure starvation, from a microbial perspective, and whether this varies with parental location. His papers include convergent shifts in host-associated microbial communities across environmentally elicited phenotypes (Nature Communications, 2018), bacterial communities of larval sea urchins under differing geography and food (2019), and bacterial exposure and resistance to Vibrio lentus in purple sea urchin larvae (2020). A 2015 paper with King and Coffman treated gene expression in sea urchin larvae responding to food availability. His later work extended to sponges, including a 2022 review of symbiont transmission and a 2023 study of maternal provisioning of an obligate symbiont.

name: Victoria E. Foe
text:
Victoria E. Foe is a cell and developmental biologist and Research Professor Emerita in the Department of Biology at the University of Washington. She earned a BS (1966) and PhD (1975) at the University of Texas at Austin, where she worked with Hugh Forrest on the induction of transcription during embryogenesis; she also worked with Charles Laird at UW on the functional organization of chromatin. With Bruce Alberts at the University of California, San Francisco, she then studied how the cell cycle relates to the shaping of embryos. She joined the UW Zoology Department in 1991 and was a founding member of the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where she held a research professorship. Her honors include a Senior Postdoctoral Fellowship from the American Cancer Society, a Guggenheim Fellowship (1990) and a MacArthur Fellowship (1993). Her FHL-connected papers span 1989 to 2022.

Foe's research asks how cell-cycle biochemistry coordinates reorganization of the cytoskeleton, as in cell division and cellularization of fly embryos, and how progress through the cell cycle relates to gene activity and cell fate. From detailed descriptions of fruit fly embryos she found that groups of cells in different regions divide on distinct schedules; these "mitotic domains", reported in 1989 papers, one with Garrett Odell, reveal early commitment of cell fates. A 1985 paper with Alberts used oxygen deprivation to visualize nuclear organization between divisions, and a 2000 paper showed how microtubules and cell-cycle phase pattern actin and myosin in early fly embryos. Later she worked with echinoderm embryos: a light microscopy chapter (2004), paired experimental and computer-modeling studies of how microtubules position the cleavage furrow (2008), and the behavior of two protein complexes during furrow specification (2012). A 2022 paper asked whether a meiotic checkpoint promotes adaptive speciation.

name: Vikram K. Iyengar
text:
Vikram K. Iyengar, a Professor of Biology at Villanova University in Pennsylvania, studies sexual selection and animal behavior; the department lists him as assistant chair. His early papers (1998-2002), from Cornell University's Department of Neurobiology and Behavior and many with Thomas Eisner, concerned sexual selection and chemical defense in the arctiid moth Utetheisa ornatrix. A 2004 paper lists the College of Wooster, and his ORCID record dates his Villanova appointment from 2004. His FHL-connected papers, from 2013 to 2026, report studies of the maritime earwig on San Juan Island that used FHL's laboratory facilities and field sites. Five are reports from FHL's summer Blinks/NSF REU/BEACON internship program with student first authors, including Nicole L. Hack (2013) and Jessica M. Kendall-Bar (2014), whose projects became journal papers; the report's network records him as research mentor to both.

His research uses insects and other arthropods to ask how mate choice, competition and body size shape reproductive success. The moth work examined female preference and offspring fitness, the heritability of body mass, male courtship pheromones and the sperm of sons of multiply mated females; at Villanova he has also studied harem mating in an amphipod (2008) and contests between moth larvae (2015). At FHL he turned to Anisolabis maritima, an earwig that lives under beach debris at or above the high-tide line and whose males carry curved, asymmetric forceps. Student reports and papers ask when earwigs share shelters (2013; 2017, with Hack), how body size and forceps affect mate choice and male competition (2014; 2017, with Kendall-Bar), how density and form differ among populations (2017), how sex affects nest intrusion and egg defense against cannibalism (2022; 2026), and how sex ratio in pairs and trios alters aggression and mating (2026).

name: Viktoria Bogantes
text: Viktoria Bogantes was a PhD student of Kenneth M. Halanych, who chaired the dissertation committee, at Auburn University (2014 to 2020), after bachelor's and licentiate degrees at the Universidad de Costa Rica. The 2020 dissertation, on annelids with emphasis on Spionidae, covered the Southern Ocean scale worm Polyeunoa laevis and its association with the soft coral Thouarella, Icelandic Laonice including the new species L. plumisetosa, larval development of Pseudopolydora paucibranchiata, and spionid phylogenomics across 17 genera. Bogantes also co-authored, with Halanych, a 2019 genome study of the tubeworm Lamellibrachia luymesi. In 2022 Bogantes joined the University of West Florida as an assistant professor of biology.

name: Vilaiwan Fernandes
text: Vilaiwan Fernandes took the 2006 computational modeling apprenticeship sponsored by Friday Harbor Laboratories, taught by Jonathan Alberts, Adriana Dawes and Kerry Kim, and interned with Kim at the Center for Cell Dynamics. Their 2009 paper tested ploidy and recombination in a segment polarity network model. Fernandes took a PhD at Simon Fraser University (2015) and became a group leader at University College London in 2018, studying Drosophila visual system development.

name: Virginia Schutte
text: Virginia Schutte was a graduate student of James E. Byers at the University of Georgia, completing a PhD in 2014. With Byers, Schutte published a 2017 Marine Ecology Progress Series paper on how variation in a simple trait of mangrove roots governs predator access to, and the community composition of, epibiotic sponges. Schutte then worked in science communication at the Louisiana Universities Marine Consortium (LUMCON), and as its social media and science communication officer co-authored a 2017 Limnology and Oceanography Bulletin article on the consortium.

name: Volker Schmid
text:
Volker Schmid (1939–2008) was a cell and developmental biologist whose published research, from 1984 to 2007, centered on hydrozoan jellyfish at the University of Basel, Switzerland. His papers from 1984 to 2005 give his address as the Zoological Institute (Institute of Zoology) of the University of Basel. A 2007 paper on jellyfish opsins, written with Hiroshi Suga and Walter J. Gehring, gives the Department of Cell Biology at Basel's Biozentrum. An obituary records that he joined Arthur Whiteley at the University of Washington in 1975, working mostly at Friday Harbor, and later became a professor at Basel. Three of his papers, from 1988 to 1992, list Friday Harbor Laboratories alongside Basel, and Basel co-authors such as Andreas Bally also give FHL addresses. A fourth paper (1995) appears in FHL's research bibliography. He is not the statistician of the same name at LMU Munich, whose ORCID record is attached to some of his papers in bibliographic databases.

Schmid's research used hydrozoan medusae, including Podocoryne carnea, to study how specialized cells can change fate and how cells interact with the surrounding extracellular matrix. A 1984 paper reported that isolated, single-nucleus striated muscle cells can transdifferentiate and form a complex regenerate. His FHL-connected papers examined the mesoglea, the jellyfish's extracellular matrix. A 1988 study with Bally found that muscle and endoderm attach to and spread on mesoglea in a highly species-specific way, through an extractable factor that appeared to be mainly a collagen. A 1991 paper extended this work on cell adhesion and spreading, and a 1992 review in International Review of Cytology surveyed transdifferentiation in medusae. A 1995 study in Podocoryne carnea identified a fibrillin-like matrix protein that forms different fibrils at different life stages. His later work dealt with life-cycle reversal in Turritopsis, the origin of striated muscle and mesoderm, the germ-line gene Cniwi and jellyfish opsins.

name: Wan Fatma Zuharah Wan Musthapa
text: Wan Fatma Zuharah Wan Musthapa, who publishes as Wan Fatma Zuharah, earned a 2010 PhD at Victoria University of Wellington and was listed as co-supervised by Nicole E. Phillips for a thesis on how mosquito predators affect endemic and exotic mosquitoes. With Philip J. Lester, Wan Fatma Zuharah published New Zealand studies on whether Culex pervigilans adults detect the backswimmer Anisops wakefieldi in larval habitats and on aquatic predators in animal drinking troughs (both 2010). Later work at Universiti Sains Malaysia, as a senior lecturer from 2010 and an associate professor from 2016, turned to dengue vectors, including a knockdown resistance mutation, A1007G, in Aedes aegypti (2021) and pyrethroid and organophosphate resistance in that species (2026). A 2026 paper lists Wan Fatma Zuharah at the university's Medical Entomology Laboratory.

name: Wanying Na
text: Wanying Na was an undergraduate researcher in Michael T. Nishizaki's lab at Carleton College, listed among its past students. With Nishizaki and labmates, Na studied how temperature fluctuations affect respiration in intertidal mussels, exposing animals in temperature-controlled chambers to either alternating daily extremes or a field-based regime built from continuous temperature records at the study site. The work appeared as a 2023 Dryad dataset and a 2026 paper in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, which lists Carleton College, Friday Harbor Laboratories and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as Na's affiliations.

name: Wei-Chun Chin
text: Wei-Chun Chin was a graduate student who worked with University of Washington bioengineering professor Pedro Verdugo. With Verdugo and Mónica V. Orellana, Chin reported in Nature in 1998 that dissolved organic polymers in filtered seawater from Puget Sound, the Arctic Ocean and the North Pacific assemble spontaneously into microgels. Further work with Verdugo covered pH oscillations in secretory granules and calcium release in goblet cell exocytosis (2002), regulated exocytosis in the alga Phaeocystis globosa (2004), and the spontaneous assembly of phytoplankton exopolymers (2009). A 2019 paper on crude oil, dispersant and the aggregation of extracellular polymers lists Chin at the bioengineering program of the University of California, Merced.

name: Wendel W. Raymond
text:
Wendel W. Raymond is a nearshore ecologist who works on seagrass, kelp and intertidal communities in the Pacific Northwest and Alaska. He earned a BS in biology at Oregon State University in 2012 and first came to Friday Harbor Laboratories as a Research Experience for Undergraduates participant in 2011. His PhD at the University of Alaska Fairbanks (2020) examined sea otters in Southeast Alaska, including their subsistence harvest and their effects on seagrass communities, and his fieldwork there included food webs in eelgrass meadows on Prince of Wales Island. From 2021 to 2023 he was a nearshore ecology research scientist at FHL, where he helped develop and co-taught the Biodiversity and Monitoring of Estuarine Ecology research apprenticeship. Since 2023 his ORCID record lists him as a nearshore ecology research scientist with the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. His census papers with an FHL address run from 2014 to 2026.

Raymond studies how nearshore habitats respond to predators, food supply, and human and climate stresses. A 2011 student report from his time at FHL tested red sea urchin feeding preferences among drift kelps, and a 2014 paper led by M. N. Dethier, with Aaron W. E. Galloway among the co-authors, showed that the food quality of decaying kelp changes differently among species. Other papers concern shelter competition between invasive lionfish and Nassau grouper (2015) and shoreline armoring in the Salish Sea (2016). His dissertation found sea otters positively associated with seagrass across Southeast Alaska, but no evidence of a link between crabs and seagrass epifauna. After the June 2021 heat wave he led a survey of shellfish die-offs that gathered 203 observations from 108 locations (2022), followed by studies of intertidal bivalves (2024) and rocky shores (2025). Recent papers concern nutrient pollution and green tides and a kelp stressor metric (2026).

name: Werner Rauh
text: Werner Rauh (died 2000) was a German botanist at the University of Heidelberg, where he became professor, directed the Institute of Plant Systematics and Plant Geography and led the botanical gardens. He supervised Wilhelm Barthlott's 1973 doctorate on cacti. Rauh worked on bromeliads and succulent plants, including the succulent and xerophytic flora of Madagascar.

name: Wilhelm Barthlott
text:
Wilhelm Barthlott is a botanist and biomimetic materials scientist who held the chair of systematic botany and directed the Botanical Garden at the University of Bonn from 1985, founded its Nees Institute for Biodiversity of Plants in 2003, and became emeritus in 2011. He studied at the University of Heidelberg, where he earned a doctorate in 1973 under Werner Rauh, on the systematics and biogeography of cacti investigated by scanning electron microscopy, and was a professor at the Free University of Berlin from 1982 to 1985. His tie to FHL is Petra Ditsche, who was a postdoctoral fellow with him at Bonn before later postdoctoral work at Kiel and FHL. They shared a 2015 paper in Applied Physics A on the elasticity of the hair cover in air-retaining Salvinia surfaces.

His research joined plant surface structure to engineering and biogeography. With Neinhuis he described self-cleaning superhydrophobic leaf surfaces in "Purity of the sacred lotus" (Planta, 1997), the basis of the Lotus effect. A 2010 paper in Advanced Materials on the Salvinia paradox examined superhydrophobic surfaces with hydrophilic pins that hold air under water, the line of work to which the paper with Ditsche belongs. He also mapped global plant diversity, as in a 1996 paper in Erdkunde toward a world map of phytodiversity, and worked with colleagues on protozoa-trapping in Genlisea (Nature, 1998). He was elected to the German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina in 1999 and received the German Environmental Prize that year.

name: Wilhelm Foerster
text: Wilhelm Foerster (1832-1921), a German astronomer, was professor of astronomy at the University of Berlin from 1863 and director of the Berlin Observatory from 1865 to 1904. With Julius Bauschinger, Foerster supervised Alfred Wegener's 1905 doctorate on the Alfonsine tables. Foerster co-discovered the asteroid 62 Erato in 1860 and from 1868 headed the commission setting German measurement standards.

name: Will Stedden
text: Will Stedden earned a PhD in biophysical sciences at the University of Chicago in 2017 with Edwin Munro as advisor. The dissertation, "Dynamic Modulation of Actomyosin Contractility and Cortical Flow by Actin Filament Recycling," used a computational model of cross-linked actomyosin networks to study how filament turnover, crosslink dynamics and motor activity shape contractile stress and flow, and included single-molecule methods for measuring actin filament turnover in C. elegans embryos. Papers with Munro include a 2014 Nature Methods report on single-molecule analysis of cell surface dynamics in those embryos, a 2017 PLoS Computational Biology model of cortical flow, and a 2018 Journal of Cell Biology study of excitable RhoA dynamics.

name: Willem Weertman
text:
Willem Lee Weertman studies how octopuses use their arms and chemical senses to find food. He earned a BS in oceanography at the University of Washington in 2018 and an MS in environmental science at Alaska Pacific University's Institute of Culture and Environment, with a thesis on how octopuses use odor plumes to find food (2023). Since 2022 he has been a PhD student in psychology (behavioral neuroscience) at the University of Washington, in David H. Gire's Laboratory of Comparative System Neuroscience; the department names Gire as his mentor. His census papers with an FHL address run from 2023 to 2025, and his recent papers list Friday Harbor Laboratories alongside the UW Department of Psychology. A 2018 UW report described his design of a diver-deployed stereo underwater video camera, lit with deep red light, for recording octopus den behavior.

Weertman combines behavioral experiments, video tracking and modeling to study octopus foraging. A 2025 PLoS ONE paper (preprinted in 2024, after a 2021 conference abstract) showed that octopuses tested in darkness moved upstream toward baited targets, with odor-gated pauses, switchbacks and cross-stream turns and fast lunges aligned with an arm; the authors argue that the suckers are the main chemosensory organs. A 2023 study with Dominic M. Sivitilli and Gire tracked arms in visually occluded, 3D-printed foraging tasks and used a simulated arm to show a contact-based search arising from local sucker coordination. With David Scheel he used DeepLabCut pose estimation on video of Octopus rubescens to show that males hold the hectocotylus, the arm modified for mating, closer to the body than their other arms (2024). He also co-authored a 2025 FHL study showing that early life stages of the endangered sunflower star tolerate current and near-future warming.

name: William B. Stickle
text:
William B. Stickle is a comparative physiologist of marine invertebrates whose career has been based at Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge. He published from its Department of Zoology and Physiology from 1973 and later from the Department of Biological Sciences, with papers into the 2020s. Papers of 1970 and 1971 list the University of North Dakota and Slippery Rock State College, and several from the 1980s the Institute for Marine Environmental Research in Plymouth, England. His doctoral thesis for the University of Saskatchewan, Regina Campus, advised by Frederick Duerr, used FHL: the snail Thais lamellosa was collected at Turn Island about monthly from 1968 to 1970 and kept at the laboratories, and he thanked director Robert L. Fernald for facilities. His FHL-connected census papers run from 1973 to 2016, including work in the 2000s with Eugene N. Kozloff of FHL.

His research asks how temperature, salinity, low oxygen and season affect the energy budgets, body fluids and survival of intertidal and estuarine animals. In Louisiana he studied the southern oyster drill, oysters and blue crabs, including responses to tidal salinity change, hypoxia, crude oil and cadmium. His FHL-connected papers began with seasonal changes in metabolism and body composition over the reproductive cycle of Thais lamellosa (1973, 1975). A 1985 paper with Richard A. Roller, probably his doctoral student (LSU, PhD 1987), measured salinity effects on larvae of four echinoderm species, and a 1990 paper compared salinity tolerance and allozymes of sea urchins from Alaska and near Friday Harbor. With Kozloff he described infection of the testes of Leptasterias sea stars by the ciliate Orchitophrya stellarum (2001-2008), and a 2016 paper with FHL's Emily Carrington and Hilary Hayford examined seasonal changes in snail tolerance of temperature and desiccation stress.

name: William E. Bemis
text:
William E. Bemis is an ichthyologist and comparative anatomist, professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at Cornell University (from 2025) and faculty curator of fishes at the Cornell University Museum of Vertebrates. He took a BA at Cornell (1976), an MS at the University of Michigan (1978) and a PhD in zoology at the University of California, Berkeley (1983). After two years as an instructor and postdoctoral fellow at the University of Chicago, he spent twenty years on the biology faculty of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, then was Kingsbury Director of the Shoals Marine Laboratory from 2005 to 2013. His tie to FHL runs through Stacy C. Farina, whose 2015 Cornell PhD on gill ventilation in ray-finned fishes he chaired, and through work with Adam P. Summers.

His research covers the anatomy, development and relationships of fossil and living fishes, including sharks, lungfishes, coelacanths, bowfins, sturgeons and paddlefishes, based on direct study of specimens. Early papers treated lungfish, among them paedomorphosis in the Dipnoi (1984) and their feeding systems (1986). With Lance Grande of the Field Museum, he published a phylogenetic study of amiid fishes based on skeletal anatomy (1998). Later work includes a 2018 study in Zoology of walking and bounding gaits in flatfishes, with Fox, Gibb and Summers, and a 2019 paper on functional coupling of suction feeding and gill ventilation in sculpins, with Farina, Knope, Corn and Summers. Bemis also co-wrote the textbooks Functional Anatomy of the Vertebrates and Vertebrate Life and was lead developer of an online course on sharks.

name: William John Nielsen
text: William John Nielsen was lab manager in Gregory A. Wray's lab at Duke University, listed among its former members. The work with Wray concerned developmental gene regulation in the purple sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus: a 2012 Evolution & Development paper on the population genetics of cis-regulatory sequences of eight genes, and a 2013 PLoS Biology paper on how natural variation in gene expression bears on the robustness and evolvability of the network that builds the larval skeleton. Nielsen was also a coauthor of a 2017 comparative-transcriptomics phylogeny of extant starfish, including Xyloplax.

name: William King
text: William King earned a PhD at the University of Washington in 2019 under Kenneth P. Sebens, with Megan N. Dethier on the graduate committee. The dissertation, "Biotic interactions shift across temperature and ontogeny in an intertidal barnacle," used the acorn barnacle Balanus glandula and the whelk Nucella ostrina. Warm water offset a drop in whelk feeding caused by warm air, and warm air slowed whelk growth while raising barnacle growth. With Sebens, King published on non-additive effects of air and water warming on a predator-prey interaction in Marine Biology in 2018. With Dethier, King wrote a 2017 Friday Harbor Laboratories report on oil dispersants in San Juan County marine waters.

name: William L. Burgess
text: William L. Burgess took an MSc at St. Francis Xavier University (2022) supervised by Cory Bishop, with Russell Wyeth on the committee. The thesis used 16S amplicon sequencing to track bacteria in the egg capsules of yellow-spotted salamanders, which hold the symbiotic alga Oophila amblystomatis. Burgess and Bishop reported in Microbial Ecology (2023) that diversity declines as embryos develop.

name: William M. Bement
text:
William M. (Bill) Bement is a cell biologist and professor of integrative biology at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where he is also a member of the Center for Quantitative Cell Imaging. Publication records place his early work at Arizona State University in 1991–1992, on the cortical cytoskeleton and cell-cycle control of Xenopus eggs with D. G. Capco, followed by work at Yale University with M. S. Mooseker on unconventional myosins and wound closure (1993–1996). His papers from Wisconsin begin in the mid-1990s. His FHL connection is through the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor Laboratories, which his 2005 Journal of Cell Biology paper gives as his address. All six of his census papers, from 2005 to 2009, were written with George von Dassow of that center, and the 2005 and 2009 cytokinesis studies used echinoderm embryos alongside frog eggs and embryos.

Bement's research asks how cells coordinate signaling and the cytoskeleton at the cell cortex during cell division and cell repair, with the frog Xenopus laevis as the main model. His lab's topics include cytokinesis, spindle assembly, wound healing, exo- and endocytosis, and cortical excitability. The FHL-connected papers center on the small GTPase RhoA. A 2005 study used four-dimensional microscopy in four echinoderm species and Xenopus to show that microtubules direct the formation and placement of a sharply bounded zone of active RhoA that precedes cytokinesis. A 2009 study led by von Dassow, using sea urchin and frog embryos, showed that a furrow-inducing signal can reach the cortex from the spindle without transport along microtubules, and that astral microtubules refine where the furrow forms. Other papers from this period introduced fluorescent actin-filament probes based on the actin-binding domain of utrophin (2007) and reviewed Rho GTPase activity zones (2006, 2008).

name: William McDowell
text: William McDowell was a PhD student of James E. Byers at the University of Georgia (degree 2014). The work addressed invasive freshwater species, including a 2013 PLoS ONE paper on climate and pH as predictors of the range of the apple snail Pomacea insularum in the southeastern United States and a 2014 Freshwater Biology paper on climate and the distribution of the clam Corbicula fluminea. A 2016 Limnology and Oceanography paper documented the death of over 99% of Corbicula in a 10-km reach of the Broad River, Georgia, during hot, dry weather in summer 2012. The Byers lab lists McDowell as an associate professor at Merrimack College.

name: William N. Colgan
text: William N. Colgan wrote a 2019 B.A. thesis at Swarthmore College with Alexis Leanza as first advisor and Bradley Davidson as second advisor. It compared the cardiopharyngeal gene regulatory networks of the tunicates Corella inflata and Ciona robusta as a case of developmental systems drift, finding trans-regulatory architecture largely conserved and cis-regulatory elements variably so. Colgan also coauthored a 2020 Genome Biology and Evolution paper on the Corella inflata genome and the tunicate Hox cluster. Colgan was a computational associate at the Broad Institute from 2019 to 2022, began a PhD at MIT in 2022, and was in Jonathan Weissman's lab at the Whitehead Institute as of 2025.

name: William N. McFarland
text:
William N. "Mac" McFarland, who died in 2004, was a biologist who studied the vision and behavior of fishes. A tribute by Ellis Loew in Visual Neuroscience records that, after posts at Cornell University and the University of Southern California, he held, at his death, a second post-retirement professorship at the Friday Harbor Laboratories. The tribute also mentions his studies at the West Indies Laboratory on St. Croix and the Wrigley Marine Science Center on Catalina Island. He was the first-named author of the textbook Vertebrate Life (Macmillan, 1979). A volume of Visual Neuroscience was dedicated to him and two other vision researchers who had recently died. The census counts nine FHL-address papers from 1996 to 2008, the last published after his death.

McFarland's research linked the light environment under water to the visual pigments and behavior of fishes. A 1973–1975 series of papers with his longtime collaborator Fred Munz built a database of visual pigments in reef and open-ocean fishes and tested ideas about how pigments suit underwater light. He proposed a "twilight hypothesis" for why most rod pigments absorb near 500 nm, and studied twilight and nocturnal behavior of California near-shore fishes with Ted Hobson (1980). His FHL-connected papers continue these themes: visual limits on the migrations of juvenile French grunts (1996), reviews of ultraviolet vision in fishes and of twilight behavior on coral reefs (1999), and visual pigments in young Pacific Northwest marine fishes (2001) and yellowfin tuna (2002). Others cover polarization sensitivity in damselfishes and vision in Hawaiian reef fishes (2003), a planktivore feeding in a current (2005) and opsin expression shifts that tune visual sensitivity (2008).

name: William R. Horsfall
text: William R. Horsfall (1907-1998), a professor of medical entomology at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, worked there from 1947 to 1976 and led the laboratory where George B. Craig did dissertation research for a 1956 PhD on the eggs of Nearctic aedine mosquitoes. Craig's memoir cites the teaching example set by Horsfall. A specialist on Aedes mosquitoes, Horsfall compiled a bibliography of medical entomology and consulted for the World Health Organization.

name: William R. Jeffery
text:
William R. Jeffery is an evolutionary developmental biologist and Biology Distinguished University Professor Emeritus at the University of Maryland, who works on ascidians and the blind cavefish Astyanax mexicanus. He earned a BS at the University of Illinois (1968) and a PhD at the University of Iowa (1971), held postdoctoral fellowships at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Tufts, and joined the zoology faculty at the University of Texas at Austin. He moved in 1990 to the University of California, Davis, working at Bodega Marine Laboratory, headed biology at Penn State (1996-1999), and then chaired biology at Maryland until 2004. His tie to FHL is Billie J. Swalla, an AAUW Sarah Berliner Postdoctoral Fellow in his Austin lab in 1988-1989, who worked on mRNAs and proteins localized in ascidian egg myoplasm.

His early papers traced the localization of maternal messenger RNA in the eggs of ascidians and Chaetopterus, including a 1983 paper on actin mRNA in ascidian development. With Swalla he studied how tailless ascidians lost the tadpole larva: a 1990 paper on hybridization between an anural and a urodele ascidian, and a 1996 Science paper on the requirement of the Manx gene for chordate features in a tailless larva. Also with Swalla, a 2023 Biological Bulletin study treated Cymric, a tyrosine kinase gene disrupted in tailless Molgula occulta. His later work addressed eye degeneration in cavefish, as in Yamamoto, Stock and Jeffery (Nature, 2004), and regeneration in Ciona. He received the Kowalevsky Medal in 2012.

name: William Robert Hardin
text: Linda G. Wordeman sat on the reading committee for William Robert Hardin's University of Washington PhD in biology (2017), chaired by Alex Paredez. Hardin developed live-cell imaging for the parasite Giardia lamblia and studied myosin-independent cytokinesis, which uses flagella to generate force (PNAS, 2017), and the ventrolateral flange, a membrane protrusion that supports attachment (PLoS Pathogens, 2022).

name: William Schneider
text: William Schneider, of California State University, East Bay, worked with James A. Murray at Friday Harbor Laboratories in summer 2015 on a Blinks-NSF REU-BEACON project. The study asked whether the nudibranch Armina californica, which shares habitat and prey with the magnetically sensitive Tritonia tetraquetra, senses Earth-strength magnetic fields. They examined pedal neurons reported as homologous to Tritonia's magnetically responsive cells while applying magnetic stimuli, and followed the reorientation of displaced animals. Neither assay gave a significant result on magnetoreception. The work is a Friday Harbor Laboratories student research paper.

name: Winsor H. Watson
text:
Winsor H. "Win" Watson III is a neurobiologist and professor emeritus of biological sciences at the University of New Hampshire (UNH). He received a BA in biology from Wesleyan University and a PhD in zoology and neurobiology from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. His UNH laboratory studies the neurobiology, behavior and physiology of marine animals, including American lobsters, horseshoe crabs, nudibranchs and fishes, with interests in biotelemetry and biological rhythms. The census counts eight FHL-address papers from 1988 to 2004. The earliest, a 1988 study with David Prior of how a neuropeptide affects the feeding motor program of the slug Limax maximus, lists both UNH and FHL. A 1992 paper on nudibranch neurons was co-authored with A. O. Dennis Willows of FHL. Later papers on the nudibranch Melibe leonina, through 2022, mention FHL in their text.

Watson's Melibe research asks how a nervous system with large, identifiable neurons produces and adjusts rhythmic behaviors such as feeding and swimming. Papers from 1992 quantified Melibe feeding and its change with prey density, examined the role of the buccal ganglia in feeding, and identified apparently homologous peptide-containing neurons across nudibranch species. With James M. Newcomb and others he mapped neurons that make nitric oxide (2001) and showed that nitric oxide modulates swimming (2002). Other studies described swimming behavior and its neural correlates (2002), the effect of light on locomotion (2004) and the central pattern generator for swimming (2005). Later papers documented circadian rhythms of crawling and swimming (2014), clock-gene transcripts in the brain (2018), the distribution of small cardioactive peptide (2020), and nerve signals from stomach distension that inhibit feeding (2022). His lobster work uses ultrasonic telemetry and underwater video to study behavior in natural habitats.

name: Xi Huang
text: Xi Huang did summer research in 2013 in Molly Jacobs's lab at McDaniel College, supervised by Jacobs and Brett McMillan. name: Yo Saiga
text:
Yo Saiga co-wrote, with Osamu Shimomura and Frank H. Johnson, the 1962–1963 papers that first described the light-emitting protein aequorin from the jellyfish Aequorea, which the Princeton group collected at Friday Harbor. In the four FHL-connected papers, all from 1962 and 1963, Saiga's address is Princeton University's Department of Biology or its Moffett Biological Laboratory, listed together with the Friday Harbor Laboratories. Saiga's other papers from 1961 to 1963 give a Princeton address, one also naming the Bermuda Biological Station. Papers from 1967 list a Yo Saiga in the chemistry department of Tokyo Kyoiku University with Noboru Sugiyama, who had co-written two 1961 papers with the Princeton group. The sources do not confirm that this is the same person, or record Saiga's position at Princeton.

The work concerned the chemistry of animal light. With Johnson and Shimomura, Saiga co-wrote papers on the luciferin and luciferase of the ostracod Cypridina and on crystalline luciferin from the luminous fish Parapriacanthus (1961), and on the luminescence system of the polychaete Odontosyllis (1963). The 1962 FHL paper reported the extraction, purification and properties of aequorin, a protein that gives off light in the presence of calcium. A footnote in it mentioned a green protein found during the purification, later known as green fluorescent protein. In 1963 the three authors published further data on aequorin, described a similar luminescent protein, halistaurin, from the hydromedusa Halistaura, and showed in Science that aequorin luminescence can be used to measure very small amounts of calcium. Shimomura later shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for green fluorescent protein.

name: Yonatan Munk
text: Yonatan Munk was a graduate student of M. A. R. Koehl at the University of California, Berkeley, studying the aerodynamics of directed aerial descent in arboreal gliding ants of the genus Cephalotes. These ants, when dislodged from a tree, stabilize in midair and glide back to it. He combined field experiments, laboratory experiments with live ants, and dynamically scaled physical models to learn how they direct their glides without obvious morphological adaptations for aerodynamic performance. With Steve Yanoviak, Koehl, and others he published field measurements of gliding performance (2015), and with Yanoviak a study of aerial maneuverability in Cephalotes atratus (2010). Earlier work covered swimming kinematics of garter snakes (2008).

name: Yordano E. Jimenez
text:
Yordano E. Jimenez is a fish biomechanist, an assistant professor of biology at Providence College as of 2026. The FHL tie starts with a summer 2015 report in the Blinks NSF REU Beacon Internship series, with Ariel Camp, J. D. Laurence-Chasen and Elizabeth L. Brainerd. It used feeding data and CT scans from largemouth bass, Pacific staghorn sculpin and striped surfperch to locate where the spine bends during suction feeding. A 2018 Biology Open paper on the same species, with surfperch and sculpin held at FHL, related neurocranial elevation and its axis of rotation to body shape and the bone behind the head. Jimenez took a PhD in ecology and evolutionary biology at Brown University in 2021, with Brainerd as advisor, on fish axial muscles in swimming and suction feeding.

With Brainerd, Jimenez recorded electromyograms throughout the epaxial muscles of largemouth bass (Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2020). Swimming always used ventral regions and suction feeding always used dorsal ones, while fast-starts and strikes on live prey activated the whole muscle. Two 2021 papers with Brainerd, one also with Richard Marsh, examined axial muscle strain and motor control in bluegill sunfish. A 2020 paper led by J. J. Lomax examined the sternohyoideus muscle in striped surfperch, with Jimenez listing both Brown and FHL. Jimenez was a postdoctoral researcher in Eric Tytell's lab at Tufts University from 2020 to 2023. A 2023 paper with Camp tested beam theory against vertebral curvature and muscle strain in rainbow trout using XROMM and fluoromicrometry.

name: Yoshimasa Hirata
text:
Yoshimasa Hirata (1915-2000) was an organic and natural products chemist and professor emeritus at Nagoya University. He was the doctoral advisor of Osamu Shimomura, who later collected the jellyfish Aequorea victoria over many summers at Friday Harbor Laboratories. In the mid-1950s Hirata took Shimomura into his Nagoya laboratory and gave him the task of purifying and crystallizing the luciferin of the sea-firefly Vargula hilgendorfii (Cypridina), so that its structure could be determined. Shimomura, Toshio Goto and Hirata reported the crystals in 1957. Shimomura took a master's degree in 1958 while working for Hirata, and Hirata awarded him a doctorate, dated 1960, although he had not been a doctoral student. That year Shimomura left for Princeton to work with Frank Johnson, who had noticed the 1957 paper.

Hirata earned a BS at Tokyo Imperial University in 1941, working on the toxic components of yellow rice under Bennosuke Kubota. He moved to Nagoya Imperial University in 1944, worked in wartime under Fujio Egami at Ueda, and took his doctorate in 1949 with a thesis on grifolin, an antibacterial substance from mushrooms. He studied steroids with Louis Fieser at Harvard from 1952 to 1953, became full professor at Nagoya in 1954, and moved to Meijo University in 1979. His research separated and determined the structures of trace bioactive natural products, notably tetrodotoxin (Goto, Kishi, Takahashi and Hirata, Tetrahedron, 1965), with further work on palytoxin and on the plant compounds anisatin, dendrobine and daphniphylline. His honors included the Japan Academy Prize (1977).

name: Younan Li
text: Younan Li was a graduate student in Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago, in the Committee on Development, Regeneration and Stem Cell Biology. With Munro, Li published a 2021 Developmental Cell study combining single-molecule analysis and modeling in one-cell C. elegans embryos. By tracking single formin particles, the work identified filament-guided filament assembly, in which existing actin filaments template the orientation of new ones and so give cells a structural memory of alignment while building the contractile ring during cytokinesis. Li also contributed to work from the lab on cortical polarity in the C. elegans zygote (2015).

name: Yuji Mizotani
text: Yuji Mizotani joined Edwin Munro's lab at the University of Chicago as a postdoctoral fellow in 2018, studying cellular and developmental biology in ascidians, after bachelor's, master's, and PhD degrees at Keio University (PhD 2018). A 2018 PNAS paper from Keio used chemical genetics in the Ciona notochord, identifying 14-3-3εa as a binding partner of the inhibitor UTKO1 and linking it to pulsatile transport toward the apical domain during lumen growth. A 2026 preprint with Munro reported how actomyosin contractility drives apical polarization and membrane transport during tubulogenesis in the ascidian notochord.

name: Yuki Wilmerding
text: Yuki Wilmerding was a student of Sandy Wyllie-Echeverria at Friday Harbor Laboratories, interviewed with him there for a 2022 Seacology article on seagrass in Puget Sound. The article describes Wyllie-Echeverria and his students at the Seagrass Lab reseeding degraded areas of nearby Westcott Bay with eelgrass, Zostera marina.

name: Yulia Ovechkina
text: Yulia Ovechkina was a graduate student in Linda G. Wordeman's lab in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Washington, working on the microtubule-depolymerizing kinesin MCAK. A first-authored 2002 Journal of Cell Biology paper showed that the MCAK neck domain is needed for depolymerizing activity and that a KIF1A K-loop could restore it in a neckless mutant. Ovechkina coauthored later MCAK work, including a 2005 paper with George von Dassow on its association with the tips of polymerizing microtubules and a 2020 analysis of cancer mutations. Earlier work at Ohio State University with Berl R. Oakley addressed spindle formation in Aspergillus (published 2003).

name: Yulia Reunova
text: Yulia Reunova joined Russell C. Wyeth's lab at St. Francis Xavier University as a research associate about 2022, working on the neuroanatomy of the great pond snail, Lymnaea stagnalis. Reunova used immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization chain reaction to label target RNAs and proteins in the nervous system, methods applied in a 2026 Journal of Comparative Neurology paper with Wyeth on the octopamine production pathway. Earlier work in reproductive biology, with experience in scanning and transmission electron microscopy, included papers from the A.V. Zhirmunsky Institute of Marine Biology in Vladivostok on sperm heteromorphism in mussels (2013) and germ plasm in Xenopus (2016).

name: Yvonne Beckham
text: Yvonne Beckham was a research scientist at the Center for Cell Dynamics at Friday Harbor, directed by Garrett M. Odell, performing molecular experiments that supported the projects of center members. Beckham earned a PhD at the University of Toronto (2003) in Richard Elinson's lab, with a thesis on orthologs of VegT and Vg1 in the direct-developing frog Eleutherodactylus coqui, comparing RNA localization in its large oocyte with Xenopus laevis; related papers appeared in 2003 and 2004. Beckham later became a research scientist in Margaret Gardel's lab at the University of Chicago, with papers on focal adhesion maturation (2012) and Arp2/3 inhibition in epithelial cells (2014).

name: Zac Swider
text: Zac Swider (Zachary T. Swider) was a PhD student of William M. Bement in the Cellular and Molecular Biology Graduate Program at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. A first-authored 2022 Molecular Biology of the Cell paper quantified cortical excitability, traveling waves of protein activity in the cell cortex, in Xenopus laevis eggs and embryos, and related wave properties to cell cycle progression and cell size. Swider also coauthored with Bement and George von Dassow on cortical excitability and pattern formation (2021, 2022). A 2017 paper on myosin filament assembly lists Swider at the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute.

name: Zach Child
text: Zach Child is listed for a 2022 project, "Assessing Pacific Sand Lance growth across the San Juan Archipelago," in the Pelagic Ecosystem Function Research Apprenticeship at Friday Harbor Laboratories, which used the laboratories' research vessels for independent research on the archipelago's open-water ecosystem. name: Zane Baki
text: Zane Baki wrote a 2023 marine biology honors thesis for a Bachelor of Science at the University of Oregon, with Aaron W. E. Galloway as primary advisor and Richard B. Emlet as biology honors faculty representative. Baki compared tridentate pedicellariae density in 100 purple urchins, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, from South Cove at Cape Arago and a jetty near the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology, finding the same mean density at both.

name: Zebib S. Abraha
text: Zebib S. Abraha was a PhD student of Charles Bradley Shuster in molecular biology at New Mexico State University, graduating in May 2022 with a dissertation on cell cycle regulation and polarity reversal of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition during sea urchin gastrulation. Abraha then completed postdoctoral training at Baylor College of Medicine on retinal vascular disease and therapies targeting Secretogranin III for ophthalmic conditions. A 2025 abstract in Investigative Ophthalmology and Visual Science dealt with development of a therapy targeting this protein for treatment-resistant neovascular age-related macular degeneration.

name: Zer Vue
text: Zer Vue is listed as a master's student of Andreas Heyland (2007-2010) on his lab's alumni page. Vue coauthored the 2011 developmental transcriptome of the sea hare Aplysia californica with Heyland and published a 2014 comparison of early development in Bursatella leachii and A. californica. Later work at Baylor College of Medicine and MD Anderson, with Richard R. Behringer, used light-sheet imaging of the developing mouse uterus (2018).

name: Zhongran Ni
text: Zhongran Ni was an undergraduate researcher at Friday Harbor Laboratories in the spring 2014 Nearshore Ecology Research course (BIOL/FISH/OCEAN 479), with Morgan Eisenlord as primary mentor and Megan Dethier as instructor. Ni's report tested how diet, temperature and salinity affect wasting disease in predatory sea stars; higher temperature and lower salinity went with more symptomatic animals.

name: Zoe Irons
text: Zoe Irons was an undergraduate research assistant for John H. Henson at Dickinson College for two summers before graduating with a B.S. in 2018. Irons coauthored the 2021 PLoS ONE paper on cytokinetic contractile ring assembly in sea urchin embryos, which used super-resolution imaging to place anillin and septin within myosin II clusters. At the University of Oregon, Irons completed a 2024 PhD with Daniel Grimes, using zebrafish to study how Daw1 times the onset of cilia motility and how the Reissner fiber and the peptides Urp1 and Urp2 act downstream in body and spine morphogenesis. Irons returned to Dickinson as a visiting assistant professor of biology in 2024.

name: Zofia Knorek
text: Zofia Knorek earned a 2018 MS at the University of Oregon, with Aaron W. E. Galloway as chair and Richard B. Emlet on her committee. Her thesis followed the invasive tunicate Didemnum vexillum at an Oregon oyster farm (2011-2016) and found no effect of Botrylloides violaceus on oysters or mussels in simulated longline aquaculture. She went on to a PhD at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

name: Álvaro Morales-Ramírez
text: Álvaro Morales-Ramírez, a marine zooplankton researcher at the Universidad de Costa Rica's Centro de Investigación en Ciencias del Mar y Limnología and Escuela de Biología, was undergraduate advisor to Marco Corrales, who earned a bachelor's degree there in 2012. The two published together on Costa Rican copepods in 2014 and on the medusa Stellamedusa ventana in 2017.
